en: The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Introduction to the Vinaya: Homage to the Venerable One of Great Compassion, who is able to take pity on all beings;
whose face is full like the rising sun, and whose eyes are pure as blue lotuses.
The Buddha was born into a family of self-discipline, and his assembly of disciples is thoroughly disciplined;
through discipline he eliminates all faults—to the Honored One among all dharmas, I pay homage.
The Buddha taught the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, with the Vinaya as the foremost.
Within this teaching, I shall briefly offer a hymn of praise:
Just as the root is supreme among trees, from which the branches and trunk arise;
so the Buddha taught that the Vinaya is the foundation, capable of giving birth to all wholesome dharmas.
Just as a great embankment cannot be overtopped by a torrential flood, so too is the Dharma of the precepts:
it can ward off the violation of prohibitions.
Thus the Buddhas realize enlightenment, and the Pratyekabuddhas possess tranquil body and mind.
And the Arhats as well— All achieve success through the practice of the Vinaya.
The sages and saints of the three times, Who have distanced themselves from the bonds of conditioned existence;
All take the Vinaya as their foundation, And are thus able to reach the place of peace and security.
If this teaching of discipline remains established in the world,
it is the treasury of the True Dharma of all Tathāgatas that shall not perish.
Morality is that which can firmly establish the lamp of the Tathāgata’s True Dharma.
Apart from this, there is no path to the peace of Nirvana.
The Buddha wanders through the world, preaching the Dharma wherever he goes;
yet the Vinaya teachings are not like that, and thus one knows they are difficult to encounter.
Just as the earth supports all living beings and can cause all plants and trees to grow;
so too is the teaching of the Vinaya, for it can give birth to all merit and wisdom.
The Buddha taught that through the teaching of the Vinaya, one can produce manifold virtues.
By upholding [the precepts], one attains liberation; by violating them, one is born in the evil realms.
Just as elephants and horses that are not tamed are controlled with hooks and whips, so too is the teaching of the Vinaya:
it subdues those who are untamed and makes them compliant with the good.
Just as a city has moats and ditches that can ward off all enemies,
so too is the teaching of the Vinaya able to prevent the breaking of precepts.
Just as the waters of the great ocean can float away a corpse, [so does the Vinaya remove defilements].
The Vinaya teachings are likewise: they can eliminate all violations of the precepts.
The Vinaya is the king among dharmas, the foremost guide of all Buddhas;
for bhikṣus it is like a merchant caravan, and this is a priceless treasure.
Broken precepts exceed the venom of a serpent; the Vinaya is like the Agada medicine.
The youthful mind is difficult to tame; use the Vinaya as its bridle and reins.
Regarding the path of virtue, the Vinaya always serves as a bridge.
It can also serve as a boat or raft across the ocean of evil destinies;
if one travels upon perilous paths, morality acts as a skilled guide;
and if one ascends the city of fearlessness, morality serves as the ladder and steps.
The Great Master, the Most Supreme Honored One, personally proclaimed the Vinaya teachings;
these two are without distinction, and all should pay homage to them.
Both the Buddha and his noble disciples abide entirely in reliance upon the Vinaya teachings.
Because he gives rise to reverence for the precepts, I take refuge in him and pay homage.
Relying on the Vinaya, I offer praise; this teaching should be honored.
Through taking refuge at the very beginning, the auspicious matters are accomplished.
The great ocean of the Vinaya is so vast its limits are difficult to know;
its diverse characteristics are infinite—how could I possibly detail them all?
The ocean of the Great Master’s Vinaya teachings is profoundly deep and difficult to fathom.
Now, according to my own ability, I shall briefly praise but a small portion.
At the time of his parinirvāṇa, the World-Honored One universally addressed the great assembly:
"After my passing, you all should revere and honor the precepts."
Therefore, I offer this praise and extolment, wishing to proclaim the Vinaya;
you, sirs, should listen with a sincere heart to the teaching of discipline.
This Sūtra of Individual Liberation is difficult to hear, even throughout immeasurable koṭis of kalpas.
Reciting, studying, and upholding [the Dharma] is likewise so; those who practice according to the teaching are even rarer to encounter.
It is a joy for the Buddhas to appear in the world; it is a joy to proclaim the subtle and sublime True Dharma.
It is a joy for the Saṃgha to be of one mind and a single vision; it is a joy to practice together in harmony with courageous diligence.
To see the noble ones is joy; to dwell together with them is likewise joy.
Not seeing those who are foolish and deluded—this is what is called constantly experiencing happiness.
To see one endowed with ethical discipline is joy; to see one of great learning is also called joy.
To see an Arhat is true joy, because of the non-arising of further existence.
There is joy in the pleasant steps at the river crossing; there is joy in conquering enemies through the Dharma.
When the fruit of right wisdom is realized, there is the joy of being able to eliminate the conceit of "I" entirely.
If one can form a resolute mind, well-subduing the senses and desires while possessing great learning;
from youth until old age dwelling in the forest, one finds joy in the tranquility and seclusion of the araṇya.
With palms joined in reverence, I pay homage to the Lion of the Śākyas;
regarding this Prātimokṣa discipline, I shall speak—listen with kindness and care.
Having heard it, you should practice correctly, just as the Great Sage has taught.
Regarding even minor transgressions, one should guard them with vigor and diligence.
The horse of the mind is difficult to restrain; it must be governed with constant and resolute determination.
The Prātimokṣa is like a bit, possessing a hundred needles of extreme sharpness.
If a person violates the rules of conduct, they can stop as soon as they hear the teaching;
like a noble steed, such a great being shall emerge from the ranks of affliction.
If a person lacks this bit, they will never experience joy.
They have perished in the battle against afflictions, Wandering deludedly through birth and death.
The Summary Verse for the Eight Pārājika Dharmas says:
Sexual misconduct, taking what is not given, Killing a human being, and claiming superhuman states.
Contacting the eight things and following after them—these are all cases of not living together.

1. The Training Rule on Impure Conduct. First: The Training Rule on Impure Conduct. At that time, the Bodhisattva was in the Tuṣita Heaven palace; as he was about to descend to be born, he first observed the world through five matters.

What are the five? First, observing the distant ancestors; second, observing the season and time; third, observing the region and country; fourth, observing the immediate kin; and fifth, observing the maternal lineage.
At that time, the gods of the six heavens of desire came to the mother’s abode and thrice purified her womb.
As Lady Māyā was reclining, she dreamed that a white elephant with six tusks descended into her womb.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways; a great radiance appeared throughout this world, illuminating everywhere, so that even the dark and obscure regions between worlds—places where the majestic light of the sun and moon could not reach—were all made brilliantly bright.
The sentient beings therein are obscured by the veil of darkness; from birth until death, they cannot even perceive their own bodies, let alone see one another.
Having encountered this light, they conceived a sense of wonder and all spoke these words:
"How is it that there are suddenly sentient beings here?
This was no different from what occurred when the Bodhisattva first descended into birth, when the great earth shook and light was radiated everywhere.
In this trichiliocosm, all those beings with whom [the Buddha] had a karmic connection who beheld this light were filled with joy and exultation, conceiving a sense of its rarity.
At that time, four great kings each had a crown prince born to them. When the Great King Brahmadatta in Śrāvastī first gave birth to his son, there was a great radiance; he then thought:
"By the power of the merit of my noble son, a great light has been emitted that shines universally upon the world; it is fitting that I name my son 'Jaya-prabha' (Victorious Light)."
Furthermore, when King Mahāpadma of Rājagṛha first gave birth to a son, there was likewise a radiance, and he thought:

"The power of my son’s merit is truly rare; at the moment of his birth, a great light shone everywhere, like the brilliant and blazing shadow-light of the solar disc. Since my wife’s name is Chāyā, it is fitting that I name my son Chāyā-jaya (Shadow-Victorious)."
Furthermore, when the Great King Śatānīka of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī first saw a radiance at the birth of his son, he thought to himself:
"The power of my son's merit brings forth a great light, like the sun first appearing to illuminate the world; it is fitting that I name my son 'Prabhāsa' (Radiant Light)."
Furthermore, in the kingdom of Oḍḍiyāna there was a great wheel-turning monarch who, upon the birth of his first son, also beheld a radiant light. He then thought:
"When my son was born, there was a supreme radiance, just as the light of a lamp can dispel great darkness; it is fitting that I name my son Dīpamkara (Light-Maker)."

Although those four kings each conceived the thought of joy, saying, "This divine marvel is entirely due to my son," how could they know that this majestic radiance was actually caused by the power of the Bodhisattva’s roots of goodness from his compassion, and was brought about by the inconceivable merit resulting from his vast cultivation?

On this very day, five hundred boys were born simultaneously, with the great Śākyan Nanda as their leader; likewise, sixty thousand girls were born simultaneously, with Yaśodharā, Mṛgajā, and Gopikā as their leaders.

Furthermore, there were five hundred male attendants, headed by Chanda, and five hundred female attendants born at the same time; additionally, there were five hundred mother elephants, headed by Kantaka, and five hundred mares, each giving birth to a single foal.
At that time, five hundred hidden treasures suddenly manifested from within the great earth, and all those border regions that had not previously submitted came to pay homage and submit.
Then, the Great Kings Śakra and Brahmā, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial hosts, respectfully honored and personally attended upon the Bodhisattva.
Furthermore, all the kings, lords of cities, towns, and villages, as well as the householders and brahmins, gathered like clouds from every quarter to behold, honor, and serve the Bodhisattva.
At that time, King Śuddhodana had this thought:

"By the power of the merit I have accumulated in past lives, a holy son has now been born into my house, and he is capable of accomplishing all supreme deeds; it is fitting, therefore, that I name my son Sarvārthasiddha (Accomplisher of All Aims)."
At that time, there was a great city in the kingdom of Magadha named Nyagrodha, which was peaceful, prosperous, and teeming with people.

In this city lived a great Brahmin also named Nyagrodha, who possessed vast wealth and many servants; his storehouses were overflowing with gold, silver, and precious jewels, and he wielded great power like King Vaiśravaṇa. Furthermore, he held eighteen extensive villages as his fief and sixteen great towns for his service, and he owned sixty billion pieces of the finest refined gold.

The Lord of Magadha, King Mahāpadma, possessed one thousand ploughs; the number of ploughs belonging to the Brahmin family was likewise equal, yet fearing the incurrence of some transgression, they reduced it by one from that total of one thousand.

However, due to the ripening of karmic fruits induced by the merit and goodness of past causes, when he sowed seeds of ordinary wheat, golden wheat sprang forth; every harvest yielded more than two hundred *shi* of grain.

Every day when this man went to have audience with the king, he would invariably offer a handful of golden barley as a longevity gift, wishing that the king’s merit and lifespan might be inexhaustible.

Later, he took a daughter from a noble family as his wife; though many years passed, they had no offspring. Constantly seeking an heir, yet never finding satisfaction, he eventually began to sacrifice to all the deities.
Although he had prayed for a long time, his wish could not be fulfilled; harboring grief and distress, he rested his cheek in his palm and sighed:
"I now possess billions in wealth and property, yet having no heir, to whom shall I entrust it?"
"In the end, I was arrested by the authorities;
I have not possessed even a hair’s breadth [of merit]. His mother said, "Why do you now sigh so deeply?"
He replied:
"How could my body and mind possibly find peace?
Though my wealth and possessions are abundant and rare in this world, I currently have no offspring and my life is difficult to preserve; once my life ends, all shall be lost."
The mother said, "Cease your grief; I shall show you a skillful means.

I have seen those in the world who have no offspring, whether they pray for themselves or entreat others on their behalf, that when they give rise to a sincere heart, there is no wish that is not fulfilled."
The son said to his mother,
"What is the matter?
His mother replied:
"Previously, I had no son; it was through my prayers at the Nyagrodha tree that you were born.
You should now exert all your effort in prayer before the sacred tree, and by asking for but one son, your wish shall surely be fulfilled."
Then, having received his mother’s instructions, the brahmin went beneath a Pippala tree in the rear garden, prepared an extensive array of delicacies, and offered this prayer:
"I humbly beseech the tree deity to grant me a son at an early date."
"If my wish is granted," he said, "I shall establish a grand shrine here and hold a great assembly to express my gratitude for this extraordinary favor.
Day after day, he constantly made such prayers and aspirations, further telling the deity:
"If my purpose is not fulfilled, I shall cut down the tree at its very roots, leaving you without a place to dwell."
At that time, the deva, perceiving this earnestness, felt fear in his heart and thought:
"I have no power; what shall I do?
He immediately went quickly to Vaiśravaṇa and said:
“Great King!
There is a brahmin who, for the sake of seeking a son, intends to cut down the trees where I dwell; I pray that you will grant your grace and deign to show me compassion and protection.”
Having heard this, the Heavenly King, realizing he lacked the power [to help], immediately ascended to the heavens and said to Śakra:
“May you deign to hear me!

Regarding the place over which I preside, there is a man who seeks a son but cannot fulfill his heart’s desire; he intends to commit acts of destruction [against the spirits]. Since he faces such distress, I pray that you will have compassion for him.”
Having heard this, the Lord of Devas addressed his attendants, saying:
"If any devaputra manifests the signs of decline, you must come and inform me.

Having given these instructions, they respectfully received the divine command. Later, at another time, a certain devaputra manifested the five signs of decay; he immediately went in haste to inform the Lord of Devas, saying:
"Now the signs of death have appeared for the Son of Heaven.
A messenger came and announced:
"You should now go to the house of a great brāhmaṇa in the city of Nyagrodha within Jambudvīpa and take birth there."
Having spoken these words, the devaputra addressed him, saying:
"Great Lord, you should know!

That brahmin, relying on his own noble status, has become deeply negligent. However, the Great Teacher, the Buddha, has appeared in the world; when his work of conversion is finished, he shall enter nirvana. I have a long-standing vow to cultivate pure conduct under the World-Honored One, and I fear that being born there will become an obstacle for me."
The Lord of Devas said:
"Do not be anxious; I shall assist you at all times so that you remain free from negligence.
After his life had ended, he went to the Nyagrodha clan and took birth there by assuming a new existence.
An intelligent woman possesses five extraordinary knowledges.
What are these five?

First, she knows when a man has a mind of desire; second, she knows the proper season; third, she knows from which person she has conceived; fourth, she knows it is a male; and fifth, she knows it is a female.
At that time, having become pregnant, the wife was filled with great joy and said to her husband:
"Do you know, my lord?
A virtuous son has now entered my womb; we ought to rejoice greatly."
Upon hearing these words, his joy pervaded his entire body and mind, and he cried out in a loud voice:
"Excellent, O Anuruddha!

From time immemorial, day and night, I have single-mindedly prayed for a son to inherit my lineage. After my passing, may you perform various meritorious deeds according to your means and capacity, always invoking my name so that these virtues may assist my parents in their future rebirths, ensuring their blessings and happiness are inexhaustible."
"I entrust all my household affairs to you.

Having spoken these words, he prepared a precious throne upon the high tower and installed his wife there. He appointed a skilled physician to provide her with specialized care, ensuring that her clothing, food, and drink were appropriate for every occasion; furthermore, he ensured that all things—whether cold or warm, astringent or slippery, sour or salty—were balanced in weight and provided at the proper time with the right temperature.
Her entire body was adorned with exquisite necklaces, and she was embellished with flower garlands of such transcendent brilliance that she resembled a celestial maiden dwelling in the Nandana Grove.

Wherever she traveled, she always moved upon couches and mats; she never walked upon the ground with her feet. As for whatever came within the range of her ears and eyes, she never listened to or beheld anything evil, whether sound or form.
When the moon was full, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was peerless and whose radiant features were as brilliant as Jambūnada gold.

His head was rounded like a parasol, his arms reached below his knees, his nose was long and straight, and his eyebrows were high and long; his forehead was broad and even, and he was endowed with all the auspicious marks.
After twenty-one days, the relatives gathered for a joyful assembly and asked,
"What name shall we give this child?
They deliberated together and said:
"This child was originally obtained from a *piṇḍapātra* tree; therefore, he should be named Piṇḍola.
Furthermore, according to his clan, he may be named Kāśyapa."
Because of this, people of that time called him Pipphalī or Kāśyapa.
He then entrusted the child to eight foster mothers, ensuring that he lacked for nothing according to his needs.
Provided with medicinal milk, clarified butter, ointments, and various other excellent nourishing substances, he grew rapidly like a lotus emerging from the water.

Upon reaching the stage of a youth, he was entrusted to a learned master to study the arts and various scriptures; having encountered them but once, they were retained in his memory without being forgotten.
He held the pure water flask (*śikya*) with proper decorum, and his every movement was clearly observed. He was thoroughly proficient in the *uṇḍuka*, *puṇḍuka*, and the four *vedas*, namely:
first, the *Ṛgveda*; second, the *Yajurveda*; third, the *Sāmaveda*; and fourth, the *Atharvaveda*—the *veda* translated as "clear wisdom."
If one understands these four, then wisdom will be all-encompassing and application will be complete.

It should be called the *Catuḥpīṭha-vidyā-śāstra*; it consists of more than one hundred thousand verses in total, which have been transmitted orally from mouth to mouth and are not to be written down on paper or leaves.

The meaning therein consists of four parts: first, a detailed explanation of ritual actions; second, an extensive presentation of eulogies; third, the exposition of the methods for medicinal offerings; and fourth, the governance of the state and the nourishment of the body.
Most Brahmins extensively recite and study these four titles;
as they cannot be translated accurately, their Sanskrit characters are retained here.
The sound "Oṃ" is the opening phrase of incantations (*mantra*).
The sound "Pong" is the word used to summon the spirits and deities.

As for the phonetic cadence of the Veda, non-Buddhists hold it to be eternal, claiming it arises spontaneously from the beginningless past; they maintain that this sound is permanent and eternally present in space, whereas its utterance by the human mouth is impermanent.
The old term "four Vedas" is an error.
Regarding all worldly matters, whether on the earth or in the sky, they examine auspicious omens and transformations, and are further proficient in ritual methods:

namely, performing sacrifices oneself and instructing others to perform sacrifices; reciting mantras oneself and instructing others to recite them; and either giving alms oneself or receiving things from others. They possess clear understanding of these six matters, and have thoroughly mastered every branch and sub-division belonging to the four *vidyās*.
He was able to elucidate his own school’s tenets and effectively refute the arguments of others; his wisdom and discernment were as sharp and penetrating as fire.
Recognized by the multitude as a preeminent talent, he was requested to serve as their teacher and guide, and he instructed more than five hundred sons of Brahmins.
When he had grown up, his father said to him: "Kāśyapa!
Do you know this now?"
"Now that you have reached maturity, you should observe the rites of marriage.
He replied,
"The sensual pleasures of the world are not what I desire."
The father further instructed him, saying:
"As a son, you must carry on the family legacy; serve your ancestors with reverence and do not allow the lineage to be extinguished.
Kāśyapa replied:
"Father, have you not heard the discourse of the ancient seers, which says:
'Those who delight in seclusion find their spirits purified and ascend to the ultimate state'?
The father said:
"Is the ritual for marriage not the orthodox canon?
He replied, "This is a recent worldly discourse; it is not the dharma of the ancient seers."
At that time, Kāśyapa sighed and said: "What a calamity this is for me!
Now I am fallen into the mire of desire from which it will be difficult to emerge for eternal kalpas;
yet the profound kindness of my parents must not be disregarded. Thus, whether advancing or retreating, there is no way to escape."
At that time, his father exhorted and instructed him with earnestness two or three times; the man, being respectful and compliant, did not dare disobey his command, yet he reflected within himself:
"By what skillful means might I escape these bonds?"
He then addressed his father, saying:
"If you now insist on forcing me into marriage, I request that you cast an image of a woman out of purple gold.
His father quickly had it made, which was completed in a timely manner; its features were distinct, its appearance lovely, and its proportions equal to those of a human being.
At that time, having observed the golden maiden, Kāśyapa said to her father:
"If I may obtain such a woman, I shall follow your instructions and enter into marriage with her."
Having heard these words, the father was inwardly filled with grief and distress; resting his cheek in his palm, he stood sighing:
"Alas! Where could I now suddenly find such a beautiful woman?"
At that time, the disciples saw his distress and asked,
"For what reason, householder, are you so sorrowful?
He then informed them of the matter:
"Who might be able to obtain this beautiful woman?
The disciples replied, "We should seek her out;

we have searched throughout the world and seen no one who possesses such a vessel yet lacks a lid. Since Kāśyapa is endowed with all manner of merit, it would be fitting to seek such a wonderful woman for him."
Then the students spoke in verse:
“Upon this vast and boundless earth, There must surely exist such a person;
Since this son possesses great merit and virtue, Do not grieve now for the sake of seeking a bride.”
"We should have three more golden female images fashioned; carrying them as we travel throughout the four directions, we shall surely hope to behold such a beautiful woman.

Thereupon, the disciples took one golden image and called it "The Golden Deity" (*Suvarṇadevī*). They beat drums and blew conch shells, making grand offerings with flower canopies spread like clouds throughout the city and its suburbs. Searching from place to place, they gradually traveled until they reached the city of Kapilavastu.
In this city there was a great brāhmaṇa also named Kapila, who possessed abundant wealth and many servants, as described in detail previously.
He took a wife from a noble family, and not long after they lived together, a daughter was born to them; her countenance was so transcendent that she was a joy for all to behold.

At that time, her parents wished to bestow a name upon her; however, this young girl was lovely in appearance and peerless in her exquisite beauty, possessed a virtuous nature, and being a daughter of the Kāpilavas, she should be named Sujātā.
At that time, as Miaoxian gradually grew up, her exquisite beauty and feminine virtue became known far and wide.
Then, various students carrying golden images of women went to every city and town, proclaiming loudly to all the men and women:
"Sirs, you should know!..."
If there are those who can make offerings of incense, flowers, and exquisite objects to the celestial deity, this deity can grant five kinds of great vows:

first, one shall be born into a wealthy and noble family; second, one shall be married into a distinguished clan; third, one shall not be slighted by one's husband; fourth, one shall give birth to virtuous children; and fifth, one’s husband shall always act according to one’s wishes.
Having heard this announcement, all the young maidens each took fragrant flowers and went to the shrine of the Golden Deity to offer their respects.
Then, the father of Subhadrā said to his daughter:
"Everyone is going to make offerings to the deity; you should also go there to present your offerings."
Suvratā replied,
"For what reason would it be necessary to make offerings to him?
Her father said:
“By honoring that deity of gold, one can fulfill five wishes:

being born into a wealthy and noble family; being married into a distinguished clan; not being treated with contempt by one’s husband; giving birth to virtuous sons; and having one’s husband act according to one’s wishes.”
Then Sujātā said to her father, "I am not by nature a woman of lustful character;
who would go of their own accord to pay homage to that celestial deity?
Her father said to his daughter:
"Although there is nothing to be gained, what harm is there in paying our respects?
You should go for a moment and observe together with the multitude.
The daughter respectfully obeyed and did not oppose her father's wish; she then took several other women as companions and went to the place of the celestial deity.
Once they had arrived there, the girl’s majestic radiance blazed so brightly that it eclipsed the golden deity, making him appear like a mass of black iron.
When the disciples witnessed this event, they were each filled with wonder and deliberated among themselves, saying:
"Where has the majestic radiance of our deity gone now?"
"Was it taken away by the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of spirits?
Or was it because this woman’s radiance eclipsed it?
How is it that the purple-gold has turned into black iron?"
Having seen this, Subhadrā returned home with her companions; the celestial form of the goddess vanished, and she was restored to her golden complexion.
At that time, the students gathered to witness this event and all marveled at its rarity, asking the people, "Whose daughter is this, whose beauty is peerless?"
"By the power of her majesty, gold has been transformed into iron.
The people replied,
"This is indeed due to the power of the majesty of that great Brahmin’s daughter, Kapila, named Bhadrā."
When the disciples heard this, they were each filled with wonder and joy; they then went together to the house of the great brahmin, prostrated themselves in salutation, and said:
"O Householder!"

To the south there is a city named Nyagrodha. In this city there was a great brahmin also named Nyagrodha, who possessed vast wealth and many servants; his storehouses were overflowing with gold, silver, and precious gems, and he held great power like King Vaiśravaṇa. He had eighteen extensive villages as his fief and sixteen great towns for his attendants, and he possessed sixty billion pieces of the finest pure gold.

The King of Mahādeva, the Great Lotus King, possessed one thousand plows; the number of plows belonging to the brahmins was equal to that of the king, yet they reduced it by one, fearing the incurrence of some transgression.

That man had a son named Kāśyapa, whose appearance was extraordinary and whose intelligence was peerless. He was proficient in the four Vedas and skilled in various arts; he could establish his own school and effectively refute the arguments of others. His wisdom and discernment were as sharp and fierce as a blazing torch. Since he had not yet taken a wife, [the father] sought one for him from afar.

At that time, the Brahmin Kapphiṇa had long admired and honored the virtue of Kāśyapa; now, hearing that [the family] was so wealthy and prosperous, his joy fulfilled his prior wishes, and he said to the people:
"I respectfully follow your intentions and shall form an alliance through marriage."
When the disciples had received this permission, they returned to their home in joy and told the great brahmin:
"We have already found a worthy wife for Kāśyapa—one who is peerless in her beauty—a daughter of a great brahmin from the city of Kapilavastu named Sujātā."
When the brahmin heard these words, he was filled with great joy and replied,
"What I have been seeking for some time has now been fulfilled according to my wishes.
Upon hearing this, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Seek out a wife for me; although it is said she has already been found, I have heard she is exceptionally excellent, yet I do not yet know what she is like.
It would be fitting for me to go there myself to observe her.
He then went to his parents, prostrated himself, and said:
"O Venerable Ones, please know this!
I now wish to travel briefly to another place to observe.
His parents replied:
"We two have you as our only son; our affection for you is deep, and the time for your marriage is approaching. You may go out with us for a brief excursion, but you must return quickly.

Having taken leave of his parents, Kāśyapa went to the city of Kapilavastu, changed his clothes and altered his appearance, and carrying a small leaf-bowl, he wandered about begging for alms. Upon learning of the householder's residence, he arrived at the entrance of the gate.
However, in this country, whenever food was to be distributed, young maidens were sent out to carry it.
At that time, when Subhadrā heard that there was a beggar, she personally took up the food with her own hands and bestowed it upon the beggar.
When Kāśyapa saw the woman, he was struck with a sense of wonder and exclaimed:
"Such exquisite beauty as this is peerless in all the world; for it to be cast away in vain is truly a great pity."
Having heard this, Subhadrā said to him,
"Has the one for whom you made that promise already passed away? Kāśyapa replied:
"He is present now. The woman said, "If that is so,
for what reason do you suddenly speak these words?"
He spoke to her again, saying,
"Although he is currently present, his heart does not find pleasure or desire [in this].
Upon hearing these words, the woman also exclaimed in astonishment:
"This is truly rare!
This is truly a virtuous deed!
I too, with utmost sincerity, do not delight in practicing sensual desire."
Kāśyapa said: "Virtuous lady! If it must be so, then I am that man.

I now make a solemn covenant with you: the instructions of one's parents truly must not be disobeyed; except for the brief holding of hands at the time of our first marriage, I vow never to touch any part of your body thereafter."
At that time, after Kāśyapa had made this agreement with her, he returned to his kinsmen to perform the great rites of marriage.

After his wife had gone home, they lived together in a one-pillar pavilion where they had prepared a bed and seat; though man and wife resided there, each occupied one side of the space to cultivate wholesome deeds. Together they grew weary of worldly affairs and focused exclusively on seeking the path beyond, never once giving rise to a thought of defiled desire.
At that time, Kāśyapa addressed Bhadramukhī, saying:
"Observing thoroughly all the faults and afflictions of birth and death, They all arise with craving and defilement as their causal conditions;
All people in the world together practice what is wrong— How can they awaken to the fact that they are long submerged in the ocean of the three realms of existence?"
He further addressed his wife, saying:
"O fair one! As it is the nature of women to be prone to drowsiness, you may sleep soundly during the first and last watches of the night; during the middle watch, I shall take a brief rest."
Later, at another time, while Subhadrā was lying down with her hands hanging over the edge of the bed, Kāśyapa was sometimes walking up and down or sitting in meditation.
When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, saw this, he thought to himself:
"I shall now go in person to test Kāśyapa; is he acting out of deceit, desiring fame and profit?"
"Is this truly seeking liberation?

He then descended from the sky and transformed himself into a snake; with its mouth agape and venom spitting forth, it manifested a terrifying appearance and moved toward Bhadrottamā, intending to bite her arm.
Having seen this, Kāśyapa hurried to the place where Subhadrā was, and raising his hand holding the handle of the precious fan,
he placed it upon the bed. At that moment, Subhadrā woke from her sleep in alarm and said to her husband,
"Noble son!..."
"Do not violate your oath!
Do not violate your oath! Kāśyapa said:
"Have you not seen the black venomous snake coming?
At that time, Suprabhā replied in verse:
"I would rather let my own body be struck by a venomous snake; I must never violate my vow by coming into contact with you."
"The venom of a snake causes only one's own body to die, but the poison of defilement leads to a sinking away into boundless depths.
Then Kāśyapa said to his wife,
"O noble lady!"
"You must cultivate pure conduct with a sincere heart.
He then spoke in verse:
"To tread upon blades and enter fire is difficult, But to practice while facing a woman is more difficult than that."
"If one can maintain their resolve without flaw or transgression, this is truly a rare occurrence in the world.
At that time, Kāśyapa further informed Sujātā of the matter, saying:
"It was not out of desire that I touched you; rather, I raised my hand with the handle of a fan to ward off the snake."
At that time, the sovereign king, seeing this, was filled with admiration and subsequently proceeded to the celestial palace.
Thereupon, the two of them dwelt in a pavilion supported by a single pillar, where they practiced pure conduct for twelve years.
As the Buddha has said:
"All accumulations come to an end; what is lofty must fall.
Those who meet will eventually part; those with life shall all return to death."
When both Kāśyapa’s parents had passed away, he took charge of the household affairs.
On another occasion, he went to the fields where the crops were being cultivated and, observing the plowing, spoke this verse:
“Behold this place of plowing; It damages the earth and harms all the insects.”
The oxen labor with great diligence, regarding him with compassion as if he were their own kin;
the farmers are worn out and haggard, their features marred by wind and sun;
exhausted from the toil of plowing and sowing, they feel a piercing ache of sorrow upon seeing him.
Then Kāśyapa asked the plowman,
"Whose field is this place for cultivation?
The plowman replied:
"It is Kāśyapa. Kāśyapa said,
"How could my family possibly possess such fields and property?"
The plowman said, "This is my father’s old business; it has not yet ceased even now.
Having heard these words, [the Buddha] addressed the plowman:

"From this day forward, I release you all; you are no longer slaves, so wander at your pleasure. As for the cattle and livestock, let them follow the water and grass as they wish, without any further restraint."
At that time, seeing this to be of no benefit, Kāśyapa spoke in verse:
"One should eat no more than a single *śroṇa* of rice; For sleeping, one needs only a small bed.
Two pieces of cotton cloth are sufficient to cover the body; Everything beyond that is merely the property of the foolish."
Then Kāśyapa said to his wife,
"O virtuous lady!
I now have a vow to renounce the world and go forth into homelessness."

Why is this so? Living at home is confining, like a prison; one is constantly entangled by all manner of suffering and afflictions, followed by evil associates, and the causal conditions for creating karma never cease.
"Leaving the household life is as vast and expansive as empty space; one can spontaneously cultivate the pure brahmacarya and swiftly fulfill it to reach the state of liberation.
Then he spoke in verse:
"The mountain forests are full of tranquility, Serene and free from fear; The householder’s life is like a thicket of thorns, Full of anxiety and dread."
One should diligently practice herein to be able to leave behind all fetters.
Right view and wrong view both arise from the mind;
dwelling in the quiet forest, the wise person should observe this.
"If a person is greedy for worldly affairs, all sufferings will constantly pursue them;
but one who transcends and leaves the net of dust can go to the palace of Nirvana.
Having spoken these words, he commanded the keeper of the treasury, saying:
“You should give me one of your lowest-quality garments; I wish to leave the household life to practice the path of renunciation.

He opened the storehouse and inspected his various robes, finding that they were all priceless. There was only a single piece of the lowest quality cotton cloth; even by a rough estimate of its value, it was worth one hundred million gold coins. Taking this, he offered it to Kāśyapa.
Having accepted it, he departed from the house.
At that time, the Bodhisattva, having observed all of old age, sickness, and death, surrounded by the devas, crossed the city walls at midnight and went forth into the forest of asceticism.
At that time, Kāśyapa also abandoned his household affairs to practice the path of renunciation, and he thought to himself:
"If there is anyone in this world who is an Arhat, I shall rely upon them and serve them with a heart of reverence."
Having thus gone forth, people of the time called him a recluse (ṛṣi).
Kāśyapa resided at the edge of the Bahuputraka Caitya.
At that time, the Bodhisattva dwelt in an araṇya; after practicing austerities for six years, he realized they were of no benefit and were merely a source of weariness.

Next, at the dwellings of the two cowherd girls, Nandā and Nandabalā, he consumed sixteen times the amount of milk gruel; the Dragon King praised him, and at the site of the human prosperity of King Bimbisāra, he received soft grass. He then proceeded to the foot of the Bodhi tree, spread his own seat of grass upon the Vajrāsana, and sat cross-legged with body erect and mindfulness established, like a sleeping dragon king.
Relying on the staff of compassion, he subdued the armies of thirty-six billion celestial Māra demons and realized unsurpassed enlightenment.

Subsequently, he went to the Deer Park at Ṛṣipatana in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, where for the five bhikṣus and their five companions, he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its three revolutions and twelve aspects.
Next, for the Brahmin Mahāsena and the two cowherd girls, he preached the sublime Dharma so that they might give rise to right view; all of them realized the first fruit [of the path].

Furthermore, he caused the one thousand followers of the Tīrthika Śikhin and others to take refuge in the Buddha, go forth, and receive full ordination. King Bimbisāra also abided in the vision of the Truths.
Next, he went to the city of Rājagṛha and stayed at the Bamboo Grove Park, where he ordained Mahāmaudgalyāyana and Śāriputra.
He then proceeded to Śrāvastī and taught the *Kumāraputra-sūtra* to King Prasenajit, bringing him to spiritual subjugation.
Next, he caused Queen Śrīmālā, General Vīra, the Rishi-son (Śiṣṭa), and others to all realize the Truths.

Such is the constant law of the Unsurpassed World-Honored One: observing the world, there is nothing he does not hear or see; he constantly gives rise to great compassion to benefit all beings, being foremost among those who provide protection and succor. He is most heroic and valiant, his word is without duality, and he dwells in concentration and wisdom, manifesting the three types of supernormal knowledge (trividyā). He has skillfully cultivated the Threefold Training (triśikṣā) and well disciplined the three types of action (trikarma).
Having crossed the four torrents and established himself in the four bases of supernormal power, he cultivated the four means of integration throughout the long night.

He abandoned the five hindrances, distanced himself from the five factors, and transcended the five paths. With his six faculties complete and the six perfections fulfilled, he universally bestowed the seven riches and opened the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment. Free from the eight worldly dharmas, he demonstrated the eightfold noble path; having forever severed the nine fetters, he was clear and proficient in the nine meditative absorptions. Filled with the ten powers, his fame reached the ten directions.

The most preeminent among all sovereigns, having attained fearlessness in the Dharma and subdued the hosts of Māra, he utters the great thunderous sound and roars the lion’s roar; throughout the six periods of day and night, he constantly observes the world with his Buddha-eye: "Who is increasing?"
Who is declining?
Who is beset by suffering and calamity?
Who is heading toward the evil destinies?
Who is mired in the mud of desire?
Who is capable of receiving transformation?
By what skillful means may they be rescued and brought forth?

He causes those who lack the noble wealth to obtain it; with the *añjana* of wisdom, he breaks the cataracts of ignorance from their eyes. He causes those without roots of goodness to plant them, and causes those who possess roots of goodness to further increase them. He places them upon the path of humans and devas, leading them safely and without hindrance toward the city of Nirvāṇa.
As it is said in a verse:
"Even if the tide of the great ocean Should ever miss its appointed time,
The Buddha, in regard to those he transforms, Never fails to deliver them at the proper moment."
Just as a mother has an only son and constantly protects his life,
the Buddha’s compassionate concern for those he transforms exceeds even that.
The Buddha’s loving-kindness toward all sentient beings is never abandoned.
"I shall strive to rescue them from their suffering and hardship, just as a mother cow follows her calf.
At that time, the World-Honored One thought to himself:
"The ascetic Kāśyapa should now be converted."

He then traveled among the people of the Kṛṣi country, arriving at the Many-Sons Stūpa in Vaiśālī where he sat beneath a tree. Desiring to guide Kāśyapa, he emitted light from his entire body that was like a mountain of exquisite gold; it was dazzling, marvelous, and radiated brilliantly in all directions.

At that time, having witnessed this event, Kāśyapa followed the light to the place where the World-Honored One was. From afar, he beheld the Tathāgata’s countenance, upright and majestic, with marks and signs of excellence beyond compare; his faculties were serene and tranquil, his mind single-pointed and undisturbed. He was like the king of mountains, radiant with a golden luster.
Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, he cried out in a loud voice: "This is my Teacher; I am his disciple."
The World-Honored One said, "So it is,
so it is! Kāśyapa!"
"I am your teacher and you are my disciple; pay homage with a sincere heart.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:

"To claim knowledge when one is truly ignorant, to claim to have seen what one has never seen, to call oneself a teacher when one is not a great master, to call oneself an Arhat when one is not an Arhat, to call oneself a Bhagavān when one is not a Bhagavān, and to call oneself a Samyaksambuddha when one is not a Samyaksambuddha—such a deceitful person shall have his head split into seven pieces."

"Kāśyapa! I am one who knows and say that I know; I am one who sees and say that I see; I am a Great Teacher and say I am a Great Teacher; I am an Arhat and say I am an Arhat; I am a Samyaksaṃbuddha and say I am a Samyaksaṃbuddha."

I have a cause and condition for proclaiming the essential Dharma for the sake of the śrāvakas; it is not without cause or condition. This is true liberation, not non-liberation; this is the refuge, not non-refuge; this is actual transcendence, not non-transcendence; this possesses supernormal powers, and is not without supernormal powers.
For this reason, Kāśyapa, you should train yourself in this way and reflect thus:
"The Dharma that I listen to is associated with the wholesome; I shall listen to it all with reverence and single-minded attention, honoring it with mindfulness and keeping my focus unwavering."

One receives [the teachings] with focused reflection and a respectful mind, thinking: "Regarding the five aggregates of clinging, I truly perceive them as suffering characterized by arising and ceasing; regarding the six bases of contact, I see them as accumulation and as obscurity; regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, I shall dwell well-established in the mind; regarding the seven factors of enlightenment, I shall cultivate and repeatedly practice them; and regarding the eight liberations, I shall personally realize and perfect them."

Toward the Great Master and my fellow practitioners of the holy life who possess wisdom, I constantly give rise to a heart of profound respect and extreme shame; my right view continues in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment, following along with my body without allowing it to be severed.
"Kāśyapa, you should train yourself in this way.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, Fascicle One.
The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume Two.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.

This concludes the remainder of the training rule on impure conduct. At that time, the Blessed One, having expounded the essentials of the Dharma for Kāśyapa and having instructed, inspired, benefited, and gladdened him, rose from his seat and departed.
At that time, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa followed after the Buddha and thought to himself:
"When the Buddha sits, I shall offer this saṃghāṭī robe, folded, to serve as his seat."
At that time, there were five hundred bandits following behind him, intending to plunder him.
Knowing this, the World-Honored One wished to sit by the side of the road; then Kāśyapa went to where the World-Honored One was and quickly folded his robe to spread it out as a seat for the Buddha.
The World-Honored One sat down and immediately addressed Kāśyapa, saying:
"This saṃghāṭī robe is extremely light and subtle; it is extremely soft.
Kāśyapa replied:
"So be it, Blessed One!
This robe is indeed light and soft; we pray that you will compassionately accept it.
The Blessed One replied:
"Would you be able to wear my rag-robes made of hemp?
He replied, "I pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will accept these light robes; I shall wear the rag-robes made of hemp bestowed by the World-Honored One."
At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion, accepted [the offering].
Then Kāśyapa, following this sequence, failed to attain any realization during the eight days; he maintained himself by begging for alms until the ninth day, when he attained the fruit of Arhatship.

At that time, Suprabhā, having no one to rely upon and being unacquainted with worldly affairs, merely observed their outward appearance and conceived a sense of reverence; she then went to the Nirgrantha ascetics and entered the religious life.

This woman’s appearance and demeanor were peerlessly upright and beautiful; when the non-Buddhists saw her, they all conceived defiled thoughts. Though they felt extreme loathing and revulsion, they could not distance themselves from her, and were consequently led by five hundred naked non-Buddhists to commit unrighteous acts together.
Sudinnā rebuked them, saying, "How can you who commit such base and evil deeds ever succeed in practicing the Path?
Your female bodies are so delicate that having been thus insulted and humiliated, the suffering is unbearable. She then reported this matter to the naked ascetic women.
The women replied,
"You should go to the Great Teacher Pūraṇa and report this matter in full.
Having heard these instructions, the woman went to the teacher's location, prostrated at his feet, and spoke as follows:
“I have now encountered misfortune and am suffering extreme hardship; I pray that you will look upon me with compassion and grant me your gracious aid.

He replied, “It is because of this assembly’s reverence and respect that I have obtained abundant offerings. If they were all to disperse as you propose, my disciples would consequently decline. I cannot comply with your wishes.”
Seeing his earnestness, he then proceeded to make mud seals and assigned two hundred and fifty people to take turns; at that time, the woman’s grief and distress gradually diminished.
At that time, there was a festival in Rājagṛha, and Bhadrottamā went along together with a naked ascetic.

Meanwhile, Kāśyapa was staying in a small hut in an araṇya near Rājagṛha; during the first part of the day, he took up his robe and bowl and entered the city for alms, where he suddenly saw Bhadrottamā and asked, "O fair-faced one!"
"Have you been dwelling in peace and happiness lately? Are you practicing the pure life?
At that time, when Subhadrā saw Kāśyapa, her eyes filled with tears and she could not contain her grief; swallowing back her sobs, she said, "With whom shall I be a companion?"
"In what place do you wish to cultivate the pure conduct?

"In the past, I dwelt with you in a pavilion with a single pillar; for twelve years within, we steadfastly cultivated sublime deeds, our pure conduct being so refined and clean that from beginning to end it never transgressed its bounds."

Originally, they did not touch hands with defiled minds; it was from a single instance of estrangement that they mistakenly joined this group. Now, gathered in a foul assembly like beasts, they have failed to achieve the state of renunciation—how could there be pure conduct?
Then Kāśyapa asked her again for the reason, and Bhadrottamā paid him homage as if to a compassionate father and informed him of the matter.
He thought to himself:
"Does this girl possess any roots of merit from previous lives?"
Concentrating his mind in contemplation, he realized that there were roots of goodness conducive to liberation. Thinking, "Who shall deliver them?
he knew they belonged to himself and replied:
"O noble one!"
"Why do you not go forth as a renunciant within this well-spoken Dharma and Vinaya?
He replied: "Noble One!"
"Do not allow this seal-method to be transmitted further within these circles.
He replied, "Cease!"
"Stop! O worthy one! Do not speak thus.

Our Great Teacher now has his myriad virtues perfected and has extinguished all obstacles; he is the true field of merit and the place of refuge. Having realized subtle, tranquil, and true liberation, how could he possibly be compared to those most inferior dharmas?"
Having heard this, Bhadrottamā was filled with joy and followed him. He then entrusted Bhadrottamā to Mahāprajāpatī, saying: "Noble Lady!
This girl Bhadrottamā delights in the sublime Dharma and possesses excellent mental attention; she may be granted the going forth."

Then Mahāprajāpatī, respectfully receiving her instructions, immediately gave her those five robes and other items; having conferred upon her the various precepts and full ordination (*upasampadā*), she said:
"You should now, within the sphere of the Buddha, seek alms for your sustenance and diligently cultivate the pure conduct."
At that time, during the first part of the day, Subhadrā took her robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for alms.
This woman’s appearance was so upright and rare among mortals that when the multitude saw her, they all marveled together:

"What is the meaning of this? This woman’s bearing is peerless; why does she waste her youth instead of enjoying sensual pleasures, being able to renounce such splendor and beauty to become a renunciant?"
Upon hearing this, Bhadrikā was overcome with shame; from that time forth, she no longer entered the city to beg for alms.
Later, when Kāśyapa encountered her, he asked:
"O fair-faced one!"
"Are you at ease?
Miao-xian (Sudatta) answered in full detail. Having heard her words, he spoke thus:
"If the Buddha permits me to reduce my alms by half and give it to Miao-xian, I shall share it with her."
He informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "Give him half as you please.
Having heard this, the Venerable One gave him half of his food to provide for his relief.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā, having witnessed this event, gave rise to a derisive laugh and slandered him, saying:

"The Venerable Mahākāśyapa previously dwelt with Bhadrikā in the Single-Pillar Pavilion for twelve years, purely cultivating the Brahma-faring; yet today he has turned back to private passion, begging for alms to support one another."
When Kāśyapa heard of this matter, he went to Bhadrottamā and instructed her in the essentials of the Dharma:
"This should be done; this should not be done. You must apply your mind well."
She then departed.

At that time, Suprabhā summoned great courage and, throughout the first and last watches of the night, remained in accord with right mindfulness. She reproached her own mind without ceasing for even a moment, and immediately realized the fruit of Arhatship, transforming into a pure woman free from birth.
At that time, Kāśyapa saw him and said:
"Now, by virtue of me as your spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), all that you had to do has been completed; you should now sustain yourself by begging for alms within the Buddha’s realm."
At that time, during the first part of the day, Subhūṣaṇā took up her robe and bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha to beg for alms in sequence.
At that moment, King Ajātaśatru had unjustly put his father to death; he was seized by great remorse and remained in his chamber filled with grief.
Although there were various kinds of drums, music, lutes, and singing, they could not dispel his sorrow and distress.
At that time, the minister happened upon Subhadrā, whose appearance was upright and whose complexion was exceptionally radiant; he then thought to himself:
"This beautiful woman is truly extraordinary compared to ordinary people; it would be fitting to present her to the King in the hope of removing his grief."

Having formed this thought, he approached the royal palace and forcibly compelled Sujātā to remove her Dharma robes and don various colored garments; he had her adorned with necklaces and anointed with famous perfumes, and sent her, attended by her personal attendants, into the presence of the king.
At that time, as soon as King Ajātaśatru beheld this woman’s exquisite and peerless beauty, his sorrowful heart was immediately relieved.

Yet, because the evil karma of Subhadrā had ripened, it could not be halted—just as a torrential flood cannot be dammed—and she was thus forcibly humiliated by the wicked king, who felt great anguish like one struck by a poisoned arrow.

At that time, on the fifteenth day when the Great Leader Mahāprajāpatī was about to perform the poṣadha ceremony, she surveyed the entire assembly of nuns but did not see Sujātā. Entering meditative concentration, she perceived that Sujātā was within the royal palace, undergoing great suffering and being subjected to extraordinary humiliation.
The nuns asked, "Venerable One!
Where is Subhadrā now? Why do we not see her alone?"
Then Mahāprajāpatī immediately commanded the nun Utpalavarṇā, saying:
"You should collect your mindfulness and observe that Subhadrā.

Having heard these words, she perceived her location; then, in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, she vanished from among the assembly of nuns and appeared within the royal palace, staying in mid-air atop a high tower, where she called out to Subhadrā from afar:
"Sister! You have already been able to shatter the various māras of the afflictions; why do you not manifest great supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) to endure this humiliation?

Then, the nun Utpalavarṇā bestowed the teaching upon her, saying: "In this manner you should act; in this manner you should cultivate [the path]; quickly discipline your own mind and manifest the power of supernormal faculties."
At that time, Bhadrottamā focused her mind to eliminate distraction, and in an instant she attained supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). Wearing secular garments, she departed through the air.
Then, Utpalavarṇā went with Bhadrottamā to the place for the *poṣadha* ceremony. When the twelve groups of bhikṣuṇīs saw them, they felt great contempt and shame, saying with derisive laughter:
"We truly cannot perform the *poṣadha* together with this palace lady."
When Mahāprajāpatī heard these words, she said to Bhadrikā,
"Venerable one!
You should go inform the King, put on your former monastic robes, and return here quickly."
At that time, Subhadrā immediately traveled by means of supernatural power to the king’s bedchamber; while the king was still asleep, she snapped her fingers in the air to make a sound.
Upon hearing it and waking up, the king was seized with great terror and his hair stood on end as he spoke these words: "Who are you?"
"Are you a deva or a nāga?
Or are you a spirit or a ghost?
Having spoken these words, at that moment Miaoxian replied from the air:
"I am not a deva, nāga, spirit, or ghost; I am merely the Bhikṣuṇī Subhadrā, a disciple of the Great Teacher.
When the King heard this, he replied with a verse:
"You currently possess neither Dharma robes nor an alms bowl, And your appearance does not resemble that of a nun."
"Since your appearance is like that of a wanton woman, you must explain how you, a layperson, act in contradiction to the Dharma.
At that moment, Miaoxian descended from her position and informed him of the matter, saying:
"Your Majesty has unjustly assailed me; you have forcibly seized my alms bowl and my dharma robes."
"You ought to grant me the inheritance of my parents; I wish to return quickly to observe the Poṣadha.
When King Ajātaśatru heard these words, he fainted and fell to the ground.

Only after cold water was sprinkled on his face was he able to regain consciousness; he then prostrated at [the monk's] feet, seeking mercy and offering thanks, immediately requesting his robes and bowl which he respectfully bestowed upon Wuxian.
Having received them, he returned to his original location and performed the *poṣadha* ceremony together with the community of nuns.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs reported the matter concerning Bhadrikā to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of these causes and conditions, the World-Honored One assembled the bhikṣuṇīs. It is the constant law of all Buddhas to inquire knowingly of what is known; to inquire at the proper time and not at an improper time; to inquire when it is beneficial and not when it is not beneficial; and to break through barriers in order to eliminate doubt.
Thus, he addressed the bhikṣuṇī Bhadrikā, saying: "Is it true that you committed such an unseemly act?"
He replied, “It is indeed so,
World-Honored One!”
The World-Honored One asked again:
"Do you experience pleasure?
He replied:
“World-Honored One!
Since I have already abandoned desire, how could I permit myself to experience pleasure?
The Buddha said:
“You are not guilty of an offense now; however, a bhikṣuṇī who engages in impure conduct commits a pārājika offense, as in the case of Soṇa.

Having considered ten benefits—as extensively explained above, up to the point of exalting the True Dharma and bringing great benefit to humans and devas—I shall establish a training rule within the Vinaya for my disciples, the bhikṣuṇīs among the śrāvakas. It should be stated as follows:”

"If again a bhikṣuṇī, having received the training rules together with other bhikṣuṇīs, does not relinquish those training rules and, while her training is weak, does not declare it herself, commits an impure act through the method of sexual intercourse—even with an animal—this bhikṣuṇī also incurs a pārājika offense and should not live in community."
Furthermore, regarding "a bhikṣuṇī," there are five kinds:

first, the bhikṣuṇī by name; second, the bhikṣuṇī by self-assertion; third, the bhikṣuṇī by mendicancy; fourth, the bhikṣuṇī by the destruction of afflictions; and fifth, the bhikṣuṇī by means of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).

Regarding the "bhikṣuṇī by name": this refers to one who has been given the designation "bhikṣuṇī," or one who is so recognized by common worldly convention, or one who belongs to the clan of bhikṣuṇīs; because of these reasons she is called a bhikṣuṇī—this is what is meant by a "bhikṣuṇī by name."
What is meant by one who claims to be a bhikṣuṇī?

If a person is not actually a bhikṣuṇī but claims for herself, "I am a bhikṣuṇī," or if one who is a "thief-dweller" (caura-vāsin) or similar status calls herself a bhikṣuṇī—this is called one who claims to be a bhikṣuṇī.
What is a bhikṣuṇī who begs for alms?
Just as worldly people constantly beg for alms to sustain their own lives, she is called a bhikṣuṇī who begs for alms.
What is a bhikṣuṇī who destroys the afflictions?

If one can sever all outflows (*āsrava*), thoroughly understand all future births and deaths—including their scorching heat and the ripening of various sufferings—and forever uproot them as if cutting off the crown of a *tāla* tree so that they are subject to the state of non-arising (*anutpādadharmatā*), she is called a bhikṣuṇī who has destroyed the afflictions.
What is a bhikṣuṇī who has received full ordination through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*?
It refers to one whose person is free from obstacles, for whom the ritual procedure is complete, and who is beyond reproach; such a person is called a bhikṣuṇī by way of the *karman*.
Regarding the meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" mentioned here, the intention is to take the fifth [category].
The word "furthermore" (punar) indicates that there are other such types as well.
"With the bhikṣuṇīs" means together with the other groups of bhikṣuṇīs.

Regarding those who have equally attained the training rules (*śikṣāpada*): even if one has previously received full ordination (*upasampadā*) and it has already been a hundred years, the matters one ought to train in are no different from those of a newly ordained person.

If a person who has newly received full ordination (*upasampadā*) is to train in the matters that ought to be learned, these are no different from those of one who has been ordained for a hundred years; namely, regarding the precepts (*śīla*), the training rules (*śikṣāpada*), and the protocols for observance and transgression, they are all identical. Therefore, it is called "attaining the training rules equally."
Regarding the phrase "not relinquishing the precepts": up to what point is one said not to have relinquished the precepts?

It means that if one relinquishes the precepts in the presence of someone who is insane, mentally deranged, afflicted by intense pain, deaf, mute, or ignorant, it does not count as a relinquishment at all.
If a person from the central region speaks in the language of the central region to a person from a border region, the relinquishment is not accomplished if [the latter] does not understand it;
it is accomplished if they do understand it.
If a person from a border region speaks in the language of a border region to a person from the central region; [the same applies].

If a person from the Central Region speaks a borderland dialect to another person from the Central Region, the renunciation is not accomplished unless they understand it; if they understand it, the renunciation is accomplished.
If a person from a Borderland Region speaks the language of the Central Region to another person from a Borderland Region, it should be understood according to the same principle as above.

If one perceives a solitary place as solitary, or perceives a non-solitary place as solitary, or perceives a solitary place as non-solitary, none of these constitute a transgression of the training rules.

If one is with respect to sleep, meditative absorption, non-humans, devas, and so forth; or to transformations of animals and various images; or at times when there is commotion and confusion; or if one does not carefully examine those with whom one dwells as being persons of their true nature—in all such cases, the relinquishment is not accomplished.
Regarding the statement "one who is weak in training does not speak," there should be four permutations:

there is one who has not relinquished the training rules and is weak in training yet speaks; there is one who has relinquished the training rules but is not weak in training and speaks; there is one who has relinquished the training rules and is weak in training and speaks; and there is one who has neither relinquished the training rules nor is weak in training and speaks.
What is meant by "not relinquishing the training rules while declaring one's weakness in the training"?

It is as when a bhikṣuṇī harbors feelings of attachment and longs to return to lay life; she has no affection for the śramaṇa’s state, and being distressed by the śramaṇa’s life, she feels shame, aversion, and repulsion.
She went to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and spoke to them as follows:
"Venerable ladies, do you know?
The holy life is difficult to establish; dwelling in solitude is difficult; living alone is difficult; it is difficult to dwell in forest glades and endure poor bedding."

I remember my parents, brothers, sisters, teachers, and masters; I wish to learn various crafts and engage in my ancestral trade, for my heart yearns to carry on our family lineage and finds no pleasure in staying here.
If a bhikṣuṇī, despite making such words of repentance, does not say,
"I relinquish the training," this is called speaking while the training is weak, but it is not a relinquishing of the training.
What is meant by "having relinquished the training rules, yet not declaring it due to being weary of the training"?
For example, there may be a bhikṣuṇī who goes to another bhikṣuṇī and speaks as follows:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!"
"I, [name], now relinquish the precepts.
This is called relinquishing the precepts.
Or one says:
"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṃgha," or he says:
"I renounce the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkās."
Some say: "I renounce my upādhyāya and ācārya. Others say:

"Knowing me to be a female novice (śrāmaṇerī), knowing me to be a laywoman, a śaṇḍha, a paṇḍaka, a female paṇḍaka; one who has defiled a bhikṣu; one who has killed her father, killed her mother, killed an arhat, caused a schism in the Saṃgha, or with malicious intent shed the blood of a Buddha; one who is a female outsider, one who has gone over to the outsiders, one who dwells as a thief, one who dwells separately, or one who is not in communion."
...and so on, up to saying:
"I am not a companion among my sisters who share the same Dharma and the same holy life.
This is called abandoning the training rules, rather than speaking while being weak in the training.
What is meant by "declining in one's training" and then declaring that one also relinquishes the precepts?
For example, there may be a bhikṣuṇī who, harboring feelings of attachment and longing, even goes so far as to say in regret:
"I relinquish the precepts."
The detailed explanation is as before, up to: "They are not of a similar class. This is called declaring one's weakness in training while also relinquishing the precepts.
What is it to not relinquish the precepts and yet not declare one's weakness in training?
This means that, excluding the aforementioned cases, this is what is called "failing to declare one's weakness as a trainee.
To speak of "engaging in impure conduct" is to engage in sexual intercourse.
To speak of "sexual desire" refers to the mutual union of two persons.
"Phenomenon" (*dharma*) here refers to what is called "phenomenon" by way of its non-phenomenal nature.
Non-virtuous bodily action is termed "performance.
This extends even to [intercourse] with animals, such as monkeys and the like.
"This" refers to that person.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who has attained the nature of a bhikṣuṇī.
What is the nature of a bhikṣuṇī?
This refers to receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*). What is meant by "full ordination"?

It refers to the formal procedure of a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*), wherein the matter to be performed is accomplished in accordance with the Dharma; because one is brought close to *nirvāṇa*, it is called "full ordination."

Furthermore, the one who receives the ordination does so with a mind of perfection, aspiring to possess the complete precepts; they pledge their commitment to receive them with a heart free from resentment.
Because this is expressed through speech and manifested through the karma of verbal action, reaching ultimate fulfillment, it is called "complete ordination" (*upasaṃpadā*).
*Pārājika* refers to an extremely grave offense, one that is utterly loathsome, despicable, and not to be relished.

As soon as a bhikṣuṇī commits it, she is no longer a female śramaṇa, no longer a daughter of the Śākyas; she loses her status as a bhikṣuṇī, deviates from the nature of *nirvāṇa*, falls and collapses, being overcome by others beyond redemption. Just as when the head of a *tāla* tree is cut off, it never grows again and can no longer flourish or expand, it is therefore called *pārājika*.

Regarding the term "not living together" (*asaṃvāsa*): it means that this offender may not live in common with the bhikṣuṇīs; nor may they participate in the *poṣadha*, the *pravāraṇā*, or any formal procedure (*karmavācanā*) consisting of a single motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha*). Furthermore, when there is business for the Saṅgha requiring the appointment of twelve types of persons, he is not eligible for such appointment. Whether in matters of Dharma or food, he shall not share in their use; thus, he should be expelled.
For this reason, it is said that one should not dwell together with such a person.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and the specific matters involved?
A summary verse says:

Engaging in sexual intercourse in three locations; with the three types of orifices, whether they are obstructed or unobstructed, damaged or undamaged, or whether the partner is living or dead; with a paṇḍaka, a woman, or a man;
engaging in intercourse while seeing another person asleep; or by means of alcohol, drugs, and the like.
One should know whether one is forced against one's will or not, and whether an offense has been committed or not.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in impure conduct—that is, the practice of sexual intercourse—with another in any of the three places, she incurs a pārājika offense.
What are the three locations?
They are the passages for feces and urine, as well as the mouth.
If a bhikṣuṇī engages in sexual intercourse with a person of any of these three types, and the organ enters even slightly into any of the three locations, she incurs a pārājika offense.
What are the three? They are:
a human male, a non-human male, and an animal male.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind intent on sexual intercourse and the intention to experience pleasure, follows a lustful thought and gives rise to a defiled mind toward a living human male, and—whether with an obstruction she inserts into an obstruction, an obstruction into a non-obstruction, a non-obstruction into an obstruction, or a non-obstruction into a non-obstruction—inserts it into the urinary tract, the anus, or the mouth, she incurs a *pārājika* offense.
As it is with a human male, so should it be understood that the same applies to non-human males and males among animals.

If a bhikṣuṇī inserts [the organ] into a dead male human at the three orifices, even if they are damaged, obstructed, or otherwise altered as described previously, she incurs the offense of sthūlātyaya.
As it is with a human male, so should it be understood that it is likewise for a non-human male and a male animal.
If a bhikṣuṇī performs an act of impurity with a sleeping bhikṣu.

If a bhikṣu, while asleep, is unaware, lacks knowledge, and does not experience pleasure during the beginning, middle, or end [of the act], there is no offense; however, the one who performs the sexual act incurs the root offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī goes to the place where a sleeping bhikṣu is, and if she knows [the situation] at the beginning and middle but is unaware at the end, there is no offense for her; however, the one who performs the sexual act incurs the root offense.
If one knows [the act] at the beginning, middle, and end, yet has no intention of experiencing pleasure, there is no offense; however, the one who performs the sexual act incurs the root offense.
If one knows [the act] at the beginning, middle, and end, and intentionally experiences pleasure, both incur the root offense.
As it is with the *śikṣamāṇā*, so it is for the *śrāmaṇerī*; the matters are identical for both.
For the *bhikṣu* and the *śrāmaṇera*, the application of the rule should be understood accordingly.

If a *bhikṣuṇī* gives various intoxicants to a *bhikṣu* to make him drunk so that he commits an impure act (*aśubha-karman*), then regarding whether the intoxicated *bhikṣu* was aware or unaware of the act at its beginning, middle, or end, and whether he experienced pleasure or not, the gravity of the offense, the presence or absence of a transgression, and even the case of giving alcohol to other members of the community to make them drunk, are all explained in detail as in the section on sleep.

Just as it is with those who are intoxicated, if one uses incantations or drugs to cause others to become deluded and engages in impure conduct with them regarding various objects, or even if members of other groups do so among themselves, the presence or absence of an offense is as described above.
If a bhikṣuṇī forcibly compels another bhikṣu to engage in unchaste conduct, and if the one so compelled experiences pleasure at the very first moment of entry, both shall be expelled.
If one does not find joy upon entering but finds joy after having entered, both are to be expelled.
If one does not find joy upon entering nor after having entered, but finds joy at the time of departure, both are to be expelled.
If one is coerced, there is no offense provided that one does not find pleasure in it during the three periods [of the day].
One who coerces another is subject to expulsion (*pravāsanīya*).
As with coercing a bhikṣu, the same applies to coercing a śrāmaṇera, a layperson (*avadātavasana*), or any other lower group; the matter is to be judged according to the preceding rules.
If bhikṣuṇīs and others mutually oppress one another, it should be understood as explained above.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa and Subhadrā—what karma did they previously perform such that, by the power of that karma, both have become so free from desire?"
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Those two individuals shall themselves experience the results of the karma they previously committed. As explained at length elsewhere, you should listen well."

"O Bhikṣus! In times past, there lived a farmer in a certain village. In the early morning, he would lead his oxen to the fields to plow and plant; when it was time for the midday meal, his wife would bring him food, while she herself went to the forest to gather firewood."

At that time, there was a pratyekabuddha dwelling beneath a tree in this forest; on another day, his wife entered the forest to gather firewood and, seeing that pratyekabuddha with a mind and body in perfect tranquility and a countenance of serene dignity, immediately prostrated at his feet and sat gazing up at him in reverence.
The farmer, surprised by her delay, thought to himself:
"Why has my wife not returned for so long?
He immediately took his plow-pole and went to that grove, where he saw his wife before the Pratyekabuddha and addressed her:
"You have committed an unrighteous act with this person.

Upon hearing these words, that Great Being, out of compassion, leaped into the air like a king of geese and manifested his supernormal powers, emitting flames from his upper body while flowing clear water from his lower body.
Upon seeing this, the farmer was filled with deep shame and remorse; he threw himself upon the ground like a great tree falling, knelt upright with palms joined, and paid homage from afar, saying:
"I pray only that you, Great Sage and Truly Pure One, will descend with great compassion to accept my offering."
The Pratyekabuddha, moved by compassion, descended from the sky and said,
"Great Being!..."
"I harbor doubts and have spoken irrational words; I pray you will grant me your forgiveness.
He then took the finest food and offered it to the Pratyekabuddha, joining his palms at the Buddha's feet and making this vow:
"My arising of evil thoughts was entirely due to desire; may both of us, in birth after birth, always be free from the defilement of desires."
"O bhikṣus, what do you think?
Was the farmer of that time anyone else?
