designating a place, fixing a time, or manifesting a sign.
What is the "appointed place"?
One replies to that person, saying:
"If you see me in a certain garden, or at a gathering of people, or in a temple, then upon seeing me at that time, know that the matter has been accomplished."
This is called the designated place.
What is the fixed time?
"If you see me from afar at dawn, or at midday, or in the late afternoon, know that the task is accomplished."
This is called the time for the fixed appointment. What is the sign?

"If you see me with my hair and beard freshly shaved, wearing saffron-colored robes, holding an alms bowl and a mendicant's staff, and carrying full vessels of ghee, oil, sugar, and rock honey—when you see this sign, know that the task has been accomplished."
This is called "indicating signs.
When stealing in this manner, one incurs an offense according to the value of the object, as previously stated.
If one steals birds, there are two preparatory methods:
This refers to lifting up from the ground or falling from the air.
What is meant by "lifting up"?
It means a bird lifts up [an object] on the ground and steals it away; whether the amount is full or not is as explained above.
How does one fall from the air?

It is like a bird-catcher who sets fire to a vast marshland in order to capture birds; when driven by the fire, he falls onto the place where a bhikṣuṇī practices walking meditation, or in front of a gatehouse. If the bhikṣuṇī takes it with the intent to steal, whether the value reaches the full measure or not is as explained above.
What are the four-footed animals?

They are elephants, horses, camels, donkeys, cattle, sheep, gazelles, deer, pigs, rabbits, and so forth. When one wishes to steal them, there are two methods: either from where they are in a herd or from where they are tethered.
When a bhikṣuṇī steals an elephant from among a herd of elephants, she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense when she reaches a place where it is still visible to the eye;
once she reaches a place where it is no longer visible, she incurs the fundamental offense (mūlāpatti).
What constitutes a place of confinement?
Whether it be an elephant tied to a pillar, a tree, or within a wall or enclosure—if a bhikṣuṇī releases it, she incurs an offense as described above.
Just as it is with stealing an elephant, so it should be understood that when a bhikṣuṇī steals other animals such as horses and the like, the case is the same as previously stated.
What are those with many legs?
They are so-called grubs, locusts, moths, various bees, ants, scorpions, and the like.
Among these, those required are found in three places:
These are the judges, the city guards, and the maritime merchants.
What are the judges?

They are those who keep many-legged creatures, such as bees and scorpions, stored inside jars. When they see a person being punished who does not submit, they cause that person to thrust their hands and feet into the jar. When the person is stung with pain, they quickly submit to the matter, or else they produce a great deal of money and goods.
What is meant by "one who guards the city"?

It refers to the one in charge of the city who stores many bees inside a fired clay jar. If an enemy comes and engages him in battle, and if they do not retreat, he then releases the jar of bees from atop the city wall; the thieves, stung by the bees, scatter and flee.
What is meant by "sea merchants"?
It refers to those who go to sea in search of precious goods and keep many bees inside unbaked earthenware jars to guard against emergencies.

When pirates arrive and they engage in battle, if they are victorious, that is well; but if they are not as strong, they take the bee-jars and hurl them from afar at the pirates' ships. The pirates can no longer fight and scatter in all directions.
The setting is the same as before. At that time, there was an arhat bhikṣuṇī named Śailā who had severed all afflictions.
There was also a young incense-seller who, upon seeing the bhikṣuṇī Śailā, conceived deep reverence for her; he approached her, paid his respects with great earnestness, and said:
"Noble Lady!..."
"If there is anything you require, take it from my home as you please; all my words of instruction, you shall receive upon your heads.
Then the bhikṣuṇī said, "Noble sir, excellent!"
"May you be free from illness.
Later, on another occasion, the bhikṣuṇī Śailā was afflicted by a serious illness and was unable to go begging for alms; meanwhile, other bhikṣuṇīs were wandering about to collect food.
At that time, the incense-seller boy saw her, paid his respects, and asked:
"Noble Lady!
For what reason has the Bhikṣuṇī Śailā not been seen?"
He replied: "O worthy one!
His body is afflicted by illness."
The youth replied,
"Venerable One!
I have already said this before:”
"If you have anything you require, take it as you please.
Yet, he was never seen coming to seek anything from me.
Whatever he may need, I pray that the Venerable One will obtain it for him.
He replied, "So be it, O noble one; may you be free from illness.
Having said this, he departed. In this manner, he made his earnest request three times.
At that time, the young bhikṣuṇī had this thought:
"I have heard what this youth has said many times; I should test whether it is false or true."
He then took a small bowl and handed it to the youth, saying,
"O noble youth! The venerable Śaila now requires a little oil."
At that time, the boy had freshly pressed oil, which he filled a small bowl with and presented to the nun,
saying: "Noble Lady,
if you require more in the future, please come and take it as you wish."
Then the bhikṣuṇī, having accepted it, departed; she immediately applied this oil to Śailā’s body, covering her hands and feet until the oil was completely exhausted.
When Śailā’s illness had healed, she went out to beg for alms. At that time, the young boy saw her and prostrated at her feet, saying:
"Noble Lady!"
"It has been a long time since we last met.
The nun then replied,
"I have recently been afflicted by illness."
He addressed him, saying:
"Venerable One!
You have already previously requested [this]:”
"If you have anything you require, take whatever you wish from my house.
Yet, she never once sent a messenger to seek anything from me;
I saw only one nun who said:
"The Noble One is ill;
please take oil from me.
I then filled a small bowl with fresh oil and presented it to that nun.
Śailā replied, "Excellent, young man!
May you be free from illness."
Having finished speaking, she departed; after completing her alms round in sequence, she returned to her residence and addressed the junior nuns, saying:
"Who was it that went to that youth selling incense and brought back this oil bowl?"
A nun replied, "Venerable One!
While I was going for alms, I saw that boy tell me repeatedly: [text missing]"
"Noble Śailā, I have already invited you, saying:
'If there is anything you require, take it as you please.
Yet, I have never seen you come to me to ask for anything."
"If that Śaila has anything he requires, I pray you will take it for him.
I then thought to myself:
"I ought to test him to verify whether his words are true or false."
He immediately took a small bowl and handed it to the youth, saying, "Venerable Śaila is currently ill and requires oil.

At that time, the youth filled the bowl with fresh oil and gave it to me. Having received the oil, I went into my cell and applied it to the body, hands, and feet of the Venerable One until it was all used up.
Then the elder nun said to the junior nun,
"Did I ever tell you to go to that boy to fetch some oil?
The junior nun replied:
"I have never caused her any harm.
At that time, there was another bhikṣuṇī who had previously harbored a grudge against this young nun; having heard these words, she said to Śailā:
"Noble Lady!..."

Now, because of your illness, this young nun has not merely taken oil from a single location; she has begged for it throughout the entire city of Śrāvastī. The number of her defeats (pārājika offenses) is difficult to calculate.
When the young nun heard these words, she felt remorse, thinking:
"Have I truly committed a *pārājika* offense?
She reported the matter to the bhikṣuṇīs, and they in turn reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked that young nun,
"With what intention did you beg for oil from him?
She replied to the Buddha:
"I merely intended to test the boy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If she acted with the intent to test him, this bhikṣuṇī is not guilty of an offense."
However, the bhikṣuṇīs should not go begging for medicine on behalf of a patient without first inquiring about their illness.
When they do go to beg, they should ask the patient:
"Are you seeking medicine for the sake of the Saṃgha’s infirmary?"
"Shall I go to the place where your faithful relatives reside?
If there are many relatives, from whom among them shall I seek it?
One should search for it according to the directions given.
"If one goes begging for alms without first inquiring of the sick person, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The summary verse says:
"Regarding goods subject to tax, carrying them to another; carrying another's belongings and departing ahead."
If one does not accept it, one should insist on wearing it, acting as if it were provided by one's parents.
Furthermore, for the sake of the Triple Gem, after paying the price, one should divide it equally;
the owner of the garment should take possession of it and have another person dye it, whether it is already dyed or not.
Imposing taxes through small gates and seizing all the goods of merchants—
this verse summarizes the origin story (*nidāna*), as clarified in the Bhikṣu-vinaya.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, Fascicle Three.
The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.

3. The Training Rule on Taking Human Life. The third training rule concerning taking human life. At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Vaiśālī, on the bank of the River Śatadrū in the Great Mango Grove (*Mahā-āmra-vana*), teaching the sublime Dharma to the fourfold assembly. He taught the meditation on impurity and praised the cultivation of the meditation on impurity, saying:
"You, members of the fourfold assembly, should cultivate the meditation on impurity; by practicing and repeatedly cultivating this meditation, you will attain great fruits and benefits."
The bhikṣus then practiced the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

Having practiced it, they developed a profound sense of revulsion toward their bodies of pus and blood; some took up knives to commit suicide, some ingested poison, some hanged themselves with ropes, some threw themselves from high cliffs, and others killed one another.
At that time, the community of bhikṣus was gradually diminishing. The Buddha, who is the knower and the seer, knowing this, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"For what reason is the community of bhikṣus gradually diminishing, such that those remaining are so few?"
Then Ānanda reported the matter in detail to the Blessed One.
On this occasion, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and asked the bhikṣus:
"Is it true that you have thus successively incited one another to kill?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The Buddha then addressed the bhikṣus:
"What you have done is not the dharma of a śramaṇa, nor is it a practice in accordance with the path; it is impure and is not an act that should be performed by those who have gone forth.
Having rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish a training rule for my disciples of the two assemblies of śrāvakas, which should be recited as follows:"

"If again a bhikṣuṇī, whether it be a human being or a human fetus, intentionally puts an end to its life with her own hand, or provides a knife, or takes up a knife herself, or seeks one who holds a knife, or encourages death, or praises death, saying: 'O woman!'"
"What use is this burden of sin and this impure, evil life?
You would be better off dead now; death is superior to life.
Thus, according to his own thoughts, he used various words to exhort and praise [the victim], urging him toward death.
If that person dies because of her, this bhikṣuṇī also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community with others.
As for the term "bhikṣuṇī," the meaning is as explained above.
A "person" refers to one who, within the mother's womb, already possesses the six sense faculties—namely, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
A "human embryo" refers to one who has entered the mother's womb but possesses only three faculties—namely, body, life-force, and mind.
"Intentionally" means that it is done with deliberate intent, not by mistake or the like.
"With one's own hand" means performing the act of killing with one's own hands.
"Taking life" means causing the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of another to cease its continuity.

Or as for "holding a blade and handing it over": if one knows that a person intends to commit suicide, one places a large sword, a razor, a dagger, or the like at their disposal, desiring that they harm themselves.

"Or holding a knife oneself" means that because one's own strength is insufficient to carry out the killing, one merely holds the knife while causing another to seize one's hand and take a human life.
"Or seeking one who holds a knife" means looking for men, women, or *paṇḍakas* (eunuchs) and so forth to have them carry out the killing.
Regarding "encouraging death," one encourages three types of persons to die: namely, those who have broken the precepts, those who maintain the precepts, and those who are ill.
How does one encourage one who has broken the precepts?

Suppose there is a bhikṣuṇī who seeks something from a bhikṣuṇī who has broken the precepts—whether it be robes, an alms-bowl bag, a water filter, a belt, or other requisites for the livelihood of a śramaṇa.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"If he remains alive while violating the precepts, I will have no means of obtaining his robes, bowl, and other belongings; I should go to him and urge him on until he dies."
He then went to him and spoke these words:
"Noble One, do you know?"
"Virtuous one, you have now broken the precepts and committed various sinful deeds; through body, speech, and mind, you constantly create manifold evils.

Even if your life, O Noble One, should endure for a long time, the evil karma you have created will only increase further. Because these evils increase, you shall suffer the torments of hell for a vast duration."
When one who has broken the precepts hears these words, they ask:
"Venerable One! What should I do now?"
He replied, "One ought to abandon the body and take one's own life.
If that bhikṣuṇī should then abandon her body or commit suicide, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī who has broken the precepts does not accept the exhortation, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

At that time, although the one exhorting death had spoken as previously described, after the words of exhortation were finished, he felt remorse in his heart; he then went to where that bhikṣuṇī who had broken the precepts was staying and spoke these words:
"Noble lady, you should know!"
What I previously said was like that of a foolish child; I failed to distinguish properly, did not deliberate with care, and spoke impulsively.

Noble one, if you can draw near to virtuous friends and speak of the removal of prior transgressions, then the unwholesome actions of your three karmas will, through their power, become purified. Because they are purified, after casting off this body, you shall be reborn in the heavens.
If one who has broken the precepts is asked by another, "Noble one!
What should I do now? what should he answer?
If she says,
"Virtuous one, do not give up your body; virtuous one,
do not commit suicide," and he does not kill himself, the bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a person who has broken the precepts hears these words but disregards them and commits suicide, the one who urged them to die also incurs the aforementioned offense.
This is called a bhikṣuṇī urging a person who has broken the precepts to death.
What is meant by "encouraging a person who upholds the precepts to die"?

For example, suppose there is a bhikṣuṇī who seeks something from a bhikṣuṇī who upholds the precepts—be it robes, a bowl, or anything else—as described at length, even to the point that she goes to her and says:
"Noble Lady!..."
Do you understand?

Since you, O virtuous one, uphold the precepts and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, and are furthermore able to give with an outstretched hand, give constantly, give with joy, give extensively, and give distributively, you shall leave behind scarcity and arrive at a place of abundant harvest.
"After casting off this body, you shall be reborn in heaven; liberation and nirvana will be as close as being separated by a thin curtain.
When a person who upholds the precepts hears these words, they ask:
"Noble One!..."
"What should I do now? He replied,
"You should cast off your body and take your own life."
If that bhikṣuṇī, having heard these words, takes her own life, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense;
if the bhikṣuṇī who maintains the precepts does not accept the exhortation, that [exhorting] bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
At that time, although she had spoken such words of exhortation to die, she felt remorse in her heart and went to where the precept-observing bhikṣuṇī was, saying these words:
"Noble Lady, you should know!"
What I previously said was like that of a foolish child; I failed to distinguish properly, did not deliberate carefully, and spoke impulsively.
Since you, O Noble One, are able to uphold the precepts and cultivate all wholesome dharmas, you will certainly be reborn in the heavens when your life comes to an end.
If one who maintains the precepts should ask him,
"What should I do now? he replies:
"Noble one! Do not abandon your body; do not commit suicide.
If she does not take her own life, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If, despite having heard the former words, one does not heed them and nonetheless commits suicide, that bhikṣuṇī also incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called a bhikṣuṇī exhorting a person who upholds the precepts to death.
What is meant by "encouraging a sick person to die"?
It is as when a bhikṣuṇī has certain expectations regarding a sick bhikṣuṇī, such as robes, alms bowls, or other requisites for sustaining life.
At that time, that bhikṣuṇī thought to herself:
"As long as that gravely ill person remains alive, there is no way I can obtain their robes, bowl, and other belongings; I should go to them and urge them on until they die."
He immediately went to him and spoke these words:
"Does the Noble One know?
Since you are gravely ill and suffering extreme distress, if you remain long in this state, your illness will only grow more severe and you will constantly endure hardship."
When the sick bhikṣuṇī hears these words, she asks:
"What should I do now? To which he replies:
"One ought to sacrifice one's body and take one's own life.
If a sick bhikṣuṇī, upon hearing these words, takes her own life out of fear of further suffering, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense;
if the sick bhikṣuṇī does not accept the exhortation, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
At that time, although that bhikṣuṇī had already spoken as before regarding the means for encouraging death, she felt remorse in her heart and went to where the sick bhikṣuṇī was, saying these words:
"Noble one, you should know!..."
What I have previously said was like that of a foolish child; I failed to discern properly, did not deliberate with care, and spoke in haste.
Noble One!

You should now seek out a spiritual friend who can find for you the medicine appropriate to your ailment, provide you with food and drink, and attend to you according to the Dharma, following your needs without opposition.
"If you can do so, before long your illness shall be cured and you will be at ease; your strength will be restored, and you may travel as you please.
If a sick bhikṣuṇī asks her, she should say:
"Noble Lady!"
"O Benevolent One, what do you now wish me to do?
He replied, "Benevolent One,
do not abandon your body, and do not commit suicide."
If she does not commit suicide, that bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense;
if the sick bhikṣuṇī, despite hearing the aforementioned words, does not follow them and instead commits suicide, that bhikṣuṇī likewise incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
This is called a bhikṣuṇī encouraging a sick person to die.
Regarding "praising death," it refers to if there is a bhikṣuṇī who utters words praising death in the presence of someone who desires to die.
"Hey, woman! is a term of address.
"What use have you now for such sinful burdens, that death is even better than life?"
These words are all expressions of contemptuous disparagement.
"Following one's own mental inclinations" means that various divergent thoughts arise according to one's own mind.
"By means of other speech" refers to using numerous expedient means to exhort another to die.
One who praises refers to someone who speaks words of praise in the presence of a sick person, desiring that they must die and have no concern for life.
If that person passes away by means of this stratagem—meaning that the bhikṣuṇī causes them to pass away through the stratagem she has spoken—it constitutes an offense.
It does not arise from other matters; that is to say, it does not arise from other factors such as wholesome states of mind and so forth.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who possesses the nature of a bhikṣuṇī.
The nature of a bhikṣuṇī refers to having received full ordination (upasampadā), as explained in detail above.
The meaning of *pārājika* is as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific matters?
A summary verse says:
Sometimes by means of one's own body, or by using external objects,
or through the combination of both internal and external factors— this is called the characteristic of killing.
What is killing by means of one's own body?
That is to say, if a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, strikes a woman, man, or paṇḍaka with even a single finger, and they die as a result of this means, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense;
or if she does not die at that time but dies later due to this very cause, this bhikṣuṇī likewise incurs a pārājika offense;
if she does not die at that time and does not die later either, she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Whether striking with a single finger, or with five fingers, a fist, a wrist, the neck, the shoulder, or other parts of the body, even down to a toe, with the intent to deprive that person of life.
If that person dies, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārajika offense;
if she does not die at that time but dies later as a result of it, the bhikṣuṇī also incurs a pārajika offense;
if she does not die, she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called taking life within one's own body.
What is killing by means of external objects?
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, shoots a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka with an arrow made of bamboo or iron, and they die as a result of this means, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense.
If one does not die immediately but dies later, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if one does not die at that time and does not die later either, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If, with the intent to kill and desiring his death, one hurls at another person a spear, a javelin, a discus, a trident, or any other weapon— even down to a jujube pit— from a distance,
and that person dies as a result of this means, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense;
even if she does not die immediately but dies later, she likewise incurs a pārājika offense.
If one does not die at that time and also does not die later, one incurs a sthūlātyaya.
This is called killing by means of external objects.
What is killing by means of both internal and external factors combined?
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, takes up a great sword and kills a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka,
and that person dies as a result of this means, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense;
even if they do not die immediately but die later, she likewise incurs a pārājika offense.
If the person does not die at that time and does not die later either, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

As it is with a large sword, so it is with all other double-edged or single-edged weapons, spears, staffs, and even blades of grass; if, with the intent to kill, one strikes or hacks at another with the desire to cause their death, [the same applies].
If one causes death through such means, one incurs a *pārājika* offense or a *sthūlātyaya*;
the details are as explained above.
This is called "killing by combining internal and external means."
The summary verse says:
If one uses powdered poison, or [acts] in two types of dwellings,
or at times with various liquors, or by means of mechanical devices and the like to harm others.
What is meant by "by means of poison"?
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, uses poison or food mixed with poison—such as cakes, rice, and so forth—to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka.
If one dies as a result of these means, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if one does not die, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
The detailed explanation is as above.
This is called killing by means of poison.
What is killing by means of powdered poison?

If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, uses various powders of poison—whether by rubbing them on the body, using them for bathing, mixing them with ointments, scattering them over incense garlands, or blending them into incense smoke—to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, and that person dies as a result of these means, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense, or a sthūlātyaya offense.
This is called killing by means of poisonous powder.
What is killing by means of a location?
This has two types:
First, detention due to the ground; second, detention due to wood.
What is meant by detention due to the ground?

If a bhikṣuṇī, with intent to kill, digs a pit in the earth and places a mechanical trap within it to ensnare the feet of a man, a woman, or a paṇḍaka, and they die as a result; [this constitutes detention due to the ground].

If she causes lions, tigers, leopards, eagles, vultures, or other such creatures to devour [the victim]; or if she causes the physical form to be consumed by wind or withered by the sun; or if she causes [the victim] to become emaciated through hunger and thirst—by such means, if the person dies, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense; if they do not die, she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.

As it is with the feet, so it is if one uses the shins, the thighs, the waist, the chest, or even the neck as a tether; or if one intends to have them eaten by lions and the like, or causes them to die through such means until they become emaciated from hunger and thirst, one incurs a *pārājika* offense or a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called "killing by detention on account of the ground.
What is "killing by detention on account of wood"?

If a bhikṣuṇī, with intentional desire to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, ties their feet to a large log, a pillar, or a stake using a wet rope or cord, and they die as a result; [this constitutes such an offense].

If, at any time, one intends to cause lions and other such creatures to eat [the victim], even to the point of emaciating them through hunger and thirst, and they consequently die by this means, one incurs a *pārājika* offense or a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called killing by causing [the victim] to linger through the use of wood.
What is killing by means of intoxication from alcohol?
If a bhikṣuṇī, with intentional desire to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, gives them rice wine to drink and they die as a result; this constitutes such an act.

If one causes lions and other such creatures to eat [the victim], or even brings about their death through such means as leaving them hungry, thirsty, and emaciated, one incurs a *pārājika* offense or a *sthūlātyaya*.

Just as it is with rice wine, so it is with wines made from roots, stalks, flowers, leaves, or fruits; whether by enchanting the wine or using medicinal wine, causing the person to drink until their mind is deranged and they are rendered senseless, thereby bringing about death through such means;
or, if out of intoxication one intends for a king, a thief, or an enemy to take their life—one incurs a *pārājika* offense, or a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called killing by means of alcohol.
What is killing by means of a mechanical bow?

If a bhikṣuṇī, with intentional desire to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, should set up a mechanical bow equipped with an iron arrow, or place various blades and so forth, and position them by the side of a road.
If she passes by a woman, a man, or a *paṇḍaka*, and they then cut off her hands and feet, or sever her head or other limbs,
and she meets death by this means, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a *pārājika* offense, or an *sthūlātyaya*.
Just as it is with a mechanical bow, if one uses a foot-activated device or other mechanisms with the intent to take a human life, the offense incurred is the same as before.
The summary verse says:
"If one raises a whole or half corpse, causes an abortion, or performs incantations..."
Pushing down, [drowning in] water or fire, or dispatching messengers to kill by cold or heat—how does one commit the "killing of a whole corpse"?

If a bhikṣuṇī, with intentional desire to kill a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, goes on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight to a charnel ground to seek a recently deceased corpse that has not yet been harmed even by ants; she then rubs the corpse with yellow earth, washes it with scented water, covers its body entirely with a pair of new cotton cloths, anoints its feet with ghee, and recites mantras over the corpse.

At that time, the corpse stretched its limbs and attempted to rise; it was placed upon a two-wheeled carriage, with two bronze bells tied beneath its neck and two double-edged blades held in its hands.
The corpse immediately rose and asked the incantation master,
"Whom do you wish for me to kill?
The incantation master replied:
"Do you perhaps recognize that certain woman, man, or paṇḍaka? He replied, "I do."
She replied:
"You may go there and sever their life-force.
If their life-force is severed, the bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense.

If, in that household, garlands and sashes made of various leaves and grasses are hung across the door and water jars are placed there; or if a cow with her calf of the same color is tied at the door, or a ewe with her lamb of the same color is tied there; or if the house has a grinding stone for medicinal herbs along with its millstone; or if there is an *indrakīla* (Indra’s pillar) at the door; or if the sacred fire is never extinguished; or if images are enshrined in the house; or if there is the true body of a Buddha; or if it is the mother of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), or she who is pregnant with a Wheel-Turning King; or if there is a Bodhisattva, or the mother of a Bodhisattva, or she who is pregnant with a Bodhisattva; or if one is about to recite the four *Āgamas*, or is currently in the midst of reciting them.

Furthermore, if one wishes to recite or is currently reciting the great sūtras, namely: the *Cūḷasuññata Sutta*, the *Mahāsuññata Sutta*, the *Pañcaka Sutta* and *Tika Sutta*, the *Māyājāla Sutta*, the *Rājovāda Sutta*, and the *Dhajagga Sutta*.
If, while guarding against such matters as these, the risen corpse is unable to enter, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If, through a lack of skill in the rite for raising a corpse, the practitioner instead kills the mantra-master, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If the mantra-master bhikṣuṇī kills that raised corpse, she likewise incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
How does the matter of the half-corpse arise?

The conditions are the same as before; the difference therein is that the chariot has but one wheel, a single bell is tied to its neck, and the blade has but one edge, up to and including the full explanation of the offense as stated above.
What constitutes killing by causing an abortion?
If a bhikṣuṇī, desiring to kill the mother who is pregnant but not desiring to kill the fetus, then crushes its abdomen;
if the mother dies and not the fetus, the bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense.
If the fetus dies but the mother does not, one incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if both die, one incurs a pārājika with respect to the mother;
if neither dies, one incurs a sthūlātyaya.
If a bhikṣuṇī intends to kill the fetus but not the mother, she then crushes its abdomen.
If the fetus dies and not the mother, the bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense;
if the mother dies and not the fetus, she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If both die, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if neither dies, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
What constitutes killing by means of incantations?

If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, undertakes the means to slay a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, she constructs a maṇḍala and installs a fire-pit; she kindles a fire, throws wood into it, and recites incantations while thinking:
"When this wood is completely consumed by the fire, may the life-faculty of that woman, man, or paṇḍaka be severed immediately."
If her life were to end while the wood in the fire was only half-burnt, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if her life ends once the wood is completely burnt, she incurs a pārājika.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, initiates the means to slay a woman, a man, or a paṇḍaka, she places one *śu* each of sesame seeds and mustard seeds into a mortar and pounds them while reciting incantations, thinking:
"If the substances in the mortar are pounded until they become powder, may their lives end."
If she causes him to die by grinding him into powder before he has reached the state of being powdered, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if he dies after he has been ground into powder, she incurs a pārājika.

If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, employs a means by placing one *śroṇa* of yellow cow’s milk in a vessel, stirring the milk with her finger while reciting a prohibitive incantation, and forms this thought:
“If the milk in the vessel is entirely transformed into blood, may that person’s life-faculty be instantly severed.”
If she dies while the milk has not yet been transformed into blood, she incurs a sthūlātyaya;
if she dies once it has been transformed into blood, she incurs a pārājika.
If a bhikṣuṇī intends to kill a person, she prepares the means by stitching a saṃghāṭī robe with five-colored thread while reciting incantations, thinking:
"Once this robe is finished, may his life come to an end."
If the robe is not yet finished when the person dies, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if the person dies once the robe is finished, one incurs a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī intends to kill someone, initiates the preparatory effort, draws on the ground with her finger, recites incantations, and forms this thought:
"If one completes the count of seven,
causing that person's life to end," if they die before the seven are completed, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*;
if they die upon completing the seven, one incurs a *pārājika*.
This is called killing by means of incantations.
What is killing by pushing down?
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to kill a person, she pushes them over a precipice, a cliff edge, or some other dangerous place so that they fall.
If the person dies because of this, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if the person does not die at that time but later dies as a result of it, one also incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if the person does not die at that time nor later as a result of it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.

Just as it is with a cliff, if one causes someone to fall by pushing them from a wall or a tree, or from an elephant, horse, carriage, bed, or seat—whether it be from the head, shoulders, waist, back, thighs, knees, calves, feet, or any other part of the body—and that person dies because of this, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if they do not die at that time but later die as a result of it, one also incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if they do not die at that time nor later die as a result of it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
This is called killing by causing to fall.
What is killing in water?
If a bhikṣuṇī, wishing to kill a person, pushes them into water.
Therefore, if the person dies, one incurs a *pārājika* offense;
if they do not die, it is a *sthūlātyaya*.
The details are as explained above.
"Water" refers to rivers, oceans, ponds, wells, and so forth, even down to pouring a single handful of water into another's mouth to cause death;
this is called killing by means of water.
What is killing by means of fire?
If a bhikṣuṇī intends to kill a person and pushes them into fire,
and the person dies as a result, the bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense.
This includes cases such as burning a village, forest, or city, or even placing burning coals in someone's mouth to cause their death.
This is called killing by fire.
What is meant by killing by instigation?
If a bhikṣuṇī intends to kill a person and dispatches that person toward a place of danger and difficulty so as to cause their death, she incurs a pārājika offense, or a sthūlātyaya.

As explained extensively above, "perilous places" refers to locations such as those infested by bandits, enemies, tigers, wolves, lions, and the like; to cause a person to pass through these so that they meet their death is called "killing by dispatching."
What is killing by cold?

If a bhikṣuṇī intends to kill a person, during a time of extreme cold when the fierce winds are severe, she places the person in the shade during the day, or at night places them in the open air and makes them sit on wet grass.
If she dies as a result of this, the bhikṣuṇī incurs a pārājika offense, or a sthūlātyaya.
The details are as explained above.
This is called "killing by freezing."
What is killing by means of heat?

If a bhikṣuṇī intends to kill a person during extreme heat when eruptions have broken out on the body, she places them in the open air during the day or in a sealed room at night, fumigating them with smoke and fire and covering them with mats, straw, woolen blankets, and the like.
If one dies as a result of this, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
The remainder is as explained above.
This is called "killing by heat."

4. The Training Rule on Falsely Claiming to Have Attained Superhuman Qualities. The fourth training rule concerning falsely claiming to have attained superhuman qualities (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*). At that time, the Blessed One was traveling through the human world and arrived at the Bamboo Grove village. To the north of the village was the Śiṃśapā Forest, where he stayed and resided.
At that time, a famine occurred and alms were difficult to obtain; even parents did not provide for their own children, let alone other beggars.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the śrāvakas:
"In this age of famine, alms are difficult to obtain; even mother and child do not provide for one another."
"You all should each go to a place that is pleasing to your friends and relatives, and observe the rains retreat in a village near Vaiśālī.
Ānanda and I shall remain here in this grove."
Having heard this, the bhikṣus assented and accepted the instruction; each followed his own friends to a village near Vaiśālī to observe the rains retreat.
When the five hundred bhikṣus saw this occurrence, they said to one another:
"Venerable sirs, you should know!"
As the Blessed One said:
"At this time of famine, alms are difficult to obtain; even fathers and sons do not support one another, much less other beggars.
You should each go with your own kinsmen and friends to dwell in the rainy-season retreat (*varṣā*) in the villages near Vaiśālī, while Ānanda and I shall remain here in this grove."

"We have no relatives here upon whom we can rely to carry out the retreat; however, there are our relatives in the village of fishermen, so we should go to visit them and temporarily establish a grass hut outside that village to observe the retreat."
Then the five hundred bhikṣus went to the village of fishermen and inquired after their kinsmen, staying temporarily in small huts outside the village.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:
"We have heard little and possess no learning; if our kinsmen come to question us, how shall we preach the Dharma for them?"
When they arrive, we should praise one another, saying:

"Your kinsmen have gained great benefit, for in your village there dwell such an assembly of sublime monks observing the rains retreat here. These bhikṣus have cultivated the perception of impermanence regarding the impermanent, the perception of suffering regarding suffering, the perception of emptiness regarding emptiness, the perception of non-self, the perception of revulsion toward food, the perception of lack of delight in all worldly things, the perception of danger, the perception of abandonment, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation, the perception of death, the perception of impurity, the perception of a livid corpse, the perception of a bloated and oozing corpse, the perception of a blood-stained corpse, the perception of a worm-infested corpse, the perception of a scattered corpse, the perception of bleached bones, and the perception of contemplating emptiness."

This bhikṣu attains the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna; he attains loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception;
and he attains the four fruits, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
Later, at another time, those kinsmen came to visit and inquire after them.
When the bhikṣus saw the kinsmen arrive, they immediately praised one another, saying:
"You kinsmen have gained great benefit, for you have such a superior and wondrous Saṃgha residing here in your village for the summer retreat."
"This bhikṣu has attained the perception of impermanence," and so on, up to "he has attained the eight liberations.
When his kinsmen had heard this explanation, they said,
"Noble One!"
"Virtuous ones, have you all realized such a supreme fruit?
They replied,
"We have all attained it."

At that time, when the common people heard that those who had attained the fruits [of the path] were being honored, they all conceived a sense of affection and joy; they failed to provide relief for their own parents, wives, children, and relatives, yet each of them supplied food and drink to the bhikṣus.
At that time, while the World-Honored One had not yet entered nirvana and remained in the world, he held two great assemblies with his disciples:

the first on the fifteenth day of the fifth month when they were about to enter the retreat (varṣā), and the second on the fifteenth day of the eighth month when the period of self-indulgence (pravāraṇā) was concluded.

Those who had entered the earlier retreat (pūrvavārṣika), having received the instructions, went to cities, towns, villages, and settlements to observe the rains retreat. When the period of *pravāraṇā* concluded, they all assembled; each knew for themselves what they had realized, while those who had not yet realized it requested the Dharma for realization.

The bhikṣus who had spent the rains retreat near Vaiśālī, having completed their robes once the three months were fulfilled, appeared haggard in complexion and emaciated in form as they took up their robes and bowls and proceeded toward the Bamboo Grove Village.

Having arrived at the village, the bhikṣus saw him coming from afar; out of compassion for their fellow practitioners of the holy life, they called out "Welcome! from a distance, went forward to receive him, and took his robes, bowl, staff, water flask, and other miscellaneous items and requisites of a śramaṇa.
They then asked: "Venerable one!..."
"In what place did you observe the rains retreat, that you have been able to come here?
They replied,
"We observed the three-month rains retreat in the village of Pāṭaligrāma, and have now come here."
He asked, “Venerable ones!
During those three months of the rainy season retreat there, was it not laborious for you to beg for food and drink?”
He replied,
“Although one may dwell in peace and happiness there, obtaining food and drink is extremely difficult.
He reported this, saying:
"It is indeed so.
I have witnessed firsthand their decline and emaciation; their complexions are haggard, and it is clear that obtaining food and drink is truly difficult.

At that time, five hundred bhikṣus from the fishing village, having completed their *varṣā* retreat, also arrived at this village carrying their robes and bowls; their complexions were bright and healthy, and their countenances were plump and robust.

When the bhikṣus saw their fellow practitioners of the holy life, they gave rise to feelings of compassion and affection; calling out "Welcome! from afar, they went forward to receive them, taking up their robes, bowls, and other miscellaneous belongings, and inquired after them in detail as before.
He even went so far as to ask:
"Is food and drink easy to obtain and is it pleasant to live in the village of fishermen?
The bhikṣu replied:
"I dwell there having truly attained peace and happiness; the food and drink I seek are easily obtained and not difficult to find.
He replied, "Venerable one!"
Observing that he was well-nourished and his complexion radiant, [the man] inferred that food and drink must certainly be easy to obtain. He then asked:
"Since this present age is one of famine where food and drink are difficult to find, and even parents and wives cannot support one another, why is it that you have such easy access to food?"
He replied, "Among my own kinsmen, I praised one another, saying:
'This bhikṣu has attained the perception of impermanence, up to and including the eight liberations.'"
Question: "Are the matters you have described real,
or are they false?"
He replied, "It is false. He asked:
"Venerable ones!
Is it appropriate for you, for the sake of a mere modicum of food and drink, to falsely claim to have attained superhuman states that you have not actually realized?
They then replied:
"Whether it was appropriate or not, we have already done it.
At that time, those bhikṣus who delighted in few desires all together censured, disparaged, and rebuked this as contrary to the Dharma, saying:
"How is it that for the sake of craving food and drink, you falsely claim to have attained the qualities of a superior person when you have none?"
Then the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. On this occasion, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣus and, though he already knew the matter, questioned them as extensively described before.
The Buddha asked the bhikṣus on the banks of the Śroṇāparantaka River: "O bhikṣus!"
"Did you truly claim to have attained the superhuman states (uttaramanuṣyadharma) when you had not?
He replied to the Buddha,
"It is true, Blessed One."
"Venerable One!
At that time, the World-Honored One rebuked them in various ways:
"O Bhikṣus!..."
This is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, nor is it a practice in accordance with it; it is something you should not do. It is not proper conduct, nor is it something to be done by one who has gone forth.
You, O bhikṣus!
You should know that there are three great thieves in the world.
What are these three? O Bhikṣus!

Suppose there were a great thief—whether leading a band of a hundred, a thousand, or even a hundred thousand—who would go to various cities and villages, break through walls and open locks to steal the property of others; who might sometimes block roads and commit murder, or sometimes set fire to burn down villages, or plunder royal treasuries, or loot towns and districts. This is called the first kind of great thief dwelling in the world.
"O Bhikṣus!

Suppose there is a great thief who, though not having a band of a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand followers, does not go to cities or villages to breach walls, pick locks, or steal the property of others; nor does he cut off roads, burn villages, or plunder the royal treasuries. Yet, he takes the firewood, grass, flowers, fruits, bamboo, timber, and other such materials belonging to the Saṅgha, selling them for his own livelihood or giving them to others. This is called the second great thief dwelling in the world."

Furthermore, O Bhikṣus! There is a great thief who does not lead a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred-thousand followers; he does not go to cities or villages to breach walls, pick locks, or steal the property of others; nor does he take the bamboo, wood, or other materials belonging to the Saṅgha to provide for his livelihood or give to others. Yet, although he has not actually realized the state of a superior person within himself, he falsely claims to have attained it. This is called the third great thief dwelling in the world.
"O bhikṣus! The first and second great thieves are not called 'great thieves';
they are called 'minor thieves. O bhikṣus!"

"If one falsely claims to have attained the qualities of a superior person when they do not actually possess them, among humans, devas, māras, brahmas, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas, such a person is a supreme thief.
He then spoke this verse:
"One who is not truly an Arhat, yet says, 'I am one,' "
"Among all gods and humans, this one is called a great thief.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had rebuked that bhikṣu in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Observing ten benefits, for the sake of my disciples—the two assemblies of śrāvakas—I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) in the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:"

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu or bhikṣuṇī, lacking actual knowledge and lacking universal knowledge, and knowing for themselves that they have not attained the superhuman state—the peaceful, noble, and sublime realization, wisdom, vision, and abiding in bliss—should nevertheless say:
'I know; I see.'"
At a later time, whether questioned or not, desiring to purify himself, he speaks thus:
"Venerable sirs!
It was true that I neither knew nor saw, yet I said that I knew and saw; it was a false, deceptive, and lying speech."
"Having committed a *pārājika* offense, one should not live in communion.

At that time, after the Blessed One had established this training rule for the bhikṣus, there were many bhikṣus dwelling in an *āraṇya* who, using coarse bedding and applying themselves with diligence, attained a slight degree of tranquility through the means of observing their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*). By means of worldly mental engagement (*lokamanasikāra*), they suppressed their afflictions so that lustful desire and malice no longer manifested.
Then they immediately said to one another:
"Venerable ones!
Do you know this now?"

That which is to be attained in an araṇya has now been attained by me: birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
"I should now abandon this forest hermitage and dwell within a village.
He then left the tranquil grove and settled in a village.
There, he frequently encountered women, as well as lay attendants and novices; living in such close proximity, his afflictions arose once more, and lustful desire and anger manifested again.
At that time, those people each had this thought:
"The World-Honored One has established training rules for his disciples within the Vinaya, as described at length above."
At that time, the bhikṣus said to one another:

"We were dwelling in an araṇya, using coarse bedding and applying ourselves with diligence; having attained a slight degree of tranquility through the skillful means of observing our own individual characteristics, we have subdued our afflictions and yet abandoned the forest hermitage to come to the village."
Having observed that afflictions were manifesting within all objects of perception, as previously explained at length, [they thought]:
"Is it not the case that we have committed a defeat?
Let us go together to the Venerable Ānanda and report this matter to him; we shall then carry out whatever he instructs."
He immediately went there and asked the Venerable Ānanda, "Does the Venerable know?
The Blessed One, the World-Honored One, has established these training rules for his disciples: [text follows]"
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣu [commits an offense], he shall not dwell together with us even as far as a pārājika.
While we were in the araṇya, afflictions did not arise; now that we have come to the village, afflictions have arisen again," and so on, as explained previously.
"We all have doubts: could it be that we have committed a *pārājika* offense?
Let us consult together and question the Venerable Ānanda; we shall act according to what he says."
For this reason, we have now come to the presence of the Venerable One, desiring to consult you in detail for a resolution; could it be that we have committed a *pārājika* offense?
At that time, having heard these words from the bhikṣus, the venerable Ānanda led the bhikṣus to the presence of the Blessed One, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and sat to one side.
Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One, you have thus established a training rule for the bhikṣus within the Vinaya, stating that if a bhikṣu [commits an offense], as explained at length, he incurs a pārājika and should not dwell together with the community."

These bhikṣus dwell in an araṇya, using remote lodgings, and are diligent in application; having attained a slight degree of the skillful means of tranquility regarding their own specific characteristics, they apply their attention to subdue the afflictions, so that desire-taint and malice no longer manifest.
Then they immediately said to one another:
"Venerable ones!
Do you know this now?"

That which is to be attained in an araṇya has now been attained by me; birth has been exhausted, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and there is no further existence.
"I should now abandon my dwelling in the forest hermitage and go among the villages.
He then abandoned his quiet retreat and took up residence in a village.

There, he frequently encountered women, as well as lay attendants and novices, with whom he lived in close proximity; consequently, his afflictions arose once more, and sensual desire began to manifest.
Those bhikṣus each gave rise to a doubt, thinking:
"Could it be that we have committed a pārājika offense?
For this reason, they have come to question me.
We did not dare to decide, so we have all come here.
Venerable World-Honored One!
Could it be that he has committed an extremely grave offense?
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda! Setting aside cases of overweening pride, he has committed no offense."

At that time, the Blessed One, through various skillful means, having exhorted and instructed those who delight in the precepts and those who revere the precepts in accordance with their needs by preaching the Dharma, addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "O bhikṣus!..."
Thus it should be understood: the former was the original prohibition, while this is a subsequent allowance.
I now speak thus for the sake of my disciples, the two assemblies of Śrāvakas:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, being truly without knowledge and without universal knowledge, and knowing for herself that she has not attained the superhuman state—the peaceful, noble, and sublime realization, wisdom, vision, and dwelling in bliss—should nevertheless say:..."
"I know; I see.
At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, desiring to be pure himself, he speaks thus:
"Venerable sirs!..."
"I truly did not know or see, yet I said that I knew and saw; this was a false, deceptive, and lying speech.
Except in the case of overweening pride (*adhimāna*), this bhikṣuṇī also incurs a *pārājika* offense and should not live in community with the others.
"Bhikṣuṇī" has the meaning as explained above.
"Lacking knowledge" means not knowing form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
"Lacking thorough knowledge" means not thoroughly knowing form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

Regarding the phrase "superior human dharma" (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*): "superior" (*uttara*) refers to the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), which is above the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), while the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) is above the form realm.
"Human" (*manussa*) refers to ordinary persons.
"Dharma" (*dhamma*) refers to the five hindrances (*pañcanīvaraṇa*) and so forth; because one can eliminate these hindrances, it is called "superior."
"Tranquility" refers to nirvāṇa.
"Noble ones" refers to Buddhas and śrāvakas.
"Exalted realization" refers to the four fruits of the śramaṇa.
The stream-enterer, once-returner, non-returner, and arhat.
"Wisdom" refers to the four knowledges:
the knowledge of suffering, the knowledge of origin, the knowledge of cessation, and the knowledge of the path, as well as other various knowledges.
"Vision" refers to the vision of the Four Noble Truths.
"Abiding in peace and happiness" refers to the four dhyānas, which are cultivated rather than innate.
"I know" refers to knowing the dharmas of the Four Truths.

As for what is called the "view of self" (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*), it refers to: seeing devas, seeing nāgas, seeing yakṣas, seeing gandharvas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, kaṭapūtanas, and piśāca ghosts; hearing the voices of devas up to the voices of piśāca ghosts; going to the abodes of devas up to the abodes of piśācas; those various devas, nāgas, up to the piśācas coming to my presence; and my constantly associating with and conversing with those devas and others, while those devas and others also come to me, constantly associating with and conversing with me.
In fact, to claim "I have realized" when one has not yet realized— meaning to say that one has attained the perception of impermanence, and so forth, up to attaining the eight liberations—
and then to speak of "another time," refers to a different occasion.
"Being questioned" means being interrogated by another.
"Not being questioned" means that one spontaneously gives rise to regret and harbors distress.
"Desiring self-purification" means wishing to emerge from the offense.
He spoke these words:
"Venerable sir!
I truly did not know."
The phrase "the one who says" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The phrase "I truly do not see" refers to the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*).
"Deceptive and false speech" refers to speaking in a manner that is inconsistent [with reality].

"Excluding those with overweening pride" means excluding persons of overweening pride who, though they have not actually realized [the fruit], claim to have already attained it; because they lack a deceitful mind, they do not commit a root offense.
"This" refers to that person. "Bhikṣuṇī" means one who abides in the nature of a bhikṣuṇī;
the detailed explanation is as above, up to the point that she should not be appointed to any of the twelve types of offices. For this reason, it is called "not to be lived with."
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense?
The summary verse says:
Seeing signs at an araṇya, Accepting an exquisite seat within a dwelling;
Being able to know their own characteristics, they manifest their bodies through skillful means.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with such a desire and such an acceptance, speaks these words:
"I have seen the devas, even down to the kaṭapūtanas."
...one incurs a *pārājika* offense. This applies even to such statements as:
"I saw a *pāṃśukūla-preta* (a ghost of refuse)."
If a bhikṣuṇī, desiring it thus and assenting thus, speaks these words:
"I have heard [of] the devas, even down to the kaṭapūtanas," she commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
...one incurs a *pārājika*.
Even down to a *pāṃśukūla-preta* (a ghost of refuse heaps), one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks such words:
If one says, "I shall go to the abodes of the devas,
even to the abodes of the kaṭapūtanas," one incurs a pārājika offense.
If one says, "even to the abodes of the pāmsupradhāvanas (scavenger spirits)," one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceitful mind, speaks thus:
"The devas have come to me," or even, "The kaṭapūtanas have come to me."
...one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
Even if it is a *pāṃśukūla-preta*, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks such words as these:
"If one says, 'I am constantly familiar with and converse with the various devas,
even down to the kaṭapūtanas,' one incurs a pārājika offense."
If one says, "I am a *pāṃśukūla* ghost," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"The devas come and constantly associate with me, conversing with me, even down to the *kaṭapūtanas*."
If she says "Pāṃśukūlika," she incurs a *sthūlātyaya*. If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind,
says "I have attained it" when she has not actually attained the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*), she incurs a *pārājika*.
Even down to falsely claiming to have attained "liberation through both doors," all such acts constitute a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:

"There are many bhikṣuṇīs who, whether residing in a village or in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*), are frequently harassed by non-human beings (*amanuṣya*); among them, those who have attained the fruit of a Stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*), Once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), Non-returner (*anāgāmin*), or Arhat (*arhat*) will no longer be harassed by non-human beings."
"If I was at that place, I was not harassed by non-human beings," [and she says this],
she incurs a *pārājika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:

“In such-and-such a house, having accepted an invitation for a meal, they have prepared an exquisite seat adorned with various colorful fabrics; only those who have attained the four fruits of the spiritual life may approach that seat to receive food and drink, and I too shall obtain that exquisite seat and its meal.”
Regarding this, if a bhikṣuṇī commits such an act, she incurs a pārājika offense.

Suppose there are many bhikṣuṇīs residing in a forest village who, though possessing few internal signs of meditative concentration, have subdued their afflictions through the mundane path so that sensual desire and ill-will do not manifest.
A bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, spoke these words:

"I too dwell in that araṇya; I have attained a slight concentration on specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa-samādhi), and by means of the mundane path (laukika-mārga), I have suppressed and eliminated the afflictions (kleśa), so that sensual desire and ill-will no longer manifest."
...whoever [does so] incurs a *pārājika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceitful mind wishing to manifest her own excellence, speaks thus:
"There is a bhikṣuṇī who has personally seen the various devas."
If he does not say,
"It was I," he incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
In this manner, up to and including seeing a *kātapatana* spirit—if one does not say, "This is me"—one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
Up to and including a *pāṃśukūla* (scavenger) spirit, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"There is a bhikṣuṇī who has heard the voices of the devas," and does not say,
"It was I," she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
In this manner, up to hearing that it is a *kattapūtana*, if one does not say, "It is me," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
up to hearing that it is a *pāṃśupreta*, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:
"A bhikṣuṇī has gone to the realm of the devas," and does not say, "It was I," she commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
Up to the realm of the kaṭapūtanas, one incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
Up to the realm of the *saṃkārajātaka* spirits, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks such words as these:
"If a bhikṣuṇī says, 'Various devas have come to me,' and so on,
up to saying that a kaṭapūtana has come, yet does not say, 'It is I,' she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense."
If it is a *pāmsu-śuṇḍika* (scavenger) spirit, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceitful mind, speaks these words:

"There is a bhikṣuṇī who constantly goes to the realm of the devas and converses and debates with them, even down to the *kaṭapūtanas*, yet they do not say 'I am she,'" she incurs the offense of *sthūlātyaya*.
If she is a *pāṃsukūla-preta* (a ghost of refuse), she incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"There are bhikṣuṇīs who come to converse and debate with various devas, even down to the *khaṭvāṅga-bhūtas* (or *kaṭapūtanas*)."
If one does not say, "This is mine," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
The case of the *pāmsupreta* (dust-ghost) is the same as before.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"If there is a bhikṣuṇī who attains the perception of impermanence— as extensively explained before— up to the point that she attains the eight liberations,
yet does not say 'this is mine,' that bhikṣuṇī incurs a sthūlātyaya offense."

Suppose there were many bhikṣuṇīs living in a forest hermitage village who were constantly harassed by non-human beings; among them, those bhikṣuṇīs who had attained the four fruits were not harassed by non-human beings.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:
"There is a bhikṣuṇī residing in that village who is not being harassed by non-human beings," and does not say,
"It is I," she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If there were many bhikṣuṇīs in a layperson’s house, sitting upon excellent seats and receiving food, and they all attained the four fruits [of the path],
yet a bhikṣuṇī with a deceptive mind spoke these words:
“There was a bhikṣuṇī who sat upon an excellent seat in that house.”
If one does not say, "This is mine," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If various bhikṣuṇīs dwelling in an araṇya village attain a slight concentration on their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-samādhi*), and through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) suppress and eliminate the afflictions such that sensual desire and ill will no longer manifest, yet they do not say, "This is mine," they incur a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a deceptive mind, speaks these words:

"There is a bhikṣuṇī residing in that village who has attained a slight degree of concentration on internal characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-samādhi*), such that even the afflictions (*kleśa*) no longer manifest."
If one does not say, "This is mine," one incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
[End of] the Fourth Fascicle of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya. Mūlasarvāstivāda Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya.
Fascicle Five.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. 5.

The Training Rule on Touching. This fifth training rule concerning touching was established while the Blessed One was residing in Śrāvastī; at that time, he had not yet prescribed that bhikṣuṇīs must not dwell in forest hermitages (araṇya).
As the Blessed One has said:
"For the sake of benefiting and compassionately pitying the śrāvakas, I have now completed all that ought to be done.

You, too, should attend to this in the same way: you should dwell in meditative concentration—whether in an araṇya, or at the foot of a tree, in a secluded and quiet place, in a mountain cave or a grass hut, or in the open air, or dwelling in the forest wilderness—and do not be negligent, lest you later regret it."
"This is precisely my instruction.
All the bhikṣuṇīs then went to the forest hermitage (araṇya) to dwell in silence and quiet their minds.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā was not free from the defilement of desire.

Before she left the household life, her countenance was upright and her appearance was peerless; beloved by all, she would only engage in amorous dalliance with men after receiving five hundred gold coins.
At that time, there was the son of a brahmin who, seeing Utpalavarṇā, became intensely attached to her with lustful passion and said,
"I desire to enjoy your company and make love with you.
Utpalavarṇā replied:
"If you seek pleasure, you may pay five hundred coins.
He replied,
"I have no money at present."
Utpalavarṇā said, "You may go and seek employment;
once you have found it, you may come here.
He then went out to work for hire.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana caused the nun Utpalavarṇā to sever all unwholesome dharmas and establish her on the path to nirvāṇa; she transcended the three realms, became free from all defilements of desire, realized the bliss of liberation, and attained arhatship. She would frequently go to the Dark Forest to dwell in silent meditation and practice concentration, experiencing the joy of liberation.
That Brahmin’s son, having obtained five hundred gold coins through his labor as a hired servant, returned to search for the nun Utpalavarṇā.
Upon hearing where she was, he left the household life; taking the five hundred coins with him, he went among the nuns and asked, "Where is the nun Utpalavarṇā now?"
The nuns replied, "She is in the dark grove.
The Brahmin’s son then went to the nuns' side and saw her sitting beneath a tree in meditative silence; he immediately addressed her, saying:
"I now possess five hundred gold coins; you may come and enjoy yourself with me.
Utpalavarṇā said, "O son of a Brahmin!"
"I have already abandoned such evil dharmas.
He then asked again:
"What do you find pleasing in my body that gives rise to defiled desire?"
The Brahmin’s son said,
“I am deeply enamored with the eyes of the Venerable One. Then,
by means of her supernormal powers, the nun Utpalavarṇā produced her own eyes and placed them within her palm, saying:
"What pleasure do you find now in this lump of flesh?
Seeing that his feelings were stirred to anger, the Brahmin’s son said,
"This shaven-headed female ascetic is practicing sorcery!"
She struck the nun’s head with her fist and abandoned her, departing.
She reported this incident to the nuns; the nuns reported it to the bhikṣus; and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Just as a lump of meat cast upon a crossroads attracts birds and beasts from all sides, so it is with women.
For this reason, bhikṣuṇīs should not dwell in forest hermitages (araṇya)."

Once the Blessed One had prohibited bhikṣuṇīs from dwelling in forest hermitages (āraṇya), the bhikṣuṇīs then entered the city of Śrāvastī and practiced meditative seclusion (dhyāna) along the public roads, where they were harassed by wicked men and thieves.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said, "A nunnery should be established.
In this city there was an elder named Viśākhā, whose faith was profound; seeing a nun, she asked her:
"Noble One, what is it that you require?
The bhikṣuṇīs related the matter in detail; having heard it, Viśākhā said:
“Noble Lady!
I have a spacious dwelling place; when the monastery is completed, out of compassion for me, I pray that you will come and reside there.
The nuns then went there and took up residence. Visākhā visited the nuns’ quarters every day to pay her respects.

Viśākhā was of upright and handsome appearance. When the nun Nandā, who wore her hair in a jeweled topknot, saw her, her heart became stained with passion. She manifested symptoms of illness and entered her room to lie down.

At dawn, Viśākhā rose early to circumambulate and pay homage at the Buddha’s stūpa; she then entered the monastery and saw one nun guarding the temple while the others were all out begging for alms. She immediately prostrated herself and asked, "Noble Lady!"
"Where have all the nuns gone?
She replied,
"They have all gone out to beg for alms."

As Viśākhā was about to leave the monastery, the nun Muktaka-Śikha-Nandā let out a loud moan from within her cell. Hearing this, Viśākhā felt compassion in her heart and went to where the nun guarding the monastery was, saying:
"Noble Lady!"
"Who is in this room making such loud moans?
He replied,
"There is a sick nun in the room."
Having heard this, he entered the room, paid his respects with devout reverence, and asked:
"Noble One, what is troubling you?"
The nun said,
"My suffering is such that it is ultimately difficult to describe.
She replied:
"Why do you not treat it?
The nun replied,
"This cannot be cured."
Viśākhā said, "Venerable One!
Is that medicine difficult to obtain?"
The nun said, "It is not difficult; however, my own wish cannot be fulfilled. Viśākhā said:
"Noble one!
Since you have gone forth, for as long as life lasts, you must seek medicine, food and drink, clothing, and bedding from others.
As the World-Honored One has said:"
"One should receive it from a *kappiya-kāraka* (a person authorized to handle requisites).
[The nun replied: "Venerable sir, please let me prepare whatever you require; I shall personally offer it as a gift.
The nun said:
"It is exactly as you have said; even one who knows the Dharma must exercise careful discernment.
Having heard this, Viśākhā felt redoubled reverence and exclaimed, "How marvelous!"
“The Bhikṣuṇī is truly one of few desires.
He then prostrated at the nun’s feet and spoke this verse:
“In the presence of the Noble One, I now give rise to pure faith;”
"Even if you require my own flesh and body, I am able to grant it to you.
When Viśākhā had spoken this verse, the nun uttered these base words:
"I pray you, perform an evil deed for me."
Upon hearing this, he covered his ears and said,
"Noble One! Do not speak such words to me."
The nun said,
"You have such an intention, yet you merely speak with forceful words.
Visākhā was about to leave when the nun spoke again:
"If you do not comply, come here and seize me by the head and my limbs.
She then seized her by the head, and the nun experienced a sensation of pleasure.
When the other nuns entered and saw this, Viśākhā felt ashamed, lowered her head, and departed. She immediately reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On this account, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣuṇīs. According to the constant practice of all Buddhas, he knowingly asked her:
"Nanda, the bhikṣuṇī Muktakaśikha, is it true that you have committed such an unseemly act?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him:
"What you have done is not the dharma of a śrāmaṇerī, it is not a practice in accordance with the path, nor is it the dharma of pure conduct.
Having rebuked her in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Considering ten benefits—and as explained at length up to—the training rule for the śrāmaṇerī vinaya is hereby established and should be recited as follows:"

"Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, together with a man who has a lustful mind, from below the eyes to above the knees, with the intent to experience pleasure, engages in physical contact or intense rubbing against him; [she commits an offense]."
"In such a matter, this bhikṣuṇī also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not be lived with.

The meaning of "bhikṣuṇī" is as explained extensively above, up to the full ordination (*upasampadā*) received through the formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun whose mind is possessed by defilement and who is bound by lustful desire.
"Together with a man of defiled mind" refers to a husband who likewise possesses a lustful mind.
"From below the eyes to above the knees" refers to the measurement of the body's parts.
"To rub and touch the body with a mind that experiences pleasure" means to experience the pleasure of tactile contact.
If there is "extreme contact," it means that by rubbing against the object with a firm touch, one incurs the root offense.
What are the characteristics of this transgression?
If a bhikṣuṇī, possessing a defiled mind, [engages] with a man who possesses a defiled mind...
If a bhikṣuṇī, from below the eyes to above the knees, has her body touched by another, whether through intense contact or firm contact, she incurs a *mūlāpatti*.
If a bhikṣuṇī with a defiled mind allows her body to be touched by a man who is without a defiled mind, she incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
If a bhikṣuṇī is free from lustful intent, and a man—whether he has lustful intent or not—touches her, there is no offense provided she guards her mind.
If the bhikṣuṇī is ill and a man massages her body, should the bhikṣuṇī give rise to lustful intent, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense for one whose mind is free from defilement, nor is there an offense for one who is afflicted by illness.
The summary verse says:
When both possess a defiled mind, [touching] from below the eyes down to the knees.
If they touch one another, this incurs a root offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If a nun has a defiled mind while a man has no lustful intent,
yet they touch one another, this constitutes a *thullaccaya* transgression.
If both are free from defiled intent, or if the man possesses a defiled mind but the nun touches him while guarding her own mind, there is no offense.
When a bhikṣuṇī is ill, if a man massages her body, [there is no offense].
If a nun gives rise to a defiled mind, she shall incur the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
The Sixth Training Rule Concerning the Offense through Eight Actions. When the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a perfume merchant in this city who was handsome in appearance and had recently married his wife.
The bhikṣuṇī Gulatā-nandā encountered him while walking and immediately conceived a lustful attachment toward him, asking: "O man!..."
"How long has it been since you took a wife?
What is her appearance like?
Do the husband and wife love one another?"
He replied, "Noble One!
The paths of the monastic and the lay are distinct; why trouble yourself to ask about this?"
The nun said,
"If you were to marry me, would that not be joyful?

The disciples of the bhikṣuṇī came outside the room to announce that the instruction was finished; as she returned inside the room, she saw the bhikṣuṇī entering and rose from beneath her bed. Mistaking the bhikṣuṇī for a thief, she became terrified and replied, "I am not a thief;
I am someone who has come by appointment."
With a defiled mind, he reached out and embraced the nun, laying her upon the bed. The nun thought to herself:
"I am the leader of the community; all people submit to me because of my precepts and virtue. If I break the *śīla*, what further use would I have?"
When the people learned of this, they all discarded it.
He replied, “Young man!
"Furthermore, let us see them release one another.
As soon as they spoke these words, they were released; the nun stepped on his chest, causing him to fall to the ground and vomit blood. The nun cried out loudly, proclaiming:
