"I have already subdued Māra and crushed my enemies.
When the nuns heard this, they rose and asked together,
"Sister!..."
"Have you realized the fruit of arhatship?
He replied, "I have not."
He asked again:

He asked again,

She replied, "I did not ask.

When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they immediately replied,
"If you had not brought him in yourself, how could he have reached the interior of this monastery?
Then the entire community of bhikṣuṇīs spoke with derision and reproach, saying:
"You have committed an evil deed; I do not approve of it.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of nuns; perceiving the benefit therein, he questioned them, saying:
“Bhikṣuṇī! Did you truly perform this unrighteous act?
She replied:
"It is true," she replied.
The Buddha then rebuked her:

After the Blessed One had rebuked them in various ways, he addressed the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
“I, having considered ten benefits, shall extensively explain in the Vinaya for the śrāvakī bhikṣuṇīs—up to the formulation of the training rule—which should be spoken thus:

‘If again a bhikṣuṇī, being herself possessed of a lustful mind, with a man who is likewise possessed of a lustful mind, engages in any of these eight acts: flirtation, playfulness, laughter, indicating a place, agreeing on a time, giving hints through gestures, mutually consenting to the advances of a man, or lying down bodily in a place where such conduct is improper; and if they thus mutually accept one another’s advances—’”
"If a bhikṣuṇī should perform such an act, she also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community.
As for "if a bhikṣuṇī," this refers to the bhikṣuṇī Khemā (Turuṇanda) or any other nun.
Regarding "a man with a defiled mind," both possess defilement and have given rise to a mind bound by desire.
First, "agitation" refers to touching while agitated by signs.
Second, "jesting" refers to mocking and playing with one another while using signs.
3. "Laughing" refers to conversing and laughing together.
4. "Pointing out a location" refers to directing one toward a specific garden or a particular shrine hall.

Sixth, regarding "manifest signs": if you see me with freshly shaven hair, wearing red robes, and holding an oil bowl in my hand, know that the matter has been accomplished.
Seventh, regarding "the mutual consent of a man and woman in coming and going": this refers to being mutually affectionate and delighted.
8. "In an improper place where sexual intercourse may be performed" refers to a concealed location where one is capable of engaging in sexual acts.

Regarding these eight matters being "mutually accepted," it means that the performance of these eight acts is done with a defiled mind; therefore, they are said to be "accepted.
The meaning of terms such as *bhikṣuṇī* is as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of offenses herein: if one commits any of the first seven acts, each incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense;
when the eighth act is committed, one incurs a grave offense (*pārājika*).
The summary verse says:
Agitation and frivolous laughter, pointing out locations and fixing times, signaling with gestures,
people coming and going, and lying down with the body stretched out in a secluded place.
The first seven incur a grave offense (sthūlātyaya); the eighth is incurable.
7. The Training Rule on Concealing Another’s Offense. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Kalyāṇamitrā slandered the venerable Sthiramati; having been driven out by the community on account of her own confession, she abandoned the path and returned to lay life.
She had a younger sister among the nuns named Kṣudramitrā, who was seen by other nuns teaching a group of disciples. She said to those nuns:
"Had my elder sister not returned to lay life, she too would have been teaching such disciples."
The nuns said, "Why must you use the name of this nun who has broken the precepts?
She replied:
“Noble One!
I too previously knew that you had committed a defeat (pārājika), and for this reason, though I was close to you, I did not speak of it.
As the verse says:”
"Even when seeing the faults of an enemy, a benevolent person does not speak of them;
how much less could they speak of the private affairs of one who is their own kin?"

She reported the matter to the Buddha, and so on, until the World-Honored One questioned her about the facts, rebuked her, and established this training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having previously known that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a pārājika offense, does not speak of it."
After that person has died, or has returned to lay life, or has departed, one should then speak these words:
"The community of nuns should know!
I previously knew that this bhikṣuṇī had committed a pārājika offense."
"In such a matter, this bhikṣuṇī also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not live in community.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a junior friend or another bhikṣuṇī.
"Knowing" means either knowing by oneself or knowing through another.
"One who has committed a defeat" refers to anyone among the eight defeats who conceals it.
"Without having spoken of it" means not having brought it to light.
"After her body has died" refers to after that nun has passed away.
The remaining text is easy to understand; it is explained in detail as stated above.
Regarding this matter, what are the characteristics of the offense?
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing such a matter, conceals it and fails to expose it, she commits a pārājika offense. 8.
The Training Rule for One Who Has Been Formally Charged. The eighth training rule concerning one who has been formally charged; the setting is the same as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Mūla whom the harmonious Saṃgha had subjected to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (act of reconciliation), and the community of bhikṣuṇīs had likewise subjected him to the *anavaśrāvaṇīya-dharma* (the rule of non-prostration). As it is explained at length, that bhikṣu desired to manifest an appearance of reverence toward the Saṃgha in hopes of seeking deliverance.
Having seen this, the nun Tullānandā said:
"Noble One!
I now offer my respects."
"Where do you wish to go?
He replied, "I have been cast out; now I wish to seek the compassion of the assembly."
The nun Thullanandā said, "Noble one!
You have gone forth from the Śākya clan; why do you suffer by seeking favors and offering apologies to others?"
"I shall provide you with all necessary requisites; settle your mind well and apply yourself to recitation and mental cultivation.
[The nun] then reported this matter to the Buddha, who addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"You should offer a formal admonition to the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇā."

"Do you not know that the community has performed the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against this person, and that the bhikṣuṇīs have imposed upon him the rule of non-prostration? Yet you provide him with robes, bowls, and other necessities so that he lacks for nothing."
"You must now relinquish this matter for which you have been formally charged.
When the bhikṣuṇīs admonished her in this manner, she remained obstinate and refused to relinquish it; they reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"A formal procedure of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman) should be performed against Pūrṇaśailā.
They acted according to the instruction, as should be understood from what follows below.

He persisted in his adherence and would not relinquish it; consequently, the Blessed One questioned him regarding the facts, rebuked him, and established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a certain bhikṣu has been subjected by the harmonious Saṃgha to the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* (the act of setting aside), and that the community of bhikṣuṇīs has likewise subjected him to the *anavaśrāvaṇīya-dharma* (the rule of non-prostration), [should still persist in her adherence...]"

That bhikṣu, manifesting an attitude of reverence toward the Saṃgha and seeking deliverance, personally requested within the boundary that the *sthāpanīya-dharma* (the act of suspension) be lifted for him.
That bhikṣuṇī replied to the bhikṣu, saying:
"Noble One!..."
Do not manifest an appearance of veneration in public places in hopes of being rescued; rather, within your own boundary, request the formal act of suspension (*niḥsargika-śikṣāpada*).
I shall provide the Venerable One with robes, alms bowls, and all other requisites so that nothing is lacking; you should then settle your mind and engage in recitation and mental cultivation.
Then the bhikṣuṇīs said to this nun:
"Do you not know? The Saṃgha has performed the *pratisāraṇīya-karman* against this person, and we bhikṣuṇīs have applied the rite of non-prostration toward him."
That bhikṣu, having aroused a humble mind, shall himself request within the boundary the formal act of release from the *sthāpanīya-karman*.
You should then provide him with robes, alms bowls, and other requisites so that he lacks for nothing.
"You must now abandon this practice of following after [laypeople].
When the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner, it is well if she abandons it.
If she does not abandon it, they should admonish her earnestly and correctly two or three times, and should reprove her according to the instruction, so that she may abandon this matter.
"If she renounces it, that is well;
if she does not renounce it, this bhikṣuṇī also incurs a pārājika offense and shall not be lived with.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūrṇa-nandā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"Knowing that bhikṣu" refers to a bhikṣu within this Dharma.
"That harmonious Saṃgha" refers to the disciples of the Buddha.
"Performing the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* of *pratisāraṇīya*" refers to performing the formal motion consisting of four parts.
This may be understood from the text; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific details?

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that the community of bhikṣus has performed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (formal act) of suspension (*pratisāraṇīya*), yet the community of bhikṣuṇīs also performs the rite of non-prostration toward her.
When these words are spoken one by one, each constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If they desist upon being admonished, it is well; if they do not desist, they incur an offense of serious transgression (*sthūlātyaya*).

From the initial motion (*jñapti*) through the second and third proclamations (*karmavācana*) of the formal act (*karman*), one incurs a grave offense (*sthūlātyaya*). If one renounces [the object] before the fourth proclamation is completed, one still incurs a grave offense;
once it is concluded, one commits a defeat (*pārājika*).
"Venerable sirs!
I have now recited the eight *pārājika* dharmas.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of these offenses, she is no longer permitted to dwell together with the bhikṣuṇīs."
As it was before, so it is after; having incurred a defeat (pārājika), one should not dwell together [with the Saṃgha].
Now I ask the venerable ones:
Are you pure in this matter?
Thus it was said three times: "Venerable sirs!
Since you are pure in this matter, as indicated by your silence, I now hold it to be so.
"Venerable sirs!"
"These twenty *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*.
The summary verse for the twenty *saṃghāvaśeṣa* dharmas says:
"Mediation, the two types of slander, the two defilements, and the four solitary acts."
Abandoning the covenant and causing schism, The two types of disputes, living alone,
Causing a split in the Saṃgha and following its companions, Polluting families and being of evil character—
These twenty formal acts of instruction (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) Should be known as consisting of eight [offenses] with three admonitions each.
1. The Training Rule on Brokering Marriages. Regarding the first training rule on brokering marriages, the setting is the same as before.

At that time, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs personally acted as matchmakers; they conveyed the intentions of men to women and the intentions of women to men, even arranging secret liaisons between men and women.
At that time, the non-Buddhists all spoke with derision: "You should know!
These śramaṇa daughters of the Śākyas do what ought not to be done; in practicing matchmaking, how are they any different from us?"
"Who else could possibly take the food and drink from the court and offer it to these shaven-headed śramaṇas, the daughters of the Śākyas?
Then the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs as before and addressed the group of twelve, saying:
"Is it true that you carry a man's intentions to a woman, carry a woman's intentions to a man, and act as matchmakers for illicit unions?"
They replied,
"It is true. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One rebuked the twelve bhikṣuṇīs:

"You are not a daughter of the Śramaṇas; you do not follow [the path], you do not practice pure conduct, you do not possess good deportment, and this is not what should be done by one who has gone forth."
At that time, the Blessed One rebuked her in various ways and even established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī acts as a matchmaker, conveying a man's intent to a woman or a woman's intent to a man, whether for the purpose of formal marriage or for illicit intercourse, even for as little as a moment, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
“Bhikṣuṇī” refers to the group of twelve or other bhikṣuṇīs.
“Acting as a matchmaker” means serving as a messenger for mutual communication.
“Communicating the man’s intention to the woman and the woman’s intention to the man” means conveying the intentions of both the male and female parties to one another.
Regarding those who act for the sake of establishing a wife or engaging in illicit sexual relations, there are seven kinds of wives and ten kinds of illicit partners.
What are the seven kinds of wives?
First, the one given by water-consecration (*udakadattā*).
2. Marriage by purchase;
3. Marriage by royal banner;
4. Marriage by mutual consent.
5. Food and clothing;
6. Living together;
7. For a brief moment.
The summary verse says:
The seven types of wives are those obtained by water-consecration, by wealth, by being won in battle,
by one's own pleasure, by food and clothing, by cohabitation, and for a moment.
Regarding the "water-bestowal" marriage for a wife: this refers to not taking any wealth or goods; instead, the parents of the girl pour water into the hand of the husband and declare:
"I now give this daughter of mine to you as your wife; you must protect her well yourself and ensure that no other person shall ever presume to deceive or violate her."
This is called a wife given by water.

As for a wife obtained through wealth (*dhana-datta*), it refers to giving away a daughter after receiving wealth and goods; as explained in detail above, this is called a wife obtained through wealth.

As for the royal banner: it is like a consecrated great king of the Kṣatriya caste who, having arrayed his military banners to strike down a rebellious kingdom, issues a proclamation once victory has been achieved, saying:
"Any women captured shall be taken as wives at will."
"This refers to obtaining a woman as a wife or concubine through the power of the royal banner.
Furthermore, if there is someone who acts as a bandit leader and captures a woman as his wife after plundering a village or city, she is called a 'wife by the royal banner.'"
Regarding "one who seeks pleasure for herself": if a woman or a young girl goes in person to the place of a man she has taken a liking to and says, "I now wish to be your wife."
If he then accepts her, she is called a wife by choice.
Regarding a wife provided with food and clothing: if a girl or young woman goes to a man’s place and says, “You should provide me with food and clothing, and I shall become your wife.”
This is called a wife for food and clothing.

As for a wife by mutual livelihood: if a girl or young woman goes to a man's place and says, "Whatever wealth I possess and whatever property you have, let us combine it all in one place to live our lives together."
This is called a wife by common consent.
As for a "momentary wife," it refers to one who acts as a wife for only a brief duration; this is called a momentary wife.
What are the ten kinds of illicit unions?
That is to say, there are ten types of protection:

protection by the father, protection by the mother, protection by brothers, protection by sisters, protection by paternal uncles, protection by maternal uncles, protection by relatives, protection by caste, protection by clan, and protection by the king or the Dharma.
The summary verse says:
The ten types consist of parents, brothers and sisters,
paternal and maternal uncles, and the royal law concerning one's own kin.
What is paternal protection?

It refers to when a maiden is still in her father’s household, her father constantly provides for and protects her; or, once she has been married, if her husband dies, or is imprisoned, or at times flees into exile, her father continues to protect her—this is called paternal protection.
Protection by the mother is likewise.
What is protection by brothers?

If a woman’s father, mother, and husband have all passed away, or have at some time been lost, and she resides in the home of her brothers, where her brothers provide protection—this is called protection by brothers.
It is the same for sisters.
What is meant by "protection by the father-in-law"?
If a woman’s parents and kinsmen have all passed away, and her husband is ill, or perhaps insane, or has wandered off and lost his way, she lives under the protection of her father-in-law.
The Great King announced: "New bride!
You may dwell by my side with a joyful heart; I cherish you as I would look upon my own child."
The Great Official then protects [them] according to the Dharma; this is called protection by the Great Official.
Protection by the Householder is likewise.
What is protection by relatives?
All kinsmen from the time of the high ancestor onward are termed "relatives"; beyond this, they are not relatives.

If a woman’s parents, brothers, sisters, or husband have all passed away, or if they are insane, or have wandered to other lands, she then relies upon and dwells with other relatives; this is called "protection by relatives."
What is protection by caste?
It refers to women of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes who abide according to their respective castes; this is called protection by caste.
What is protection by clan?
It refers to certain lineages among the Brahmins and others, such as the daughters of the Bhāradvāja, Śāṇḍilya, Vatsa, and so forth; because of this protection, it is called "protection by clan."
What is protection by royal law?
If a woman has no kinsmen and stands alone, because of the royal law no one dares to欺 (deceive or harm) her; this is called protection by royal law.

Furthermore, there is that which is called "Dharma-protection" (*dharmarakṣā*): if there is a woman who, being a widow, maintains her integrity, preserves her pure conduct, and keeps her heart chaste, such that no one deceives or violates her—this is called Dharma-protection.

Regarding the Sangha: if one commits this offense, one must undergo the prescribed disciplinary procedure in reliance upon the Sangha and attain purification from the offense in reliance upon the Sangha, not by relying on an individual.
*Śeṣa* means "remainder.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits any one of the eight *pārājika* rules, there is no remainder; she may not live in community with others.
These twenty dharmas, although committed by a bhikṣuṇī, leave a remainder; because they are subject to treatment, they are called *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
Furthermore, because the offense is removed through the instruction of the community (*saṃgha*), they are also termed *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (Community Instruction).
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offenses and their specific details?
As with the aforementioned states of separation from wives, there are seven kinds.
A summary verse says:
"During the fight and after the fight, / Breaking the grass and throwing three tiles,
/ 'According to the Dharma, she is not my wife'— / Proclaiming this as testimony to many people.
What are these seven?"
1. Separation while in the midst of fighting;
2. Separation after the fighting has ceased;
3. Separation by breaking a blade of grass into three pieces.
4. Separation by throwing a tile in the three directions;
5. Separation by acting according to the law before one's relatives;
6. Separation by declaring, "She is not my wife."
7. Universal Separation from the Multitude.

If a bhikṣuṇī, seeing a layperson in the process of causing separation between a husband and his first wife due to quarrels and the like, should reconcile them at the initial stage of their separation so that they are reunited, she incurs one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one performs the second act of mixing them apart, one incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one performs the third act of mixing them apart, one incurs three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
If one performs the fourth, fifth, or sixth act of mixing them apart, one incurs, respectively, one, two, or three *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If one causes a seventh separation from a spouse, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If, among the remaining four types of wives or ten types of illicit unions, one causes a separation through any one of the seven kinds of separations, and the bhikṣuṇī subsequently reconciles them again, she incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense in all such cases.
The summary verse says:
Receiving for oneself and receiving through a messenger; the two nuns and the four modes of conduct;
walking together in front and behind; the causes for honor and disgrace, as well as the specific matters.
If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message herself, goes to deliver it herself, and returns herself to report it, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message herself, goes to deliver it herself, but dispatches a messenger to return with the report, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself receives a message, sends a messenger to deliver it, and returns herself to report it, she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself receives a message, sends a messenger to deliver it, and has the messenger return to report it, she commits a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message from a messenger, goes herself to deliver it, and returns herself to report it; or receives a message from a messenger, goes herself to deliver it, and dispatches another messenger to report it; or receives a message from a messenger, dispatches another messenger to deliver it, and returns herself to report it; or receives a message from a messenger, dispatches another messenger to deliver it, and dispatches yet another messenger to report it—she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense in each case.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message from a messenger, goes in person to deliver it, and returns in person to report; or receives a message from a messenger, goes in person to deliver it, and sends another messenger to report; or receives a message from a messenger, sends another messenger to deliver it, and returns in person to report; or receives a message from a messenger, sends another messenger to deliver it, and sends yet another messenger to report—she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense in each case.
If two bhikṣuṇīs receive a message from another, both go to deliver it, and neither returns a reply, both commit two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If two bhikṣuṇīs receive a message from another, neither goes to deliver it, and neither returns a reply, both commit one *sthūlātyaya* offense each.
If two bhikṣuṇīs communicate with each other, and one says:
"Convey my words to him and report back," and the other acts according to those instructions, both incur a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If two bhikṣuṇīs receive a message from someone together, and one says,
"I shall go to deliver the message but will not return to report it," while the other returns to report it,
the one who went to deliver the message and returned to report it incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
Regarding those who do not go to deliver the message nor return with a reply, they incur two *sthūlātyaya* offenses.
If two bhikṣuṇīs receive the request themselves, one says:
"I will not go to deliver the message, nor will I return with a reply."

If one who goes to deliver the message and returns to report it incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, while one who neither goes to deliver the message nor returns to report it incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
If a single bhikṣuṇī travels along the same road together with one man and one woman, [the same applies].
If that man says to the bhikṣuṇī:
"Noble Lady!
Could you perhaps speak to this woman and say such words as these?"
"Would you be able to become the wife of this man, or dwell with him for even a short time?
Or again, a woman might say to a bhikṣuṇī:
"Noble Lady!..."
"Could you speak to this man and say these words:
'Would you be able to become the husband of this woman, or dwell with her even for a short time?'?
If this bhikṣuṇī, having accepted this request, then speaks on his behalf and reports back [the result], she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
Just as it is with walking, so should it be understood that standing, sitting, and lying down are to be treated accordingly.
Likewise, if two bhikṣuṇīs and two men, or two women; or three bhikṣuṇīs and three men and three women, and so forth—as explained at length—one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If two bhikṣuṇīs are traveling together, one preceding and the other following, and the one who precedes receives the message herself, delivers it, and returns with the report, the preceding one incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense, while the following one is not guilty of an offense.

If the bhikṣuṇī who is traveling ahead receives the message herself and dispatches the bhikṣuṇī following behind to go and speak, and once the truth has been ascertained, the bhikṣuṇī traveling ahead returns to report it herself, the bhikṣuṇī traveling ahead incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses, while the bhikṣuṇī following behind incurs one *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If the bhikṣuṇī who goes ahead receives the message herself and goes to deliver it herself, and then dispatches a bhikṣuṇī following her to report back, the bhikṣuṇī who went ahead incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses, while the bhikṣuṇī who follows incurs one *sthūlātyaya* offense.

If the bhikṣuṇī who went ahead has already accepted the message herself and then dispatches the bhikṣuṇī following behind to deliver it and report back, the bhikṣuṇī following behind incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses, while the bhikṣuṇī who went ahead incurs one *sthūlātyaya* offense.
One should understand that the amount of offense incurred by a bhikṣuṇī who acts as the leader is the same as previously described;
likewise, one should understand that the amount of offense incurred by a bhikṣuṇī who is sent as a follower for the sake of the leader’s task is to be explained by analogy.
There are two types of householders: first, those who have autonomy; second, those who do not have autonomy.
Those said to have autonomy are masters of their own affairs, taking and giving among their own sons and daughters according to their own wishes.
If one goes before government officials or to places where crowds gather, even when speaking of false matters, people will nevertheless believe and accept them; this is called "mastery" (*vaśitā*).
"Lack of mastery" (*avaśitā*) has the meaning of being lowly or inferior; it refers to having no power over one's own sons and daughters in matters of giving or taking.
If one goes before a government office or a gathering of many people, and although one speaks the truth, others do not believe or accept it, this is called "lack of autonomy.

If a nun receives a message from a person who lacks such authority, conveys it to a person with authority, and returns to report it back to that authoritative person, she incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message from one with authority, goes to deliver it to that person with authority, but returns to report it to one without authority, she incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and one *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message from one with authority, goes to deliver it to one without authority, but returns to report it to that person with authority, she incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and one *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message from one who lacks authority, goes to deliver it to one who lacks authority, and returns to report it to one who lacks authority, she incurs one *sthūlātyaya* and two *duṣkṛta*s.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message from one who lacks authority, goes to deliver it to one who lacks authority, but returns to report it to one who possesses authority, she incurs two *duṣkṛta*s and one *sthūlātyaya*.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message from one who lacks authority, goes to deliver it to one who has authority, and returns to report it to the one who lacks authority, she incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses and one *sthūlātyaya*.

If a bhikṣuṇī receives a message from one who lacks authority, goes to deliver it to one who has authority, and returns to report it to the one who has authority, she incurs two *sthūlātyaya* offenses and one *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one receives a message while lacking autonomy—neither being able to deliver it nor being able to return a reply—one incurs three *duṣkṛta* offenses.

Furthermore, there are three circumstances under which a bhikṣuṇī acts as a matchmaker; even if she has received the three [messages], if she does not communicate them by speech, the act of matchmaking is nonetheless established.
What are the three?
First, the designated place; second, the fixed time; and third, the manifested sign.
What is meant by the designated place?
He tells that person:
"If you see me in a certain garden, or at a certain shrine, or in a place where people gather, you should know that the matter has been accomplished."
This is called the appointed place.
What is the fixed time?
"If you see me at the time of the morning meal, or at midday, or at the afternoon hour, then you should know that the matter has been accomplished."
This is called the fixed time.
What are the signs?

"If you see me with my hair newly shaved, or wearing a new outer robe (*saṃghāṭī*), or holding a mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), or at times carrying an alms bowl filled with ghee or oil, you should know that the matter has been accomplished."
This is called "indicating signs.
These are the three conditions by which, although one has received a message, even if one does not reply with words, it constitutes the act of matchmaking.
Furthermore, there are three other matters that constitute the act of matchmaking at the time of being dispatched as a messenger.
What are the three?
First, speech; second, writing; third, hand gestures.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal mission and conveys it verbally or reports back verbally, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal messenger, conveying the message verbally and reporting it in writing, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal messenger, conveying the message in writing and reporting it back verbally, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal message and conveys it by means of a letter, and receives a reply by means of a letter, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal message and conveys it by means of a letter, but receives a reply by indicating a place, or by fixing a time, or by displaying a sign, she likewise incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
This is called the fivefold distinction regarding verbal messengers and written messages.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal messenger and conveys the message verbally while returning the report verbally, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal message, conveys it verbally and returns a reply by means of a hand gesture, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal message, conveys it by means of a hand gesture and returns a reply verbally, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal mission and conveys it by means of a hand-sign, and receives a reply by means of a hand-sign, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī herself accepts a verbal mission and conveys it by means of a hand-sign, but receives a reply by indicating a place, or by specifying a time, or by manifesting a sign, she incurs a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
This is called the fivefold distinction of speech combined with hand-seals.

Just as there are two sets of five differences between speech combined with written seals, so too should one provide an extensive explanation for written seals combined with speech, hand-seals combined with speech and writing, and the mutual combination of speech, writing, and hand-seals.
If a preceptor bhikṣuṇī goes to a donor’s house and speaks as follows:
“Why does this girl not go out to marry now that she has grown up?
Why does this boy not take a wife now that he is already grown?”
These [remarks] all constitute an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If one says:
"Why does this woman not go to her husband's house? [it is likewise an offense].
If one says,
"Why does this man not go to his wife's house?
it is likewise an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If a gate-teacher bhikṣuṇī goes to a donor’s house and utters words of opposition or contradiction, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) in every case.
There is no offense for one who is a first-time offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.
2. The Training Rule on Groundless Slander. The second training rule concerning groundless slander. The setting is the same as before.

The nun Tullā-Nandā, through her quarrels and disputes, caused distress among sentient beings; she then slandered others with the *pārājika* offense based on groundless allegations. Consequently, the bhikṣuṇīs could not dwell in peace, they were hindered from cultivating wholesome deeds and practicing meditative concentration, and all became filled with anxiety and distress.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣuṇīs, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, he said: "I shall now establish a training rule for the community of bhikṣuṇīs, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, harboring malice and refusing to let it go, intentionally slanders a pure bhikṣuṇī with a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to ruin her pure conduct.'"
If, at a later time, whether questioned or not, one knows that this matter is groundless and was spoken out of malice by someone slandering that bhikṣuṇī, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or others of a similar class.
“Harboring anger” means that resentment has arisen in the mind.
“Not relinquishing” means that the malice does not cease.
"A pure bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma.
"Without offense" means not committing that act. "With groundless [accusation]" means being without the three grounds:
[the ground of seeing, the ground of hearing, and the ground of suspicion].
The roots of seeing, hearing, and doubt.
Regarding the *pārājika* dharmas, one is described according to any one of the eight matters.
As for "dharma," it refers to speaking of what is not dharma as being dharma.
"Slander" means to speak of what is untrue.
It is the desire to ruin that practitioner of pure conduct, and the desire to damage that person's pure training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
"At another time" refers to a different occasion.

"Whether asked or unasked" means that after having spoken a slanderous accusation, one feels regret and remorse; it is not because of another's questioning that one realizes this matter was groundless slander arising from a dispute.
There are four kinds of disputes:
namely, disputes involving quarrels, disputes involving verbal abuse, disputes involving transgressions, and disputes involving legal matters.
To speak such words out of malice is precisely to utter slanderous speech.
Regarding the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, it has already been explained as before.
The third training rule concerning false accusation based on a pretext (*mūlaka-śikṣāpada*). The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika took a similar matter and slandered a bhikṣuṇī; as explained in detail above, they all became filled with grief and distress. To establish a training rule, it should be stated as follows:
"If again a bhikṣuṇī, harboring anger and refusing to let it go, intentionally slanders a pure bhikṣuṇī by means of a groundless *pārājika* offense, desiring to ruin her pure conduct."

At a later time, whether questioned or unasked, if one knows that this is an irrelevant matter and yet, due to malice, falsely slanders a bhikṣuṇī by means of a slight resemblance of facts, saying such words, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense.
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or others of her kind.

“Matters that are different and not one’s portion”: “different” means *nirvāṇa*, because it is contrary to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); the eight *pārājika* dharmas are not one’s portion [in that context].
Regarding the *pārājika* offenses: among these eight, if one slanders another by means of even a single matter, such a slanderer falsely accuses that person.
By doing so, they destroy the pure conduct of that practitioner, intending to cause them to fall away from their pure conduct.
The details are as extensively explained previously.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are its specific instances?
If one slanders a pure bhikṣuṇī, there are ten matters that constitute an offense and five matters that do not constitute an offense.
What are the ten? They are:
not having seen the matter, nor heard it, nor suspected it, yet forming such a false and deceptive notion.
Although one has no actual seeing and so forth, one falsely claims, "I have seen, heard, or suspected. When one makes such a statement, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Whether one forgets after hearing or forgets due to doubt, yet forms such an interpretation and such a conception as to say,
"I have not forgotten what I heard or doubted," when one makes this statement, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
Some hear and believe; some hear and do not believe, yet say, "I have seen it.
Some hear and doubt; some hear and do not doubt; or some merely doubt themselves, yet say:
"If I saw it"—
when one speaks thus, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
These are called the ten matters that constitute an offense.
What are the five cases where there is no offense?
They are: when one has not seen, heard, or suspected, yet possesses the conviction that one has seen and so forth, possesses the perception that one has seen and so forth, and speaks these words:
"I have seen, heard, or suspected."
There is no offense if [the person] has not heard it.
Or, if one has heard it but forgotten, or suspected it and forgotten, yet speaks as if one had heard it or similar, there is likewise no offense.
Just as when slandering a pure person, there is an offense in ten cases and no offense in five cases, it is the same when slandering a pure person who appears impure.
If one slanders a person who is not impure, there are eleven matters that constitute an offense and six matters that do not.
What are the eleven? They are:

when one has neither seen, nor heard, nor suspected [an offense], yet forms such an understanding and such a conception, and while having no actual seeing and so forth, falsely declares: [that one has seen, etc.]...
If one says, "I have seen, heard,
or suspected," at the time of making such a statement, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense. Or, having seen but forgotten,
or heard but forgotten, or suspected but forgotten, if one forms such an understanding and such a conception, and says:
"I do not forget what I have seen, heard, or suspected.
When one makes such a statement, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
This applies whether one has heard it and believes it, or has heard it and does not believe it, yet says:
"I saw it," he says;
or having heard it, he doubts; or having heard it, he does not doubt; or he merely doubts himself, yet says: "I saw it."
When one speaks in this manner, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
These are called the eleven matters that constitute an offense.
What are the six matters that do not constitute an offense?

That is to say, although they have not seen, heard, or suspected, they possess the conviction that they have seen and so forth, and they possess the perception that they have seen, heard, and so forth, and thus they speak:
"I have seen, heard, and suspected."
There is no offense in these cases:

if one has seen but forgotten, heard but forgotten, or doubted and forgotten; or if one has the understanding that one saw [and so forth], or the perception that one saw [and so forth], yet speaks of having seen, heard, and so on—these are all likewise without offense.

These are called the six matters for which there is no offense. As for the rest, the detailed account of the past causes and conditions concerning Śrīgupta’s son is fully explained as it appears in the *Mahābhikṣu-nidāna*.
4. The Training Rule on Trading with Men of Lustful Intent. The fourth training rule regarding trading with men of lustful intent; the setting is the same as before.
In this city there was a perfume seller of handsome appearance.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Muktakaccha-Nanda went to that man to purchase various goods; the bhikṣuṇī then conceived a lustful desire for the man, and the man likewise harbored defiled intentions toward her.
At that time, the man took little payment and gave much merchandise.
If there were other nuns who had needs, they all relied upon this nun for their transactions, and all of them gave rise to defiled thoughts.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs and, knowing the facts, intentionally questioned the bhikṣuṇī Muktaka-Keśa Nanda:
"Is it true that you, with a lustful mind, engaged in mutual exchange with a man who was likewise lustful?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him as before, and eventually established the rule of training, which should be recited as follows:
"If again a bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, receives [an offering] from a man with a lustful mind, whatever object she may take, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"Regarding the bhikṣuṇī, this refers to Śuklakuṭī Nanda or any other nun.
Regarding 'with a defiled mind,' this means that those two individuals each harbored lustful desire."

"Whichever object one takes" means that according to whichever various objects one takes, one commits an offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class, and so forth, including other offenses, as explained extensively above.
If both parties possess a defiled mind, whatever object is taken constitutes an offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class.
If the nun has a defiled mind while the man is free from defilement, she incurs a thullaccaya offense.
If the nun is free from a defiled mind while the man has a defiled mind, she incurs a dukkaṭa offense.
If both parties are free from defiled minds, there is still an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*), because it is improper to engage in commercial transactions with such a person.

Fascicle Six.
