The Training Rule on Admitting One’s Own Faultlessness. The fifth training rule concerning the admission of one’s own faultlessness; the setting of the occasion is the same as before.
Once the Blessed One had established this rule, if any bhikṣuṇī, with a lustful mind, takes any object whatsoever from a man who is free from lustful intent, she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā was still away receiving [alms], when another nun asked her,
"Where have you come from?
She replied:
"I shall go and fetch some goods.

The nuns replied, "Has not the Blessed One already established this training rule: 'If a nun, with a lustful mind, takes any object whatsoever from a man who is free of lustful intent, she incurs a grave offense (thullaccaya)'?"
The nun Thullanandā asked,
“Do you have no lustful intent?
The nun replied:
"I have none," she replied. The Thullanandā nun said,
"If you take an object from a man with lustful intent while you yourself are free of lustful intent, what fault is there on my part?"
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of nuns and asked Pūraṇa-Dhanadā:
"Did you truly speak these words?"
"Since you took the object from a man with a defiled mind while you yourself were free from a defiled mind,
what fault is there on my part? She replied,
"It is indeed so."
The Blessed One rebuked her as before, and eventually established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should speak thus to another bhikṣuṇī:
'Since you have accepted the goods of a man with a lustful mind while you yourself were free from a lustful mind, what fault is there on my part?'"
"Whoever [does so], it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūrṇaśailā (Tulananda); the explanation of the characteristics and the determination of the offense are the same as before.
6. The Training Rule on Staying Overnight Alone at a Layperson’s House. The sixth training rule concerning staying overnight alone at a layperson’s house:

The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha. The bhikṣuṇī Kalyāṇamitrā slandered the bhikṣu Sthiramati with false accusations. Facing the other bhikṣus, she confessed that she had violated the precepts; she then returned to lay life and subsequently fell ill.
There was a sister bhikṣuṇī named Jñātikā. Her good friend was gravely ill and was about to pass away; with faith, she said to Jñātikā:
"I am now afflicted by illness and about to die; you should come quickly so that we may see one another."
When her friend arrived, that very night the good friend passed away.
Her husband returned briefly during the night and, seeing his wife’s body dead, beat his breast and cried out loudly, saying:
"Who shall now provide for my sons and daughters?"
The family members replied,
"This female friend of yours may be brought here to serve as a substitute.
Having heard this, the friend thought to herself:
"I fear that if I speak of my retribution, I shall be subjected to humiliation," she thought,
and so she remained silent.
When dawn broke and she knew her friend was about to depart, her husband said to her:
"Aunt, where are you going now?
You should stay here to care for our son and daughter.
Since we are kinsmen, how could you not feel compassion for us?"
The husband then stepped forward, intending to seize his companion; the nun rebuked him with a loud voice, saying:
"Whether you, along with all your sons and daughters, perish together at once, what concern is that of mine?"
She immediately ran back to the nunnery.
When the other nuns saw her, they asked,
"With whom did you stay overnight last night, and at what place?"
She replied,
"I have no companion.
The nun said:
"If you encounter an evil person, will they not surely destroy your pure brahmacarya?
He replied,
"If I were to converse with him, I would certainly incur this transgression."
The nun questioned her, and she answered fully.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community of nuns and questioned Jñātikā:
"Did you indeed go from the nunnery to stay overnight at another place?
She replied, "It is true."
The Buddha said:
"This is not something that should be done by a woman who has gone forth.
The World-Honored One rebuked her as before, and eventually established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī stays overnight alone in another place after departing from a nunnery, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
Regarding the term "bhikṣuṇī," this refers to a female companion or any other person.
"Alone" means having no companion.
"Staying overnight elsewhere" means leaving one's own monastery to stay overnight at another's house.
The explanation of the characteristics and the determination of the offense are both the same as previously stated.
7. The Training Rule on Going Alone to Lay Homes. The seventh training rule concerning going alone to lay homes. The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Khujjuttarā went alone, without any companion, during the day to the house of a layperson to preach the Dharma to an elder and others.
The nuns said to her, "Do not go alone to another's house during the day; we fear there may be obstacles to your pure conduct.
Tullanandā replied:
"You have not seen that when I, the incense-seller’s man, stepped on him with my foot, blood flowed from his mouth.
The nuns said,
"It is not necessarily the case that all people are as cowardly as he."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On this account, the Buddha assembled the nuns as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, he established the training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, being alone, goes from a nunnery during the day to a layperson's home, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
"A bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūraṇa-dhītā (Tulā-nandā) or any other such person.
To travel alone without a companion to the house of a layperson until sunset constitutes an offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class.
If one travels together with a female śrāmaṇerī, one commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one travels together with a śikṣamāṇā, one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
The eighth training rule concerning traveling alone on a road. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there was a caravan traveling toward Rājagṛha, and the nun Tullāraṇanda followed it alone; she likewise traveled alone to six other cities.
Later, when she returned and arrived at her original residence, the nuns massaged her to relieve her fatigue and allow her to rest, asking:
"Where have you been traveling alone during this time?"
She replied,
"I have traveled alone to all six cities.
The nuns said to her:
"If one travels alone without a companion and encounters evil people who come to oppress and assault one, would this not make pure conduct a great hardship?
Having heard this, he replied:
"Did you not hear? When the incense-seller came to harass me, I struck him down so that he lay prostrate on his back."
As soon as she stepped on his mouth, he vomited hot blood.
"How could any other person dare to provoke or offend him?
The nuns replied:
"It is not necessarily the case that all these people are as cowardly as she.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the nuns as before, questioned her regarding the facts, and after reprimanding her, established the training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again travels alone on a road, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
Regarding "bhikṣuṇī," this refers to Pūraṇa-dhītā (Tulananda) or any other such person.
"To travel alone on the road" means to travel on the road without a companion; this constitutes an offense of transgression of the many rules (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
If one goes together with a female novice (śrāmaṇerī), it constitutes a grave offense (sthūlātyaya).
If one goes with a female trainee (*śikṣamāṇā*) and crosses [the river], one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
The Ninth Training Rule on Crossing a River Alone. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, a group of bhikṣuṇīs was traveling through the countryside and arrived at the Aciravatī River, where a boat was on the opposite bank.
There was a bhikṣuṇī named Kālikā whose husband had previously been a boatman;
the nun said, "I shall enter the river and swim across to fetch the boat."
He then entered the river and swam until he reached the middle,
where he became exhausted. The nuns said to him, "Kālika!
Do not fear! Do not fear!
You must exert yourself with diligence.
The nun replied, “I am now exhausted;
it was only when I was on the verge of death that I managed to cross the river.

The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. On account of this matter, as before, the Buddha assembled the nuns, questioned her about the facts, and having rebuked her, established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should again swim across a river alone, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Kālika or any other such person.
To swim across the river alone means to cross the river by swimming through the water without a companion; this constitutes an offense of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* class.
If one crosses by binding together rafts, one incurs an offense of *duṣkṛta*.
If one crosses a river together with a female novice (śrāmaṇerī), one commits a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one crosses together with a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā), one incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
The tenth training rule concerning crossing with other women: The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, King Prasenajit had a great general named Kṛpāṇagraha who was constantly engaged in military expeditions.
While he was away, his wife, tormented by lustful desires, began to have illicit relations with an outsider.

When the general returned later, he heard of this matter and consequently increased the application of the whip and staff; yet, though she suffered the torments of punishment, she did not cease her misconduct. The general then thought:
"I have brought other districts under submission for the sake of the King and caused them to be compliant; how is it that I cannot even bring my own wife to order?"
Having formed this thought, he went to inform the king:
"I pray only that Your Majesty establish a decree for women:
if there be any who fail to cultivate the virtues of a wife and thereby defile the laws, they shall be punished by the ultimate penalty."
The king said, "A good thing.

Later, at another time, there was the daughter of a general who had violated the laws of this kingdom and been separated from her husband; she petitioned the king to act according to the law, and so the woman went to inform the judicial officer, saying:
"I have committed one transgression; I pray that you will graciously grant me your forbearance.
The judge said, "This cannot be pardoned."
The woman said, "I shall certainly not escape death; I beg for seven years of life.
The official said:
"No. "If you do not permit it, then I pray that I may live for six years, five, four, three, two, or even one year."
The official said,
"It cannot be. [The monk replied,] "In this way, let me go free for seven months, down to one month."
The official said, "It cannot be. [The monk replied,] "If that is so,
I would be grateful if you would allow me to stay for seven days."
The official said,
"As you wish.
Having received this permission, he formed this thought:
"I shall surely cut off my own body in seven days," she said, her tears flowing as she cultivated various meritorious deeds.
At that time, the nun Cūḍapanthaka, carrying her robes and bowl, entered the city for alms during the morning meal. Arriving at the woman's house, she saw her weeping and addressed her, saying:
“O maiden! For what reason do you weep with a grieving heart as you practice giving?
She replied:
"I am not far from death myself.
The nun said,
"Do not utter such inauspicious words."
The woman then went and wept as she recounted the events in sequence.
The nun said, "If that is so, why do you not renounce worldly life and go forth?
She replied:
"Who else will accompany me and take me along?
The nun said,
"I shall ordain you."
The woman then prostrated at his feet and replied,
"Noble One!
Grant me my life."
Tulānanda then granted her ordination.
When the General Holding a Sword heard that the wicked woman had now become a nun, he spoke these words:
"Could she have entered the City of Fearlessness?"
"When the seven days are complete, I shall take her life.
Upon hearing these words, the nun immediately sought out companions for the girl's sake and went to the place of the group of twelve nuns, saying:
"This is the daughter of a certain official; she has already taken refuge in the Buddha and taken refuge in the Dharma, and now she takes refuge in you all."
He related the matter in sequence.
The group of twelve said:
"This is an excellent thing; we shall now accept it. Who else would dare to speak against it?"
"If anyone should come here, I shall explain it myself.
She then led her daughter to Mahāprajāpatī and said,
"Noble Lady!..."

"You should know that this is the daughter of such-and-such an official; she has taken refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha with her body and mind, and now comes to take refuge at the feet of the Great Mistress.
When she was asked the reason for this, she explained it in full detail.
The Lord of the World said:
"Sisters! What is the use of this practice of non-action?"
Tulananda then took this woman to Lady Śrīmālā and said, "Lady! This is the daughter of a certain official;
she has already taken refuge in the Triple Gem and now comes to take refuge in you."
He asked her the reason for this, and she recounted everything as before.
The lady said,
"For what reason has this woman of no conduct been ordained so hastily?"
"It would have been improper for him to leave the household life;
this matter has already passed, and I shall inform the King.
Having arrived at the King's presence, he related the circumstances in detail. The King said:
"This is indeed contrary to the Dharma, yet this matter is difficult to adjudicate.
If I were to execute him according to the law, it would harm the Buddhist teachings and bring me an evil reputation.
If I were to release him now, it would further damage the administration of justice. Thus, whether advancing or retreating, there are two paths from which it is difficult to reach a decision."
He immediately dispatched a messenger to inform General Sword-Bearer of the matter in detail.
The general replied in his report:
"The strict decree that was established is known by all; how can this queen wish to violate the regulations and grant a release?"
The king said,
"This one should be released, and let it serve as a warning to others.
Having heard this, the general spoke at length with derision and reproach:
"How can one ordain such a woman who acts contrary to the Dharma?
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, as previously described, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, established the training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another woman has committed an unlawful act, is universally despised by the public, and has been abandoned by her husband, and furthermore informs the king of this, yet proceeds to ordain her and allow her to go forth, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanadā or any other such person.

“Knows” means she knows for herself; the full explanation continues until: it is improper for such a person to go forth into homelessness. If anyone ordains her, they incur an offense requiring formal instruction (saṃghāvaśeṣa).
11. The Training Rule on Seeking Lost Property. The eleventh training rule concerning the seeking of lost property. The setting is the same as before.
In this city there was a householder whose family was immensely wealthy; he suddenly fell gravely ill, and though treated by physicians for a long time, his condition did not improve.
Knowing that his own life would not last much longer, the elder extensively practiced the giving of alms, making offerings to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, and the widowed.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulmavilāsinī, having dressed and taken her bowl at the time of the morning meal, entered the house for alms and said to the elder:
"May you be free from illness."
"Are you at peace?
The householder replied,
"Noble One!"
"I have no desire for my own life or body, nor do I seek any further recovery; I shall give away all my household possessions to practice generosity and cultivate merit.
The nun said, "O noble one!"
“I deeply rejoice; this is most appropriate.
However, as a woman, my gains and offerings are meager; please accept a small portion from what I have set aside for distribution.
The householder replied:
"I have already given away all my wealth; why did you, O Noble One, not come earlier?
The nun replied, "To cause me to depart from my home empty-handed would have been a great harm."
The householder said, "Venerable One!
I have no other possessions; what would you wish to do with them?"
The nun said,
"O worthy one! You must provide me with some small amount of assistance."
At that time, the householder had only promissory notes for debts owed by others; he immediately showed them to the nun, saying:
"Noble Lady! These are the only documents I have in my home; if you require them, you may accept them."
The nun said, "Noble sir,
if you will give it to me, I shall take it myself.
She then took the contract and further addressed the elder, saying:
"By virtue of this merit from giving, the mind attains sublime adornment;
constantly receiving all necessary provisions, one shall reach unsurpassed bliss.
The elder said:
“Noble one!
That debtor’s household circumstances are impoverished and he cannot repay the full amount; please take whatever he can afford to provide, according to his means, and do not trouble him.”
The nun said, "O worthy one!
I am an ordained person; how could I not deliberate before causing distress to another? This is unreasonable."
Before long, the householder passed away.
When the nun heard of his death, she seized the debtor and began dragging him along by force at a crossroads.
Upon seeing this, the brahmin householder reviled her in disgust:
"How is it that a bhikṣuṇī, relying on a death-contract with another, drags along a debtor?
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, as before, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, established the training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, relying on an old agreement with another, seeks for herself the property of a deceased person, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūraṇa-dhanadā or any other nun.
"Relying on another's old contract" refers to a debt contract belonging to someone else.
"Seeking for oneself the property of a deceased person" means that after another has died, one uses the contract to demand and seek to take the property for oneself.
If there is anyone who seeks [the property] back, they incur an offense of many instructions (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
There is no offense if one pursues the matter with reason for the sake of the Saṃgha.
Twelfth: The Training Rule on Unjustified Release from Suspension (*muktaka-uddhāra-śikṣāpada*). The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Rāgacittā (Disordered Mind) who was by nature prone to anger; she constantly reviled and insulted one another with harsh words, so that the entire community of nuns came to despise and loathe her.
When she went out to beg for alms, the nuns saw that she was not there and immediately gathered together to discuss her misconduct.
She had a daughter named Śāntā; seeing the people speaking of her mother’s faults, she went to where her mother was begging for alms and told her everything.
Having heard these words, he gave rise to even greater anger and addressed the nuns with coarse speech and insults.
The assembly immediately inquired:
"Who is it that has incited this strife between the two sides?"
Śāntā informed her mother of this, and the assembly immediately performed the *jñapti-karman* of suspension (*pratisedha*) against her.
The girl went weeping to her mother’s place, prostrated at her feet, and said:
"The nuns have performed the *karman* of suspension against me."
Having heard this, Kālaṃkāra’s anger redoubled, and he spoke these words:
"I wish for you to perform the *pratisedha-kaṛman* (act of suspension) against all the people of the country.
He then took his daughter out beyond the boundary and performed the rite of release for her.
The nuns said, "The community has performed the *jñapti-karman* of *pratisedha* against your daughter; for what reason have you come outside the boundary to revoke it?
She replied:
"If a group performs the ritual, what fault is there in my understanding?
He asked, "In what place and with whom did you perform the ritual?"
He replied,
"This is my resolution with others outside the boundary.
The nun said:
"Is it appropriate to interpret the method in this way?
He replied, "Whether it is appropriate or not is already settled; why should it concern you?"
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the nuns as previously described, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reproaching them, established the training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣuṇī has been subjected by the community of bhikṣuṇīs to the formal act of suspension (pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman), should go outside the boundary and perform the rite of release for her, it is a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
“Nun” refers to one whose mind is distracted, or perhaps another nun.
“One who knows a bhikṣuṇī” refers to one who is tranquil.
“The assembly of nuns” refers to the assembly of śrāvakī nuns of the Tathāgata.
To perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations) refers to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
To go outside the boundary and perform the rite of release refers to the ritual for releasing the *karman*.
To incur an offense requiring communal instruction (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*) refers to the first transgression.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī arbitrarily goes outside the boundary to perform the formal act of *utkṣepaṇīya-karman* (suspension), she incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.

13. The Training Rule on Not Abandoning Wrong Views. The thirteenth training rule on not abandoning wrong views was occasioned at Śrāvastī. There was a bhikṣuṇī named Kālika who had formerly been a non-Buddhist; she constantly engaged in disputes and disturbances with the other bhikṣuṇīs, frequently saying:
"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

"It is not only this Śramaṇī daughter of the Śākyas who possesses such observance of the precepts, virtuous conduct, a sincere and upright disposition, and pure brahmacarya; there are likewise such virtuous persons in other places, and I shall go to them to practice the brahmacarya."
The nuns reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the nuns:
"You should privately admonish this nun of black complexion, or any other nun who acts likewise."
He should admonish her thus: "O Black Nun!
When engaged in a dispute, do not say:..."
"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

It is not only this Śramaṇī of the Śākya clan who possesses the virtue of observing the precepts and whose disposition is upright, pure, and good in her holy life; there are likewise such virtuous persons elsewhere. I shall go to them to practice the holy life."
“Kālī! You should now abandon such an evil view.
When the nuns followed the instructions and offered a private admonition, that nun remained stubbornly attached to her position and refused to relinquish it, speaking as follows:
"Only this is true; all else is false.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha told the nuns:

"You should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations) to admonish the nun Kālī. Ring the *ghanṭī*, and once the assembly of nuns has gathered, let one nun make the motion, followed by the *karman*."
“‘Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This Bhikṣuṇī Kālika has given rise to evil views; while engaged in a dispute, she spoke these words:
“I now renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha.”’”

"It is not only this Śramaṇī daughter of the Śākyas who possesses the virtue of observing the precepts and whose disposition is upright and purely good as a practitioner of the Brahma-faring; there are likewise such virtuous persons elsewhere, and I shall go to them to practice the Brahma-faring."
The bhikṣuṇīs went to admonish her in private; while being admonished in private, she did not relinquish her evil view, saying:
"This alone is true; all else is false."

"If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha authorize that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now perform the formal act of *karmavācanā* for this Bhikṣuṇī Kālī, who refuses to relinquish her wrong view."
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This black-clad bhikṣuṇī gave rise to an evil view and, during a time of dispute, spoke these words:
"I now renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

It is not only among these śramaṇa daughters of the Śākya clan that there are those who maintain the precepts and possess virtuous conduct, whose dispositions are upright and pure, and who practice the holy life; there are likewise such virtuous persons elsewhere. I shall go to them to practice the holy life."
The bhikṣuṇīs went to admonish her in private, but while being admonished, she did not relinquish her evil view, saying:
"This is the truth; all else is false."
"The Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha now performs the formal act of *karma* for this Bhikṣuṇī Kālika to relinquish her refusal to abandon a wrong view.
If the Venerable Ones consent to performing the *karma* of relinquishing the refusal to abandon a wrong view against the Bhikṣuṇī Kālika, let them remain silent; if you do not consent, please speak."
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are performed in the same manner.
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has completed the formal act of not relinquishing a wrong view against the Bhikṣuṇī Kālī."
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; I now hold it thus.

At that time, when the assembly of nuns acted according to the instruction and performed the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to admonish that nun, she remained obstinate regarding her matter and did not relinquish her evil view, saying:
"This is the truth; all else is false. What is it that I am holding to that you would have me relinquish?"
On account of this incident, the bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

For this reason, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, he explained the matter at length until he established the training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having engaged in quarrels and disturbances with other bhikṣuṇīs, should speak thus:”
"I renounce the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

It is not only this Śramaṇī of the Śākya clan who is endowed with precepts, endowed with virtue, and possesses superior wholesome qualities; other śramaṇas as well are endowed with precepts, endowed with virtue, and possess superior wholesome qualities. I shall go to them to practice the holy life."
Then the bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
"You should abandon this sinful and evil view.
When she was thus admonished, it was well if she abandoned it.
If he does not relinquish it, he should be earnestly and formally admonished up to three times, and questioned in accordance with the instruction, so that he may relinquish this matter.
If he relinquishes it, it is well;
if he does not relinquish it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
"Furthermore, regarding 'a bhikṣuṇī,' this refers to the Bhikṣuṇī Kālī or any other bhikṣuṇī.
The detailed explanation is the same as before.
If she relinquishes [the matter] when thus admonished, it is well."
If he does not relinquish it, he should be admonished two or three times, and then subjected to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* up to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, as explained in detail previously.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific circumstances?
If a bhikṣuṇī does not relinquish her position when being admonished individually, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense for each instance.
If she relinquishes it during the formal motion (jñapti), it is well; if she does not relinquish it, she incurs a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one relinquishes [the offense] at the time of the first *karmavācanā*, it is well; if one does not relinquish it, the offense is the same as before.
At the conclusion of the second recitation, one also incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one does not relinquish it when the third *karmavācanā* is completed, one incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (offense requiring formal meeting of the Saṃgha).

If they perform what is contrary to the Dharma yet the assembly is harmonious; or if they perform what is in accordance with the Dharma yet the assembly is not harmonious; or if they perform what resembles the Dharma yet the assembly is harmonious; or if they perform what resembles the Dharma yet the assembly is not harmonious; or if they carry out a legal procedure in a manner that is neither according to the Dharma, nor according to the Vinaya, nor as taught by the Buddha—the procedure is not validly established, and in all such cases there is no offense.
That bhikṣuṇī, having ascended the seat, shall address the great assembly, saying:
"Venerable sirs!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], have committed a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense."
If [she] does so, it is well.

If she does not speak, then until her offense has been confessed and expiated according to the Dharma, if she performs any of the formal procedures—ranging from a *jñapti-karman* to a *jñapticaturtha-karman*—together with other bhikṣuṇīs, for each instance she incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

14. The Training Rule on Speaking of Others’ Attachment and Hatred. The fourteenth training rule concerning speaking of others’ attachment and hatred was established while the Buddha was residing in Śrāvastī. At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika was constantly engaged in quarrels and disturbances with other bhikṣuṇīs, remaining in a state of harbored resentment.
The bhikṣuṇīs said: "Noble one!
Do not remain harboring resentment due to this quarrel."
They replied, “You all possess desire, hatred, fear, and delusion; therefore, regarding those who engage in quarrels, some are restrained while others are not.
The nuns reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"You should admonish the bhikṣuṇī Toraṇadā in private, saying:
'Do not speak such words.'"
"You who possess craving, aversion, fear, and delusion—some among those engaged in quarrels will restrain you, while others will not.
Sisters! You should cease these words and abandon this view.
When the bhikṣuṇīs admonished her in accordance with the Buddha’s instructions and teachings, she still did not repent and said:
"This teaching is true; all others are false.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"You should perform the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* against the bhikṣuṇī Pūrṇaśailā; it should be done in this manner:
ring the *gandī*, spread out the seats and mats, and when the Saṃgha has all assembled, one bhikṣuṇī shall make the formal motion (*jñapti*):"
“‘Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This Bhikṣuṇī Toraṇadattā constantly quarrels with and disturbs the other bhikṣuṇīs, dwelling in resentment.
The nuns admonished them, saying:
"Venerable ones!
Do not engage in quarrels and disturbances."
He replied:
"You possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; thus, regarding those who engage in disputes, some are restrained while others are not.
He remained obstinate and refused to relinquish his position, saying: "Only this dharma is real; all else is false."

"If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their consent, let the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permit that this Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā undergo the formal procedure of a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for not relinquishing her state of being possessed by craving, hatred, fear, and delusion."
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā constantly quarreled and caused disturbances with the other bhikṣuṇīs, dwelling in a state of resentment.
The bhikṣuṇīs admonished her, saying:
"Noble Lady!..."
"Do not engage in quarrels or disturbances.
They replied, "You possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; therefore, regarding those who engage in quarrels, you sometimes prohibit them and sometimes do not."
“‘Only this dharma is real; all others are false,’ she stubbornly clings to this and refuses to relinquish it.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the sake of the Bhikṣuṇī Cūḍāpanthaka (Tulanandā) to compel her to relinquish her attachment, hatred, fear, and delusion.”

Venerable sirs, if you approve of performing the *karman* of "not relinquishing" against the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā for her attachment, hatred, fear, and delusion, remain silent; if you do not approve, speak.
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third are also spoken in this manner.
'The Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha has completed the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for the nun Taurā regarding her refusal to relinquish [her state of] attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion.'"
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṅgha has already granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; I now hold it to be so.
Having thus admonished her earnestly and repeatedly, one should follow the instruction and interrogate her, causing her to relinquish this matter.

Having heard the Buddha’s instruction, the bhikṣuṇīs performed the formal procedure of *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (one motion and three proclamations) with the nun Tāpanī up to three times; however, she remained obstinate in her attachment and did not repent or relinquish her position.
Furthermore, on account of this matter, the bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
For this reason, as before, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, established a training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again engages in quarreling and strife with other bhikṣuṇīs..."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Sister! Do not engage in quarreling and disturbance."
This bhikṣuṇī speaks as follows:
"You possess attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; therefore, regarding those involved in a dispute, you either obstruct them or do not obstruct them."
The bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
"Venerable lady!
When others are admonishing you, do not speak in this manner."
"You have attachment, aversion, fear, and delusion; therefore, regarding those who engage in quarrels, you may either obstruct them or not obstruct them. "Sister!
Let this speech cease."
When the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner, it is well if she relinquishes [the matter].

If she does not relinquish it, they should admonish her earnestly and correctly two or three times, and following the instruction, they should interrogate her so as to cause her to relinquish that matter.
"If she renounces [this], it is well;
if she does not renounce it, it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense.
"Nun" refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
"Those who speak to the bhikṣuṇīs" refers to the nuns within this Dharma; that is, one should admonish them to cease quarreling and disturbances.
If they say they are acting out of attachment, aversion, fear, or delusion, one may offer a private admonition; if they abandon [the misconduct], it is well.

If he does not reform and repent, the same procedure of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*) shall be performed as before; he must be earnestly and formally admonished, and interrogated in accordance with the teaching.
If he relinquishes [the offense], it is well; if he does not relinquish it, he incurs the offense of a formal communal instruction (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*).
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are the specific matters?
If one relinquishes [the position] during the private admonition, it is well; if one does not relinquish it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing).
If one relinquishes it during the formal announcement (*jñapti*), it is well; if one does not relinquish it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* (grave offense).
If one relinquishes [the offense] at the time of the first *karmavācanā*, it is well; if one does not relinquish it, one incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense.
