The Training Rule on the One-Month Cloth. The third training rule, concerning the one-month cloth. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣus kept many extra robes; some obtained dark-blue cloth but did not immediately make a robe, instead merely keeping it in storage while hoping for more, thinking:
"If I obtain such similar material, I shall then make a robe."
Just as it was with the blue robes, so too did they collect yellow, red, and white ones, as well as those that were thick or thin.
At that time, the bhikṣus of few desires felt resentment and contempt, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu possess so many garments, accumulating and storing them away rather than making robes from them?"
The bhikṣu reported this to the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī has finished making her robes and the kaṭhina robe is subsequently suspended, and she obtains an out-of-season robe that she wishes to accept, she should accept it; having accepted it, she must quickly have the robe made up."
If there is a source from which one expects to obtain [the requisite], and one seeks to have it fulfilled, then if it remains insufficient, one may keep it for up to one month.
If this period is exceeded, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma.
Regarding the completion of the robes and the emergence from the kaṭhina period, there are four cases, as explained in detail previously.
Regarding the expression "obtaining out-of-season robes," what constitutes the season and what constitutes the non-season?
If the *kaṭhina* robe is not spread at the residence, the season lasts for one month, specifically from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the ninth month.

If the *kaṭhina* robe is spread in a residence, there is a period of five months; that is, from the sixteenth day of the eighth month to the fifteenth day of the first month is called "the proper time," while the remainder is called "the improper time."
"Having a source of expectation" means that one has few robes and seeks more.
"May be kept for one month" means that there is an expectation from parents, brothers, sisters, teachers, preceptors, or others that they will provide one with robes;
or that at a five-year assembly, a six-year assembly, a *cūḍā* assembly, or a youth assembly, one will obtain robes.
If one possesses [the full set], it is well; if one lacks even one of the five robes, one may keep them for up to one month.
If one keeps them beyond that, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, as explained in detail previously.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offenses and their specific details?
A summary verse states:
"Places where there is expectation and where there is no expectation; When expectation is severed, it is not the same as [wearing] the robe."
The distinctions between new and old, as well as discarded rags, and the measurements of strips and cubits are as follows:
if a bhikṣuṇī obtains a small piece of blue cloth on the first day of the month and keeps it without yet having made [a robe], [she incurs an offense].
If there is a source of expectation, thinking, "When I obtain such a garment of the same color,

I shall make it into a robe," and on that very day she obtains a garment of the same color, that bhikṣuṇī must, within ten days, either make it into a robe, keep it, discard it, or perform the formal ritual (karmavācanā).

If one does not keep, does not relinquish, and does not perform the formal ritual (*dharmakarma*) until the appearance of the dawn on the eleventh day, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī does not obtain another robe on the first day, but obtains one on the second day, or on the third day, or even up to the tenth day, that bhikṣuṇī must, within those ten days, make a robe from it, and she must keep it, relinquish it, or perform the formal ritual.
If one neither retains, nor discards, nor performs the formal ritual (karmavācanā), until the dawn of the eleventh day, it is likewise a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī does not obtain another robe on the tenth day, does not obtain one on the eleventh, does not obtain one on the twelfth, and so on until she does not obtain a robe on the nineteenth day, but only obtains another robe on the twentieth day, she should immediately perform the ritual as previously described.
If one does not perform the formal rite, one commits an offense of forfeiture and transgression (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

If a bhikṣuṇī has not obtained another robe for twenty-one days, and subsequently obtains another robe on the twenty-ninth day, she must, within the thirtieth day, either wear it, forfeit it, or perform the ritual of distribution.
If one does not perform the formal act [of relinquishment], and the dawn of the thirty-first day breaks, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Just as it is with obtaining a garment of blue color, the same applies to obtaining garments of any other color.
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a blue garment on a certain day and keeps it without processing it, having no other expectation for obtaining more, she then forms this thought:
"If I obtain another garment of the same color, I shall make a robe."
If on that very day she obtains a robe of a similar kind, the bhikṣuṇī must, within ten days, either make it into a robe or perform the formal relinquishment (nissaggiya).
If she does not perform the formal relinquishment, when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, it constitutes a nissaggiya-pāyattika offense.
If one does not obtain another robe on the first day, but obtains one on the second day, or even on the thirtieth day, it is as explained in detail above.
Just as it is with obtaining a blue robe, the same applies to obtaining robes of other colors and similar matters.

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a blue garment on a certain day and keeps it without making it into a robe, provided there is a source from which she hopes to obtain more; however, if that source is far off in time, does not meet her requirements, or she lacks the power to acquire it, or if she obtains a blue garment on that very day, she must make it into a robe within ten days.
Thus it is explained in detail, up until the point where it is obtained after thirty days.
The same applies to other colored robes as previously described.

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a blue robe on a certain day and keeps it without making it into a formal robe, provided there is a source from which she expects to obtain more; even though she has not yet received the expected robe, her intention does not cease. Or, if on that very day she obtains a blue robe, it is to be explained in detail as before.
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a blue-colored robe on a certain day and keeps it without processing it, provided she has the expectation of obtaining more;
if the source of her expectations is completely cut off, that bhikṣuṇī must, within ten days, either keep the robe she obtained or relinquish it, as explained in detail previously.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying: "Bhadanta,
how many kinds of robes are there?"
The Buddha said:
"There are two kinds:
first, new; second, old."
"New" refers to what has been newly woven; "old" refers to that which has already been worn for four months.
Upāli! Furthermore, there are five kinds of robes:
1. Robes offered by a donor; 2. Robes without a donor; 3. Robes obtained through exchange; 4. Robes from a corpse; 5. Refuse rags.
What is clothing with a donor?
It refers to clothing for which a male, female, or *paṇḍaka* acts as the donor.
What is clothing without a donor?
This refers to cases where neither men, women, nor *paṇḍaka* serve as the donors.
What is meant by "clothing for returning"?

It is when the relatives of a deceased person, out of grief and remembrance, present clothing with the corpse and place it upon the body to be taken to the cremation site; once the cremation and burial are complete, they bring back this clothing and offer it as a gift to the Saṃgha.
What is a "dead person's garment"?
It is the garment of one who has died in a charnel ground, which is not claimed or possessed by anyone.
What is a "rag-robe" (pāṃśukūla)?
There are five kinds. What are the five?
First, clothing discarded on the road; second, clothing from a refuse heap; third, clothing discarded by a riverbank; fourth, clothing worn by ants; and fifth, tattered clothing.
Furthermore, there are five kinds:
first, clothing burned by fire; second, clothing soaked by water; third, clothing gnawed by mice; fourth, clothing chewed by oxen; and fifth, clothing discarded by a wet-nurse.

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains new cloth and wishes to make robes, she should wash, dye, cut, and sew it: two layers for the saṃghāṭī, two layers for the niṣīdana, one layer for the uttarāsaṅga, and one layer for the antarvāsaka.

If a bhikṣuṇī has made a saṃghāṭī of two layers and wishes to add a third layer, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense at the time of patching it; when the dawn light appears on the eleventh day, she commits the offense of naiḥsargika-pāyattika.

If a bhikṣuṇī removes the old lining from a new saṃghāṭī with the intention of using it for another purpose, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense at the time of removal; when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, she commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī removes the lining from a new saṃghāṭī, washes, dyes, and sews it, and intends to reattach it, there is no offense.
However, if she has not finished reattaching it by the time the dawn of the eleventh day appears, it is a naiḥsargika offense.
Just as it is with the *saṃghāṭī*, the same applies to the *niṣīdana*.

If a bhikṣuṇī has a new *uttarāsaṅga* with a second patch, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of patching; when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, she commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
The same applies to the *antarvāsa*.

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains an old garment and wishes to make robes from it, she should wash, dye, and sew it; four layers are made for the *saṃghāṭī*, four layers for the *niṣīdana*, and two layers for the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *antarvāsa*.

If a bhikṣuṇī possesses two layers of an uttarāsaṅga and an antarvāsaka, and wishes to add a third layer, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense at the time of patching it on; when the dawn of the eleventh day appears, she commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, regarding this heavy robe, wishes to remove it, or whether she places it on or does not place it on [the body], there are offenses and non-offenses as explained in detail above.
If a bhikṣuṇī goes back and forth with a corpse’s robe that has an owner, one should know [the rules] based on its newness or oldness and its weight.
When it comes to *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) robes, one may, according to one's inclination, make them in any number of layers without limit.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhadanta!..."
“How many kinds of saṃghāṭī robes are there,
and what are their measurements?
The Buddha told Upāli:
“There are nine distinct types.
What are the nine? They are:
those with nine strips, eleven strips, thirteen strips, fifteen strips, seventeen strips, nineteen strips, twenty-one strips, twenty-three strips, and twenty-five strips.”

"Upāli! The first three types of robes have two lengths and one shortness; the next three types of robes have three lengths and one shortness; and the last three types of robes have four lengths and one shortness. These should be made and worn; beyond these measurements, they become patched rags (pāṃśukūla)."
Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Venerable Sir,
how many distinctions are there regarding the size of robes?"
The Buddha said:
"There are three types of saṃghāṭī robes:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior."
The superior [robe] is three cubits in height and five cubits in width; the inferior is two and a half cubits in height and four and a half cubits in width;

those between these two are called the middling. As for the *uttarāsaṅga* and the *antarvāsaka*, there are likewise three types—superior, middling, and inferior—their measurements being as described for the *saṃghāṭī*.
"Upāli! Furthermore, there are two kinds of *antarvāsas*:
one with two vertical sections and five horizontal sections, and one with two vertical sections and four horizontal sections."
If the antavaśa (undergarment) is placed at the very bottom so that it covers only the three wheels [of the body], it is the smallest among the types of robes to be worn.
If the niḥsargika-cīvara (robe subject to forfeiture) is of the most extreme minimum size, it measures only one cubit in both length and width.
If a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika), she should perform the three procedures as described above.
Herein, the rules for the three robes are stated in brief; the details regarding the *guṇakā* and the *saṃkakṣikā* are fully explained in other places.

4. The Training Rule on Having a Bhikṣu Who Is Not a Relative Wash Old Clothes. The fourth training rule concerning having a bhikṣu who is not a relative wash old clothes. At that time, the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita Heaven and took birth in the house of King Śuddhodana in the city of Kapilavastu; at that moment, a great reputation spread in the four directions, saying that a prince had been born into the Śākya clan.

On the slopes of the Snowy Mountains, by the banks of the Salt River, at the dwelling place of the seer Kapila, not far from there lived a brahmin seer named Asita, who was skilled in the interpretation of omens and physiognomy. The king summoned him to examine [the child], and he prophesied two possibilities:

"If he remains at home, he will become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin) ruling over the four continents, a great holy sovereign endowed with the seven treasures—namely, the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the military-commander-treasure. He will have a full thousand sons of great power, peerless in valor and strength, capable of subduing all enemies. Throughout this entire earth, reaching to the very limits of the four oceans, there will be no thieves nor cruel punishments; he will govern the people according to the Dharma, and they shall dwell in peace and security."

If one leaves the household life, shaving off hair and beard and departing from home for the homeless state with right faith, one shall attain the state of a Buddha, an Arhat, a Samyaksaṃbuddha, whose fame shall spread throughout the ten directions as he extensively delivers all classes of beings.

At that time, the great kings of all the nations, having heard and learned that the Śākya Prince had been born on the Snowy Mountains and was extensively saving all classes of beings, each thought to themselves:
"I should now go to serve the Prince, so that in the future I may receive his blessings and prosperity."
He further thought to himself:
"At present, I have no opportunity to see the Prince; however, if I serve King Śuddhodana, it will be as if I am serving the Prince's person."
At that time, all the kings dispatched envoys bearing their national credentials to King Śuddhodana.

Later, as the Bodhisattva was raised in the inner palace and gradually grew older, he became distressed at heart upon witnessing old age, sickness, and death; he subsequently departed for the forest to abandon worldly affairs.
When the various kings heard of these matters, they all thought to themselves:
"The reason we serve King Śuddhodana is that we wish to serve the Prince;

yet now that the Prince has gone to the forest seeking liberation, why should we continue to serve him in vain, wasting our resources? We shall therefore sever all communication with his messengers and the envoys from our various kingdoms."

At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala and King Śuddhodana shared a bordering realm; although the exchange of gifts had ceased, envoys still traveled back and forth between them. From time to time, they dispatched messengers to inquire after one another, and the minister sent by [King Prasenajit] was named Gopaka.
At that time, Guptaka went to King Śuddhodana; after discussing matters of state, he took up residence in the house of the minister Udāyin.
Whenever King Śuddhodana sent a messenger to inquire after King Prasenajit, he would dispatch the minister Udāyin to go.
At that time, Udāyin arrived at the city of Śrāvastī and met King Prasenajit. After discussing matters of state with the king, he took up residence in the house of Guptā.
At that time, Guptā had a wife named Gopā, who was of upright and dignified appearance and pleasing to behold. Then Udāyin committed an unrighteous act with Gopā.
At that time, having heard that his wife had a secret and intimate liaison with Udāyin, Guhyaka thought to himself:
"I shall take the lives of these two wicked people."
Later, he reflected further:
"If I were to kill him, it would throw the royal city into turmoil and cause great alarm.
How could I, for the sake of this sinful woman, kill a Brahmin?"
He then abandoned the matter and did not inquire further.
Later, at another time, Guptika died; because King Prasenajit had no son, all of his wealth and possessions were taken into the royal treasury.
When Udāyin heard of this matter, he thought to himself:
"How can I ensure that Guptā has no one to rely upon while I am still alive?"
He then contemplated the matter of benefit and harm during the night, and at dawn went to King Śuddhodana and addressed him thus:
"Your Majesty, since your kingdom borders that of King Prasenajit, and seeing such unstable circumstances as these, you ought to dispatch an envoy there to deliberate upon them."
"If you do not inquire, you will surely invite disaster and ruin.
The King then replied,
"If that is the case, you shall serve as an envoy and go there to deliberate."
Then Udāyin immediately set out for Śrāvastī, thinking to himself:
"Should I see the Great King first, or should I see the ministers first?"
Having had this thought, he further reflected:
"The principle for seeking a matter is to begin from the bottom.
He then went to the royal minister and set forth his original intention, saying:
"I wish to request King [Śrīgupta] for Gupṭā; I pray that Your Majesty will favor me by assisting my request.
Having heard this, the minister agreed to the matter.
Thereupon, Udāyin went to King Prasenajit to discuss state affairs, and he said to the king:
"I pray that Your Majesty will grant me a place to stay.
The King asked,
"Where have you stayed previously?"
He replied,
"I previously stayed at the house of Guptaka.
The king said:
"It would now be appropriate to return and stay at that place.
He then addressed the king, saying,
"Mihuhu has died."
The king said,
"Even though the master of the house has died,
how could the house itself die? Udāyin replied:
"Although the householder himself does not die, his property and possessions have all vanished.
The King commanded his ministers, saying:
"Seek out a place where Udāyin may find rest and security."
The minister said, "There is no other place for them to stay.
However, he previously had an illicit liaison with Guptā; it was for this reason that I originally intended to report the matter."
“If Your Majesty can now accept this man, you will have accepted King Śuddhodana as well.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit immediately dispatched a messenger to summon Udāyin, and said to him: “Udāyin!
"I truly did not know that you and Gupta had previously been intimate.
Now I give Gupta to you as a wife; I shall also provide you with both the house and its wealth."
Then Udāyin bowed in thanks and departed.
At that time, when Gopā heard that Udāyin had come to her house, she immediately went out to the door and wept aloud.
When Udāyin arrived at the door, he asked Gopā,
"For what reason are you weeping? Gopā replied:
"The husband I love has passed away; would you, O Benevolent One, now likewise abandon me?
Udāyin replied, "I came here specifically for your sake, and have already informed the King."
"You and your household goods have both been granted to you;
will you remain here for this reason, or will you go toward the city of Kapilavastu?
Guptā thought to herself:
"If I go to Kapilavastu now, the Brahmin’s wife will not spare my life; it would be best for me to remain at my own home.
At that time, Udāyin came to have two residences:
one in his own house and one in the house of the Brahmin.
One was in Kapilavastu and one was in Śrāvastī.

At that time, after the Bodhisattva had practiced asceticism for six years without possessing anything, he then desired to partake of superior and exquisite food according to his wish. He immediately smeared his body all over with rice, food, and various ghee and oils, and bathed himself with warm water; he then proceeded to the village of Vijitāvin to visit two cowherd girls:
the first named Nandā and the second named Nandabalā.
Having received sixteenfold milk-rice and eaten his fill, he went again to where the man Sudāna was; as he took the *śara* grass, the Naga King Kālika offered praise.
The Bodhisattva approached the foot of the Bodhi tree, personally spreading the grass so that it was not disarrayed, and sat down cross-legged.
With body upright and mind focused, he thought and spoke these words:
"If I have not yet completely severed all outflows (*āsrava*), I shall never break this cross-legged posture."
At that time, before the Bodhisattva had even finished breaking his cross-legged posture, all delusions were completely exhausted.

Then, after the World-Honored One had subdued the armies of thirty-six billion māras and realized all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*), he accepted the invitation of the Brahma King and proceeded to Vārāṇasī. There, he turned the Wheel of Dharma with its twelve aspects in three revolutions, delivering the five bhikṣus and those who followed them. He then traveled to the Śuklodana Forest, where he delivered the sixty members of the Bhadravarga and established them in the vision of the Truth (*satyadarśana*).
Furthermore, he arrived at the village of Jayasena, where he delivered two cowherd girls and caused them also to realize the Truth.
He then proceeded to the vicinity of the Uruvilvā forest, where he ordained one thousand non-Buddhist practitioners as renunciants and conferred upon them full ordination.
Furthermore, he went to the summit of Mount Gayā and manifested the three miraculous transformations, teaching and transforming beings so that they might abide in the peace of *nirvāṇa*.

He then proceeded to the Śāla Grove, causing King Bimbisāra, the lord of Magadha, to dwell in the vision of the Truth (*satyadarśana*), while also delivering eighty hundred thousand celestial hosts who had gathered there, as well as immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Brahmins from the kingdom of Magadha.
Next, he arrived at Rājagṛha and accepted the Bamboo Grove Monastery (Veṇuvana-vihāra), where he also granted Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana the going forth and full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
Subsequently, he went to Śrāvastī and accepted the Jeta Grove Anāthapiṇḍada Park (Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍadārāma).
Next, having arrived in Kośala and delivered the *Kumāra-sūtra*, he caused King Prasenajit to attain the vision of the Truth (*dṛṣṭi*) and then resided in the Jetavana Grove.
At that time, King Prasenajit dispatched a messenger with a letter to King Śuddhodana, saying:
"Great King!..."

"O King, rejoice now! The Prince has already realized unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment and causes all sentient beings to partake of the nectar of immortality; he currently resides within the Jeta Grove."
When King Śuddhodana heard this message, he rested his cheek in his hand and sighed with sorrow:
"In the past, when Prince Sarvārthasiddha was practicing austerities, I constantly sent messengers to inquire after his well-being."
The messenger returned shortly after to report my location, yet despite sending messengers one after another, not a single one has returned.
Now that you have arrived within the Jeta Grove, what is the state of affairs?
Then the minister Udāyin went before the king and said to him: "Great King,
why do you sit with your hand supporting your cheek, dwelling in sorrow?"
The king said,
"How could I not harbor anxiety now? In the past,
when Prince Sarvārthasiddha was practicing austerities, I constantly dispatched messengers to inquire after his well-being."
The messenger soon returned to report my whereabouts; however, since he was sent to inquire, not a single person has returned.
Now there is news saying:
"The Prince Sarvārthasiddha has realized unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, and he has invited all sentient beings to partake together in the nectar of immortality at the Jeta Grove."
"Would you not then have cause for concern?
At that time, Udāyin addressed the King, saying:
"If it be so, I request to serve as an envoy and return with this letter."
The King said,
"If you go, you shall remain there and not return. Udāyin replied:
"Having received the Great King’s command, how could I dare not come?
At that time, King Śuddhodana composed a letter himself, saying:
"From the very moment of conception, I nurtured the World-Honored One;..."
The fire of afflictions burns constantly; I have always longed for the tree of supreme victory.
Now that you have attained Buddhahood, your assembly is infinite in number;
while other people enjoy peace and happiness, I alone have not yet removed my suffering.
Having finished writing and affixed the seal, he gave it to Udāyin.

Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately spoke a verse for the sake of his father, the King:
"The disciples of the Muni all possess great majesty and virtue;
whether it be the three knowledges or the six supernormal powers, there is none among them who is not fully endowed with these."
At that time, King Śuddhodana thought to himself:
"It is not only my son who possesses great majesty and power; there are other bhikṣus as well who possess such great supernormal powers."
The pride that had previously arisen was immediately severed.
At that time, the king thought again:
"Now the World-Honored One accepts offerings only from humans; I do not see any devas."
Mahāmaudgalyāyana, knowing the king’s thought, addressed him, saying:
“Great King!
I now wish to return to the presence of the World-Honored One.”
He replied, "As you wish.

Then King Śuddhodana also went to where the Buddha was. At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts of his father the king, immediately transformed the entire Kūṭāgāra forest into crystal (*sphaṭika*).
When the king wished to enter through the eastern gate, the gatekeeper reported,
"Great King!
Do not enter."
The king asked,
"What is the meaning of this?
The gatekeeper replied:
"The Buddha is now preaching the Dharma exclusively for the devas.
The king asked his gatekeeper:
"Worthy sir!"
"Who are you? The gatekeeper replied,
"Great King!"
"I am Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Heavenly King of the East.
He then proceeded toward the southern gate, wishing to see the World-Honored One, whereupon the gatekeeper addressed him, saying:
"Great King!"
"Do not enter.
The king asked,
"For what reason?"
The gatekeeper replied,
"The Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma exclusively for the devas.
The king asked the gatekeeper:
"O noble one! Who are you? He replied:
"I am Virūḍhaka, the Heavenly King of the South.
He then proceeded toward the western gate, desiring to see the World-Honored One, whereupon the gatekeeper addressed him, saying:
"Great King!..."
"Do not enter.
The king asked,
"For what reason?"
The gatekeeper replied,
"The Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma exclusively for the devas.
The king asked the gatekeeper:
“O noble one! Who are you?
The gatekeeper replied:
"I am Virūpākṣa, the Heavenly King of the West.
He then proceeded toward the northern gate, wishing to see the World-Honored One, whereupon the gatekeeper addressed him, saying:
"Great King!
"Do not enter.
The king asked,
"For what reason?"
The gatekeeper replied,
"The Buddha is currently preaching the Dharma exclusively for the devas.
The king asked the gatekeeper:
"O worthy one! Who are you?
The gatekeeper replied:
"I am Vaiśravaṇa, the Heavenly King of the North.

At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal power, empowered King Śuddhodana so that he saw from outside the gate the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma to the assembly of devas.
When the king saw this, he thought to himself:
"Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is not only being venerated by the multitude of people, but is also being personally attended by the various devas who have come here."
Once King Śuddhodana’s pride had been quelled, Mahāmaudgalyāyana withdrew his supernormal powers.
He then led King Śuddhodana to see the World-Honored One; having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, he sat down to one side.

At that time, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the inclinations, latent tendencies, and dispositions of King Śuddhodana and the other members of the assembly, preached the Dharma according to their capacities. He caused King Śuddhodana to shatter the high mountain of the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity) with the vajra-thunderbolt of wisdom, thereby attaining the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Having realized this fruit, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

What I have now realized was not created by my ancestors, nor was it created by my parents; it was not created by kings, nor by devas, nor by śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, nor could it have been created by any of my kinsmen.

It is by relying on the World-Honored One as my spiritual friend that I have now attained this matter: I have been rescued from and delivered out of the three evil realms of hell-beings, animals, and hungry ghosts, and established in the human and celestial realms;
I shall exhaust the limits of birth and death until the end of the future, dry up the vast oceans of milk and blood, and cross over the great mountain of white bones.
That which has been accumulated since beginningless time—the cave-dwelling of the view of a self—is now entirely cast aside, and this wondrous fruit is realized.
O Virtuous One!
I have now emerged from the stream of birth and death.
I now take refuge in the Triple Gem of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, and become a lay follower (*upāsaka*).

May the World-Honored One, out of compassion, deign to witness this: from this day forth until the end of my life, I shall refrain from taking the lives of sentient beings and so forth, up to refraining from drinking all kinds of intoxicants; I reverently accept these five precepts of training from the World-Honored One.
Then King Śuddhodana, having paid homage to the Buddha, departed and went to King Śuklodana, saying:
"Brother, you should now accept the royal throne. He replied:
"What is your intention?
the king asked.
He replied, "I have now realized the Truth; I cannot serve as king."
He asked, "When? and he replied:
"Today," he replied,
"I attained the vision of the Truth on the very day the World-Honored One first arrived."
Next he went to King Droṇodana, and afterwards to King Amṛtodana, hoping to offer them the royal throne;
they both replied, "We have already seen the Truth."
King Śuddhodana said, "If this is so,
whom do I now wish to anoint on the crown of the head to receive the royal throne?
He then replied:
"The Śākya youth named Bhadrika shall succeed to the royal throne.
Understanding the King's intention, he silently accepted.
Then, King Śuddhodana immediately performed the consecration upon his head and bestowed the royal throne upon Bhadrika.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus entered the royal palace every day to receive his offerings. Then King Śuddhodana thought to himself:

"Now these disciples of the Buddha were formerly followers of non-Buddhist paths; though their minds are upright, their bodies are not well-proportioned, for due to their former asceticism their appearances are emaciated and haggard."
"How may we cause the disciples of the World-Honored One to possess such a pleasing appearance that those who see them give rise to wholesome thoughts?
If members of the Śākya clan were to accompany the World-Honored One, then they would truly be dignified and worthy of the respect of all."
At that time, King Śuddhodana assembled the Śākyas and addressed them, saying:
"Gentlemen, you should know:
if Prince Sarvārthasiddha does not renounce the household life, what will he do?"
They all replied,
“He will become a wheel-turning monarch.
He asked again:
"What are you doing? they asked.
They replied, "We have declared ourselves subjects and serve as your attendants."
The King spoke again, saying:
"Now that Prince Sarvārthasiddha has realized the Dharma of the Deathless and intends to let all sentient beings partake of this flavor as well, for what reason do you not follow him?"
They all replied, “We wish to go forth; we will follow behind the World-Honored One.
The king said:
"Go each according to your own wish.
The Śākyas said,
"Are we to go as an entire family together?"
"Is it one person from each household?
The king replied,
"One person from each household."
At that time, King Śuddhodana shook his bell and issued a proclamation, addressing the Śākyas:
"One person from each household shall renounce the world to serve the Buddha; those who refuse will surely incur blame and reprimand."
At that very moment, five hundred Śākyas, including Bhadrika and Aniruddha, all went forth from the household life.
As the Blessed One had said:
"Those who renounce their noble lineage to go forth will receive much gain and support."
At that time, the five hundred Śākya bhikṣus received an abundance of offerings and requisites.
