The remainder of the training rule concerning washing old robes with a bhikṣu who is not a relative. At that time, the Blessed One had this thought:
"These sons of the Śākyas originally left the home life seeking liberation, yet now they have abandoned their few desires and become attached to wealth and profit.
Desiring to sever their pursuit of offerings, the World-Honored One immediately returned to the city of Śrāvastī and stayed in the Jeta Grove, dwelling there as he had before.

Then, during the first part of the day, the Venerable Udāyin took his robe and bowl and entered the city of Śrāvastī; proceeding on his almsround, he arrived at the gate of the former house of Guptā and stood there.
At that time, Gopā saw him from afar and recognized him immediately; she struck her breast with her hand and said, "Udāyin!
For what reason have you now abandoned me to go forth into the religious life?"
He replied: "O noble one!

When our World-Honored One was a bodhisattva, he renounced his precious consort Yaśodharā, Gopikā, Mṛgajā, and sixty thousand other court ladies to leave the household life. Who could possibly sink into the mire with you, who are but a speck of dust?"
Guptā replied, "If that is so, I too shall go forth.
He answered:
"Excellent! Gupatā said,
"I shall now settle my household affairs and soon go forth into the religious life."
Udāyin said, "You should go quickly and not delay," and then he departed,
leaving him behind.
However, at various times Udāyin came frequently to visit and inquire after him, saying,
"You have not yet gone forth.
He replied:
"My household affairs have not yet been concluded. Udāyin said,
"Must you wait until the Kingdom of Kośala has been reduced to ashes before your household affairs can be finished?"
Guptā said, "I shall gather my belongings this very day; tomorrow I shall go forth into the religious life.
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself:

"At this time, due to my past worldly entanglements, I am already held in contempt by my fellow practitioners who carry black alms bowls; how much more so would it invite further ridicule if I were to cause them to go forth, leading others to say:
'The group of six bhikṣus have ordained bhikṣuṇīs'?"
He then felt regret.
When dawn broke, he took up his robes and bowl and headed for Rājagṛha; having arrived there, he entered the rains retreat.
At that time, having entrusted her household affairs to them, Gupta went to the Jetavana Grove on another day and asked the bhikṣus,
"Where has he gone?"
The bhikṣu asked, "Who is that? He replied:
"Noble Udayin! the bhikṣus replied,
"He has already departed for the great city of Rājagṛha."
Having heard these words, she immediately wept. The bhikṣu asked, “Guptā!
For what reason do you weep?”

She replied, "The noble Udāyin told me to renounce worldly life and permitted my ordination; I have already entrusted my household estate to him, yet he has now abandoned me and departed. I am neither a laywoman nor an ordained nun; how could I not be distressed?"
One man replied, "He went toward the royal city for the sake of a razor, wishing to obtain a new blade to shave your hair anew.
At that time, the community of bhikṣuṇīs had come to the Jetavana Grove to request instruction; seeing Guptā walking along, weeping and despondent, they asked her:
"Guptā! For what reason are you weeping?
Guptā then related the preceding events in detail to the bhikṣuṇī.
The nuns replied, "You are truly ignorant; how could a bhikṣu ever ordain a bhikṣuṇī?
We shall instead have you ordained by the community of nuns."
"Come with me to Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī; she will ordain you and allow you to leave the household life.
Then the community of nuns took Gupṭā to Mahāprajāpatī’s place and said to her, "Noble Lady!"
"This woman Gopā wishes to go forth [into the religious life].
Then Mahāprajāpatī immediately granted her the going forth.
At that time, Udāyin was in Rājagṛha and had this thought:
“It is because I wish to protect and cherish those who carry black alms-bowls that I did not grant Guptā ordination; otherwise, I would have lost my waist-straps and other personal requisites.
If some other holder of a black bowl were to ordain Guptā, I would have no means even to catch a fleeting glimpse of her.”
Although he remained in retreat during the summer rains, his mind was constantly dissatisfied.
At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who, having completed the summer retreat at Śrāvastī, arrived at Rājagṛha.

At that time, Udāyin was standing by the side of a major road outside the Bamboo Grove Monastery, looking about as he waited. He then saw from afar an elderly bhikṣu approaching; his hair was like reed blossoms, his eyebrows were long and drooped down over his face, and with hunched shoulders and arms hanging low, he walked with slow steps.
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself,
"Who is this approaching senior monk?
Having drawn near, he addressed him, saying:
"Welcome! Welcome! Elder!"
The elderly bhikṣu said:
"I pay homage to the ācārya!
I pay homage to the upādhyāya!"

At that time, Udāyin, seeing that he behaved without restraint and did not recognize his two teachers, realized immediately that he must be a mahallaka. He then led him into the monastery and asked, "Where have you come from?"
He replied,
"I have come from Śrāvastī.
At that time, Udāyin thought to himself:
"If I were to ask about Guptā’s news first, those who hear it would find it shameful and offensive; therefore, I should ask in due order.
Since you, Mahallaka, have come from there, do you know if the World-Honored One is free from illness and affliction, and whether his daily life is light, easy, and peaceful?"
"Is he observing the summer retreat in Śrāvastī?
He replied, "The World-Honored One is free from illness and at ease; he is observing the retreat there."
He asked again:

"Are the assemblies of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas and upāsikās, all free from illness and dwelling in peace and comfort as usual; and do they, from time to time, pay their respects to the World-Honored One and listen to the True Dharma?"
He replied,
"The persons you asked about have all attained peace and security, and from time to time they come to hear the True Dharma.
He asked again:

"Are the venerable elders who have attained mastery in the teachings—such as Kauṇḍinya, Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others—as well as the Great Lady Gautamī, King Prasenajit, the householder Vijayin, the long-time friend Mṛgāramātṛ Viśākhā, and the lady Sujātā, all dwelling in health and peace?"
He replied, "They are all dwelling in peace and happiness.
He asked again:
"Do you recognize the householder's wife, Guptā?
He replied, "I do;
she was the former wife of the Venerable Udāyin."
Udāyin said, "Is she still the wife of that elder even now?
He replied:
"He has already gone forth.
Udāyin asked, "Who ordained him?"
He replied, "It is Mahāprajāpatī.
Udāyin then thought to himself:
"Since you have gone forth as a renunciant, it is possible we may meet again.
He then called out, "Māhāra!"
"Come now, let us wash our feet.
Then Udāyin took his robes and bowl and hung them upon a very high ivory peg; he then gave him much oil for anointing his hands and feet, saying:
"In this room there is food and profit; you should dwell here with a mind of peace and joy."
He replied, “I do not wish to stay here.
Then Udāyin handed over the keys and said:
"As the World-Honored One has said:
'A bhikṣu should not abandon his dwelling place and depart without due cause. O Mahāla!"
"This is the lock and key; you should know it for yourself.

Having said these words, he set out on the road and gradually reached Śrāvastī. Inside the Jeta Grove, he swept and cleaned the rooms, smeared them with cow dung, closed one door, and lay down upon his bed, chanting the True Dharma in a melodic voice.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had come there to request instruction. When the other bhikṣuṇīs heard the sound of this recitation and recognized its melody, they went together to Udāyin and asked him:
"Venerable Sir!..."
When he had walked away, [the other] asked, "From where have you come? He replied,
"I was previously heading toward the city of Rājagṛha."
Having learned this from the nun, she returned and told Guptā:
"You are now filled with joy; the Ācārya has already arrived. Guptā asked:
“Who is this ācārya? He replied, “It is Udāyin!”
Guptā said: "For what reason is he my ācārya?
How could I have received instruction in the studies from him!"
The nuns replied, "You speak such words without understanding; there are many nuns who are closely associated with the great bhikṣus. You should now go and inquire after their well-being."
He then took powdered incense, oil, and bathing requisites, went to that room, knocked on the door,
and called out. Udāyin asked,
"Who is knocking at the door?"
She replied, "I am Gopā. Udāyin said:
"Welcome! Welcome!
Lady of the householder, please enter as you please."
At that time, Gupṭā entered and said,
"Venerable Sir,
am I truly the wife of a householder?"
"I have already left the household life.
He asked, "Who ordained you?"
He replied,
"Noble One! It is Mahāprajāpatī."
Udāyin said, "I have other business that requires me to go to Rājagṛha; for what reason do you so urgently seek to leave the household life?
He then replied:
"Is it not true that the Venerable One previously said these words:
'You should gather in your household affairs; I shall ordain you and let you go forth'?
Relying upon this instruction, I entrusted my family estate to him, yet the Venerable One abandoned me and went far away toward the royal city."
"If the Great Mistress of the World had not delivered me, I would truly be neither a layperson nor one who has gone forth.
Udāyin said, "How could I have personally taken up this heavy burden at that time to promise to instruct you? For now, you may sit, and I shall preach the Dharma for you."
Having paid his respects, he sat down and listened to the Dharma with a composed mind. Then Udāyin preached the Dharma for him, recalling past instances of laughter and joy, and asked:
"Do you remember how, in the past, at such-and-such a garden, grove, forest, or shrine, you partook of such exquisite and delicious food?"
When these words were spoken, lustful thoughts immediately arose and her mind became deranged.
It is a characteristic mark of wise women that they possess a unique discernment, enabling them to know whether a man has lustful intentions or not.
Guptā, perceiving that Udāyin’s lustful mind was burning intensely, said to him:
"Venerable One!
I must go out for a moment; I will return as soon as my business is finished."
Udāyin thought to himself,
"Is he wishing to go out for the sake of relieving himself?
He then allowed him to go out for a moment.
Having emerged, Gupta pulled up her robes and fled in haste.
Hearing the sound of her running, Udāyin then went outside his room and pursued her, calling out:
"Shaveling woman, where are you going?"
He pursued her even more urgently; as his generative organ touched her thigh, his semen was discharged. Once his lustful desire had subsided, he stood there, pacing back and forth.
Knowing this, Gupta returned and said, "Noble One!..."
"If I were to remain [in this state], I would not be a bhikṣuṇī,
and you, sir, would not be a bhikṣu. Udāyin said, "Sister!"
As the Blessed One has said:
"If one protects oneself, that is protecting others; if one protects others, that constitutes protecting oneself.
In what way does protecting oneself constitute protecting others?
Because one attains realization through personally practicing and cultivating [the path] repeatedly, protecting oneself thereby constitutes protecting others.
How is it that protecting others becomes the protection of oneself?
"To be without vexation, without anger, and without a mind of enmity or harm, always giving rise to compassion and pity for all beings— this is called protecting others,
which simultaneously constitutes protecting oneself. Gupitā replied, "Noble One!"
"You may take off your lower garment and bring it here; I shall wash it for you.
At that time, Udāyin immediately handed over the garment.
When Gopā saw the semen upon the garment, remorse arose within her, and she thought to herself:
"Since my body has not yet been touched or seen by a noble one (*ārya*), I shall not follow this unwholesome course.
Having thought thus, his defiled mind increased all the more. As stated in a verse from the Buddha’s sūtras:
"Those who are addicted to desire do not perceive what is beneficial."
"Nor do they contemplate wholesome dharmas; they always walk in darkness.
At that time, because her mind was agitated by desire, Guptā took a single drop of semen and placed it in her mouth, and then took another drop and inserted it into her female organ.
The workings of sentient beings' karma are inconceivable; at that time, the intermediate state aggregates of his final birth arrived and took up residence there.
When Guptā reached the monastery, she immediately began washing the robes.
When the nuns saw her and questioned her, Gupitā related the matter in full.
The nuns said to her, "We thought you had gone to the Great Virtuous One to seek the sublime Dharma; how could we have known there was such an evil deed?"
Guptā replied, "That venerable one is a keeper of the precepts; since his ordination, he has never again touched my body.
The nuns said:
"If such a thing occurs even when there is no physical contact with the body parts, what would you do if there were actual contact?
When the bhikṣuṇīs learned of this matter, they went and informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"That nun has not committed a pārājika offense.
If she is pregnant, she should be placed in a secluded room and provided with food and supplies so that her needs are not lacking."

"In the future, you shall give birth to a son who shall be named Kumāra-Kāśyapa; he will go forth as a renunciant within my Dharma, sever all outflows, and become an Arhat. Among my disciples, he shall be foremost in possessing eloquence and skill in preaching."
At that time, the Blessed One thought to himself:
"If there is a bhikṣuṇī who washes old clothes for a bhikṣu who is not a relative, such a fault will arise."

For this reason, the Blessed One assembled the community as before, questioned her regarding the facts, and rebuked her. He spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī has a non-relative bhikṣu wash, dye, or beat a used robe, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
"Regarding the term 'bhikṣuṇī,' it refers to Gupatā or any other nun.
As for the term 'relative,' it means that those descending from both the paternal and maternal ancestors up to the seventh generation are all kin; beyond this, they are no longer so."
"The bhikṣu" refers to Udāyin.
"Old clothing" refers to any one of the seven types of robes.
What are the seven?

First is *roma*; second is *bimbara*, which does not exist in this region; third is *śaṇaka*, which does not exist in this region; fourth is *karpāsika*, meaning white cotton cloth; fifth is *dukūlaka*, meaning linen cloth; sixth is *kauśeyaka*, meaning a fine woolen cloak, which does not exist in this region; seventh is *āpānandika*, which is the name of a place in the north, and it is there that this garment is produced.
There is also an interpretation which states that these refer to types of coarse silk (*śāṭaka*) and so forth.
"Washing" means soaking with water.
"Dyeing" refers to applying color even as little as a single immersion.
"Striking" means even striking once with the hand.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" is explained in detail as before.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances?
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a bhikṣu is not a relative, perceives him as such, and has him wash an old garment, she commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture;
the same applies to having him dye or beat it.
Regarding these three matters, one may cause all three to be performed together, or cause two to be performed, or cause only one to be performed;
furthermore, whichever one of the three is undertaken first, if it involves a bhikṣu who is not a relative, one incurs the full offense.
If it is not a relative bhikṣu, yet one suspects so, there is also a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If he is a relative, but one perceives him as a non-relative, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If he is a relative, yet one gives rise to doubt, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

5. The Training Rule on Receiving Robes from a Bhikṣuṇī Who Is Not a Relative. This fifth training rule concerning receiving robes from a bhikṣuṇī who is not a relative was established at that time when the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, before the prohibition against bhikṣuṇīs dwelling in forest hermitages had been enacted.
At that time, there were several bhikṣuṇīs who went to a forest grove to practice meditative concentration and experience the bliss of superior absorption.

Then, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, together with her retinue of five hundred people, went to the Dark Forest (Andhavana), sat cross-legged beneath a tree, and entered the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
At that time, after the sun had set, the other nuns each desired to return toward Śrāvastī, and some spoke thus:
"Noble Lady Utpalavarṇā, we shall call her to rise."
Others said, "The Noble One possesses great majestic power; perhaps he will enter the monastery ahead of us.
Thus, they did not call for him to rise, but each returned to their own quarters.
When it was time for the lotus-colored one to emerge from meditative absorption at the end of the day, she surveyed all around and saw that all the nuns had departed.
She then thought to herself: "Shall I enter the city, or shall I remain here?"
He then entered into meditative concentration.
At that time, a band of five hundred thieves, having completed their robbery, arrived at the edge of this forest. The thieves deliberated, saying:
"Let half the men divide the loot, and let the other half act as guards."
Thereupon, within the grove, he saw a nun who had entered meditative absorption;
some said, "This is wood," while others said:
"This person. Some say: "A bhikṣu."
At that time, there was among those bandits a former monk who replied,
"This is a bhikṣuṇī, not a bhikṣu. The others asked:
"How do you know this? He replied,
"The bhikṣus sit in the full lotus posture (paryaṅka), while the bhikṣuṇīs sit in the half-lotus posture (ardhaparyaṅka)."
"Since she is sitting in the half-lotus posture, it is clear that she is a nun.
At that time, the bandits gave rise to a sense of wonder, saying:
"You all should know!"
"In such a terrifying great forest of darkness, a single bhikṣuṇī was able to stay overnight.
He then went to where the bandit general was, and the general asked him,
"Did you see anything extraordinary within the forest?"
He replied, "I have seen it;
in such a terrifying, great forest of darkness, a single bhikṣuṇī is able to stay here.
Having heard this, the general said to the guards:
"I shall go and see for myself.

Upon arriving, he beheld a bhikṣuṇī whose countenance was so upright and beautiful that all who saw her were filled with delight; her deportment was so serene and composed that they felt profound reverence at the mere sight of her. He sighed in admiration, saying:
"In this grove today there are two things truly lovely: the radiance of the bright moon, and the wondrous, extraordinary beauty of this bhikṣuṇī."
The general said, "You should call him up; I shall offer him food.
The layman who had returned to secular life replied:
"This is not eating at an improper time.
The general said, "The bhikṣuṇīs in the forest possess two things that are lovely: namely, their upright and graceful deportment, and their abstention from eating at improper times."
The general said,
"Order him to drink wine.
He returned and reported:
"This one does not drink alcohol.
The general said, "In this grove there are two other things that are lovely: namely, the beautiful countenances of the bhikṣuṇīs and their abstention from all kinds of liquor."
The general said,
"Now that I have fortunately encountered a field of merit, yet I have failed to offer even a single meal.
He then wrapped superior food in expensive layers of cloth, hung it upon a tree branch, and spoke thus:

"Just as the Venerable One’s countenance and deportment are tranquil and composed, perceiving all and knowing all, I now leave these robes and food; I pray that out of compassion you will graciously accept and make use of them."
Having spoken these words, he abandoned her and departed.

Then, when the night had turned to dawn, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā arose from meditative absorption. Seeing the tracks where the great multitude had passed, she entered meditative concentration and observed that those five hundred bandits had come to this place and then left.
He further examined himself to see whether there was anything unseemly or improper about him,
and he knew that he was without fault.
Then, seeing the wrapped food hanging from a tree branch, he thought to himself:
"This is brought about by the power of a pure mind and reverent faith. He further thought:
"If I wait for another person to distribute the food, I fear that birds or beasts might come and spoil this pure offering. I should now take this excellent food and offer it to the Saṃgha myself."
"However, the Buddha has taught:
'If a bhikṣuṇī has previously touched a bhikṣu, she is pure; if a bhikṣu has previously touched a bhikṣuṇī, he is also pure.
Having said this, she took it in her own hands and went to the Jeta Grove.
It was the constant practice of the group of six that two or three of them would always remain stationed at the entrance of the monastery.
At that time, Upānanda was walking up and down in front of the temple gate when he saw a bhikṣuṇī approaching from afar and asked her:
"Sister!..."
"Is it that the city gates have already opened before dawn?
The nun said,
"Venerable Sir!"
"I did not stay overnight in the city; I have come from the Dark Forest.
She replied, "Sister!..."
"I once entered that forest during the day and felt such terror that my hair stood on end; how could you, Great Sister, dwell there alone?
What is that object you hold in your hand?"
Then the bhikṣuṇī related the circumstances in full:
"This was left by a thief with a pure heart. Upānanda said:
“Sister! Because they saw your dignified demeanor, the thieves conceived a sense of respect and affection for you, which enabled them to obtain this object.
Had they seen me, they would surely have administered a beating and forced me to carry the goods away.”
Upānanda said, "Sister!

If one obtains this fine new white cotton cloth and sews it into a double-layered saṃghāṭī robe, then to dwell with few desires and cultivate all manner of wholesome qualities would truly be excellent!"
The nun said,
"Venerable One,
do you need this robe?"
He replied,
"If there is indeed anything remaining, you may dispose of it as you see fit.
He answered:
"Wait a moment!
I shall take this first meal to offer to the Saṃgha, and upon my return here, I will bestow this robe upon you.
Thus did Upānanda think.
"If there should be any other black-bowl wearer who sees this, they will surely beg for this robe,
and I shall have no way to obtain it. She replied, "Sister!"
"You may stay here; I shall go and summon someone to receive the first meal.
The nun consented.
At that time, Upānanda entered the monastery and saw the person receiving the food standing there idly, so he said to him:
“Venerable one!
The donor is laboring at the door-eaves while providing food; you, however, remain idly in your room with nothing to do. You ought to go quickly and receive that alms-food.”
He then took his bowl and went to the gate of the monastery, where he received the first portion of food from a bhikṣuṇī.
After she had given him the food, he took a piece of white cotton cloth and offered it to Upānanda.
Having received the robes, he joyfully offered this prayer of blessing:
"May the object you have given serve as a necklace for the mind and as an aid to the mind; adorned with concentration and wisdom, may you attain the paths of humans and devas."
"Enjoying excellent and exquisite garments according to your wishes, you shall ultimately attain unsurpassed, peaceful Nirvana.
Having said this, he departed.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā thought to herself:
"Should I now return to my original place,
or should I pay homage to the World-Honored One?
Having come here now, I shall pay homage at the Buddha's feet."
She then went to where the Buddha was, prostrated before the World-Honored One, and sat to one side.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs’ five robes were tattered and worn; seeing this, the World-Honored One said to Ānanda:
"Was the community of bhikṣuṇīs sufficiently provided for during the rainy season retreat?"
Ānanda said to the Buddha,
“It is sufficient.
The Buddha said:
"For what reason is the nun Utpalavarṇā’s five robes so tattered?
Ānanda replied, "Venerable Sir!"

This bhikṣuṇī possesses firm and deep faith and a pure, virtuous disposition; she joyfully relinquishes whatever she acquires among the Three Jewels and never frustrates the intentions of those who come to beg from her. Now that she has obtained an excellent large woolen blanket at her residence, she offers it to the Venerable Upānanda.
The Buddha asked Ānanda,
"Did the bhikṣu receive the robe from a nun who is not a relative?
He replied:
“Accepted.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“However, a bhikṣu who is not a relative does not give rise to this thought:”
"Does this bhikṣuṇī possess the five robes?
Whenever she was given anything, she would accept it all; however, if it was a bhikṣu who was her relative, she did not act in this way, refusing to accept the robe when she saw that he was in need.
At that time, the Blessed One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"From the place where the robes are stored within the Great Hall, you should take five robes and give them to the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā."
Then Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s instruction, took the five robes and presented them to the nun Utpalavarṇā.
At that time, for this reason, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"One should likewise not receive robes from a bhikṣu. Furthermore, I shall establish a training rule for my disciples of both divisions; it shall be spoken thus:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī should take a robe from a bhikṣu who is not a relative, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.

After the Blessed One had thus established this training rule, there was a householder in Śrāvastī who was very wealthy, possessing great riches and abundant enjoyments; his entire estate was like that of King Vaiśravaṇa, and he took a wife from a family of noble lineage.
Although they had lived together for a long time, no son or daughter was born; consequently, his heart was filled with anxiety and he thought to himself:

"Though there is much wealth within my house, there is not a single heir to succeed me. After my death, because I have no son, all my assets will be confiscated by the royal house, and I have not yet prepared provisions for the journey to the next world."
He sat with his hand supporting his cheek, sighing deeply.
His wife asked him,
"For what reason do you sit here supporting your cheek, your heart filled with such sorrow?"
He replied, "O worthy one!
How could I not be filled with sorrow now?"
He related the matter in detail.
His wife asked,
"How does one cultivate the provisions for future lives?"
He replied, "O worthy one!

If you can provide excellent food and drink for the Buddha and the Sangha, and after they have eaten, present each person with a pair of fine white cotton cloths, this is called preparing the provisions for the journey to the next world."
The wife said,
"Why do you not do so? At that time,
the elder went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha's feet, and sat to one side.
The Buddha taught the sublime Dharma, instructing, exhorting, benefiting, and gladdening them, and then remained silent.
At that time, the elder rose from his seat, adjusted his robe over one shoulder, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."
“I only pray that you will have compassion for me and the community of bhikṣus, and accept my humble offering at my home tomorrow.
The World-Honored One accepted by remaining silent.

Knowing that the Buddha had graciously accepted, the elder prostrated at his feet and departed. That night, he prepared various kinds of exquisite food and drink, arranged the seating and pure water vessels, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha.
In the early part of the day, the Blessed One dressed himself, took his bowl, and together with a company of bhikṣus, went to the house of the elder and sat down upon the prepared seats.

Once the elder had seen that the Buddha and the saṅgha were seated according to the Dharma, he personally served them with exquisite food and drink until they were fully satisfied; when the meal was finished and the ritual rinsing was completed, [he withdrew].
The Buddha and the assembly of monks each received a pair of exquisite white cotton cloths; they then took low seats and listened to the sublime Dharma before the World-Honored One.

The Buddha, according to their faculties and natures, instructed, exhorted, benefited, and gladdened them by preaching the essentials of the Dharma. Having offered his customary blessings, he rose from his seat and departed.

At that time, the householder followed the World-Honored One out, circumambulated him three times, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew. Standing upon a high terrace, he cultivated the mindfulness of renunciation and said to his wife, "O virtuous lady!
"You should feel great joy, for I have now prepared the provisions for future lives.
His wife then replied,
"Although you have now made them, I have not yet practiced."
The householder replied,
"Is not the merit being cultivated now shared?
His wife said:

"Although I know this is shared by all, it is my sincere wish to invite the Great Lady Mahāprajāpatī and the community of bhikṣuṇīs to my home for a meal; having eaten, I shall offer each of them a pair of exquisite white woolen cloths (*karpāsa*). This, indeed, shall be my provision for future lives."
The householder said:
"Excellent! Excellent!"
"Do as you wish.
Thereupon, the householder’s wife went to the place where the bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī was, prostrated at her feet, and sat to one side.
Having heard the sublime Dharma, he rose from his seat and said:
"O Noble One and assembly of bhikṣuṇīs, I pray that out of compassion you will come to my home tomorrow."

As described at length above, until she had finished washing and rinsing her mouth, the householder’s wife then took a large chest filled with fine white cotton cloth, opened it before the Elder, and stood there.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī thought to herself:
"The World-Honored One has established the precepts, forbidding bhikṣuṇīs from accepting exquisite garments.
If I were to accept them now, I would be violating the rules of training."
"If she does not accept it, she will obstruct the merit of the donor, and the bhikṣuṇīs will lose their offerings.
Each member of the community thought to herself,
"It would truly be excellent if Mahāprajāpatī were to accept this robe."
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī, having understood the minds of the assembly, thought to herself:
"The Blessed One, too, should permit the acceptance of fine robes on account of this very matter.

Then Mahāprajāpatī accepted the robes on behalf of all; after reciting verses of blessing for the wife of the householder, she rose from her seat and went to the place where the Blessed One was. With her usual dignified demeanor, she reported the entire matter to the Blessed One.
The Buddha addressed Mahāprajāpatī:
“Excellent! Excellent!”
"You already know that I have not yet permitted it.
From this day forward, I allow bhikṣuṇīs to receive expensive robes and exchange them with bhikṣus."
Then Mahāprajāpatī, having received the Buddha’s instruction, prostrated at his feet and departed. Arriving at the nuns’ residence, she announced:
“The World-Honored One has given this teaching: ‘I permit bhikṣuṇīs to accept expensive robes and exchange them for coarse ones with bhikṣus, to be used as they please.’”
When the bhikṣuṇī had received the robe, she went to Jetavana with the other bhikṣus, intending to exchange it.
At that time, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs took expensive robes and went to where the group of six was, saying:
"Noble ones!..."
The Blessed One has given this instruction:
"It is permitted for a bhikṣuṇī to receive a garment of high value and exchange it with a bhikṣu.
Now, you should take this fine garment and give me your coarse one.
The group of six replied:
"Sisters! We would not even accept a gift offered directly to us; how much less would we exchange it with you, who are foolish, ignorant, and lack autonomy?"
The other nuns each followed their own inclinations, taking the robes they had obtained to the elderly bhikṣu. They recounted the aforementioned matters and offered to exchange the robes with him.
The elderly bhikṣu said, "Sisters, wait a moment!"
"I shall ask the Buddha about this.
Then that bhikṣu went to where the Buddha was and addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Sir!"
"There is a bhikṣuṇī who has brought fine clothing and wealth to me, seeking to exchange it for coarse garments; I do not know how to proceed.
The Buddha said, "I permit bhikṣus to receive clothing from bhikṣuṇīs, with the exception of exchanging them."
"When changing clothes, you should cause the bhikṣuṇīs to feel joy and free from resentment.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts, fewness of desires, and contentment, and addressed the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"The former was the original prohibition; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated thus:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī should take a robe from a bhikṣu who is not a relative, except in exchange, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding the meaning of "one's own" versus "not one's own," there are seven types of robes, as explained in detail above.
With the exception of those obtained through trade, there is no offense.
The rules for the forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-prāyaścittika*) are both as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If a bhikṣuṇī perceives a bhikṣu who is not a relative as not being a relative, or entertains doubt about it, and takes a robe from him, she incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī perceives a bhikṣu who is a relative as one who is not a relative, or if she entertains doubt regarding this, she incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).

Furthermore, there is no offense in the following cases: if a bhikṣu gives robes to the Saṃgha; or gives them for the purpose of preaching the Dharma; or gives them at the time of full ordination (upasampadā); or gives them because he has been robbed by thieves; or if he has acquired them through purchase; or if he has acquired them through exchange—in all these instances, there is no offense.
If a bhikṣu, who is widely known among the people as one who receives great offerings of sustenance, takes his robes and goes before a bhikṣuṇī, places the robe on the ground, and speaks these words:
"Sisters!..."
"I now have much wealth such as this; I pray that you will compassionately accept it for me.
Having spoken these words, he abandons it and departs; if one takes it, there is no offense.

6. The Training Rule on Begging for Robes from a Non-Relative Householder. The sixth training rule concerning begging for robes from a non-relative householder was established with its origin in Śrāvastī.

At that time, Upānanda begged for robes and other items from a householder; the full account is as detailed in the *Mahābhikṣu-vinaya*. It is explained at length until the formulation of the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should beg for a robe from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*."

At that time, the Blessed One first established a training rule for his śrāvaka disciples. At that moment, there were many bhikṣus traveling through the countryside who were plundered by bandits and left without any clothing.
At that time, the bhikṣus deliberated together, saying:
"As the Blessed One has prescribed:
'It is not permitted to beg for robes from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative.'"
"I have no kinsmen here; it would be best for me to return to Śrāvastī and seek clothing from my fellow practitioners of the holy life."
"How can we depart with our bodies exposed?
They then reported this matter to the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"For this reason, there shall be an exception for other times. If a bhikṣu’s robes have been stolen, lost, burned, blown away, or carried off by water, this constitutes such a time."
What was previously established as a formal prohibition is now further expanded by this allowance; it should be stated thus:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should beg for robes from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative, except at the appropriate times, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika."
"Other times" refers to when a bhikṣuṇī has had her robes taken away, lost them, had them burned, blown away by the wind, or carried off by water; these are the [permissible] times.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who is within this Dharma; the meaning of "robes" and so forth is as explained above.
"Begging" means to solicit from another.
"Robbed of one's robe" refers to being robbed by a thief.
"Lost one's robe" refers to losing it oneself.
"Regarding 'burned robes,' they have been consumed by fire.
Regarding 'blown away robes,' they have been carried off by the wind.
Regarding 'floated away robes,' they have been swept away by water. If there is such an occasion of hardship, there is no offense in requesting [robes]."
If it is otherwise, one who acquires [the object] commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense?
There are three types of matters:
This refers to value, color, and quantity. Regarding value:

if a bhikṣuṇī, without being prompted by difficult circumstances, begs from a non-relative for a robe worth one kārṣāpaṇa—the meaning of *kārṣāpaṇa* has already been explained in detail above under the precept against taking what is not given—and if she obtains a robe worth one *kārṣāpaṇa*, there is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of begging, and upon obtaining it, there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

In this manner, as the number increases up to fifty *kāṛṣāpaṇas* and so forth, one should understand that the gravity of the offense corresponds to the amount received upon each request, as detailed above.

If a bhikṣuṇī asks a non-relative for a robe worth one kārsāpaṇa and receives one worth two kārsāpaṇas, there is an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) at the time of requesting it, but there is no offense at the time of receiving it.

In this manner, up to fifty *kārsāpaṇas* and so forth, one should understand that whether there is an offense or no offense when begging for little and receiving much follows the same principle. Regarding the color:

if a bhikṣuṇī begs from another for a garment of blue color and receives a garment of blue color, there is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of begging, and she incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (forfeiture and confession) upon receipt.
Just as it is with blue, so it should be understood for yellow, red, and white, as well as for thickness and thinness.
If a bhikṣuṇī requests a garment of blue color and receives one that is yellow, there is an *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of the request, but no offense at the time of receipt.
In the same way, it should be understood that the same principle applies to other colors, whether thick or thin, when they are compared with one another.

Regarding the measurement: if a bhikṣuṇī begs for a five-cubit garment from another and receives exactly five cubits, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of begging, and a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* (offense involving forfeiture) upon receipt.
If one begs for five and receives ten, or even fifty, and so forth, it should be understood according to the above principle.
These are called the three matters.
If one begs for thread and receives a small fragment, or if one begs for a small fragment and the other gives a wide garment, there is no offense in either case.
Furthermore, there is no offense for one who is a first-time offender.
7. The Training Rule on Begging for Excess Clothing. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, a great many bhikṣus had been plundered by bandits. Upānanda said to those bhikṣus:
"For what reason are you wearing these tattered robes? Why do you not beg for more from others?"
"The World-Honored One has permitted that those who have encountered bandits may beg for [robes] without offense.
They replied,
"We cannot beg for robes from others."
Upānanda said, "If you cannot seek it yourself, I shall beg for it on your behalf.
He replied:
"As you wish.
Thereupon, on account of this matter, Upānanda went to the homes of various brahmins, householders, and elders, where he taught the Dharma and converted them, obtaining many robes.
Because those of superior quality were all taken for himself, he broke them up and gave the pieces to the bhikṣus.
At that time, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, as before, the Buddha assembled the community, questioned him about the facts, and reprimanded him; the full account continues until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣuṇī, having had her robes stolen, lost, burnt, blown away, or carried off by water, should beg for robes from a householder or a housewife who is not a relative.
If that person offers many robes and a bhikṣuṇī requires them, she should accept two robes: one for the upper body and one for the lower body.
If she accepts more than that, it is a niḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
“Nun” refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
“Taking away robes,” etc., is as explained above.
Regarding “one who should receive the two types of upper and lower robes,” there are two kinds of upper and lower robes:
First, the upper and lower robes of a bhikṣuṇī; second, the upper and lower robes of a layperson.
Regarding the upper and lower robes of a bhikṣuṇī: if they are new garments, the saṃghāṭī should be made of double thickness, with three vertical strips and five horizontal strips.
If it is a *nivāsana*, it is two spans high and five spans wide.
For laypeople, the upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*) is eleven cubits long and three cubits wide;
the lower garment (*antaravāsaka*) is seven cubits long and two cubits wide.
"Should receive" means to accept with a conscious intention.
"If one receives in excess" means exceeding the aforementioned number.
At the moment one obtains the robes through begging, one commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
The remaining meanings are as explained extensively above.
Regarding this matter, what are the characteristics of the offense?
If a bhikṣuṇī requests upper and lower garments from a layperson, she may receive them according to the prescribed measure.
If one begs for more than that, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense; once it is obtained, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one begs for the upper and lower robes of a bhikṣuṇī, the matter is treated in the same way.
When begging for the upper and lower robes of a layperson from another, even if they are smaller than the standard measurement for laypeople, one should not beg for more.
If there is any excess, it must be returned to the owner.
When begging for the upper and lower robes of a bhikṣuṇī from another, if they are insufficient to meet the standard measurement for a bhikṣuṇī’s robes, one should beg for more.
If there is an excess, it should be returned to the owner.
If it is a layperson’s robe and one lacks enough, one should ask for more.
If it is a bhikṣuṇī’s robe and one has an excess but does not return it, the gravity of the offense should be understood according to the specific circumstances.

If one originally intends to seek [an object] by means of deception, at the time of seeking it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; upon obtaining the object, one commits the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If, after having committed the offense, one further obtains other objects, all are likewise offenses; the detailed explanation is as previously stated.

8. The Training Rule on Begging for a Robe from a Layperson Who Has Offered Consent. The eighth training rule concerning begging for a robe from a layperson who has offered consent. The setting of the缘 (nidāna) is the same as before.
In this city there was a householder who abandoned his own wife and committed illicit acts with another woman.
His wife said to him, "Noble sir, you should not commit such illicit acts."

Although his wife repeatedly admonished him, her husband did not follow her words; she became resentful and jealous, and began to engage in secret unions with other men. Her husband constantly gave household goods to that illicit wife, and she likewise gave household goods to that unfaithful husband.
The husband and wife squandered their wealth until it was nearly exhausted.
The elder was violent by nature; he beat his maidservant and constantly gave her tattered clothes and poor food, saying to her:
"It is because of you that my family's assets have been dissipated."
The maidservant said,
"I have indeed known for a long time the reason for this dissolution.
However, as both of you are my masters, I did not dare speak of it directly."

At that time, the husband and wife, realizing that the maidservant had been sarcastic, were both filled with shame. The full account is as detailed in the *Mahābhikṣu-vinaya*, up until the World-Honored One’s reprimand and his extensive discourse on establishing the training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be stated as follows:

"Should any bhikṣuṇī have a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative prepare the price for a robe, intending to buy such a pure robe to give to a certain bhikṣuṇī for her to use at the proper time."
This bhikṣuṇī, having not previously received an invitation, went to that person's house upon being informed by another and spoke these words:
"Excellent, worthy sir!
For my sake, you should purchase such pure cloth with the price provided for clothing and give it to me in a timely manner, so that it may be of good quality."
"If one obtains such a robe, it is an *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.
"A *bhikṣuṇī*" refers to one who is a member of this [monastic] community.
The distinctions between "relatives" and "non-relatives," etc., are as explained above.
"Price of clothing" refers to gold, silver, cowries, and so forth.
"To procure" means to seek out.
"Such clothing" refers to the seven types mentioned above.
"Buying" means purchasing from another.
"Pure" means obtaining such a robe as is fit for use.
"Giving" refers to the time when the robe is offered.
"Such-and-such a person" refers to Upānanda.
"Not having accepted the invitation" means he had not previously given his word of assent.

"Because of being informed by another" means that upon seeing someone else making a request, he went to that person to seek a robe and forcibly demanded its price for the sake of obtaining something superior; if he obtains the robe at that time, he commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
The meaning of the characteristics of offenses has been explained above.
In this context, what are the specific instances of these characteristics?
There are three types of instances:
That is to say: price, color, and measure. What is meant by "price"?
If a bhikṣuṇī receives a robe worth five kārṣāpaṇas from a person who is not a relative, there is no offense at the time of receiving it.

If one does not accept this robe but seeks further, at the time of seeking, one commits an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); at the time of obtaining it, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
This applies even up to fifty *kārsāpaṇas*; whether seeking or obtaining, the gravity of the offense should be understood according to the above principles. This is what is meant by "price."
What constitutes the offense regarding color?
If a bhikṣuṇī receives a blue-colored robe, there is no offense at the time of acceptance.

If she does not accept this robe but further requests one beyond [the permitted limit], there is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) at the time of requesting, and she incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture and confession) at the time of obtaining it.
Just as it is with blue, so it should be understood for all other colors accordingly; this is what is called "color.
What is meant by "measure"?
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a robe of five cubits, she may accept and take possession of it without offense.
If one does not accept this robe and seeks more than that, one incurs the same offense as before.
This applies even up to many cubits; the gravity of the offense in each case is identical to what was stated previously. This is what is meant by "measure."
The method for relinquishing this *naiḥsargika* robe is also the same as previously described.

There is no offense if one requests thread or cotton and receives only a small fragment; nor is there an offense if one requests a small fragment and the other person gives a full robe. These cases are all without offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense for the very first person. 9.
The Training Rule Concerning Begging for a Robe from a Layperson Who Has Specifically Offered One. The setting and circumstances of the ninth training rule are the same as before.
At that time, there was an elder and his wife, each of whom had been having illicit affairs with outsiders.
Upānanda preached the Dharma for them, leading them to abandon evil and cultivate goodness; the circumstances were identical to those previously described.

The only difference was that two people had each prepared the price for a robe; they then caused those two prices to be combined into a single robe, which resulted in the elder undergoing great hardship. [The Buddha] spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī has a non-relative householder or householder’s wife who have each prepared the price for a robe, thinking, 'We shall buy such a pure robe and give it to a certain bhikṣuṇī'..."
"Without having previously received an invitation, this bhikṣuṇī, upon being informed by another, went to that person's house and spoke these words:
'Excellent, O worthy one!'"
"If you have prepared the price for robes on my behalf, you may purchase such pure robes together and give them to me in a timely manner, for the sake of their quality.
If he obtains the robes [in this manner], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Regarding this, there are three different aspects of the offense, all of which are as previously explained.
10. The Training Rule on Soliciting Robes Beyond the Limit. The setting for this tenth training rule is the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣu Upānanda was observing the rains retreat in Rājagṛha. In the morning, he donned his robes, took up his bowl, and went for alms; he entered the house of the brahmin minister Varṣākāra and preached to him the Sūtra on the Three Bases of Meritorious Action—namely, giving, ethical discipline, and cultivation.
Having heard the Dharma, the minister Vārṣika was filled with joy; developing pure faith, he spoke these words:
"Noble One! I shall offer sixty gold coins as a gift."
The details are as found in the *Mahābhikṣu-vinaya*, up to the point where the training rule (*śikṣāpada*) is established and should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when a king, a minister, a brahmin, a householder, or others, sends a messenger to deliver the price for a robe to a bhikṣuṇī..."
The messenger, carrying the price for the robes, went to the bhikṣuṇī’s location and said:
"Noble Lady!
These goods have been sent by such-and-such a king, minister, brahmin, or householder, and I have been dispatched to deliver them."
"Noble one!
Please accept this out of compassion.
Then that bhikṣuṇī said to the messenger:
“Virtuous one, I should not accept this price for robes; rather, if I obtain a pure robe that is appropriate for the season, I should accept it.
The messenger replied, “Noble one!”
"Is there anyone in charge?
The bhikṣuṇī who requires robes replied, "There is!"
"Whether it be a monastic attendant (*śrāmaṇera*) or a female lay follower (*upāsikā*), these are the persons who attend to the needs of the bhikṣuṇīs.
That messenger goes to the person attending to their needs, gives them the price for the robe, and says:
"You should use this price for the robe to purchase a timely and pure robe and give it to the bhikṣuṇī [Name] so that she may wear it."
Having properly instructed the attendant, that messenger returns to the bhikṣuṇī and says: "Noble Lady!
I have already given the price for the robe to the attendant you indicated; you should receive the pure robe."
If a bhikṣuṇī requires robes, she should go to the person in charge of affairs and, after reminding them two or three times, say:
"I require robes."
"If he succeeds, it is well.
If he does not succeed, he should go to that place up to four, five, or six times, remaining silent wherever he stands.
If he obtains the robe after four, five, or six visits, it is well."
If she does not obtain the robe, yet seeks to obtain a robe beyond that [time limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If she still does not obtain the robe at all, that bhikṣuṇī should go herself or send a trustworthy person to the place where the price for the robe was sent, and announce:
"The price for a robe was sent by you for the sake of such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī; however, that bhikṣuṇī did not ultimately obtain the robe."
“O Benevolent One, you should know and not let this be lost; now is the time.
As for “a nun,” it refers to one among those who follow this Dharma.
As for “a king,” whether male or female, or even others who have been consecrated by the rites of royal law, all such persons are called kings.
The ministers are those who hold the affairs of state and stand in mutual dependence upon the king.
The brahmins are those of noble lineage and great learning.
The householders (gṛhapati) refer to those who are wealthy and affluent while remaining at home, as well as other various miscellaneous classes.
"Sending a messenger" refers to a woman, a man, or a eunuch.
"One who sends the price for the robe" refers to gold, silver, money, and so forth.

"He who holds the price for the robe and so forth" refers to one who, holding the price for the robe, arrives at the place of the bhikṣuṇī and says, "Noble Lady," thereby addressing the person before her.
"This item belongs to such-and-such a person" refers to the source from which the robe was sent; [the recipient] should say, "I pray you accept it.
Regarding "this bhikṣuṇī," etc., [the response] is that she should not accept it.
"Pure according to the proper time" means obtaining [the requisites] in accordance with reason.
He instructs the bhikṣuṇīs and others to inquire of the person in charge.
When the bhikṣuṇī says "it is available," she points out and informs that person.
"Those who are monastic attendants (śrāmaṇera) of the Saṃgha" refers to the attendants of the great assembly.
"Those who are upāsikās" refers to those who have taken refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts.
The phrase "those messengers and so forth" clarifies the intention of the messenger.
"Buyer" refers to one who either purchases or weaves.
"To such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī" indicates the person to whom it is given.
"Pure" means that it is fit for use.
"One who teaches oneself well" refers to one who skillfully instructs and informs a bhikṣuṇī regarding the full report.
"Twice, thrice, or so on" indicates the number of times she should go back and forth.
"Causing her to remember and obtain what is good" means that it accords with her own intention.
If one does not obtain [the object], and remains silent at a location for as many as four, five, or six times, this refers to the count of silent stays.
Regarding "at a location," there are four types of locations:
first, an open space; second, a house; third, a field; and fourth, a shop.
"Chang" refers to places such as potteries where earthenware vessels are made, or locations for shaving the hair;
"she" refers to residential dwellings;
and "tian" refers to fields such as those for rice and sugarcane.
A "shop" refers to a place where goods are sold.
There are six points of interrogation; having observed those six statements, one should interrogate accordingly according to the matter at hand. What are these six?
If they should ask,
"By what means have you now arrived?
the bhikṣuṇī should answer:
"I have come for that purpose.
If he says, "Welcome, sir; you should sit here," [one should do so].
He replied, "I have come for that matter. If he says:
"Eat your rice," he replied,
"I have come for that matter."
If one says,
"I am eating rice," the response is:
"I have come for that purpose.
If he says, "I am drinking water," [one should say: "I have come for that purpose."
He replied, "I have come for that matter. If,

among these six types of questioning, one perceives another's speech and immediately responds upon hearing the sound without answering slowly, thereby leaving the other person no opportunity to utter further words, this is not called a complete and excellent sixfold interrogation.

If, when hearing another's speech regarding any particular matter, one waits for the sound of their words to cease before responding slowly and calmly—thereby allowing the other person the leisure to formulate further speech—this is called the complete and excellent sixfold method of interrogation.
If, while seeking in this manner, one obtains the robe, it is well.
If one does not obtain the robe, yet obtains it by seeking beyond this limit, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Exceeding" means that after three verbal requests and six silent requests, one goes again to seek the robe;
if one ultimately does not obtain the robe, one may either go oneself or dispatch a trustworthy person from the place where the robe was obtained.

Regarding those whose words are trustworthy, this refers to disciples and followers who may be entrusted with the information; one should inform them so that they may collect [the items] and prevent their loss, for this is the proper method for reporting back.
If a bhikṣuṇī has sent a messenger with a report, and that attendant comes to the bhikṣuṇī’s place and speaks thus:
"Noble lady,
please accept this price for a robe."
The bhikṣuṇī should reply to her, saying:
"I have already relinquished this price for the robe; you should return it to the place from which the robe was sent.
To report thus is virtuous; if she takes the robe, she commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If the attendant should speak thus: "Noble one!
You may accept this price for the robe; I shall consult with that donor together so as to make his heart rejoice."
"If it is done in this manner, there is no offense in taking the robe.
However, if a bhikṣuṇī does not act in this way but accepts the robes in sequence, she commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika)."
Once the offense has been committed, the method for relinquishing and repenting it is explained at length as before.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific circumstances?

If one acts as a donor, an agent, or a servant, and receives robes in accordance with the Dharma, there is no offense; otherwise, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (an offense involving forfeiture and confession).

If a human being acts as the donor, a human being acts as the messenger, and a non-human being acts as the servant, and one obtains a robe in accordance with the Dharma, there is no offense; otherwise, it is an act of wrongdoing (dukkaṭa).
If a human being acts as the donor, a non-human being acts as the messenger, and a non-human being acts as the attendant, it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), as previously stated.

If a human being acts as the donor, a non-human being acts as the messenger, and a human being acts as the attendant, it is a *nissaggiya-pācittiya* (offense involving forfeiture), as previously stated.
If the donor is not a human being, the messenger is not a human being, and the attendant is not a human being, it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), as previously stated.

If the donor is not a human being, the messenger is not a human being, but the attendant is a human being, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture and confession), as previously stated.
If a non-human is the donor, a human is the messenger, and a non-human is the attendant, it is the same as the previous offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a non-human is the donor, a human is the messenger, and a non-human is the attendant, it is the same as the previous offense of *duṣkṛta*.

If a bhikṣuṇī requests the price for a robe from a non-human, she incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); upon obtaining it, she incurs an offense of expiation with forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).
If she requests the price for a robe from a nāga, she incurs an offense of wrong-doing; upon obtaining it, she incurs an offense of expiation with forfeiture.

If a bhikṣuṇī, by means of a messenger according to the prescribed method, requests [an item] using a letter or a seal, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense at the time of the request; once she obtains it, it becomes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
Furthermore, regarding those who are exempt from offense, the detailed explanation is as previously stated.

The second summary verse says:
Handling gold and silver; receiving and disbursing; Buying and selling; begging for bowls; and begging for thread.

The Training Rule on Taking Precious Objects. The eleventh training rule concerning the taking of precious objects: At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the six groups of bhikṣus personally handled gold and silver, or instructed others to handle them, using them to construct dwellings or to place upon beds and seats.
When the non-Buddhists saw this, they felt contempt and said:
"These śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, personally grasp gold, silver, coins, and the like, or instruct others to grasp them."
The details are as explained above.
All other laypeople are likewise; what distinction is there between them and us?
How can one cause other brahmins and householders to give rise to deep respect and faith, and offer various foods and drinks to these shaven-headed men?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes hold of gold, silver, coins, or the like, or instructs another to take hold of them, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“To grasp with one’s own hand” means to take hold with the hand.
“Gold and silver” refers to gold, silver, and cowrie shells.
"Money" refers to gold coins and the like.
To instruct another person [to do so] is likewise; in all such cases, one commits an offense requiring forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).
The method for forfeiture and repentance is explained in detail as above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how is it constituted?
When instructing another to take [something], there are eighteen different types of such acts that all constitute an offense.
That is to say, one tells the other:
"Take this object; take it from here; take this much!
Carry this object; carry it from here; carry this much!"
"Set this object down; you set it down here; you set down that much!
Take that object; you take it there; you take that much!"
You shall take that object; you shall take it there; you shall take that much!
You shall set down that object; you shall set it down there; you shall set down that much!

Regarding the statement "you take this object," it refers to instructing another to take items such as gold or silver that are within sight; for doing so, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense, and at the moment of actually grasping and lifting them, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

Regarding the statement "you take from this," it means that if one instructs another to take items from various bags or containers made of iron, wood, or other materials, the offense incurred is the same as before.
All subsequent phrases regarding offenses are identical to this.
"Take that much" refers to commanding another to take items such as hundreds, thousands, or billions.
"Bring this object" refers to commanding another to bring objects such as gold and silver.
"To take this from here" means to instruct another to take an object from within a pouch, a box, or a container.
"Take this much from here" refers to instructing another to take a quantity such as hundreds, thousands, or billions when taking it.
"To place this object" refers to gold, silver, and so forth; it means when instructing another to place them.
"To place this in here" refers to within chests, vessels, and the like; it means when instructing another to set them down therein.
The phrase "you set aside this much" refers to quantities such as hundreds of thousands of billions when instructing another to set them aside.
These nine cases all concern visible objects and involve instructing another to perform the action.

Regarding the statement "you take that object," it means that if one instructs another to take an object such as gold or silver from a place where it is not visible, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense; at the moment of seizing and lifting it, one commits a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
"To take from there" means to instruct another to take items from various bags or containers made of iron, wood, and so forth.
"To take that much from there" means to instruct another to take items numbering in the hundreds, thousands, tens of millions, and so on.
"To take that object" refers to instructing another to bring items such as gold or silver.
"To take from that" refers to instructing another to retrieve an object from within a bag, a box, or a container.
"To take so much of that" refers to instructing another to take hundreds of thousands of billions of items and the like.
"To set aside those objects" refers to instructing another to set aside gold, silver, and so forth.
"To place it there" means to set it within a chest, a vessel, or similar container.

"To have it placed there by you to such an extent" refers to when one instructs another to place hundreds of thousands of billions [of items] and incurs a fault identical to that mentioned previously.
These nine cases all refer to instances where one instructs another to perform the act in an out-of-sight location.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes hold of gold, silver, coins, or cowrie shells, she commits an offense of forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣuṇī takes hold of gold or silver, whether finished or unfinished, she commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣuṇī takes hold of gold, silver, coins, shells, or teeth that possess their characteristic marks, she commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If a bhikṣuṇī touches a mani-jewel or a vaiḍūrya-jewel, she commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣuṇī grasps currency used for common transactions in various regions, she commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one holds currency not used in one's own country, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one holds red copper, brass, bronze, iron, lead, or tin, there is no offense.
Thus, after the Blessed One had established the rules of training for the śrāvakas, he was staying at the Jetavana Grove.
At that time, there was a householder living in this city in the kingdom of Campā; he was deeply faithful and purely virtuous, and he practiced giving with the most excellent things.

At that time, the householder constructed a dwelling for the Buddha and the Sangha; with its doors, windows, and railings exquisitely adorned and magnificently decorated, it was a delight to behold, serving as a path to rebirth in heaven.
A large number of bhikṣuṇīs had been observing the rains retreat there; once the retreat was concluded and the *pravāraṇā* ceremony finished, they said to the elder:
"We now wish to go to Śrāvastī to pay homage at the feet of the Great Teacher and to visit the senior and venerable elders."
"If a bhikṣuṇī is currently lacking robes, you should give them to her at that time.
The householder replied,
"Noble Lady!"
"The people here have no superior, exquisite garments or fine fabrics; however, we have now heard that a caravan is about to arrive. When they reach this place, we shall offer them to you.
The bhikṣuṇī said, "Householder!"
"If there are no fine items, give me those that are coarse and poor.
The householder replied,
"Noble One!"
"It is my nature to always give excellent things; why then do you now give me something inferior?
If you will not wait, you may take the money for the price of the garment and go."
He replied, "Householder!
The World-Honored One has established a precept prohibiting me from handling money."
The householder replied,
"If that is the case, I would rather not give at all than bestow something of poor quality upon others.
At that time, the community of nuns, having received nothing at all, departed immediately.
As they proceeded along the road and reached Śrāvastī, the nuns saw them and said, "Welcome, sisters!
Did you not receive much clothing at your place of residence during the rainy season retreat? Why have you come here wearing such coarse and tattered garments?"
He replied, "There are no robes to be obtained.
The bhikṣuṇī said:
"In what place do you dwell for the rains retreat?
He replied,
"In the kingdom of Campā."
He asked again:
"Upon what do you rely for your dwelling? He replied:

"Venerable ones," [the nun] said, "I have heard that this householder is fond of giving fine upper garments; will he not give one? The nuns replied: "He will. [The nun continued: "Then let us go together. They went to the householder's residence. When they arrived, the householder saw them from afar and, seeing them, he rose from his seat, approached them, paid homage at their feet, and sat down to one side. As he was seated there, the nuns said to him: "Householder, we have heard that you are fond of giving fine upper garments; will you not give one? He replied: "Venerable ladies, I am indeed fond of giving fine upper garments; I shall give one. He then took a fine upper garment from his own body and offered it to them. The nuns said: "Householder, we have many robes; do not give us this one. He replied: "Venerable ladies, please accept it. They accepted it. The householder then rose from his seat, paid homage at their feet, circumambulated them three times, and departed. The nuns then said to one another: "Sisters, we have obtained a fine upper garment; let us divide it among ourselves. They then divided it among themselves. At that time, the householder returned home and asked his wife: "Wife, did those nuns receive a fine upper garment? She replied: "Yes, husband, they did. He asked: "Did they divide it among themselves? She replied: "Yes, husband, they did. The householder thought: "Alas, these nuns are shameless and lack modesty; how can they divide a single fine upper garment among themselves? Having thought this, he went to where the Blessed One was, paid homage at his feet, and sat down to one side. As he was seated there, the householder said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, I have committed an offense; may the Blessed One accept my confession of that transgression. The Blessed One said: "Householder, you have committed an offense; you should confess it. By so doing, you will grow in wholesome qualities. The householder then confessed his transgression before the Blessed One. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him. The Blessed One then addressed the Venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to the nuns' quarters and say to them: 'Sisters, the Blessed One has rebuked the householder regarding your conduct. The Venerable Ānanda replied: "As you command, Blessed One," and having paid homage at the Blessed One's feet, he departed. He then went to the nuns' quarters and said to the nuns: "Sisters, the Blessed One has rebuked the householder regarding your conduct. The nuns said: "Venerable Ānanda, what was the Blessed One's rebuke? The Venerable Ānanda related it all in detail. The nuns then said to one another: "Sisters, we have committed an offense; we should confess it. By so doing, we will grow in wholesome qualities. They then confessed their transgressions before the Venerable Ānanda. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the monks: "Monks, if a nun should divide a single fine upper garment among herself and others, she commits a *pācittiya* offense. The Blessed One further addressed the monks:

"Monks, if a nun should divide a single fine upper garment among herself and others, she commits a *pācittiya* offense. This is the rule of training. If a nun divides a single fine upper garment among herself and others, she commits a *pācittiya* offense. "Fine" means: it is considered fine if it is worth five *māsakas* or more. If she intends to divide it but passes away in the state of being absolutely deceased and then divides it, she incurs no offense. If she intends to divide it but passes away in the state of being completely extinguished and then divides it, she incurs no offense. If she intends to divide it but passes away in the state of being totally extinguished and then divides it, she incurs no offense. She replied,
"It is precisely because of this that I have not obtained the robe.
The nuns asked:
"What is the reason for this?
She recounted the matter in detail.
Having heard it, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:

"There are Brahmins, householders, and lay devotees who, out of reverence and faith, joyfully wish to offer the price for robes to the bhikṣuṇīs; my disciples also desire to obtain these robes. I should establish a rule so that the bhikṣuṇīs may receive them without any deficiency."
He addressed the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

"If there is a gift of cloth-price offered by another, you may accept it as needed; having accepted it, you should maintain it with the mental attitude that it belongs to that person. Furthermore, the bhikṣuṇīs should seek out an attendant."
The bhikṣuṇīs did not know whom they should seek out.
The Buddha said:
"They should seek out a monastery attendant or an upāsikā."
"Those belonging to the monastery" refers to the *kappiyakārakas* (lay attendants).
"Upāsikās" refers to those who have received the three refuges and the five precepts.
One should ask them as follows:
"Can you act as my patron?
If he says, "I can," [then proceed].
As for those [who say this], they should entrust the person with the mind of a steward and keep the items; they may have someone else hold them and should not grasp them themselves.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who, while traveling to another region, had this thought:
"I have now arrived here, yet I still have no donor."
She gave rise to a sense of remorse.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Even if they have gone far away, as long as those persons remain alive, they shall always be the donors.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who had not yet found a donor; when another person gave her an object, the bhikṣuṇī hesitated and did not dare to accept it. The Buddha said:
"She should accept it."
Having received the object, she should address a bhikṣuṇī, saying:
"Venerable one, please attend to me.
I, the bhikṣuṇī [name], have obtained this impure object; I shall exchange this impure object for pure wealth."
"Thus it was said three times: 'Use [this] as you see fit according to your needs; do not harbor any doubts.
At that time, there was a donor who built a monastery in a remote border region and offered it to the Sangha.
From time to time, bandits came to cause alarm and fear, and those bhikṣuṇīs abandoned the monastery and departed, whereupon the bandits arrived to seize the monastery's property.
The Buddha said:
"Whether it be the property of the Saṃgha or the property of a stūpa—including all gold, silver, coins, jewels, and so forth—one must securely store and secure them before departing."
Although she said to "send it away and hide it," the nun did not know whom she intended to send.
The Buddha said:
"It shall be a *karmadāna* (pure person) or an *upāsaka* (lay follower)."
He ordered it to be stored away, but the one who stored it then stole the object. The Buddha said:

"If there is a deeply faithful upāsaka, have him store it; if there is no one of deep faith, you should have a śrāmaṇerikā do so; if there is no śrāmaṇerikā, the bhikṣuṇī herself should store it with her own hands."
The nun still did not know how to store it away.
The Buddha said:
"One should dig a pit."
"Who should be employed?
the Buddha said,
"One should employ a *karmadāna* (pure person) or an *upāsaka* (lay follower)."
If he should steal the items, one should have a person of faith do it.
If such a person is not available, one should have a female novice (śrāmaṇerī) do it.
If there is no female novice, one should dig them up oneself.
"After the bandits have departed, you may take [the goods] as before, and the items shall be returned to the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said:
"Regarding what I have permitted as an exception for difficult circumstances, once those difficulties have passed, it should no longer be practiced."
"If you continue to practice this, you will incur an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
**The Twelfth Training Rule on Seeking Profit from Lending and Borrowing.** The setting for this training rule was the city of Śrāvastī.

The World-Honored One was staying at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park. Far and near, everyone heard that in the Middle Kingdom a Buddha had appeared in the world, and that his śrāvaka disciples possessed great supernormal powers, performed various transformations, and extensively preached the sublime Dharma.
