"If there are those who can make offerings to his disciples, they will obtain great rewards and their benefits will increase and expand.
At that time, there were merchants from the north who, hearing this reputation, said to one another:
"Gentlemen, you should know!..."
"We ought to go to the Middle Kingdom to engage in trade; first, we shall obtain great profit, and second, we may make offerings to the Triple Gem.
Thereupon, the merchants took a large quantity of goods and arrived at the city of Śrāvastī.
In this city there was a naked ascetic who was well-versed in celestial astrology and divination; he went to the merchant leader and said, "Welcome, merchant leader!"
"Your father’s name was so-and-so and your mother’s name was so-and-so; you brought such-and-such goods to this region, and by a certain day you obtained such-and-such profit.
Upon hearing this, the merchant leader thought to himself:

"I have previously heard that the disciples of the World-Honored One possess great supernormal powers, such as emitting smoke and pouring down rain, and discerning things before they have even sprouted. This must be such a person."
He then took a crimson woolen cloak from the north and various exotic fruits and presented them to the non-Buddhist practitioners.
Once they had received them, he immediately donned the cloak and went to his companions; when they saw him, they questioned him, and he related everything in detail.
A fellow disciple said to him:
"O virtuous one!
We are constantly held in contempt by the śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, who always say to us: [text continues]"
"You have never associated with noble and virtuous people, but have instead only familiarized yourselves with lowly laborers and the outcaste class of Caṇḍālas.
You should now don these noble robes and go to the place of the Śākya sons to pierce their hearts."
He immediately donned his woolen cloak and went to the Jetavana Grove.
At that time, Upānanda was walking back and forth outside the gate of the Jetavana Grove; seeing him coming from afar, he thought to himself:
"That which this outsider wears is a fine and precious thing. If I cannot obtain this garment, I shall no longer be called Upānanda!"
As they gradually drew closer, he asked, "Outsider!
Have you now recently returned to the lay life?"
He replied,
"I shall not return to lay life.
[The other] asked, "If that is so, why are you wearing these lay garments?"
He related the matter in full. Upānanda said,
"This is not a good thing!"
"This is not a virtuous act!
How can one who is advanced in years and physically decayed permit himself to break the precepts?
You ought to sit for a moment and briefly listen to the essential points of the Dharma."
At that time, the non-Buddhist follower sat down as soon as he was told; Upānanda, with a joyful heart, preached the Dharma for him.
Whenever Upānanda proclaimed the Dharma of renunciation and giving, those who heard it all desired to cut the flesh from their own bodies to offer it in exchange.
He further addressed the non-Buddhists:

"Your great teacher is by nature fond of the coarse and the base; he teaches his disciples to go naked, to pluck out their hair, to eat little, to dwell for short periods, and to constantly lie upon the ground.

If your great teacher were one who delighted in fine clothing and food, he would surely permit you to wear garments of exquisite quality worth ten million coins, to consume food of a hundred flavors at will, and to reside in dwellings worth a hundred thousand."
Because of their narrow-mindedness, they could not tolerate this;

however, my Great Master possesses a vast heart, permitting his disciples to wear clothing worth ten thousand pieces of gold, to eat food of a hundred flavors, and to dwell in residences valued at several thousand pieces of gold.
If you were to go begging for alms while wearing these expensive and fine garments, those who possess faith and respect would think:
"Now this non-Buddhist practitioner has broken his moral conduct in body."
"As for food and drink, it is difficult to sustain myself with them.
You should give me this upper garment of yours; I have a woolen cloak which I will exchange for it, and I shall wear it while going from house to house to beg for alms."
If a person of pure faith comes to question me, I shall answer him thus:
"There was a naked ascetic named so-and-so who withheld [his food] and bestowed it upon you.
He will then know that you are a person of deep faith; and when you go for alms, if he sees you, he will offer you a copper vessel filled to the brim with wine dregs as an act of veneration.
When that naked ascetic heard these words, he was filled with faith and joy, and spoke thus:
"Venerable sir! If it is so, you may take this robe."
Upānanda then offered a blessing, saying:
"May you be free from illness and long-lived; however, your followers are constantly in a state of poverty and suffering, and when they hear of your giving, they will surely snatch it back from you."
He said, "Venerable sir!
Is this woolen cloak indeed his property?"
"This is my own property; you may take it with confidence. "If that is the case, I shall accept it.
Having accepted it, he immediately gave him a coarse, thick-fleeced woolen cloak.
Then that outsider put on the garment and departed; having reached his fellow practitioners of the holy life, they asked him:
"Venerable sir, where did you obtain this garment?"
He then related in detail the circumstances of the clothing exchange.
Upon hearing this, they all spoke in anger:
"O virtuous one!..."
"This son of the Śākyas constantly intends to kill me; though others may deceive him, he is not like the group of six, for among those six, none surpasses this one.
If you were to bestow [this gift] upon other virtuous ones, I would likewise rejoice."
"Yet Upānanda wishes to drink my blood; who could endure having his robe given to him?
You should go and demand it back.
It would be well if you can get it."
"If you do not obtain it, I shall likewise expel you, move your seat, and cover up your food vessels; you need not speak with me.
He then became terrified and went to Upānanda’s place.
Seeing him approaching from afar, he thought to himself:
"Judging by this outsider's movements and demeanor, he will surely seize my fine woolen cloak.
He then hurriedly entered his room, closed the door, and remained there.

The non-Buddhist practitioners immediately arrived, knocked on the door, and called out; however, Upānanda remained silent and did not respond. When the bhikṣus saw this, they asked, "Non-Buddhist practitioner!
What do you require?"
He replied,
"I am looking for my woolen cloak, which is why I have come to seek you.
The bhikṣu said:
"If you wish to obtain [this], go to the World-Honored One and seek his compassionate protection.
Thereupon, that non-Buddhist practitioner went to where the Buddha was.
At that time, the World-Honored One saw the non-Buddhist practitioner approaching from afar and addressed the bhikṣus:
“Do you see those non-Buddhist practitioners coming?
They replied to the Buddha,
“We see them.”
The Buddha said,
"He has come for the sake of a woolen cloak.
If he can obtain it, that would be well."
"If I do not obtain it, I shall vomit hot blood and meet my end.
A non-Buddhist came to where the Buddha was and addressed him thus:
"Venerable One!"
"Upānanda has taken my woolen cloak; I pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion and pity, will cause him to return it to me.
If he does not return it, my fellow practitioners of the holy life will expel me."
As previously related in detail,
at that time the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda, saying:
"Go yourself and say to Upānanda:..."
"I hope you are free from illness," he said, and further addressed him:
"You must return that woolen cloak to those non-Buddhist practitioners; if you do not return it, you shall vomit hot blood and die."
Then the Venerable Ānanda, acting upon the Buddha’s words, informed him; having heard these words, he immediately rose from his seat and said:
"I now pay my respects; how could I dare to contravene the unsurpassed, venerable teaching?"

If it were not for the Buddha’s sending me back, even if non-Buddhists as numerous as bamboo and reeds filled the entire continent of Jambudvīpa were to vomit hot blood and perish all at once, not a single hair of my Upānanda would stir.
"Venerable Ānanda, you may go; I shall return there myself.
He then said to the non-Buddhist:

"Your great teacher previously practiced false speech to deceive the world; after his life ended, he fell into the Avīci Great Hell. Upon his tongue there are five hundred plows that plow and till day and night."
Your current falsehood is twice as grave as that; a thousand plows shall forever till your tongue.
You have already put on my woolen cloak, yet I have never used your belongings.
The non-Buddhist replied, "I, too, do not wear it.

Then Upānanda took that woolen cloak, untied its edge-knots, folded it into four layers, placed it in his left hand, and with his right hand he slapped and spread it open, draping it over the man's head. The man then fell to the ground, and Upānanda kicked him in the ribs, saying:
“Heretics, depart quickly!
Depart quickly!
Do not let your filth defile my field of merit.”
The non-Buddhist replied,
"Venerable One!
As long as I remain alive and am able to leave, I shall never again dare to enter the Jeta Grove."
This was the origin of the event, yet the Blessed One had not yet laid down the precept.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in various forms of lending at interest: they would take or give, produce or pledge; they would exchange what was already finished for what was finished, exchange what was unfinished for what was finished, exchange what was finished for what was unfinished, and exchange what was unfinished for what was unfinished.

Regarding "taking": this refers to actually taking possession of whatever goods one desires from another direction, transporting them away, and seeking out guards while establishing various contracts; this is what is meant by "taking."
Regarding "giving" (*datta*): this refers to giving another object on the eighth or tenth day and establishing a formal contract as proof; this is called "giving. Regarding "arising" (*jāta*):

this refers to the arising of profit, such as giving a small amount of goods to another and taking back much grain or barley, adding five percent, or even one or two times the original amount, and storing it by measure while establishing a promissory note; this is called "arising."

Regarding "pledge" (質): this refers to taking jewels, pearls, and so forth as collateral; as previously described, one establishes a contract and requests a reliable guarantor to hold the property for him—this is called a pledge.
Regarding "taking what is finished with what is finished," this refers to using vessels made of gold, silver, or other materials to take another's finished vessel.
Regarding "taking what is finished with what is unfinished," this refers to using a gold ingot to take another's gold vessel.
"Taking what is already finished with what is not yet finished" refers to taking another's gold ingot using a gold vessel.
"Taking what is not yet finished with what is not yet finished" refers to taking another's fragmented gold using a gold ingot.
When the bhikṣus engaged in such trade to seek profit, the various non-Buddhists, brahmins, householders, and elders, having witnessed this, all felt contempt and disparagement, saying:
"How is it that these śramaṇa sons of the Śākya produce goods to seek profit; how are they any different from the laity?"
"Who is able to provide him with clothing and food?
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, as previously [described], the Buddha assembled the community, questioned them regarding the facts, and reprimanded them. He spoke at length, up until the point where he established the training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again seeks profit through various forms of lending and borrowing, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
Regarding the term "bhikṣuṇī," it refers to a nun within this Dharma.
"Various kinds" refers to more than one type of thing.
"Seeking profit through receipts and disbursements" means engaging in the taking and giving, the receiving and spending, in order to seek a surplus profit.
Regarding the commission of the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the detailed explanation is as given above.

Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of seeking profit, collects goods and employs various expedients, driving carriages to other regions, establishing contracts and guarantors, and transporting taxable goods—even before she has obtained the profit, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); once she obtains the profit, she incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).

If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of seeking profit, provides various goods such as gold, silver, and other valuables to others and enters into a formal contract of guarantee, she incurs an offense as extensively explained previously.

If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of seeking profit, takes various goods or grain and entrusts them to another person, using measures such as bushels and pecks to calculate the amount and establishing a formal agreement, she incurs an offense as previously described.

If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of seeking profit, accepts precious gems, pearls, shells, or jade, and calculates the interest accrued over time—whether she actually obtains the profit or not—it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of profit, exchanges her own robe with another, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense; if she receives the profit, she commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
At that time, the Blessed One was staying in the High Hall by the side of the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī.

In this city, the Licchavis and others, seeing that the dwellings of the bhikṣuṇīs were lowly compared to their own residences which rose six stories high, immediately constructed for them elegant houses seven or eight stories high.
After a long time, the dwellings had mostly fallen into ruin; seeing this, the donors all thought to themselves:
"While we are still alive, the temples have all been destroyed; what will become of them after our lives have passed?"
"We ought to provide inexhaustible materials for her to carry out the construction.
Having thus taken the offerings, they went to where the bhikṣuṇīs were and said,
"Noble Ladies!"
"This is an inexhaustible gift intended for repairs; you should accept it.
The bhikṣuṇīs replied, "The World-Honored One has established the precepts; we are not permitted to accept it."
Then the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"If there is something to be constructed for the sake of the Saṃgha, one may accept inexhaustible goods."
"However, a bhikṣu-vihāra should be constructed with three stories, whereas a bhikṣuṇī-vihāra should be constructed with two stories.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs obtained inexhaustible goods and placed them within the monastic storehouse.
At that time, a donor came and asked,
"Venerable One!
For what reason has the vihāra still not been repaired?"
The bhikṣuṇī replied,
"O noble one! It is because we have no food or drink."
The donor asked,
"Have I not given inexhaustible goods?
He replied:
"O Worthy One!
How could we dare to consume these inexhaustible goods? They have been placed securely within the monastery treasury and remain there to this day.
The donor replied:
"The inexhaustible goods are not suitable for such a purpose; surely there is no place for them in my home. Why do you not exchange them to seek profit?
The nun said, "The Buddha has prohibited us and does not allow us to seek profit."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If it is for the sake of the Saṃgha, one should seek profit."

Having heard the Buddha’s words, those brahmins and householders who possessed faith made offerings of inexhaustible goods for the sake of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. These goods belonging to the Triple Gem should also be circulated to seek profit, and the resulting gains should be returned to the Triple Gem as an offering.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs returned these items to those donors; when they demanded interest, much contention arose, and they spoke thus:
"Noble ladies!..."
"How could it be right for my own belongings to be the cause of quarrels?
Then the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"One should not engage in lending with them.
Furthermore, when lending to those who are wealthy and noble, if they refuse to return the goods when they are demanded because they rely on their official power, the Buddha said:
"One should not engage in such transactions with them."
Furthermore, if they lend money at interest to a poor person and there is nothing to repay when it is due, the Buddha said:

"When giving the loan, one should clearly provide double the amount as collateral; record the terms in a formal contract, establish guarantors, note the year and month, and record the name of the presiding elder (sthavira) as well as the names of the administrators."
"Even if a lay follower (upāsaka) with faith receives the five precepts, he should likewise receive double the amount as collateral.
The Thirteenth Precept on Buying and Selling. The setting for this rule is the same as before.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus engaged in various kinds of transactions, taking and giving, buying and selling; they purchased cheaply and sold dear, storing up goods as they lived. When the brahmins and householders saw this, they all reviled and despised them.
The bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the community as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and rebuked them. He then established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī engages in various kinds of buying and selling, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
“Bhikṣuṇī” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“Various kinds” means not just one thing.
Regarding “taking, giving, buying, and selling”: “taking” means that if goods are cheap in another place but expensive here, one takes them from that place.
"Bestowing" means that if something is of low value here but of high value elsewhere, one takes it from this place and carries it away.
One purchases it during times of abundance and sells it during times of scarcity.
"Naiḥsargika" is explained in detail as previously stated.

Regarding the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī engages in buying and selling for the sake of profit, there is a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of purchase, and she incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) at the time of sale.
If she purchases for the sake of profit but does not sell for the sake of profit, there is a *duṣkṛta* at the time of purchase, but there is no offense at the time of sale.
If one buys for profit but sells without profit, there is no offense at the time of purchase, but at the time of sale, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If one buys without profit and sells without profit, there is no offense in either case.
If one purchases goods from another region not for the purpose of seeking profit, there is no offense even if a profit is made when selling them upon arrival.

The Fourteenth Training Rule: On Begging for a Bowl. The detailed account of the origin (nidāna) is as fully explained in the Bhikṣu-vinaya, up to the point where the training rule was established and should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī has a bowl that is less than five patches worn but is still fit for use, yet seeks another bowl for the sake of desiring something better, and obtains it, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
That bhikṣuṇī shall relinquish this bowl in the midst of the community; the community shall take the lowest-ranking bowl and give it to that bhikṣuṇī, saying:

"This bowl is returned to you. You should not keep it as a formal possession, nor should you treat it as a separate property, nor should you give it away to others. You should examine it carefully and use it slowly, maintaining it until it breaks."
"This is the Dharma.
Regarding "bhikṣuṇī," this refers to a nun within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Less than five patches" means not reaching five patches.
"Fit for use" means having obtained and maintained [the bowl].
"Seeking another bowl for the sake of beauty" means seeking a second bowl out of a desire for something beautiful;
"beauty" refers to excellence and fineness.
"Obtained" means having acquired it through seeking and brought it into one's possession.
"Naiḥsargika" is explained in detail as above.
"That bhikṣuṇī" refers to the person who has committed the offense.
That bhikṣuṇī who is to relinquish this bowl within the assembly should appoint one bhikṣuṇī from among the assembly to carry out the distribution of the bowl of the offender.
If there is no one possessing the five virtues, she should not be appointed; even if appointed, she should not be made to perform it.
What are the five? They are:
being possessed by craving, hatred, fear, delusion, and ignorance regarding what should and should not be done.
If one possesses these five qualities, they should be appointed if not yet appointed, and once appointed, they should be made to perform their duties.
What are the five? They should be understood as the reverse of the above.
He should appoint them in this manner: having struck the *ghanṭī* to assemble the community, he first asks:
"Are you able?
Can you, [Name], act as the distributor of the bowl for the Saṃgha that has been found guilty of an offense? He replies:
“Can you? Then, one bhikṣuṇī shall perform the formal motion (jñapti-karman); this should be done in detail as in the *Ekottarakarmaśataka*.
The Buddha said:
"I shall now declare the rules of conduct for a bhikṣuṇī who is traveling with a bowl that has been formally declared as having an offense.
That bhikṣuṇī should make the following formal announcement (jñapti) within the harmonious assembly:
'Venerable sirs!'"
"I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], shall perform the procedure for the bowl that has been transgressed against.
Venerable sirs!
Tomorrow, each of you should bring your own bowl and come to the midst of the Saṃgha."
When the following day arrived, the bhikṣuṇī who distributes the alms bowls spread out the mats and seats, struck the gaṇḍī, and each of the bhikṣuṇīs took her own bowl and went into the assembly.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī who is walking with the alms-bowl should hold the bowl and stand before the elder, praising it: "Elder!
This bowl is pure, complete, and fit for use; if you wish to have it, you may take it as you please."
If the senior monk (sthavira) accepts this bowl, the person distributing the bowls should take the senior monk’s previous bowl and pass it on to the second senior monk.
If he does not accept it, it is passed on to the third.

Regarding the third instance of taking: if the senior monk requests it again, it should not be given at the first request, nor should it be given at the second request; however, it should be given at the third request. The senior monk incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma (vayadharmāpatti) and must confess it according to the Dharma.
In this manner, it continues until even the smallest person among the assembly takes this bowl.
While the distribution is not yet finished, if someone from the third group seeks the bowl, the rule for them is similar to that for the senior monk (*upādhyāya*).

When the distribution of the bowls has been completed and one bowl has been obtained, the bhikṣuṇī who was distributing the bowls should take this bowl and hand it to that bhikṣuṇī, saying: "Bhikṣuṇī!..."
This bowl should not be discriminated against, nor should it be given away to others; one should use it carefully, slowly, and in accordance with the Dharma until it breaks.
This is its proper rule.
"If a bhikṣuṇī who is walking with the alms bowl does not act according to the Dharma, she incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
The Buddha said:
"I shall now establish the rules for the conduct of a bhikṣuṇī who has received an alms bowl."
One should keep two bowl-covers: the superior one should be used for the spare bowl, and the inferior one for the old bowl.
When going on alms-round, one should carry both bowls; if one receives dry rice, it should be placed in the spare bowl, and if one receives moist rice, it should be placed in the old bowl.
Having arrived at the dwelling, one should construct a maṇḍala and place two bowls upon it; one should eat from the old bowl.
After eating, one should first wash the extra bowl, and then wash the old bowl.
In this manner, even down to the stages of drying and storage, the long bowl is always to be treated first.
When placing it inside a niche or when fumigating it with fire, one should always place the long bowl first in the most favorable location.
When traveling on a journey, one should have someone carry the old bowl while carrying the extra bowl oneself.
If there is no one to hold it for you, place the extra bowl on the left shoulder and the old bowl on the right side, and proceed.
If a bhikṣuṇī who has received an alms-bowl does not abide by this rule of conduct, she commits an offense of transgressing the Dharma (vayadharmāpatti).
This disciplinary measure shall remain in effect until the end of her life, or until the bowl is broken; during that time, she should guard it well.
The details regarding what constitutes a *naiḥsargika* offense are as explained extensively above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression?

If a bhikṣuṇī’s bowl is broken such that it can be mended with a single patch, and although the patch has not yet been applied, she is still able to use it, yet she seeks another bowl: at the time of seeking it, she commits an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); once she obtains it, she incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
If a bhikṣuṇī’s bowl is broken such that it can be mended twice, she may still continue to use it even before the repairs are made; yet if she seeks another bowl, her offense is the same as before.
The matters concerning three or four repairs are also as previously stated.

If a bhikṣuṇī’s bowl is broken and can be repaired with one patch, and having applied that one patch she is currently using it, yet she seeks another bowl—when she seeks it, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing); once she obtains it, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
The same applies up to four repairs; the offense incurred is likewise.
If a bowl can be repaired five times, whether it has been repaired or not, or whether it is functional or not, there is no offense in seeking another bowl.
If the bowl was obtained by purchase or received as a gift, there is likewise no offense.

The Fifteenth Training Rule: On One’s Own Account Begging for Thread and Having a Weaver Who Is Not a Relative Weave a Robe. The setting and detailed explanation are fully as stated in the Bhikṣu-vinaya, up to: "He established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, on her own account, begs for thread and has a weaver who is not a relative weave a robe [for her], [she commits an offense].'"
If she obtains the robe, it constitutes a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Requesting thread oneself" refers to [requesting] one *liang*, half a *liang*, or similar amounts.
"Employing a non-relative" is explained at length as above.
"A weaver" refers to a hired weaver.
There are seven kinds of robes, as explained above.
If one obtains a robe, one commits an offense of expiation with forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*); the procedure for forfeiture is as stated above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances?
If a bhikṣuṇī requests thread from one who is not a relative and has that non-relative weave it, she incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta) for both acts;
when she receives the robe, she commits an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).
If a bhikṣuṇī requests thread from a non-relative and has a relative weave it into a robe: at the time of requesting, it is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); upon obtaining the robe, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī requests thread from a relative and has a non-relative weave it: at the time of requesting, there is no violation; upon obtaining the robe, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If a bhikṣuṇī requests thread from a relative and has a relative weave it, there is no offense in either case.

If a bhikṣuṇī requests thread from one who is not a relative and weaves the cloth herself, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of the request, and also an *dukkaṭa* when the garment is finished.
If a bhikṣuṇī requests thread from a relative and weaves it herself, there is no offense at the time of the request, but when the garment is completed, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If she provides payment for the work, there is no offense.

16. The Training Rule on Exhorting Weavers. The sixteenth training rule concerning exhorting weavers is explained in detail according to the Bhikṣu-vinaya, up to: "The training rule is hereby established and should be recited as follows:
If a bhikṣuṇī has a householder or a householder’s wife who is not a relative commission a weaver who is not a relative to weave a robe for her."
This bhikṣuṇī, having not previously received an invitation, conceived a contrary thought and went to the weaver’s workshop, saying these words:
"Do you know this now?"
"Please weave this robe for me.
Excellent weaver!

You should weave it well, combing it cleanly, selecting the fibers carefully, and beating it thoroughly. I shall provide you with a small portion of alms-food, or something similar to alms-food, or even the monetary value of such food."
"If a bhikṣuṇī gives such items to a weaver and obtains a robe [thereby], it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
The meaning of "one's own kin" versus "non-kin," as well as the seven types of robes, is explained in detail as above.
"Not having previously accepted an invitation" means that one has not been informed beforehand.
"Conceiving a divergent thought" means that the mind desires to obtain the robe.
Regarding the phrase "addressing those weavers and others," it means he was expressing his own intention.
The words "weave for me" clarify that it is for his own person.
The instruction "it should be woven well" is because he wished for the robe to be long and properly conform to the prescribed measurements.
"Thoroughly combing and grooming" refers to the desire to make the cloth wide and bright white.
"Skillfully selecting" means removing the knots and frayed edges to make it fine and refined.
"Beating it until extremely firm" is intended to make it smooth, lustrous, and dense.
"When I shall give food from a bowl" refers to the five kinds of *khādanīya* (solid foods) and the five kinds of *bhojanīya* (soft foods).
"Or things of the class of bowl-food" refers to raw grain and the like.
"Or again, 'the price for food' means providing its value.
'Bhikṣuṇī' refers to a nun within this Dharma.
'With such an object' refers to the aforementioned matter."
"Obtaining the robe" means the robe has come into one's hand.
"Naiḥsargika" is as explained above.
What are the characteristics of the offense and its specific circumstances herein?

If a bhikṣuṇī, for the sake of obtaining robes, rises from her seat, adjusts her robes, and gives two sets of five items of food or the like to a weaver, urging him to weave them well, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense; once she obtains the robes, she commits a naiḥsargika-pāyattika offense.
The categories of relatives and non-relatives are as explained above. 17.
The Training Rule on Taking Away Robes. The setting for this seventeenth training rule is the same as before.
At that time, the Bhikṣu Nandika gave a robe to his disciple and said:
"I shall travel through the human realms together with you.
The disciple was unwilling to go, so the bhikṣu Nandika snatched his robe away.
At that time, the bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha.

For this reason, the Buddha, as before, assembled the community and questioned them regarding the facts, reprimanding them. He spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī gives a robe to another bhikṣuṇī, and the latter, at a later time, out of malice, anger, or abuse, giving rise to a mind of resentment or contempt, should take it back herself or instruct another to take it back, saying:
'Give me back my robe; I will not give it to you.'"
"If a robe is separated from that person's body and she uses it for herself, it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma.
"To give to a bhikṣuṇī" means to give to another nun.
There are seven kinds of robes, as explained in detail previously.
"To give a robe" means to give it to a co-resident (sārdha-vihārin), a gatekeeper (dvāra-pāla), or others of a similar class.
"At a later time" means on another day.
"Causing distress, anger, reviling, or giving rise to a mind of contempt and disdain" refers to manifesting signs of hatred through body, speech, or mind.
"Taking it oneself or causing another to take it, thereby removing the robe from the body" means that it is completely separated from the body.
Regarding "for one's own use," this means it belongs to oneself.
As for the explanation of the offense, it is as extensively described previously.
In this context, what are the characteristics and the specific matters of the transgression?
There are three types of characteristics:
namely, those of the body, of speech, and of both together. Regarding the body:

if one first gives a robe and subsequently harbors resentment, and with one's own hand seizes it—either pulling or tugging—but does not speak, then as long as even a corner of the robe has not left the body, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); at the moment it leaves the body, one incurs an offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*). This is called bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Regarding "speech," it refers to uttering angry words to take away another's robe without moving the body or hands; the offense is established as before.
Regarding "both," it refers to taking away their robe by means of both body and speech; the offense is established as before.
Regarding "instructing another": if one instructs a bhikṣuṇī to take away that robe, when the robe has not yet left the body, both incur an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing);
if it has left the body, both incur a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture), and the owner incurs the fault of relinquishment.
If one instructs a bhikṣu to seize [the property], the offense is likewise; for the three lower assemblies, all incur the offense of duṣkṛta.
If laymen or laywomen seize it, they incur immeasurable sin.
There are two types of cases where there is no offense:
first, for the sake of difficult circumstances; second, for the sake of complying with the teachings.

Regarding "difficult circumstances": if one's two teachers see their own disciples in places of terror and so forth, or crossing dangerous terrain at an improper time on a riverbank, and they forcibly seize those disciples' robes out of fear that the disciples might lose them, in all such cases there is no offense.

Regarding "acting in accordance with the teaching": if a teacher sees that a disciple is associating intimately with evil companions or traveling along the same path with them, he may take away the disciple's robes so as not to allow him to commit evil; this is called acting in accordance with the teaching.

18. The Training Rule on Diverting Community Property to One’s Own Use. The training rule on diverting community property to one’s own use, the eighteenth, is explained in detail with its setting as found in the Bhikṣu-vinaya, up to: “The training rule is hereby enacted and should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that an item was given to the community, diverts it for her own personal use, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.’”
“Bhikṣuṇī” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“Knowing” means either knowing by herself or being informed by another.
“Saṃgha” refers to the disciples of the Buddha, the Śrāvakas.
"Various objects" are of two kinds:
namely, objects consisting of food and objects consisting of clothing; what is referred to here is objects consisting of clothing.
"To divert" means that when an object is already determined to belong to another, one transforms it and takes it for oneself.
Regarding the *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*, the explanation of the offense is as above.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this case?

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that an object belongs to another bhikṣuṇī and diverts it for her own use, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of diversion; once she has acquired it, there is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
In this manner, even if one knows that the property belongs to two persons, three persons, or the Saṃgha, yet diverts it for oneself, the offense incurred is the same as before.

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that an object belongs to a single bhikṣuṇī, and diverts it to give to another person, there is a duṣkṛta (wrongdoing) at the time of diversion, and there is also a duṣkṛta at the time she acquires it.
In this manner, even up to the point where one knows that an object belongs to a single person, yet diverts it to two people, three people, or the Saṃgha, the offense incurred is the same as before.

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that an object belongs to the Saṃgha, yet diverts it to a single person, there is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of diversion, and there is also an *duṣkṛta* at the time of acquisition.

In this manner, even up to the case where one knows that an object belongs to the Saṃgha and diverts it to two or three individuals: at the time of diversion, it is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing), and upon acquisition, it is also an *duṣkṛta*.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that an object belongs to a single Saṃgha and diverts it to multiple Saṃghas: at the time of diversion, it is an *duṣkṛta*, and upon acquisition, it is also an *duṣkṛta*.
If one knows that [an offering] was given to the community of bhikṣuṇīs, yet redirects it to the community of bhikṣus;
or knows that it was given to the community of bhikṣus, yet redirects it to the community of bhikṣuṇīs;
or knows that it was given to both communities, yet redirects it to the community of bhikṣus;
If one knows that [an item] was given to the Saṃgha of both divisions, yet redirects it to the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha;
or if one knows that it was given to the Bhikṣu Saṃgha, yet redirects it to the Saṃgha of both divisions;
or if one knows that property was given to the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, yet redirects it to the Saṃgha of both divisions.
If the Saṃgha has split into two factions, he knows that what was intended for this faction is diverted to that faction;
or he knows that what was intended for this monastery is diverted to that monastery; or he knows that what was intended for this room is diverted to that room;
or he knows that what was intended for this corridor is diverted to that corridor.

Or if one exchanges items between different corridors, or exchanges items from between these pillars to between those pillars, or exchanges items from between the pillars to the doorway, or exchanges items from the doorway to the upper gallery—and so on, as explained at length—even if they are exchanged back and forth in such a manner, all constitute an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that an object was intended for this particular Buddha image, diverts it to another Buddha image;
or knowing that an object was intended for this particular stūpa, diverts it to another stūpa;

or knowing that an object was intended for the first step of the stairway, diverts it to the second step and so forth, or diverts it to the main body of the stūpa, or to the eaves and tiers; [she commits an offense].

Whether one diverts materials from this side to another side, or diverts them to a covered bowl, or to the first tier of a square pedestal, wheel-base, and so forth up to the precious vase, Dharma-wheel, or pillar, or again diverts them from these down to the lower foundation—such mutual transferences as described above all constitute an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If one turns [the gift] over due to the power of the king, there is no offense.
If one intends to give this poor person's item but turns it over to give it to that other poor person, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If one cannot find [the intended recipient], turning it over [to another] is without offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī gives food to one animal and then diverts it to another animal, she incurs an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
If she is unable to find [the intended recipient], diverting it is not an offense.

If one intends to give an object to an animal and instead gives it to a human, or intends to give an object to a human and instead gives it to an animal, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one intends to give an object to a renunciant and instead gives it to a layperson, or conversely, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing;
however, there is no offense if one searches for the intended recipient and cannot find them.

In this same manner, regarding women, men, *paṇḍakas*, bhikṣus, and the three lower classes of monastics—whether many or few—if they exchange [robes] with one another, it should be explained according to the preceding rules.
If one cannot find [the required items], there is no offense in complying with others' wishes even though it contradicts one's own original intention. 19.
The Training Rule on Taking Medicine for More Than Seven Days. The nineteenth training rule concerning taking medicine for more than seven days; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the disciples of the Venerable Pilindavatsa handled all kinds of medicinal substances themselves or had others handle them; they mixed them with food or drink, either as fine powders or by blending them together, or allowed similar substances to contaminate one another. Keeping them all in one place, they did not know whether they should discard them or not, nor distinguish between the proper and improper times for use, consuming them at will according to their own inclinations.
Some bhikṣus of few desires, having seen this matter, gave rise to feelings of aversion and contempt and reported the circumstances to the Buddha.

On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:

"As the Blessed One has said, it is permitted for sick bhikṣuṇīs to consume all medicinal substances according to their needs—namely, ghee, oil, sugar, and honey—and to keep them for seven days, provided they maintain possession of them and consume them after they have been kept overnight."
"If a bhikṣuṇī consumes [it] beyond seven days, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"As for 'the World-Honored One,'" this refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"To explain" means to provide instruction and clarification.
"A sick bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma whose body is afflicted by illness.
"To consume whatever medicines as one pleases" means to take those that are suitable for the specific ailment, pure, and fit for consumption.
"Ghee" refers to various types of ghee;
"oil" refers to various types of oil;
"sugar" refers to granulated sugar.
"Honey" refers to honey from bees.
"For seven days" means for seven nights and days.
"One should personally keep it overnight and consume it" means that one may take it up oneself and eat it.
"Exceeding seven days" means to pass the limit of the prescribed period.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" means that this object must be relinquished and the offense must be confessed.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains medicine on the first day of the month, she must, within seven days, either formally take possession of it herself, relinquish it, or give it to another;
if she neither takes possession of it, nor relinquishes it, nor gives it to another, then when the dawn of the eighth day appears, she incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains medicine on the first day, does not obtain it on the second day, and then obtains it again on the third through the seventh days, she must, within those seven days, either take formal possession of it herself, relinquish it, or give it to another;
if she neither takes possession of it, nor relinquishes it, nor gives it to another, when the dawn of the eighth day appears, she incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains medicine on the first day and also obtains it on the second day, she must maintain the medicine obtained on the first day within the seven-day period; as for the medicine obtained on the second day, she may either relinquish it or give it to another, or she may herself maintain the medicine obtained on the second day while relinquishing or giving away the medicine obtained on the first day.
If she neither maintains, relinquishes, nor gives it to another, then when the dawn of the eighth day appears, she incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī performs the ritual procedure in mutual consultation for one day or two days, and likewise for two days, three days, up to six or seven days, the remainder is as prescribed by the aforementioned rule.
If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a large quantity of medicine on the first day of the month, she must, within seven days, either take formal possession of it herself, relinquish it, or give it to another;

if she neither takes possession of it, nor relinquishes it, nor gives it to another, when the dawn of the eighth day appears, she incurs an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a large quantity of medicine over the course of one day, and likewise up to seven days, she must, within those seven days, either take formal possession of it herself, relinquish it, or give it to another;
if she neither takes possession of it, nor relinquishes it, nor gives it to another, when the dawn of the eighth day appears, she incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains many medicines on the first day and also obtains many medicines on the second day, she should maintain the medicines obtained on the first day within the seven-day period; as for the medicines obtained on the second day, she should either relinquish them or give them to another.
Alternatively, she may maintain the medicines obtained on the second day herself, while relinquishing or giving away the medicines obtained on the first day.
If she does not relinquish them nor give them to another, when the dawn of the eighth day appears, she incurs an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If a bhikṣuṇī does not obtain many medicines on the first day, nor on the second day, and so on until she finally obtains many medicines on the sixth or seventh day, she should maintain the medicines obtained on the sixth day within the seven-day period; as for the medicines obtained on the seventh day, she should either relinquish them or give them to another.
If she neither relinquishes them nor gives them to another, when the dawn of the eighth day appears, she incurs an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.

If a bhikṣuṇī has any medicinal substances that she has touched herself or caused others to touch, or that have come into contact with other foods or fine powders, or that have been mixed together, or that are of similar types and blended such that they cannot be distinguished when kept in one place, these medicines should be given to the temple attendants (śrāmaṇeraka) or bestowed upon a female novice (śrāmaṇerikā).

Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī, regarding these various medicines, does not touch them herself nor cause others to touch them; does not allow them to come into contact with other foods or fine powders; nor mixes them with one another, nor allows those of different kinds to contaminate each other, nor keeps them in the same place; and if she can properly distinguish between what is relinquished and what is not, between what is timely and what is untimely—then within seven days, she may personally maintain them and take them for her own consumption.
One should maintain it in this manner: before midday, having washed one's hands clean, one should receive the medicine and speak thus to a fellow practitioner of the holy life:
"Venerable one, please attend to me!"
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], having this occasion of illness, now formally accepts these pure medicines for myself and for my fellow practitioners of the holy life, to be consumed by me within seven days.
The second and third days were also spoken of in this same manner.
Having taken the medicine for one day, he then informed his fellow practitioners of the holy life:
"I have taken this medicinal decoction for my illness for one day; six days remain, and I shall continue to take it."
In this manner, one should inform [the donor] for up to seven days.
If, after the seven days have passed, there is still medicine remaining, it should be given away to a lay attendant (upāsaka) or to a female novice (śrāmaṇerī).
If one does not relinquish it, then upon the appearance of the dawn on the eighth day, one commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*).

If a bhikṣuṇī possesses medicine subject to forfeiture and does not give it away to others, does not set it aside, and does not confess the offense, yet obtains further medicine, she commits an offense of expiation involving forfeiture for all of it, because of the taint of the prior [offense].

If a bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) regarding medicine, even though she has already forfeited it, has not yet created an interval [of purification], and has not yet confessed and atoned for the offense, if she further obtains other medicine, she commits an offense involving forfeiture in all cases, because of the prior defilement.

If a bhikṣuṇī commits an offense involving forfeiture of medicine, even though she has already forfeited it and there is an interval of time, if she has not yet confessed and atoned for the offense, and she subsequently obtains further medicine, she commits an offense of forfeiture in all such cases.

If a bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) regarding medicinal requisites and has not yet performed the three prescribed acts, should she further obtain other items—such as a bowl-bag, a waist-band, or any other articles used by śramaṇas for their livelihood—and accept and keep them, she commits an offense involving forfeiture due to the influence of her prior transgression.

If a bhikṣuṇī has committed an offense involving forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika) regarding medicine, and she has already forfeited it, maintained the required interval of time, and confessed and repented for the offense, there is no violation if she subsequently obtains other medicine.
20. The Training Rule on Keeping an Extra Alms Bowl. The twentieth training rule concerning the keeping of an extra alms bowl. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs merely knew how to store the extra bowls they had obtained; they neither used them themselves nor gave them to others.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, as before, the Buddha assembled the community, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī keeps an extra alms-bowl, she may do so for one night."
"If it exceeds [this limit], it is a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*.
A bhikṣuṇī may keep an extra bowl for only one night; "exceeding one night" means exceeding that single night.
Regarding the "extra bowl" (*atireka-pātra*): with the exception of the bowl that is formally maintained, any other is called "extra.
Regarding "keeping": it means forming the intention that it belongs to oneself.
If one keeps more than this, one incurs the offense of *naiḥsargika-pāyattika*; the method of relinquishment is as described above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a bowl on the first day of the month, within that same day she must either keep it, distribute it, discard it, or give it to another. The sequence of these actions and the manner of raising the question are explained in detail as in the previous precept concerning robes; even the formalities for its relinquishment are entirely the same as before.
If the object is small or white, or if it is intended for one who is about to receive the full precepts, there is no offense.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, Fascicle Ten. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.
Fascicle Eleven.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
The third summary verse says:
Not inspecting [the robes], relinquishing or not relinquishing, requesting gold, silver, or dye-money, obtaining profit—these five distinctions; buying medicine and clothing—the two prices. 21.
The Training Rule on Not Inspecting the Five Robes. The second training rule on not inspecting the five robes: the occasion was at Śrāvastī.
Women by nature have little memory; thus, the nuns did not know which was the saṃghāṭī,
which was the uttarāsaṅga, and which was the antarvāsaka.
"What is *kūsulaka*? What is *saṃkakṣikā*?
Then Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to the Blessed One, prostrated at his feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and informed the Buddha of the matter. The Buddha said:
"For this reason, nuns must keep the five robes in custody for half a month.
Once the Buddha had commanded that they be kept, the nun Pātayantī did not keep them in custody every half-month.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha convened the bhikṣuṇīs as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, he spoke at length until he said: "For the sake of the bhikṣuṇīs, I shall establish a training rule within the Vinaya, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī does not inspect her five robes for maintenance during the half-month, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
The robe must be relinquished, and the offense must be confessed.

Regarding the characteristics of the transgression herein: within every half-month, if a bhikṣuṇī does not look after her five robes, she incurs an offense of relinquishment and forfeiture (naiḥsargika-pāyattika).

22. The Training Rule on Discarding the *Kaṭhina* Robe Out of Season. The second training rule on discarding the *kaṭhina* robe out of season. The setting and circumstances are the same as before; the Buddha commanded that the bhikṣuṇīs should discard the *kaṭhina* robe.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā wished to relinquish the robes at an improper time, and she said to the other nuns:
"What is the use of storing these robes?
We should relinquish them together; when else would we wait?"
She then urged her to give it up.
As the bhikṣuṇīs were each traveling through the countryside with only five robes, another nun asked them:
"Noble ladies!..."
"Did you not spread the kaṭhina robe?
He replied, "I have already spread it."
"If you have spread it out, for what reason do you travel with only five robes?
She then related the matter in detail to him.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs as before.
The Buddha asked Pūraṇa Nandā:
"Is it true that you, in such a manner, caused the kaṭhina robe to be relinquished at an improper time?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him, and after speaking at length, he established the rule of training, saying: “It should be recited as follows:”
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, should discard the kaṭhina robe at an improper time, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūrṇa-nandā or any other nun.
What is the time for the *kaṭhina* robe?
It refers to the period from the sixteenth day of the eighth month until the middle of the first month; apart from this, all other times are considered "non-seasonal.
Regarding its relinquishment, it means relinquishing it by performing the formal ritual of a motion and a second proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*).
In all such cases, one incurs a *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* offense; the robe must be relinquished and the transgression confessed.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein:
if there is anyone who makes it at an improper time, it is entirely a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if one has been robbed by thieves. 23.

The Training Rule on Not Releasing the Kaṭhina at the Appropriate Time. The twenty-third training rule concerning not releasing the kaṭhina at the appropriate time; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

In accordance with the instruction of the Blessed One that all bhikṣuṇīs should relinquish the kaṭhina robe at the proper time, Pūlananda alone refused to relinquish it; she was thus guilty of the same offense as before.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On this account, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs as before and questioned Pūraṇa-Dhanadā:
"Has the time truly arrived, and do you not wish to relinquish the kaṭhina robe?
He replied, "It is indeed so."
The Blessed One rebuked her and, after speaking at length, established this training rule:
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not relinquish the kaṭhina robe at the proper time, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
"Time," "non-time," and so forth, have meanings as explained above. 24.
The Training Rule on Begging for Gold. The twenty-fourth training rule on begging for gold; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there was a goldsmith who had been married for not long. Later, on another occasion, the goldsmith thought to himself:
"Is my wife capable of managing the household affairs so as to increase our prosperity?"
"Now you may try it.
Having thought this, he immediately took the gold ring and placed it before the woman, then departed from the house.
At that time, Pūraṇa-Dāsa, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, entered her house for alms and said to the goldsmith's wife:
“O virtuous lady!
You may give me some food.
The woman then entered her room and brought out some parched grain to offer it; seeing the golden ring, the nun said:
"You previously gave me roasted flour, which is inauspicious; you may give me gold instead.
Upon hearing this, he remained silent.
The nun, thinking he would give her gold, immediately took his gold ring and departed from the house.
The goldsmith arrived later and asked his wife,
"Where is the golden ring?
His wife replied:
"A renunciant has come and taken away the golden ring.
The goldsmith followed after him and said,
"Venerable One!"
"Why have you stolen my gold and gone?
The nun replied,
"O worthy one!"
"If no one has given it to me, how would I dare take it?
The goldsmith replied,
"Then you must return my gold."
The nun placed the gold ring inside her mouth; the goldsmith struck her severely, forced her mouth open, and seized the gold, leading to various criticisms and complaints.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs as before and asked Pūraṇa Nandā:
"Did you truly commit this unseemly act, which is not the dharma of a śramaṇī?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him and, proceeding until he had established the rule of training, declared: "The precept should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī again solicits gold or silver, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūrṇaśailā (Tulānandā) or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"Begging" means wandering from house to house to solicit from others; the remaining meanings are as stated above.
The twenty-fifth training rule: Using the price for dyeing robes to procure food. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the nun Tullānandā’s five robes were worn out. During the mealtime, she put on her robes, took her bowl, and went to the residence of Queen Vaidehī. Upon arriving, she was provided with a seat and sat down; after preaching the Dharma for her, she remained there in silence.
The lady asked,
"Why are your robes torn?
The nun Khujjuttarā replied:
"How could I possibly have a husband or a son who might give me a robe?
The lady said, "Noble One!"
"I shall give you five robes.
He replied, "May you be free from illness; now is precisely the right time."
The lady immediately brought out her wardrobe and said,
"Noble One!
Please take whatever you wish."
The nun said, "Although there is merit in giving, there is no merit in mere consumption; you must provide the price for sewing and the price for dyeing.
The lady also gave these.
Having received them, Pūrṇa-nanda sold them and used the proceeds for food.
As before, she again put on her old clothes and went to the lady’s quarters. Upon seeing her, the lady said, "Noble One!..."
"For what reason do you wear these old clothes?
The nun replied, "You should simply rejoice that we have escaped the eight difficulties; those previously offered are now within the Inexhaustible Treasury."
The lady said, "Noble One!
What will you do with the robe once you have obtained it?"
The nun replied, “I pass through as is appropriate; I have but a *pāṃśukūla* (rag-robe) to cover my body—what need is there for clean, fine clothing?
The lady observed her and felt a sense of disrespect arise within her mind.
"How can a bhikṣuṇī use the benefit of the five robes for the purpose of food?
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

For this reason, the Buddha, as before, assembled the bhikṣuṇīs and questioned them regarding the facts, reprimanding them. He spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī takes the value of cloth for the purpose of providing food, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhananda or any other nun.
“Obtaining the price for dyeing robes” refers to the seven kinds of robes mentioned above;
“price for dyeing” means obtaining their value.

Regarding those who intend to use [the items] for food: having obtained such garments and other articles, they sell them and consume the proceeds as the two types of fivefold food (*pañcavidha-bhojana*).
The remaining meaning is as explained above.
The Twenty-sixth Training Rule: Using the Benefit of Separate Garments for Food. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

The nun Tūlanandā, wearing a worn-out robe and carrying her alms bowl, entered the city and went from house to house among the brahmins, householders, and elders, preaching the essentials of the Dharma for them.
A lay traveler asked,
"Noble one!
For what reason do you wear these tattered robes?"
The nun said, "How could I have husbands, sons, daughters, or slaves from whom I might give clothing? It is only through the gifts and provisions you provide that I am able to sustain myself.
The lay travelers replied:
"We shall offer whatever we can to the Noble One.

Some offered thread, others the price for robes, some the price for sewing, and others the price for dyeing; the nuns sold all these items to provide for their food and drink. Yet, wearing the same worn-out robes as before, they went to the house of the householder to teach him the essentials of the Dharma.
The householder’s wife asked,
"Venerable one, why are you still wearing these tattered robes?
The nun replied as she had before, explaining at length until she reached the point where the lay travelers were criticizing and disparaging her.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs as previously described, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, he established this training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If any bhikṣuṇī should receive a separate gift of clothing for the purpose of providing food, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhananda or any other nun.
“Obtaining separate clothing offerings” means receiving individual gifts from others.
“Using them for food” means selling them to provide for eating and chewing.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as described above. 27.

The training rule concerning using the value of bedding and furniture to supplement food. The twenty-seventh training rule concerning using the value of bedding and furniture to supplement food. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
The nun Tullanandā was inside the monastery when a householder and his wife came to visit her. The nun preached the Dharma for them, and they both gave rise to pure faith and felt great joy, saying:
"Noble Lady!..."
"If you have anything we require, please inform us;
we shall offer it to you. The nun said, "I need bedding."
Having heard these words, he took his bedding and offered it to this nun.
Once she had received it, she sold it to provide for her food and drink, and then went again to the houses of householders and brahmins.
They asked, "Venerable One!
We previously gave the funds for bedding; has it now been completed?"
The nun then said, "This body is filthy;
it is used according to its needs, so why must one provide such exquisite bedding?
Upon hearing this, the lay travelers all expressed their derision and disdain.
“How is it that a bhikṣuṇī uses bedding and requisites to procure food for consumption?
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, as previously described, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs, questioned them regarding the facts, and rebuked them. Having explained the matter at length, he established the training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having obtained a gift of bedding, should use it for food, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūraṇa-dhanadā, or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"Obtaining the benefit of bedding and requisites" refers to material wealth.
All other meanings are as explained above.
The twenty-eighth training rule concerning the use of benefits from temple construction and the rainy season retreat for food. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā thought to herself, "The monastery where I reside is now completely dilapidated; who will repair it?

Subsequently, wives of brahmins and householders came to pay homage at the nuns' feet and sat to one side. The nun preached the essentials of the Dharma to them and then led the women all around to show them the damaged areas.
Those women, wishing to repair [the monastery], each reduced their own wealth and offered it with a pure mind.
Once the nuns had received it, they ate it just as before.
Later, when the women came again and saw that the temple was in ruins, they asked:
“Noble one!
Why have you still not repaired it?
The nun then replied:
"A small hut or room is sufficient for the rains retreat; what need is there for such elaborate decoration?
Having heard this, they spoke with derision and suspicion:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī take property belonging to the Saṃgha and divert it into her own possession for personal consumption?"

When the nuns heard this, they informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the nuns as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should receive temple profits for the purpose of personal consumption, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
The nuns and so forth are as described above.

Regarding "benefiting the monastery," this refers to the donor’s original intention to provide for the benefit of the Tathāgata and his community of śrāvakas, as fully explained previously; the remaining meanings are also the same.

29. The Training Rule on Appropriating for Oneself Benefits Received from Many People. The twenty-ninth training rule on appropriating for oneself benefits received from many people. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
As the Blessed One had said, "A great assembly should be held every five or six years.

At that time, many bhikṣuṇīs arrived. On account of this, Pūraṇā entered the city of Śrāvastī and begged from the wives of householders and brahmins; having obtained much gain and offerings, she then took them for herself.
When the nuns heard this, they informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the nuns as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having received a gift intended for many, diverts it into her own possession, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
The explanation of the title is the same as before.
The thirtieth training rule concerning the misappropriation of communal property for one’s own use. The setting for this thirtieth rule is the same as before.

While the bhikṣuṇīs were observing the three-month rains retreat, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa (Tulānanda) solicited offerings from lay travelers during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony; whatever benefits for the community she obtained, she kept entirely for herself.
Upon hearing this, the laypeople all criticized and disparaged her, saying:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī, having begged for goods on behalf of the community, take them entirely into herself?
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

For this reason, the Buddha, as before, assembled the bhikṣuṇīs and questioned them regarding the facts. Having rebuked them, he spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should divert communal property for her own personal use, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or any other nun.
“Obtaining the community’s benefit” means that because of the community of nuns, two kinds of benefits are obtained:
either clothing or food.
"Returning it to oneself" means taking it for one's own personal use.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
**The Thirty-first Training Rule: Buying Medicine to Release from Bondage.** The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Muktaka-Śikhā-Nanda felt a lustful attachment toward a certain perfume-seller; she went to his shop to purchase various medicinal herbs, repeatedly tying and then untying her bundle, and while doing so, they conversed and took pleasure in each other’s company.
The nuns saw this and admonished her,
saying, "Noble lady, do not do such a thing.
She would not accept their advice.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of this matter, as before, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs, questioned them regarding the facts, and after reprimanding them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī purchases various medicinal substances and ties them up and then unties them, or unties them and then ties them up again, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Śuklā Nandā or any other nun.

“Purchases various medicinal substances” and so forth, up to “furthermore unties,” means that she takes goods from another with a mind of defiled attachment, unties what was bound, and experiences pleasure.
Regarding *naiḥsargika-pāyattikā*: the object must be relinquished, and the offense of transgression (*pāyattika*) must be confessed.
Within this context, as for the characteristics of the offense: whenever there is an act of binding or untying, one incurs the offense of transgression.
32. The Training Rule on Possessing Expensive and Heavy Clothing. The thirty-second training rule concerning the possession of expensive and heavy clothing. The setting is the same as before.

At that time, King Prasenajit of Kośala bestowed expensive and heavy garments upon his military commander. The commander then gave these garments to the nun Dharmadinnā; having received them, the nun placed them upon a rack.
At that time, the nun Ratnacūḍānandā entered the room of Dharmadinnā to pay her respects; seeing these precious garments, she asked,
"Noble lady, where did you obtain these?"
He replied,
“A spear-bearing military officer brought it here to give to me.
The nun Muktikā said:
"The Noble One’s merit is profound; he is venerated by humans and devas.
Fali said to the nun:
"Is there something you desire?"
The nun Muktikā said,
"Venerable One,
withered flowers from a shrine must be discarded as soon as they fade."
Having heard these words and understood their intent, Dharmadinnā took the garment and gave it to Maṇicūḍā.
Once she had received it, she immediately put it on and entered the city to beg for alms. When the common folk saw her, they all mocked her, saying:
"Look at this nun! She is so obsessed with sensual pleasures that how can she wear such royal attire as this and wander about everywhere?"
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the nuns as before; having questioned them and learned the facts, he rebuked her:
"You are difficult to support and difficult to satisfy, possessing great desire and lacking contentment."

The Blessed One praised being easy to support and easy to satisfy, having few desires and knowing contentment, and the virtues of the dhūta practices as a sublime adornment. He addressed the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"I now establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī possesses a costly and heavy robe, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to Śuklācīrṇa Nandā or any other nun.
“Holding a costly, heavy robe” means a robe weighing one hundred *liang*, worth twenty *kārsāpaṇas*, or even more than this—namely, fine Kāśi cloth or high-quality silk.
"Keeping" means taking possession for oneself.
"Naiḥsargika-pāyattika" has the meaning as explained above.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is also as stated above.
33. The Training Rule on Possessing Expensive Light Garments. The third and final training rule on possessing expensive light garments has the same setting as before.
At that time, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra gave an expensive light garment to Queen Vaidehī; the Queen then offered the garment to Mahāprajāpatī, who placed it upon a rack.

When Muktāśikha Nanda came and saw her, the exchange of questions and answers was as before; eventually, having obtained the robe, she went out to beg for alms, which drew the derision and reproach of the lay travelers.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

For this reason, the Buddha gathered the bhikṣuṇīs as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī possesses a costly, light garment, it is a naiḥsargika-pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Śuklācūḍā Nandā or any other nun.
“Holding a precious, light garment” means one that is high in value, worth twenty kārṣāpaṇas or more, and light in weight, weighing five *liang* or less; the remaining meanings are as stated above.
"Venerable sirs!
I have already recited the thirty-three *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* rules.
Now I ask the venerable sirs:"
"Is there purity herein?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable sirs!
Since there is silence, you are pure herein; I now hold it to be so."
4. One Hundred and Eighty *Pāyattika* Dharmas:
"Venerable sirs, these one hundred and eighty *pāyattika* dharmas are recited every half-month within the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*."
The initial summary verse says:
False slander and divisive speech, Exposing faults and speaking in unison,
Speaking of offenses and claiming superhuman states, Following favoritism and acting with contempt.
1. The Training Rule on Intentional False Speech. First: At that time, the Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the Venerable Rāhula was dwelling in a grove of hot springs near this city.
Then, a great multitude of faithful brahmins, householders, and others came to his place and asked:
"Venerable sir!..."
"Where does the Blessed One reside now?
If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was in the Bamboo Grove, Rāhula, fearing he might disturb his Great Teacher, would immediately reply:
"He is at Vulture Peak Mountain."
If he is in the Pipphalavana Cave, report:
"He is in the Senāniguhā Cave.
If he is in the Senāniguhā Cave, report: [He is in the Piṇḍolabhāradvāja Cave].
“At the Piṇḍola Cave.
At that time, those people, wishing to pay homage to the Buddha, were unable to see him; their bodies grew weary and they fell into extreme exhaustion, so they went to the place where Rāhula was.
At that time, Rāhula asked the people, saying:
"Virtuous ones, have you been able to see the World-Honored One?
They replied:
“I did not see it.
The people replied,
“Noble One!”
"For what reason do you trouble us?
He replied, "It is indeed so;
it was my deliberate intent to trouble you."
At that time, those people each gave rise to feelings of disdain and contempt.
The bhikṣus then informed the Buddha of these circumstances.

Having heard these words, the World-Honored One, during the first part of the day, took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Rājagṛha. He went on his almsround in sequence and returned to his original dwelling place.
When the meal was finished, after the time of eating, he immediately went to the Hot Springs Grove, to the dwelling place of Rāhula.

At that time, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, Rāhula prepared a seat for the Buddha, set out a water jar and a foot-washing basin, and having washed his own hands, went forth to welcome the World-Honored One. Taking up the upper robe, he said:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!"
"I pray that you will take a seat upon this throne.

Once the Buddha had taken his seat, he took water from a jar and washed his own feet. He poured out most of the water from the foot-washing vessel, leaving only a small amount remaining, and said to Rāhula:
"Do you see the little water left in the vessel?"
