He replied, “I saw it. “Rāhula! [the Buddha said.]
If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks falsehoods, being devoid of shame and lacking remorse,
I regard such a foolish person as one who possesses but a meager portion of the qualities of a śramaṇa.
The World-Honored One again poured the small amount of water remaining in the vessel onto the ground and said to Rāhula,
"Do you see that the little water has been entirely discarded upon the earth?"
He replied, “I have seen them.
The Buddha said:
“Rāhula! If one intentionally speaks falsehoods without shame or remorse,
I regard such a foolish person as having utterly abandoned the dharma of a śramaṇa.”
The Blessed One again tilted the vessel toward the ground and asked Rāhula,
"Do you see this vessel tilted?
He replied:
“I have seen it.
“If a bhikṣu intentionally speaks falsehoods,” [the Buddha] said, “and so forth, up to: this is called a leaning away from the dharma of a śramaṇa.
The Blessed One again overturned his bowl upon the ground and questioned Rāhula as before, until he declared it to be a leaning away from the dharma of a śramaṇa.
"Furthermore, Rāhula!
It is like a drunken elephant king who possesses great power and strength, with tusks as thick as chariot axles; he is stout, fierce, and skilled in combat.
When he goes to the battlefield to fight others, his four feet, two tusks, tail, back, and flanks all exert their full force, yet only his trunk remains curled and does not emerge."
"Rāhula! For the sake of protecting his life, this elephant does not use its trunk to crush that army.
The elephant trainer then thought:
"This elephant king cherishes his own body and life. Rāhula!

If, when that elephant king is engaged in battle, he extends his trunk to fight, at that time the elephant trainer immediately knows that this elephant does not begrudge his life; whether encountering his own army or the enemy's army, he will destroy them as soon as the opportunity arises, committing no evil that he would not do.
Thus it is, Rāhula!
If a bhikṣu deliberately utters a falsehood, being devoid of shame and lacking remorse,
I say that such a person is capable of committing no evil.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"If a person violates the true Dharma And deliberately utters false and deceptive speech,
Until the end of their life, There is no transgression they will not commit."
“It would be better to swallow a red-hot iron ball, blazing like a fierce flame, than with a mouth of broken precepts to consume the food offered by the faith of others.
This was the origin of the rule; at that time, the Blessed One had not yet laid down the formal precept.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika intentionally spoke a falsehood.
On account of this matter, the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
For this reason, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs as before and asked Pūraṇa Nandā:
"Is it true that you intentionally spoke such a falsehood? She replied:
"It is indeed so.
Having rebuked her in various ways, he continued: "I now establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī should intentionally speak falsehoods, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or any other nun.
“Intentionally” means that she does so with a deliberate mind, knowing it to be untrue.
Regarding “false speech,” there are nine types of false speech, as well as eight, seven, six, five, four, three, and two types, which differ according to their distinctions.
What are the nine kinds of false speech? They are:

making false claims based on groundless charges of a *pārājika*, a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, a *pāyattika*, a *pratideśanīya*, or a *duṣkṛta*; and making false claims based on groundless charges of a breach of morality, a breach of view, a breach of conduct, or a breach of right livelihood.
What are the eight kinds of false speech?

They are: [accusing another] with groundless cases of pārājika, saṃghāvaśeṣa, pāyattika, pratideśanīya, or duṣkṛta; and [accusing another] with groundless claims based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
What are the seven kinds of false speech? They are:

groundless charges of violation of the precepts, violation of views, violation of conduct, or violation of right livelihood; as well as groundless claims based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected.
What are the six kinds of false speech?
If a bhikṣuṇī intends to speak falsely, she gives rise to this thought:
"I shall speak falsely."
While speaking a deliberate falsehood, one thinks:
"I am now speaking a deliberate falsehood.
Having spoken the falsehood, one thinks:
"I have spoken falsely, based on groundless seeing, hearing, or suspicion.
What are the five kinds of false speech?
They refer to speaking falsely by means of groundless charges regarding the five classes of offenses.
What are the four kinds of false speech? They are:
groundless accusation of breaking the precepts, breaking right view, breaking proper conduct, and breaking right livelihood.
What are the three kinds of false speech?
That is to say, it is based on groundless seeing, hearing, or suspicion.
Furthermore, there are three kinds of false speech, involving such thoughts as:
"I shall speak falsely," "I am now speaking falsely," and "I have spoken falsely."
"What are the two kinds of false speech? They are:
'I am currently speaking falsely' and 'I have already spoken falsely.
There is not even one kind that constitutes false speech [in itself]."
Furthermore, there are five kinds of false speech. What are they?
There is false speech that incurs a *pārājika* offense;

there is that which incurs a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense; there is that which incurs a *sthūlātyaya* offense; there is that which incurs a *pāyattika* offense; and there is that which incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
How does one incur a *pārājika* offense through lying?
If a bhikṣuṇī, having not actually attained the state of a superior person (*uttarimanussa-dhamma*), claims to have attained it, this lie constitutes a *pārājika* offense.
How does one incur a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* through false speech?
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī is pure and free from offense, slanders her with a groundless *pārājika* charge, this false speech constitutes a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*.
How does one incur a *sthūlātyaya* for speaking falsely?

If a bhikṣuṇī, while in the midst of the community of nuns, intentionally speaks falsely—speaking what is not Dharma as Dharma, speaking Dharma as not Dharma, speaking what is not Vinaya as Vinaya, or speaking Vinaya as not Vinaya—this false speech incurs a *sthūlātyaya*.
How does one incur a *duṣkṛta* for lying?

If a bhikṣuṇī, when the *poṣadha* is performed every half-month and the *Prātimokṣa* Sūtra is being recited, is asked whether she is pure, yet knowing herself to be impure and having committed an offense, remains silent with the intention to conceal it—this lie constitutes a *duṣkṛta*.

Aside from the four types of false speech previously mentioned, all other instances of lying incur a *pāyattika* offense; this term carries the meaning of "scorching and falling. That is to say, the offender falls into the miserable realms of hell, the animal kingdom, or the hungry ghosts, where they undergo the suffering of being scorched and boiled.
Furthermore, if this offense is not confessed with earnestness, it can obstruct all wholesome dharmas.
Because it possesses these various meanings, it is called a *pāyattika*.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī has not seen, heard, sensed, or known something, yet forms such a thought and accepts it as such, saying:
"I have seen, I have heard, I have sensed, I have known."
When speaking in this manner, for every single utterance, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī has previously seen, heard, sensed, or known a matter but has forgotten it, yet forms such a thought and accepts it as such, saying:
"It is not false."
For every such statement, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If, having actually seen, heard, sensed, or known something, one subsequently develops doubt, yet forms the notion that it is so and accepts it as such, saying:
"Regarding what was seen and so forth, I have no doubt," [one incurs an offense].
Each time such words are spoken, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
If one has not seen, heard, sensed, or known [an object], yet possesses the perception that one has seen it and so forth, and with that understanding says:
"I have seen it."
When each such statement is uttered, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If, in reality, one has not seen [the object] but has heard, sensed, or known it, yet forms the notion that one has seen it and accepts it as such, and later says:
"I saw it; there was no hearing or the like," [one incurs the offense].
When each such statement is made, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If, in reality, one has not heard [the words] but has seen, sensed, or known them, yet forms the notion that they have heard them and accepts it as such, and later says:
"I have heard them, though I have not seen, sensed, or known them."
Each time he speaks thus, he incurs the fundamental offense.
If, in reality, he has not perceived [the object], yet he has seen, heard, or known it, and he forms the notion that he has done so, accepting it as such, but later says:
"I have perceived it, but I have not seen, heard, or known it."
When each such statement is uttered, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If, in reality, one does not know, yet has seen, heard, or sensed [something], and having formed such a thought and such an acceptance, later says:
"I know it, though I have no seeing, hearing, or sensing."
When each statement is made, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually seen but forgotten it, while having heard, sensed, or known without forgetting, yet forms the thought that this is the case and later says:
"I saw it and did not forget it; I also heard, sensed, and knew it without forgetting."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually heard [the teaching] but forgotten it, while having seen, sensed, or known it without forgetting, yet forms the thought that this is so, and later says:
"I have heard it and have not forgotten it; I have also seen, sensed, and known it without forgetting."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one has actually perceived but forgotten it, while having not forgotten what was seen, heard, or known, yet forms the thought that it was not forgotten, and later says:
"I perceived it and did not forget it; I saw, heard, and knew it, and I likewise did not forget it."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.
If one actually knows [the truth] but forgets it, while not forgetting what was seen, heard, or sensed, yet forms the thought that it has been forgotten, and later says:
"I know it and have not forgotten it; what was seen, heard, and sensed, I too have not forgotten."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the fundamental offense.

If one has actually seen but doubts it, while having heard, sensed, or known without doubt, yet forms the thought that "I have seen without doubt, but I doubt what I have heard, sensed, or known," and later says:
"I saw it without doubt; I doubt what I heard, sensed, or knew."
When each statement is spoken, one incurs the full offense.
If one has actually heard [the teaching] but doubts it, while having seen, sensed, or known it without doubt, yet forms the thought that it is otherwise and later says:
"I heard it without doubt, but I have doubts regarding what I saw, sensed, or knew."
When this is spoken, it constitutes the original offense.

If one has actually perceived but doubts it, while having seen, heard, or known without doubt, yet forms the thought that "I have perceived without doubt, but I doubt what I have seen, heard, or known," and later says:
"I perceived without doubt, but I doubt what I saw, heard, or knew."
When one speaks thus, it constitutes the fundamental offense.
If one actually knows [the fact] but is doubtful, while having no doubt regarding what was seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, speaking in such a manner is also as described above.
If one has not actually seen it and forms the perception that one did not see it, yet having heard, sensed, or known it, forms the perception that one heard, sensed, or knew it, and later says:
"I saw it, but I did not hear, feel, or know it.
At the time of speaking these words, the fundamental offense is incurred.
If one has truly not heard it and forms the perception that one has not heard it, yet has seen, felt, or known it and forms the perception that one has seen, felt, or known it, and later says:
"I heard it, but I did not perceive or know it.
At the time of speaking these words, one incurs the fundamental offense.

If, in reality, one has not perceived it yet forms the thought that one has not perceived it, but having seen, heard, or known it, one forms the thought that one has seen, heard, or known it, and later says:
"I have perceived, yet I do not see, hear, or know.
To speak thus constitutes the fundamental offense.
If one truly does not know and forms the perception that one does not know, yet has seen, heard, or perceived and forms the perception that one has seen, heard, or perceived, and later says:
"I know, yet I have not seen, heard, or sensed.
At the moment of saying this, he incurs the fundamental offense.
If he has actually seen, heard, sensed, or known, yet forms the thought that it was otherwise and later says:
"I did not see, hear, perceive, or know it.
When one speaks thus, it constitutes the primary offense.
If, however, one has truly seen, heard, perceived, or known it and does not forget the matter, yet forms this thought and later says:
"I saw, heard, sensed, or knew it, yet I have forgotten the matter.
At the moment of saying this, the fundamental offense is incurred.
If one has truly seen, heard, sensed, or known it and has no doubt, yet forms such a thought and later says:
"I have seen, heard, sensed, or cognized, yet I have a doubting mind.
At the moment of saying this, the primary offense is incurred.
If one has actually seen, but not heard, sensed, or cognized, yet forms such a thought and later says:
"I did not see it, but I heard, sensed, and knew it.
At the moment he says this, he incurs the fundamental offense.
If he actually heard it but did not see, sense, or know it, yet forms such a thought and later says:
"I did not hear it, but I saw, perceived, and knew it.
At the time of speaking these words, he incurs the root offense.
If he actually perceived it but neither saw, heard, nor knew it, yet forms this thought and later says:
"I did not perceive it, yet I saw, heard, and knew it.
At the time of speaking these words, he commits the fundamental offense.
If he actually knew it, but neither saw, heard, nor perceived it, and he forms this thought, later saying:
"I do not know, yet I have seen, heard, sensed, or cognized.
At the moment of speaking these words, the primary offense is incurred.
If one has actually seen and does not forget it, but has forgotten what was heard, sensed, or cognized, and while having that perception, later says:
"I forgot what I saw, but I did not forget what I heard, perceived, or cognized.
Speaking thus constitutes the original offense.
If, in fact, he did not forget what he heard but forgot what he saw, perceived, or cognized, yet forms this thought and later says:
"I forgot what I heard, but I do not forget what I perceived through sight.
At the time of speaking, this constitutes the primary offense.
If one has actually perceived and does not forget, yet forgot what was seen, heard, or known, and while harboring that thought, later says:
"I forgot what I perceived through mental cognition, but I did not forget what I saw, heard, or knew.
To speak thus constitutes the original offense.
If, in fact, one has not forgotten what was known but has forgotten what was seen, heard, or perceived, yet forms this thought and later says:
"I forgot what I knew, but I did not forget what I saw, heard, sensed, or cognized.
At the time of speaking these words, it constitutes a primary offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If one has actually seen something without doubt, yet has doubts regarding what was heard, sensed, or cognized, and while harboring such thoughts, later says:
"I have doubt regarding what I have seen, but no doubt regarding what I have heard, sensed, or known.
At the time of speaking these words, he incurs the fundamental offense.
If, in reality, he has no doubt regarding what he has heard, but does have doubt regarding what he has seen, sensed, or known, yet he forms this thought and later says:
"I have heard [it] with doubt, but I see, perceive, and know it without doubt.
At the moment of speaking these words, he incurs the primary offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If he has actually perceived it without doubt, yet sees, hears, or knows it with doubt, and while forming that very thought, he later says:
"I have doubt regarding what I have sensed, but I have no doubt regarding what I have seen, heard, or known.
At the time of speaking these words, the primary offense is incurred.
If one actually knows without doubt, but has doubt regarding what was seen, heard, or sensed, and while harboring that thought, later says:
"I know there is doubt, yet I have no doubt regarding what was seen, heard, sensed, or cognized.
At the moment of speaking these words, the fundamental offense is incurred.

If one has actually seen something and forms the perception of having seen it, but has not heard, sensed, or known anything and forms the perception of not having heard, sensed, or known it—forming that specific perception—and later says:
"I did not see it, but I heard it, perceived it, and cognized it.
At the moment of speaking these words, he incurs the fundamental offense.

If he has actually heard it and forms the perception that he has heard it, and he has not seen, perceived, or cognized it but forms the perception that he has not seen, perceived, or cognized it, and while forming this perception, he later says:
“I did not hear it, but I saw, perceived, and knew it.
At the moment of saying this, the fundamental offense is incurred.

If one actually perceives and forms the perception of perceiving, yet does not see, hear, or know and forms the perception of not seeing, hearing, or knowing—forming such a perception and later saying:
"I did not perceive it, yet I saw, heard, and knew it.
At the time of speaking these words, the primary offense is incurred.

If one actually knows [something] but forms the perception that one knows it, or does not see, hear, or perceive [something] but forms the perception that one does not see, hear, or perceive it—forming such a perception and later saying:
"I do not know, yet I have seen, heard, or perceived.
When one speaks thus, one incurs the fundamental offense (*mūlāpatti*).
If a bhikṣuṇī speaks any words that contradict her mind, she incurs the fundamental offense in all such cases.
If one speaks without contradicting one's own mind, there is no offense in either case.

The Training Rule on Slandering Speech. The second training rule, on slandering speech: At that time, the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus would constantly speak disparagingly of other bhikṣus, saying:

"You blind man! You lame man! You hunchback! You dwarf! You who are too tall! You who are too short! You who are too coarse! You who are too thin! You deaf man! You blind man! You mute man! You who walk with a crutch! You with swollen feet! You with a shaven arm! You with a large head! You with drooping lips! You with protruding teeth!"

At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus uttered such disparaging words, the other bhikṣus, having heard them, were filled with shame and distress, finding no joy; they completely neglected their recitation and contemplation, remaining in a state of sorrow.
At that time, some bhikṣus of few desires, having witnessed this incident, all felt revulsion and contempt, and spoke words of disparagement:
"How can a bhikṣu revile another bhikṣu, calling him 'one with squinting eyes' and so forth?"
As described above,
the bhikṣus reported these circumstances to the Buddha. Thereupon,
the World-Honored One, for this reason, assembled the two assemblies of monks and even questioned the group of six:
“Did you truly utter disparaging words to harass the bhikṣus, calling them ‘one-eyed’ and so forth?
The group of six replied,
“It is true.”
"O Venerable One!
The World-Honored One then rebuked him in various ways, as extensively explained above, up until: "This is not the conduct of a śramaṇa; it is not a task you should perform."
Why is this? You should listen!
In ages past, there was an elder in a village who had recently married and lived in joyful intimacy with his wife; before long, they gave birth to a daughter who gradually grew up.
The elder personally labored as a plowman.

At that time, there was the son of a householder whose parents had both passed away; he regularly made his living by selling firewood in the forests and wilds. Carrying his load of wood, he came to the place where the elder was plowing, and set down his pole at the edge of the field beneath a tree to rest his shoulders.
Seeing that elder personally engaged in plowing, he approached him and asked, "Uncle!
For what reason do you toil so hard yourself in your declining years? You ought to be living in a village, yet instead you are here in the fields."
He replied, "Welcome, nephew!
I have no brothers and no children; how could I provide for my own clothing and food without farming myself?"
He replied, "Uncle!
I shall plow for you for a while; you should rest for a moment."
He immediately took up the plow to work in his stead until midday.
When the food from the house arrived, he called out, "Nephew!"
"Come, let us eat together.
After they had eaten together, he said, "Uncle!"
"You should return home.
However, as I do not yet know the location of my uncle's residence, I shall go outside the village after the sun has set; we shall meet on the road.
Having heard this, the elder immediately returned to his house.

At that time, the householder’s son had been plowing until evening; he released his oxen into the green grass and, carrying a shoulder-pole with bundles of straw and a load of firewood, drove the animals back home.
Upon reaching the edge of the village, the elder met him and led him directly to his residence.
At that time, the householder’s son cleaned the barn, spread dry earth over it, set up a fire and smoke, and provided a great deal of fodder for the oxen.
When the elder saw this, he thought to himself:
"Because of this son of mine, I now enjoy peace and happiness; I shall give my young daughter to him as a wife."
After having him eat, he said to him: "Nephew!
You should remain here and diligently attend to the family business; I give this young girl to you as a wife."
He replied, "Very well!
and immediately followed those instructions to establish his livelihood through manual labor.

"At that time, the householder had two oxen whom he employed for labor. The larger one was by nature gentle and well-behaved, while the smaller one was dull-witted and gluttonous; despite being restrained, it was its constant habit to commit acts of violence."
The youth, filled with indignation, hurled a stone from afar and broke off one of its horns; thus it was named "Bald-Horned.
Later, on another day, as the animal continued to trespass upon the young crops just as before, he released a sickle and cut off its tail; consequently, it was named "Bald-Tailed Bald-Horned."
Later, at another time, the householder’s son said to the elder:
"Uncle! Please fulfill the marriage alliance you previously promised."
At that time, the householder said,
"Very well," and then addressed his wife:
"O worthy one! You should prepare the robes and ornaments; our young daughter will soon be ready for marriage.
His wife then asked:
"How can you provide for it when you have never given anything to others?
The elder replied,
"I have already given it to others."
The wife asked, "Who is it?
He replied:
"O son of this householder," his wife said, "I do not know the origins of this man's clan;
he is like white pepper, whose place of origin is unknown. How can you rashly form a marriage alliance with him?"
"In all matters of marriage, when relatives come and go, share food and drink, and call upon one another, I shall give my daughter only if our clans correspond.
He said to his wife:
"O virtuous lady!..."
Since this son of a householder came to my home, I have been able to enjoy peace and comfort by having him take over my labors.
Were he not here, I would once again be beset by hardship and could not avoid the toil of manual farming myself.
The wife replied to her husband, "I truly cannot give my beloved daughter to a servant.
People of the world generally follow their wives' words; at that time, the elder thought to himself:
"If I were to reply that I will not give her to you, this laborer would leave me this very day, and I myself could not avoid having to take up the plow.
For now, I shall employ a deceptive expedient so that he does not depart immediately."
At another time, that laborer said to the householder: "Householder,
you ought to arrange a marriage."
He replied, "Nephew!
My family and kinsmen are numerous; when we gather, there is a great need for food and drink. It would be best to wait until the autumn harvest of rice is gathered."
Once the grain had been gathered, he announced that the wedding was to take place, saying: "Nephew!
We require sugar; you should wait for the sugarcane."
Once he had accepted this, the man further announced that they were to be married, saying:
"Nephew! These flour and pastries are for your sustenance; you shall wait until the wheat is ripe."
Once the wheat had been harvested, he announced that the wedding was to take place again, saying:
"Nephew! The old rice is nearly exhausted; you should wait for the new non-glutinous rice."
At that time, seeing that [the other] was making excuses and delaying, the householder’s son conceived this thought:
"It is impossible for the crops in the field to ripen all at once; judging by these circumstances, he is surely deceiving me."
"I should now go and inform the people; if they do not give it to me, I shall take the matter to the authorities for a final decision.
He then addressed the assembly, saying: "Uncle!"
"A marriage may be arranged.
Having heard this, the people said to the elder, "The agreement was made long ago; why have you not yet performed the marriage?"
At that time, the elder became angry and said:
"Gentlemen, you should know that this man is a hired laborer in my house; for what reason would I have him marry?"
Then the householder’s son thought to himself:
"I have neither obtained the money nor the wife; time is being wasted in vain without any success.
I should now harm this man so that I may depart as I please."

He then took the two oxen and drove them for half a day, subjecting them to many blows and lashes. He tied them to a withered tree and exposed them to the scorching sun before intending to return home.
At a time near the beginning of the kalpa, animals were able to understand human speech. The large bull then addressed the householder’s son: "Previously you cherished me and loved me together;

our kindness was like that of parents, and you knew my toil. For what reason do you now inflict so many lashes upon me, tie me to a withered tree, and expose me to the scorching sun? Why do you abandon me and return home?"
"What fault or offense have I committed against you?
The householder’s son replied, "You have no fault;
however, your master has committed an offense against me."
The ox asked,
"What fault has he committed?
He replied:
"You previously promised to give me your daughter, yet now you violate your word.
The ox said,
"Why do you not take this to the authorities?"
The man replied, "Because there is no witness.
The ox said:
"We shall serve as witnesses for you. The man asked,
"Are you speaking as human beings?"
"Shall I make the sound of an ox?
He replied, "I shall not speak human language; I will manifest signs, and you should enter into a covenant to lead me as a witness so that people may know it."

"Lead my two oxen and tie them inside the barn, giving them neither water nor fodder. After seven days have passed, release me into a place on the ground where there is abundant water and grass, so that bystanders may come and see the proof."
"We shall hold our tongues and not eat water or grass; we will manifest this appearance so that the king and his ministers may believe your words to be true, and then we shall drink and eat.
At that time, having heard this plan, the man immediately released them all together into the lush grass and went himself to the king's presence, paid his respects, and said to the king:
"Great King!"
"A householder of such-and-such a village promised his daughter in marriage, yet after she had served for many years, he has now reneged.
The King summoned the householder and questioned him regarding the truth of the matter; the householder replied, "I truly did not give my consent."
The king asked the man:
"Do you have any witnesses?
The man replied to the king:
"Yes," [he replied]. The King asked,
"Is he a human being?"
"Are you a non-human being?
He replied, "I am a non-human being."
The king asked,
"What is this? and [the messenger] replied:
"It is a cow.
The king asked,
"Does it speak the language of humans?"
"Is it some other kind of speech?
He replied, "I do not speak the language of humans."
The King asked,
"How can this be proven? He replied:
"He possesses genuine faith that can be made known to others.

For seven days, keep this ox tied inside the stable and do not give it water or grass. Once the seven days have passed, release the ox into a place on the ground where there is abundant water and grass. I shall lead [the ox] as proof; there will surely be a miraculous sign, such that even before the Great King has yet placed his trust in me, the ox will never eat."
"If this be false, I shall deserve the death penalty.
The king commanded his ministers, saying,
"One must rely upon these words to observe the evidence."
The minister, having received these instructions, took the two oxen and tied them inside a barn, providing them neither water nor fodder.
Then the bald-horned, bald-tailed ox said to the great bull:
"Is this some kind of perversion? Why is it that we alone have the sun rising in the west, being confined within this barn without hearing of water or fodder?"
The great ox replied,
"Is it not true that I promised to act as a guarantor for the son of the householder, so that he might remain fasting for seven days, not eating grass or water until the king has gained faith?"
The bald-tailed, bald-horned one replied to the great ox, saying, "If you release me, I would devour even a rock upon encountering it; how much more so water and grass?
The great ox replied:
"This son of a householder loves and cares for us as his own parents; how could we violate our word and deceive him?
The Bald-Tailed and Bald-Horned one replied, "Though he truly loves and cherishes us with affection equal to that for his own two parents, he constantly calls me 'Bald-Tailed' and 'Bald-Horned'."
"When I hear you calling, I intend to pierce its belly with my horns.
Having heard this, the great bull remained silent.
Later, when the householder’s son came again to look at it, he asked the bull:
"Are you at peace?
The great ox replied,
"I am indeed at peace, but you are not."
The householder’s son asked,
“What is the meaning of this?
The great ox explained it in detail.
The householder’s son said, "If it is so, I shall flee in haste this very night; my life is in the balance, for I am being deceived by the king.
The great ox replied:
"You need not flee; I shall have my tail shorn and my horns trimmed, and a nose-rope shall be passed through my nostrils with its tether fastened securely to my horns.
On the day I am released, if he violates his promise and consumes water or grass, I will lift his nose upward with both my horns."
You then replied:
"Now these two oxen have informed the fifth world-protector.
It is commonly agreed upon by the people of the world that there are five protectors, namely: earth, water, fire, wind, and the sun.
Then the householder’s son proceeded to pierce its nose. The bald-tailed, bald-horned ox said to the great bull, "Virtuous one, you should observe this cruel oppression being inflicted upon me.
The great bull said:
"What suffering could there be in wearing these ornaments?
he said, and then tied the elder calf's head with a halter.

When seven days had passed, the king and his ministers went together to observe them; they released the cattle into a field abundant with water and grass to let them graze. Upon seeing the water and grass, the calves with shorn tails and horns immediately desired to eat; at that moment, the great bull used both its horns to lift the younger calf by the nose and gaze toward the sun.
The king asked his ministers,
"For what reason are these two oxen gazing toward the sun?
At that time, there was a wise minister who replied:
"Great King!

Now these two oxen wish to inform Your Majesty of this matter; it is not merely we two who serve as witnesses, but we also appeal to the fifth world-protector, the clear and bright sun, to assist us in our testimony."
When the king saw this matter, he was filled with extreme wonder and said to his ministers:
"Even a beast, lacking in knowledge, can act as a guarantor for a human being. Since the matter is not false, it is fitting that she be given in marriage to him."
He then released both oxen so they might eat grass and drink water together.
At that time, having achieved victory, the householder’s son took the girl as his wife.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"You should know this!
Even those in the realm of animals harbor thoughts of malice when hearing words of disparagement, let alone humans.
Therefore, O Bhikṣus!"
"One should not speak harsh words or disparage others.
This was the origin of the rule, though the precept had not yet been formally established.
The Buddha further addressed the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, there lived in a certain village an elder whose livelihood was by means of driving carts.
He had two female oxen:
one named Nandā and the other named Rasā. During the spring season, each gave birth to a single calf, both of which were variegated in color."
As they gradually grew up, the son of Joyful had broad and long horns, while the son of Fine Flavor was bald-headed and hornless.
At that time, the elder established names for them: the first was named Joyful Long-Horned, and the second was named Fine-Flavored Bald-Headed.
When they had grown strong and were both possessed of great vigor,
at another time, some people driving carts gathered at the edge of the pond because they had been drinking their oxen there, and spoke these words:
"Whose ox is the most excellent?"
Each said, "My ox is superior.
The elder replied,
"My ox is far superior."
How is this known?
One may have a heavy cart pulled up a steep slope and make a clear agreement together, wagering five hundred gold coins.
Having made this resolve, he took his own oxen to the steep slope and hitched his heavy cart.
Then the elder called out to the oxen, saying:
"O Joyful Long-Horned One, you should pull swiftly; O Delicious-Tasting Bald-Headed One, you too must haul with haste!"
When the shaven-headed ox heard these disparaging words, it immediately stopped and refused to pull the cart.
The elder grew furious and began to lash it with a heavy cudgel.
The others reported, "Do you intend to kill this ox now?"
"Since he is not as capable as we thought, he ought to be released.
At that time, the elder paid five hundred gold coins and, in a state of extreme rage, gave him many lashes with a cow-whip and tied him to a withered tree.
The ox, having understood human speech as previously described, replied:
"Now, because of you, they have fined me gold coins. The ox said: [The householder replied: "Now, because of you, they have fined me gold coins. The ox said:
"It was due to the verbal transgression of the master.
The elder asked,
"What was my verbal transgression?"
The ox said, "Why do you humiliate and insult me before others?
If you say that my reputation is good and you will not disparage me, let us pull a double load up a steep slope together; let us establish a clear agreement and double our wager to one thousand."
The householder replied,
"Do you now wish to double my fine?
The ox said:
"Do not disparage me; I shall certainly exert all my strength.
Later, he made a pact with another man to pull a cart drawn by an ox up a steep slope. He then called out to the ox, saying:
"O Joyful One, you should pull quickly! O Delicious One, you must haul swiftly!"

Upon hearing this, the two oxen were filled with joy; they exerted all their strength to pull the cart until it reached level ground, and having achieved victory, they obtained one thousand gold coins.
At that time, a deva in the midst of the sky spoke a verse, saying:
"Though there be an extremely heavy load, And it rests upon a steep slope below;
If the two oxen’s hearts are joyful, They can pull this chariot out."
If one speaks words that accord with their wishes, the two oxen will hear them with joy;
drawing the cart out [of the mud] will not be difficult, and the master will obtain a reward of a thousand pieces of gold.
Therefore, always speak with affectionate words; do not utter speech that is harsh to the ear.
"When one utters words of loving-kindness, one is free from fault and always dwells in peace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"When those of the animal realm hear such disparagement, they can still bring harm to their master; how much more so for human beings!"
"Therefore, you bhikṣus, you should not speak words of disparagement toward others.
Having rebuked them in various ways, he spoke at length until: "I shall establish a training rule for my disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, speaks disparagingly, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma.
"Speaking disparagingly" means uttering words that manifest acts of humiliation toward another person.
When he understands [the offense], he incurs a *pāyattika* offense; the detailed explanation is as above.
What are the characteristics of the transgression in this context?
A summary verse says:
Lineage, craftsmanship, karma, physical form, and disease—these five;
offenses, the category of afflictions, and abusive speech as the final one.

Weavers, wool-workers, and needle-makers; those who work with iron, copper, and leather;
potters and barbers; wood- and bamboo-workers, as well as slaves.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣuṇī of the brahmin caste and speaks thus:
"Noble one!
You are a woman of the Brahmin caste who has gone forth; you are now neither a female śramaṇa nor a female Brahmin.
When that bhikṣuṇī hears these words, whether she is thereby distressed or not, this nun incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣuṇī of the kṣatriya caste and speaks as previously described, up to and including whether she causes distress or not, this bhikṣuṇī also incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If one goes to the place of a Vaiśya-caste nun and speaks these words:
"Noble lady!
You are a woman of the Vaiśya caste who has gone forth; you are now neither a female śramaṇa nor a female brāhmaṇa."
Having heard these words, she may either be distressed or not distressed.

Regarding the phrase "this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pāyattika," all subsequent passages likewise contain the phrase "whether distressed or not distressed"; fearing that the text would become too voluminous, I have not translated them.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣuṇī of śūdra birth and speaks thus:
"Noble lady!
You are one who has gone forth from a śūdra family; you are now neither a female śramaṇa nor a female brāhmaṇa."
Upon hearing this, that nun incurs a *pāyantika* offense.
This concludes the discussion on castes.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣuṇī of the Brahmin caste and speaks as above, up to: "She is neither a female śramaṇa nor a female brāhmaṇa."

You should now learn your own crafts and various technical skills, namely: the Brahminic codes of conduct and ritual procedures, the practice of purification, the handling of the water-pitcher, the taking up of ashes and earth, the rules for recitation with a jar-like or rustling voice, the four Vedas, and the methods for performing and receiving various sacrificial offerings and assemblies.
Upon hearing this, the former nun incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.

Whatever be the dignified conduct and formal protocols of a kṣatriya—namely, riding chariots and horses, wielding bows and arrows, turning and advancing, handling hooks and ropes, using spears and lances, the arts of cutting, hacking, stabbing, boxing, wrestling, archery, and the like.
Upon hearing this, that nun incurs the same offense as before.

"If it concerns the modes of conduct and rules of the Vaiśyas— namely, plowing fields, tending cattle, engaging in trade, and so forth"—

whatever the Śūdras' deportment and rules may be—namely, carrying firewood on their shoulders and feeding the livestock."
Upon hearing this, that nun incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If a nun goes to the quarters of nuns who are weavers and speaks as above, even saying: "You should now learn your own crafts, namely the making of large and small blankets, as well as garments for covering and clothing made of hempen or flaxen thread."
Upon hearing this, that nun incurs an offense as previously described.

If she goes to the place of a wool-weaving nun and speaks as above, even saying, "You should now learn your own craft, namely the making of large and small carpets, whether thick or thin, or square and round cushions and mats," [she incurs the same offense].
When that nun has heard this, she incurs the same offense as before.

Upon hearing this, that nun incurs the same offense as before.

If she goes to the quarters of a nun of the blacksmith caste and speaks as above, even saying, "You should now learn your own craft, namely the making of iron needles, razors, axes, pickaxes, and so forth," [the offense is the same].
Once that nun has heard it, this [speaker] incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If she goes to the quarters of nuns who work in copper and speaks as above, explaining at length up to: "You should now learn your own craft, namely the making of copper plates, bowls, and other such items."
Having heard this, that nun incurs the same offense as before.

If she goes to a nun who works with leather and speaks as above, even saying, "You should now learn your own craft, namely the making of *phala* (boots), shoes, saddles, bridles, seats, and other such items."
Having heard this, that nun incurs the same offense as before.

If she goes to the quarters of nuns of the potter caste and speaks as above, explaining at length up to: "Now you ought to learn your own craft, namely the making of jars, pots, bowls, and other such vessels."
When that nun heard this, she incurred the same offense as before.

If she goes to a nun of the hair-cutting class and speaks as above, explaining at length up to: "You should now learn your own craft, namely such matters as cutting hair, clipping nails, dressing, and folding."
When that nun heard this, she incurred the same offense as before.

If a nun goes to the quarters of nuns who work in wood and speaks as above, explaining at length up to: "You should now learn your own crafts, namely the making of beds, seats, windows, houses, and so forth."
When that nun had heard this, the rest is as explained above.

If a nun goes to the dwelling of a nun who makes bamboo articles and speaks as described above, up until: "You should now learn your own craft, namely the making of baskets, winnowing fans, mats, fans, umbrellas, parasols, and nose-pipes."
When that nun heard this, the rest is as explained above.

If a nun goes to a nun of the *dāsa* or *dāsī* caste and speaks as above, even down to: "Learn your own crafts, namely such tasks as washing the feet of others, bathing their bodies, and performing menial labor for them."
Having heard this, the nun’s remaining actions are as described above.
This concludes the discussion on craftsmanship.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣuṇī of Brahmin descent and speaks as follows:
“You are one who has gone forth from the Brahmin caste; you are neither a female ascetic (śramaṇī) nor a female Brahmin.
You should now perform your own proper work—that is, the conduct and ritual observances of a Brahmin, such as the duties of washing and carrying the water-pitcher, as explained at length previously.”
When that nun has heard this, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
Likewise, if a Kṣatriya causes her to perform her own work, as explained in detail above, he incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If the work performed by Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or other classes of slaves and servants— as described in detail previously— is undertaken according to their respective duties,
and if she uses their tools and implements, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pāyattika offense.
This treatise has completed its exposition of the actions.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣuṇī who is lame or crippled and speaks thus:
"You are a lame or crippled renunciant; you are neither a śramaṇī nor a brāhmaṇī."
When that bhikṣuṇī hears these words, she incurs a pāyattika offense.
This applies likewise even when speaking to one who is one-eyed, blind, humpbacked, a dwarf, deaf and mute, or has a deformed gait and loathsome appearance.
Upon hearing these words, all these nuns incur a *pāyattika* offense.
This concludes the discussion on physical appearance.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to a bhikṣuṇī suffering from leprosy and speaks as follows:
“You are a leprous renunciant; you are neither a śramaṇī nor a brāhmaṇī.
When that nun heard this, she incurred the same offense as before.
In this way, there arise all manner of diseases such as scabies, balding sores, hiccups, vomiting, consumption, feverish malaria, wind-disorders, insanity, dropsy, hemorrhoids, fistulas, and tumors.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to such a sick bhikṣuṇī and speaks as described above, she incurs an offense identical to the previous one.
What constitutes this offense?
If a nun, with the intent to disparage, goes to where another bhikṣuṇī is and speaks thus:
"You have committed a pārājika offense; you are not a śramaṇī, nor are you a brāhmaṇī."
Upon hearing this, that nun incurs the same offense as before.
Likewise, "If you commit a *saṃghāvaśeṣa*, *sthūlātyaya*, *pāyattika*, *pratideśanīya*, or *duṣkṛta* offense, you are no longer a female śramaṇī, nor a female brāhmaṇī."
When that nun has heard it, this bhikṣuṇī incurs the same offense as before.

What are the afflictions?
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to disparage, goes to another bhikṣuṇī and speaks thus:
"You are full of anger; you are not a daughter of the Śramaṇas, nor are you a daughter of the Brāhmaṇas."
Having heard these words, whether he is thereby afflicted or not, he incurs the same offense as before.

Likewise, if you harbor resentment, concealment, affliction, envy, stinginess, flattery, deceit, lack of shame, lack of dread of blame, evil conduct, and wrong views, you incur the same offense as before; this is called an affliction (*kleśa*).
What is abusive speech?
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intention of disparaging another, goes to where that bhikṣuṇī is and utters various kinds of vulgar and indecent words as an insult.
Having heard these words, she incurs the same offense as before.
There is no offense if there are several bhikṣuṇīs with the same name residing in one monastery; if another asks about her and does not recognize her, she should reply to that person:
"The bhikṣuṇī of such-and-such a kind, such as a Brāhmaṇa [family], and so forth."
It is said that there is no offense in all such cases.
**The Third Training Rule on Divisive Speech** The setting for this rule is the same as before.

At that time, when the group of six bhikṣus engaged in divisive speech toward other bhikṣus, those bhikṣus became mutually resentful and felt great shame. Each harbored sorrow and distress, unable to dwell in happiness; they neglected their cultivation of the right practice, their recitation, and their reflection, and the long-standing bonds of affection were thereby severed.
When the bhikṣus who possessed few desires heard of this matter, they felt revulsion and contempt in their hearts and spoke these words:
"How can a bhikṣu engage in divisive speech toward other bhikṣus?"
She immediately reported this matter to the Buddha.

The World-Honored One assembled the community, questioned her regarding the facts, and rebuked her; he then established a training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
"As in the Great Bhikṣu Vinaya, if a bhikṣuṇī, out of divisive speech, [causes a schism], it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma, or others of a similar class.
Regarding “slanderous speech”: if a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to cause division, utters any such words toward another bhikṣuṇī, she incurs a pāyattika offense.
The meaning is as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and the specific matters involved?
A summary verse states:
Lineage and craftsmanship, Action, physical form, and illness—these five;
Offenses and the categories of afflictions, With verbal abuse as the final one.
The summary verse says:
"Lineage" refers to the four castes, even down to the lineage of slaves;
their crafts and skills are all the same, and their occupations are likewise so.
Among them there are various classes, such as weavers, wool-workers, and needle-makers.
Ironsmiths, bronze-workers, leather-workers,
potters, barbers, carpenters, and bamboo-workers—
these eleven distinct classes have the slaves as the lowest of all.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to cause division, goes to the dwelling of a bhikṣuṇī of the Brahmin caste and speaks thus:
"Noble lady! A certain bhikṣuṇī says:..."
“You are one who has gone forth from the Brahmin caste; you are neither a śramaṇī nor a brāhmaṇī. He asked, “Who is this?”
He replied, "I, [Name].
To disclose his name in this manner constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
To speak of one's caste is also an *dukkaṭa* offense.
For a *kṣatriya*, the offense is likewise as before.
If one reveals the name and caste of anyone from a *vaiśya* down to a slave, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The detailed explanation therein is as in the training rule concerning disparaging speech. 4.
The Training Rule on Rebuking. The setting for the fourth training rule on rebuking is the same as before.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus, knowing that the harmonious Saṃgha had already settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma, further proceeded to rebuke one another regarding the formal ritual (karmavācanā). Thereupon, the World-Honored One reprimanded them, saying:
"I shall establish a training rule for my disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha has settled a dispute in accordance with the Dharma and that the matter has been extinguished, [should cause it to be reopened]...'"
"If one subsequently raises the issue again at the place of the *karmavācanā*, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Nun" refers to a nun within this Dharma.
"Knowing" means that she understands it herself and speaks of it to others.
"Harmonious" means being of one flavor.
"The assembly" refers to the disciples of the Buddha.
"Deciding according to the Dharma" means according to the Vinaya and according to the Teacher’s instruction.
"Disputes" refers to the four types of disputes:
namely, disputes concerning legal matters (*adhikaraṇa*), disputes concerning verbal abuse (*abhivāda*), disputes concerning offenses (*āpatti*), and disputes concerning formal procedures (*kṛtya*).
"Already extinguished" means that the matter has been eliminated.
"Subsequently raising [the matter] during the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act)" means to raise the matter so that it does not cease.
The meaning of "falling" (*pātayantika*) is as explained above.
What are the characteristics of the offense in this case? What are its specific details?

If a bhikṣuṇī, regarding a legal case of censure, perceives it as a legal case of censure, and knowing that the case has been settled, perceives it as settled—or if she harbors doubt—yet raises the matter again, it is a pāyattika.
If one suspects that a matter has not been settled yet conceives the thought that it has been settled, and then raises the issue again, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī, regarding a dispute over censure (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), conceives the thought that it is a dispute over verbal abuse (*adhikaraṇa-adhikaraṇa*), and knowing that the matter has been settled, conceives the thought that it has been settled—or if she entertains doubt—yet raises the issue again, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The remaining offenses are the same as before.

If a bhikṣuṇī, regarding a dispute over criticism, perceives it as a dispute over an offense, and knowing that the matter has been settled, perceives it as settled—or if she entertains doubt yet raises the issue again—it is a pāyattika.
The remaining offenses are the same as before.

If a bhikṣuṇī, regarding a dispute over criticism (*adhikaraṇa-vivāda*), forms the perception that it is a dispute over what is not a matter (*adhikaraṇa-avastu*), and knowing that the matter has been settled, forms the perception that it has been settled—or if she entertains doubt—yet further raises the issue again, the offense incurred is the same as before.

Just as taking *adhikaraṇa-śamatha* (settlement of legal issues) as the first [category] and comparing it with the other three types of disputes (*adhikaraṇa*) results in four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*), one should understand that the same applies when taking the other disputes as the primary categories; in full, there are sixteen permutations in total.
There are five types of individuals. What are the five? They are:
the host, the person performing the *karmavācanā*, the person giving consent (*chanda*), the person stating their own view, and the guest.
The "host" refers to one who understands the beginning, middle, and end of the matter of dispute.
The "person who performs the *karmavācanā*" refers to one who presides over the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) regarding this matter of dispute.
"One who gives consent" refers to one who grants their consent at that time.
"One who states their own view" refers to one who expresses their personal perspective during the performance of the *karmavācanā*.
Regarding "the guest": this refers to one who does not understand the beginning, middle, or end of a matter of dispute.
Among these five types of persons, if the first three know that the harmonious Saṃgha has rightfully settled the matter of dispute, yet they raise the matter again, they incur a *pāyattika* offense.
If those latter two persons raise the issue again during a formal legal proceeding (*adhikaraṇa-samatha*), they incur a *duṣkṛta* offense.
The categories of objects and perceptions (*viṣaya-saṃjñā*) should be understood as usual.

5. The Training Rule on Speaking Dharma Alone with a Man for More than Five or Six Words. This fifth training rule, concerning speaking dharma alone with a man for more than five or six words, has the same setting as the preceding one.

At that time, Udāyin was skilled in interpreting bodily signs. During the first part of the day, he took up his robe and bowl and entered the city of Śrāvastī to go on almsround. Arriving at the houses of brahmins and householders, he explained to them their secret and violent characteristics.
Eventually, the Blessed One rebuked him and addressed the bhikṣus: “I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣuṇī should preach the Dharma to a man for more than five or six sentences, except when a wise woman is present, it is a pāyattika. (The full context and conditions are as explained in the Mahābhikṣu-vinaya.)
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“Man” refers to one who understands speech that is wholesome or unwholesome.
“One must not exceed five or six words” means that when speaking five sentences of the Dharma, if one intentionally proceeds to a sixth; [this constitutes an offense].
When speaking the Dharma in six phrases, the intentional mind extends to the seventh.
As for "Dharma," it refers to that which is spoken by a Buddha or spoken by a Śrāvaka.
As for "speaking," it means to proclaim and set forth with the mouth.
"A wise woman" refers to a woman who possesses understanding.
The meaning of *pāyattika* is as explained above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances?
If a bhikṣuṇī preaches the Dharma to a man using five or six phrases, and intentionally continues to the sixth or seventh phrase, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense in each case.
The Sixth Training Rule: On Reciting or Studying the Text Together with One Who Has Not Yet Received Full Ordination. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the group of six bhikṣus were reciting word-for-word together with those who had not yet received full ordination, creating a great clamor in their dwelling place, like Brahmins reciting various non-Buddhist treatises, or like laypeople in a schoolhouse practicing their lessons in loud voices. Consequently, for the sake of the disciples of both divisions, this training rule was established and should be spoken as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī recites word-for-word together with one who has not yet received full ordination, or teaches him the Dharma, it is a pāyattika."
“Nuns” refers to those nuns within this Dharma.
Regarding “those who have not received full ordination,” there are two types of fully ordained persons:
namely, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; all others are termed those who have not received full ordination.
Regarding "phrases and sentences," there are parallel phrases and preceding phrases.
What are parallel phrases?
When one who is fully ordained says, "Commit no evil," one who is not yet fully ordained says, "Commit no evil" at the very same moment; this is called a parallel phrase.
What is meant by the "preceding phrase"?

It refers to when one who is fully ordained has not yet finished uttering the words "Commit no evil," at which moment those who are not yet ordained simultaneously voice this same phrase; they then proceed to say first, "Practice all that is good. This is called the preceding phrase.
What is meant by "identical syllables"?
It refers to when one who is fully ordained utters the syllable "akāśa" (evil), and one who is not yet ordained simultaneously utters "akāśa"; this is called identical syllables.
What is meant by "the preceding word"?

It refers to when one who is fully ordained utters the sound of the word "evil" (*pāpa*), and before that sound has ceased, one who is not yet fully ordained utters the word "evil" in unison; yet, he subsequently says "good" (*kuśala*) first—this is called the "preceding word."
"Reciting" refers to receiving and retaining [the words].
"Dharma" refers to the teachings spoken by the Buddha and his disciples.
*Pāyattika* has the meaning as explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī recites the Dharma with a person who is not fully ordained—either by repeating the same phrases or by reading ahead of them—she incurs a root offense.
If the preceding word and the subsequent word are identical, one incurs the same offense as before.
There is no offense if the person stammers, is of an impatient temperament, or speaks rapidly; in these cases, there is no violation.

Whether during the instruction for recitation or the instruction for questioning, there is likewise no offense; the two meanings of "ordination" (*upasaṃpadā*) and "full possession" (*paripūrṇa*) both apply here.
The Seventh Training Rule: Prohibiting the Disclosure of Gross Offenses to One Not Fully Ordained. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, because he had not yet abandoned desire, committed an offense subject to the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules and sought to purify his transgression by undertaking the *parivāsa* (probation).
The group of six [bhikṣus] informed laypeople, causing them to lose faith; [the story continues] at length until the Blessed One rebuked them and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall now establish the training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to one who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rules for the bhikṣuṇīs, there was a bhikṣu named Pūrṇamukha and a bhikṣuṇī named Śākhā in the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, these two individuals engaged in defiling domestic affairs within the houses of laypeople and displayed unwholesome conduct, thereby causing people to lose their faith and respect.
Then the community of bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣuṇīs:
"You should appoint one bhikṣuṇī to inform the people at various lay households, saying:"
"The improper acts were committed by the bhikṣu Pṛthupāla and the bhikṣuṇī Śiṃśapā.
If a bhikṣuṇī does not possess five qualities, she should not be appointed; even if she has been appointed, she should not be sent away.
What are the five? They are:
being motivated by affection, by ill-will, by fear, by delusion, or not knowing what has been said and what has not been said.
One who possesses these five qualities should not be appointed or sent; conversely, one who possesses the opposite of these five qualities should be appointed and sent.
One should spread out the seats and strike the *khaṇḍi* drum; once the assembly has gathered, one should inform them with words and first inquire whether they are capable, saying:
"Can you, [Name], go to the households of the laity and speak of the unlawful conduct of those two persons?"
He replies, "I can.
Then, one bhikṣuṇī shall perform the formal ritual (jñapti-karman) in this manner:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
These two, the bhikṣu Pṛthugalla and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā, have committed various improper acts in the homes of laypeople, thereby causing people to lose their faith and respect."
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], is capable of going to the homes of laypeople to proclaim the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant permission, may the Saṃgha authorize that the Bhikṣuṇī [Name] be appointed by the Saṃgha to go to the homes of laypeople and proclaim the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukola and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is performed:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu Viśālamukha and this bhikṣuṇī Śiṃśapāskandha have committed various unlawful acts within the households of laypeople, thereby causing people to lose their faith and respect.
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], is capable of going to the homes of laypeople to speak of the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthūcchada and the bhikṣuṇī Śāṇakā.

If the venerable ones permit this bhikṣuṇī [Name] to speak of the transgressions of others in the homes of laypeople—specifically to speak of the unlawful conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthūcchada and the bhikṣuṇī Śāṇakā—then remain silent;
if you do not permit it, speak up.

"The Saṃgha has now authorized this bhikṣuṇī, [Name], to speak on behalf of others in the homes of laypeople, to report the improper conduct of the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā toward those lay households."
"Because she remained silent, I now maintain this rule.
O Bhikṣuṇīs! I shall now establish the rules of conduct for those bhikṣuṇīs who speak ill of others in the homes of the laity."
That bhikṣuṇī should go to a layperson’s home and speak as follows:
"O worthy ones, listen!

There are those who defile the household life and there are those who defile the life of renunciation. It is like a rice field where the grain grows lushly but then encounters frost and hail, causing the entire crop to be destroyed."
Furthermore, it is like sugarcane: when its stalks and branches are in full bloom, they may be struck by the "red-knot" disease, which ultimately destroys them until nothing remains.
You should know, O virtuous ones, that those two evil persons are just like this!
Virtuous ones, do not dwell in association with him, lest you bring harm to the holy teaching.
You should know that this person has ruined himself; like a scorched seed that no longer sprouts, he can no longer grow within the discipline and doctrine of the holy teaching.
"You all should contemplate the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, and you should also contemplate the Elder:

the Venerable Ājñātakauṇḍinya, the Venerable Vāṣpa, the Venerable Aniruddha, the Venerable Bhadrika, the Venerable Mahānāman, the Venerable Yaśas, the Venerable Pūrṇa, the Venerable Vimala, the Venerable Gavāmpati, the Venerable Subāhu, the Venerable Śāriputra, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the Venerable Kuṭhila, the Venerable Mahācunda, the Venerable Mahākātyāyana, the Venerable Piṇḍola-bhāradvāja, the Venerable Naṭa-bhāradvāja, the Venerable Gayā-kāśyapa, the Venerable Mahākāśyapa, and the Venerable Nandika."
You should observe these great bhikṣus.
Furthermore, you should observe the great bhikṣuṇīs:
Cundā, Mṛḍā, Pāṭhā, Pāṭaccarī, Aṭavikā, Khaśmā, Candraprabhā, Jotikā, Utpalavarṇā, and Mahāprajāpatī; you should observe such a multitude of great bhikṣuṇīs.
Then, having instructed the bhikṣuṇīs thus regarding the householders, she immediately left that house.
When the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā heard of this matter, she said:
"Did you speak of my faults to the householders?"
He replied, "I have received the Sangha’s instruction in accordance with the Dharma.
He answered:
"If this matter suits me or not, I shall split open your belly, pull out your intestines, and hang them upon a tree.
Upon hearing these words, she was struck with great terror and informed the nuns in full:
"I can no longer speak of this matter in the homes of the laity."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"That foolish person may deceive an individual, but he cannot deceive the Saṃgha. Therefore, the Saṃgha should perform a *jñapti* (formal motion) to detail his transgression."
Having spread out the seats and struck the *khaṇḍi* gong, once the assembly has gathered, one should announce the matter.
One bhikṣuṇī should act as follows:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!..."
This bhikṣu Viśālamukha and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā have performed unrighteous acts in various households of the laity, thereby causing many people to lose their faith and respect.
At present, there is no one else capable of pointing out their faults and misdeeds within the homes of laypeople.

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant permission: if the Saṃgha sees the bhikṣu Pṛthukūṭa and the bhikṣuṇī Śākhā committing unrighteous acts in the homes of laypeople, they should then point out their transgressions.
“Thus it is reported.

Following the Buddha’s instruction, the community of nuns went to those dwelling places and announced this to the lay families, informing them whether they were aware of the situation or not. Consequently, people ceased to feel respect or faith, making it difficult for those who go on almsround to obtain food and drink.
She reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"In the case of lay households, you should speak of a bhikṣuṇī’s misconduct only where it is known that she has committed such acts; do not speak of it where it is unknown."
"From this you should know that [the rule] is set aside except in the case of a formal act of the Saṃgha (saṃghakamma).
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts and, having taught the Dharma of few desires according to the occasion, addressed the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
"The former was the original prohibition; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated as follows:"
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has committed a grave offense, should speak of it to one who is not yet fully ordained—except by formal authorization of the Saṃgha—it is a pāyattika.
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
Regarding the term “fully ordained” (upasampadā), there are two kinds:
namely, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; others are called “not yet fully ordained.”
Regarding what is called "coarse and evil," there are two types:
those arising from the causes of *pārājika* offenses and those arising from the causes of *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offenses.
This "coarse and evil" has two characteristics:
First, coarseness of intrinsic nature; second, coarseness of causal origination.
"To speak" means to reveal the matter.
"Excepting the *saṃgha-karman*" means excepting when the assembly performs the ritual procedure for one's sake.
*Pāyattika* has the meaning explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī, at a lay household she does not know, forms the perception that she does not know it—or harbors doubt—and speaks of another's grave offense to them, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, regarding a household that is known [to her], forms the thought that it is unknown or entertains doubt, and speaks of it to that person, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense.

There is no offense if, regarding a household that is unknown [to her], she forms the thought that it was previously known; or if the matter has been discussed in detail by the assembly, or if at that time the people have all heard of it—just as when a mural painting is viewed by all people alike—and she says, "It is not that I alone know this," then there is no fault in speaking.

8. The Training Rule on Proclaiming One’s Attainment of the Higher Human States to an Unordained Person. The eighth training rule concerning the proclamation of one’s attainment of the higher human states to an unordained person; the setting and circumstances are as before.

At that time, a great number of bhikṣus applied themselves with diligence and refined their practice, maintaining mindfulness in their cultivation; as described at length, they even attained the fruit of arhatship. They all spoke of the benefits of these fruits to their own followers to manifest their own majestic virtue, and even went so far as to reprimand them, saying: "For the sake of the disciples of both divisions, a training rule shall be established, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having truly attained the state of a superior person, should speak of it to one who has not yet received full ordination, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
“Having actually attained” means that the fact is true.
Regarding “the qualities of a superior person,” these are all as extensively explained previously in the fourth *pārājika* for a *bhikṣu*.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī, without a deceptive intent and with the perception that it is true, speaks to one who is not yet fully ordained, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
Regarding the distinctions therein: what was previously termed a *pārājika* offense is here called a "falling away" (*patanīya*);
what was previously termed a "grave offense" (*sthūlātyaya*) is here called a "misdeed" (*duṣkṛta*).

The Ninth Training Rule on Slandering the Diversion of Community Property. The detailed account of the origin of this rule is fully set forth in the Mahābhikṣu-vinaya, up until the formulation of the training rule, which should be stated as follows:
"If, moreover, a bhikṣuṇī first agrees in concert [with others] and later says:
'Venerable ones, you have diverted the property belonging to the Saṃgha to private individuals according to their personal intimacy.'"
"Whoever [does so] commits a *pāyattika* offense.
"Nun" refers to one who belongs to this community.
"Having previously agreed with a common mind" means having previously consented to that matter.
"Speaking thus later" means uttering such words at a subsequent time.

"According to those with whom one is intimate" refers to the two teachers with whom one is intimate—namely, the preceptor and the instructor who share the same teacher—as well as other friends and spiritual mentors; when these individuals regard one another, they are all considered intimate associates.
"Sangha" refers to the disciples of the Buddha.
There are two kinds of material benefits:
first, the benefit of clothing and requisites; second, the benefit of food and drink.
In this context, "benefit" refers to the benefit of robes.
"Having brought it into the assembly and diverting it" means transferring monastic property to another individual.
The meaning of *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) is as explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and the specific circumstances?

If a bhikṣuṇī, regarding whatever amount of property belonging to the Saṃgha there may be, first gives her consent with a harmonious mind, but later speaks as follows, she incurs an offense of falling (pāyattika).
If the Sangha has not actually granted [the robe], and one takes it back and gives it away on one's own initiative, there is no offense when this is reported.
The Tenth Training Rule: The Precept on Contemptuously Rebuking the Vinaya. The setting was in Śrāvastī. The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Every half-month, you should recite the Prātimokṣa Sūtra."
At that time, the bhikṣus followed the Buddha’s instruction and recited the Prātimokṣa Sūtra every half-month.
When the six group of bhikṣus heard it being recited, they spoke these words:
"Why do you repeatedly inflict wounds upon our sores?"
"When these minor and secondary precepts are recited every half-month, they cause the bhikṣus who hear them to feel distress and give rise to remorse.
The bhikṣus of few desires all felt disdain and shame, until the Blessed One rebuked them and established the training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is being recited every half-month, speaks as follows:"
"Venerable ones!
What is the use of reciting these minor and lesser rules of training?
When these precepts are recited, they cause the bhikṣuṇīs to give rise to remorse, distress, regret, and anxiety."
"If one thus disparages the precepts, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Nun" refers to a nun within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Half-month" means that one month is divided into two parts.
"Precepts" refers to [the training] beginning from the eight defeats (*pārājika*) and ending with the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
"Discourses" (*sūtra*) refers to that which is arranged in sequential order.
"Brief exposition" refers to the time when they are being proclaimed.
"Venerable ones" refers to recounting one's circumstances to manifest a state of distress.
"Reproaching the precepts lightly" means uttering disparaging words to inform the person before one.
The meaning of "falling" is as explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī, during the fortnightly recitation of the eight pārājika rules, up to the recitation of the seven methods for settling disputes, should speak as follows:
"Venerable one!..."
"If one asks, 'Why must these minor and very minor precepts be taught, causing the bhikṣuṇīs to feel remorse?
one incurs a *pāyattika*.
Or, if one causes them to feel vexation, regret, or distress, or says:"
"He thinks of worldly affairs," or it is said:
"He does not delight in leaving the household life."
Or if one says,
"Return to lay life"—
uttering such words as these all constitutes an offense of falling (pāyattika).

In this way, it should be understood that when these matters are being discussed in the context of the other sixteen sections, the *Kṣudrakavastu* (Miscellaneous Matters), the *Nidāna* (Origins), the *Mauktika* (or *Muktaka*) sections, and in those sūtras associated with the Vinaya teachings—or whenever they are spoken in other contexts—if a bhikṣuṇī should speak thus:
"What is the use of reciting these minor and lesser precepts? Reciting them at such times causes remorse to arise."
Those who say this all fall into an offense.
If, when proclaiming it during the recitation of other sūtras, one speaks so as to cause others to feel distress or regret, they incur an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Volume Twelve.
The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume Thirteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The second summary verse says:
Seeds, lightness, and instruction; Arranging beds, grass mats, and pulling.
One should firmly stay on a bed with detachable legs; when watering grass, one should do so two or three times.
11. The Training Rule on Destroying Living Seeds. The eleventh training rule on destroying living seeds. At that time, the Blessed One was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the six bhikṣus, acting both as principals and as agents, cut down trees and various types of living grasses, even taking and using flowers and fruits as they pleased.
When the non-Buddhists saw this, they were filled with disdain and shame, and made this deliberation:
"These śramaṇas, the sons of the Śākyas, personally and through others, cut down grasses and trees."

However, we worldly people, such as Brahmins and even laborers, likewise personally or through others, cut down trees and kill grasses; in this regard, what difference is there between us who have left the household life and those who remain in the world?
"Who would ever make offerings to such shaven-headed śramaṇas?

The bhikṣus informed the Buddha of this matter. On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community as before, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī herself destroys a village of seeds or sentient beings, or causes another to destroy it, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to one who belongs to this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
