Regarding the “village of seeds,” there are five kinds of seeds:
first, root-seeds; second, stem-seeds; third, joint-seeds; fourth, node-seeds; and fifth, seed-seeds.
What are root-propagated plants?
They refer to nut-grass, sweet flag, yellow ginger, white ginger, *ākanda*, and *vatsanābha*—these substances all grow from planted roots; therefore, they are called root-propagated plants.
What are plants propagated from stems?
They refer to the pomegranate tree, the willow tree, the grapevine, the bodhi tree, the udumbara, nyagrodha, and so forth.
All these arise from stems, and are therefore called "stem-seeds" (*kāṇḍabīja*).
What are "joint-seeds" (*parvabīja*)?
They refer to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, and the like; all these grow from the joints, and are therefore called "joint-seeds."
What are seeds that propagate by splitting?

These refer to the seeds of plants such as *lānxiāng* (Cymbopogon), *yúnsuī* (Coriandrum), and *júyòu* (Citrus). All such seeds are produced only after they split open; therefore, they are called "seeds that propagate by splitting."
What are seed-propagations?
They refer to rice, wheat, barley, various beans, mustard seeds, and so forth; because all these are produced from seeds, they are called seed-propagations.
These are collectively termed the "village of seeds.
What is the "village of sentient beings"?

Sentient beings refer to locusts, butterflies, mosquitoes, gadflies, dung beetles, ants, snakes, scorpions, and various bees; these sentient beings all rely upon grasses, trees, and wood to dwell as their nests and lairs.
If a bhikṣuṇī pulls up, breaks, or cuts grass, trees, or wood, it is a pāyattika; the meaning is as previously explained.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein, what are the specific matters?
A summary verse says:
Perceiving roots and so forth as seeds, Cutting trees, grass, and flowers.
In places such as beneath trees or along walking paths, or on green moss and bottle-stands, if a bhikṣuṇī perceives a root-plant as a root-plant,
or perceives a living thing as a living thing— or has doubt regarding it— and she herself cuts it or instructs another to cut it, she incurs a *pāyantika* offense.
If one perceives dry matter as being living or harbors doubt regarding it, in both cases one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).

If a bhikṣuṇī perceives a root-plant as a stem-plant, or perceives it as living, or harbors doubt regarding it, and she herself cuts it or instructs another to cut it, she incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
If one perceives dry objects as being living or harbors doubt regarding them, then at the time of cutting or destroying them, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense in all cases.

Regarding these root-propagated seeds, when compared with joint-propagated, node-propagated, and seed-propagated seeds, there are four permutations for each; they should be treated according to the preceding rules.

Furthermore, regarding the seed from the stem, when compared to itself and to each of the other four types of seeds, there are four permutations for each; whether it be a perception or a doubt, one incurs both a *pārājika* offense and an *dukkaṭa*, as explained in detail according to the specific circumstances.
If a bhikṣuṇī herself or causes another to cast five kinds of seeds into fire, with the thought:
"May these seeds all be destroyed."
If [the seeds] are destroyed, one incurs five *pārājika*-level offenses; if they are not destroyed, one incurs five *dukkaṭa* offenses.
If one personally or causes another to cast five types of seeds into water, it is also as previously stated.
If one places five seeds in a mortar and pounds them with a pestle so that the seeds are damaged, one incurs five *pārājika* offenses;
if they are not damaged, one incurs five *dukkaṭa* offenses.

If one places five kinds of seeds on dry ground or in a hot location, or mixes them together with alkaline ash, *gomeya*, dry soil, and so forth, with the intent to destroy them, one incurs an offense of light or heavy gravity according to the specific circumstances, as previously described.
If one places five seeds into the broth, stew, or rice-water and causes them to be damaged, the offense incurred is the same as before.
If one cuts down a tree using a single method, one incurs one *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) and one *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
If one cuts two trees with a single blow, one incurs one *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) and two *pācittiya* (offenses entailing expiation).
If one cuts many trees with a single blow, one incurs one *dukkaṭa* and numerous *pācittiya* offenses.
If one cuts down a single tree with two strokes, one incurs two *dukkaṭa* offenses and one *pācittiya* offense.
If one cuts down two trees with two strokes, one incurs two *dukkaṭa* offenses and two *pācittiya* offenses.
If one cuts down many trees with two strokes, one incurs two *dukkaṭa* offenses and numerous *pācittiya* offenses.
If one cuts down a single tree with many strokes, one incurs many *dukkaṭa* offenses and one *pācittiya* offense.
If one cuts down two trees with many strokes, one incurs many *duṣkṛta* offenses and two *pāyattika* offenses.
If one cuts down many trees with many strokes, one incurs many *duṣkṛta* offenses and many *pāyattika* offenses.
As it is with trees, so it is with wild grass, lotuses, and the like; the gravity of the offense incurred according to the facts is the same as previously stated.
If a bhikṣuṇī pulls up the roots of a tree, she incurs a pāyantika offense.
If one damages the rough bark of a tree or its non-firm, moist parts, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
if one damages its firm or moist parts, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation).
If one damages a flower that has not yet opened, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If [the grass] has already ripened and it is destroyed, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
If, at a place where the grass is still growing, one pours hot water or cow dung and mud over it to cause damage, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation) in all such cases;
if it is not damaged, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* in all such cases.
If one acts with the intention of pouring out or scattering substances, and has no intent to cause damage, there is no offense in any case.
If a bhikṣuṇī, while walking upon a patch of living grass, gives rise to such a thought as:
"I shall cause the grass to be damaged."
Regarding this, for every blade of grass destroyed, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
If one merely walks upon it with the intention [to harm], there is no offense.
If, on a patch of living grass, one drags firewood or pulls a mat with the intent to destroy it, one incurs an offense of downfall.
If there is no corrupting of the mind, there is no offense.
When walking for meditation upon ground covered in green moss, there is an offense or no offense as previously stated.
If one drags firewood, spreads mats, or handles other various objects on this ground, the transgression incurred is the same as before.

If one picks up duckweed leaves or green moss from water, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) as long as they have not been removed from the water; once removed from the water, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
If one pulls mushrooms from the ground, one incurs a *duṣkṛta*;
if there is the intention to damage the ground, one also incurs a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī, upon jars, pots, and the like, or on clothing, or on mats, cushions, and the like, or on clothing racks, food, drink, and the like, should have green mold or white mildew grow, if she acts with the intention of damaging them, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing);
however, if she causes others to know [of the mold] and only then uses it after it has been purified, there is no offense.
If one causes others to perceive purity through the five kinds of seeds, there is likewise no offense. 12.

The Training Rule on Contemptuous Disparagement and Despising. Regarding the twelfth training rule on contemptuous disparagement and despising, the detailed account of its origin is as found in the Mahābhikṣu-vinaya, up to the point where it says: "The training rule is hereby established and should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī again shows contempt, disparages, or treats another bhikṣuṇī with disdain, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Those who revile, disparage, or treat with contempt" refers to expressing oneself directly face-to-face or by resorting to pretexts regarding other matters to manifest one's intent through speech.
*Pāyattika* has the same meaning as explained above.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense?

If a bhikṣuṇī, having been formally censured by the Saṃgha through a ritual procedure, disparages or slanders those among the twelve types of persons who have been appointed by the assembly while the matter has not yet been resolved, it is a pāyattika;
if she treats them with contempt, it is a pāyattika.
If one feels resentment, slanders, or treats with contempt those who have been censured, it is a *pāyattika*.

Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī, after having been formally censured by the Saṃgha through a ritual act, feels resentment or slanders those among the twelve types of persons appointed by the assembly—even though the matter has already been settled—it is a *pāyattika*;
if she treats them with contempt, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one disparages or treats with contempt those who have been censured, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣuṇī, while the formal act of censure by the Saṃgha has not yet been performed against her, disparages those among the twelve appointed persons whose business has not yet ceased, she incurs an *dukkaṭa*;
if she treats them with contempt, she incurs an *dukkaṭa*.
If one feels resentment, disparages, or treats with contempt those who have been censured by the Saṃgha through formal legal action, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī, even though she has not been formally censured by the Saṃgha, feels resentment or disparages those among the twelve types of persons who have been appointed by the Saṃgha for a task—even if the matter has already been settled—she incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense;
if she treats them with contempt, she incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one feels resentment, slanders, or treats others with contempt and disdain, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).
The categories of objects and perceptions should be understood according to the specific circumstances.
Furthermore, there is no offense in the case of the very first offender, or for one who is insane, mentally deranged, or overwhelmed by intense physical pain.

13. The Training Rule on Contrary and Annoying Speech. The thirteenth training rule concerning contrary and annoying speech. The detailed account of the origin (nidāna) is as found in the Mahābhikṣu-vinaya, up to: "He established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī again contrarily annoys another with her speech, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Furthermore, 'a bhikṣuṇī' refers to a bhikṣuṇī within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
'To act in contradiction to and disturb the verbal instruction' means to express oneself with words intended to cause disturbance to others."
*Pāyattika* has the meaning as explained above.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If there is a bhikṣuṇī who goes to another bhikṣuṇī and speaks as follows:

“Āḷavika, did you see a bhikṣuṇī with freshly shorn hair and beard, wearing a crimson outer robe, carrying a bowl substituted for her usual one, holding a mendicant’s staff in her hand, and departing while carrying a bowl filled to the brim with ghee, honey, granulated sugar, or rock sugar?”
When questioned by him, she replied:
"I truly did not see a bhikṣuṇī with such physical characteristics; however, I saw a bhikṣuṇī walking away on her two feet."
If a bhikṣuṇī, having seen one thing but speaking of another, intentionally speaks in such a way as to cause distress and confusion to others, she incurs a pāyattika.
The same applies, up to and including śikṣamāṇās and śrāmaṇerīs, who incur a pāyattika through the same questions and answers as previously described.
If someone else comes and asks:
"Have you seen any laypeople passing by here carrying sugarcane, bamboo poles, firewood, grass, or jars of clarified butter?"
He then replied:
"I truly did not see such a person; I only saw two feet walking away.
If a bhikṣuṇī sees one thing and speaks of another, thereby causing such vexation, it is a pāyattika.
If someone were to ask:
"Have you seen any laymen wearing blue, yellow, red, or white garments, carrying vessels of clarified butter and so forth, passing by here?
and [the monk] replies as follows:
"I only saw two feet walking away.
One should understand that this is explained in detail; when speaking with a vexed mind, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.
As it is with speech, so it is with silence; in both instances, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
There is no offense if, for instance, a bhikṣuṇī sees hunters pursuing deer or other game entering the monastery; having seen them, the hunters ask:
"Noble Lady!..."
"Have you seen any deer running past here?
He should not answer,
"I have seen one."
If it was during the cold season, he said to the hunter:
"Worthy sir!
You may enter the heated chamber for a short while to warm yourself by the fire."
If it is during the heat, one should say:
"O worthy one!
You may enter a cool room for a moment to drink some clear, cold water and rest awhile."
If the hunter says, "I am not tired;
I am asking about the fleeing deer," one should first examine one's own fingernails and reply to that person as follows:
"Na-kha-bha-sha-mi.
If asked again, one should look into the great void and reply to that person:
"Na-va-bha-sha-mi."

This Sanskrit language, with its diverse dialects and distinct phonetics, is extremely difficult to interpret; unless one thoroughly understands the hidden intent, how could one possibly grasp the meaning of these words?

Unless one points to oneself, it is difficult to bring about awakening; thus, both the fingernail and empty space are described as being "without characters. There are extensive commentaries on this, as found in other places.
If a hunter says,

"I do not ask about the fingernails nor about empty space, but I ask whether it is permissible to kill sentient beings here or not," the bhikṣuṇī should immediately survey the four directions and form this thought:
"In the ultimate truth, all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are fundamentally devoid of sentient beings.
To this, he replied:
"I do not perceive any sentient beings."
In all these cases, there is no offense.
However, if a bhikṣuṇī does not speak truthfully when questioned by others, she incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
The Fourteenth Training Rule: Regarding the Placement of the Saṃgha’s Requisites on Open Ground. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home for a meal; then, during the first part of the day, the bhikṣus took up their robes and bowls and went to the householder’s residence.
At that time, the World-Honored One was residing within the monastery and had people bring him food.
There are five reasons for which the Buddha eats while staying in the monastery.
What are these five?

First, for personal quietude; second, to preach the Dharma for the devas; third, to visit the sick; fourth, to inspect the bedding and furniture of the Saṃgha; fifth, to establish rules of training for the bhikṣus.

At that time, the Buddha wished to inspect the bedding and seating of the Sangha and to establish a training rule (śikṣāpada). With this as the occasion, while residing within the monastery, he had people bring him food.

Then, after the assembly of monks had departed, the World-Honored One took the keys and inspected all the dwellings within the monastery, extending even to the gardens and groves nearby outside the monastery, observing them all thoroughly.
Next, he arrived at the monks' quarters. In this hall, many bedding and sitting mats were spread out in the open air when, suddenly, an unseasonable wind and rain began to fall heavily.
The Buddha thought to himself:

"These bedding and mats were all given to the Saṃgha by faithful brahmins and lay devotees who, seeking superior merit, have afflicted their own bodies and diminished the portions of their wives and children."
When the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs were using them, they did not know the proper measure and failed to guard them well, casting them away wherever they pleased.

As wind and rain were about to arrive, the World-Honored One perceived this and exercised his supernormal powers to ward off the storm; yet heavy clouds gathered and spread, refusing to disperse, waiting for the World-Honored One to fold up his bedding.
The World-Honored One himself took his bedding and arranged it within the room; then, taking up his rain-cloak, he went outside the chamber intending to bathe.
He immediately withdrew his supernormal powers, whereupon thunder and lightning darkened the day, and a torrential rain fell, moistening both the high and the low ground alike.
After the Buddha had washed his body, he washed his feet, entered his room, and remained there in silent seclusion.
When the bhikṣu who was to take the food arrived with it, he set it aside and went to where the World-Honored One was, prostrating at his feet.
It is the constant custom of the Blessed One to exchange pleasant greetings with those who bring food, asking:
"Has the community of bhikṣus received sufficient food and drink to be satisfied?
They replied:
"Venerable Sir!
All have been fully satisfied.
He then presented the food to the World-Honored One.
Having finished his meal, he remained in silent seclusion until the time of the afternoon meal, when he sat upon his usual seat.
Once seated, he addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"Just now, after the Saṃgha had gone out for alms, I took the keys and inspected the dwellings; I saw that many bedding mats were laid out in the open air."
"At that time, when it was about to rain, I used my supernormal powers to ward off the rain entirely and personally gathered up [the offerings].
He addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"There are donors who, by afflicting their own bodies, give to the Saṃgha in pursuit of merit; yet you are unable to use these offerings in accordance with the Dharma, thus wasting the gifts of faith."
He then spoke in verse:
"Regarding the gifts of others' faith, One should know the proper measure in their enjoyment;
Thus one attains peace for oneself And causes the merit of others to increase."

At that time, the World-Honored One praised contentment and, having accepted the offerings of the faithful in accordance with the Dharma, addressed the bhikṣus, speaking at length as previously described, up to: "I now establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having placed monastic bedding or various seats in an open area, departs without herself putting them away or instructing another to put them away, it is a pāyattika.'"

Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rule for the bhikṣus, there was a certain bhikṣu who, following a caravan, traveled through the countryside and arrived at a dwelling where he sought lodging. Later in the night, the caravan departed.
A person came calling; upon hearing the call, the bhikṣu immediately rose in haste. Because he spent time handing over his bedding, he was subsequently robbed by bandits as he followed along.
They reported this matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there are bhikṣus at the place where you reside, you should entrust your affairs to them before departing.
When the bhikṣus heard the Buddha's instruction, those who had such reasons all entrusted their affairs and departed.
In the city of Śrāvastī there were two householders who had been mutual enemies throughout their successive lives:
one possessed faith, while the other was devoid of faith.
The one with faith reflected as follows:
"Why do I now increase my enmity?
I should abandon this malice and go forth into homelessness.
When those without faith heard this, they harbored resentment and said:
"Even if you were to run and hide inside the horn of a bull, I would never let you go.
Upon hearing this, the bhikṣu thought to himself:
"I have gone forth into homelessness out of fear of him; could I possibly encounter that same fear again in this very place?"
"I should now flee to another region.
Having thought this, he said to his upādhyāya,
"Where can I go to escape this calamity?"
The preceptor said,
"Since you have such fear, you may wander among the people.
The disciple then departed.
Upon hearing this, the pursuer took provisions for the journey and set off in pursuit.
The bhikṣu traveled only at the proper time and not at improper times, whereas the layman did not cease his pursuit, whether at the proper or improper times.
Along the way, there was a monastery. When the elder caught up with him, the bhikṣu saw him from afar and immediately entered the monastery.
The elder thought to himself:
"I shall know for myself tomorrow when we are on the road."
Having formed this thought, he sought another place to stay.
When the night had turned to dawn, that bhikṣu addressed the other bhikṣus:
"Examine the bedding; I wish to set out."
He asked, "Where do you wish to go?
He replied:
"I wish to go to Rājagṛha.
The bhikṣu replied, "You should follow this path; do not take any other road."
He replied,
"May you dwell well," and then proceeded forward.
Then, at dawn, that householder entered the monastery and asked the bhikṣu,
"Which path did you take?
He replied:
"This is the way.
Following the path, he hurried along until he caught up with the bhikṣu and said, "Hey!
“Where does this shaven-headed śramaṇa wish to go?
The bhikṣu replied,
“O noble sir!”
"I have already left the household life, desiring to eliminate enmity and strife.
He then replied, "I am doing so now,
for the sake of eliminating enmity and strife."
He beat him severely with a staff until he was nearly dead; his robes and bowl were shattered, and only his life remained. He returned to the monastery and related the matter in detail.
The bhikṣus of the monastery said to him, "If we had not told you where to go, you certainly would not have encountered such suffering."
He then reported this matter in detail to the World-Honored One. The World-Honored One said:
"Except for specific circumstances, one must otherwise entrust [the bowl] to another.
The previous rule was the original enactment; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī places monastic bedding and various seats in an open area, and upon departing does not herself put them away nor instruct another to do so."
"If any bhikṣuṇī, without having given her formal notice, [enters a village], except for other circumstances, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one among those in this Dharma; the rest of the meaning is as above.
"Monks" refers to the disciples of the Tathāgata.
"Requisites for bedding" refers to large beds, woolen rugs, mattresses, blankets, and the like.
"Miscellaneous items" refers to small beds, stools, benches, and other such articles of utility.
"An open space" means it is without a covering.
"When departing" means having left the boundary of influence.
At that time, the Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Venerable Sir!
When one is separated from bedding and furniture, at what distance does it come to be called the ‘sphere of influence’ (sīmā)?
The Blessed One replied:

"Just as when the Brahmin Jātivāda plants mango trees according to the proper method, spacing each tree seven *vyāmas* apart so that their branches grow tall and lush and their flowers and fruits are abundant, there are forty-nine *vyāmas* within the space of ten trees."
"When bedding and mats are placed in an open space, one must entrust them to someone else for this distance; once beyond this boundary, they must be gathered up.
To "not gather them up" means neither to lift them oneself nor to instruct another to do so.
"Regarding 'there being a bhikṣuṇī,' it means there is currently someone present who is capable of receiving the entrustment.
There are five kinds of entrustment. What are the five?"
One should reply to the host, saying:
"Venerable one! This is the dwelling; this room may be inspected; these are the bedding and furnishings; these should be maintained; and this is the key to the door."
If there are no bhikṣuṇīs at that place, one should entrust [the keys] to a śrāmaṇerī;
if there is none of these, one should entrust them to a layperson;
if there is none of these, one should look around the four directions, hide the door key well, and only then depart.
If one encounters [the object] on the way, one should inform [the owner] that it may be collected at such-and-such a place.
Regarding the phrase "except for specific circumstances," this refers to the exception of difficult conditions.
As for *pāyattika*, the meaning is as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣuṇī has arranged bedding or mats for the Saṃgha and intentionally departs without entrusting them to someone else, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) as long as she has not yet moved beyond the boundary (*sīmā*).
Once she has moved beyond the boundary, she incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).

If a bhikṣuṇī places monastic bedding on an open space and enters her room with the intention of sitting in stillness to quiet a distracted mind, she may only leave as she pleases once she has attained meditative concentration. If, by the time of the first watch of the night, she has not damaged the bedding, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense;
if she has damaged it, she incurs a pāyattika offense.
The Venerable Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, Great Virtuous One!
How many kinds of damage are there to bedding and seats?"
The Buddha told Upāli:
"There are two kinds of destruction:
namely, wind and rain."
"If it is blown away and gathered up by the wind, this is called destruction by wind; if it is soaked through by rain, this is called destruction by rain.
If a bhikṣuṇī leaves her bedding and requisites exposed at sunset and fails to gather them up by the time of the middle watch, neither guarding them herself nor having another do so.
If it is not damaged, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
if it is damaged, one incurs a *pācittiya* (offense entailing expiation).

This applies likewise for one watch, one and a half watches, two watches, two and a half watches, three watches, three and a half watches, four watches, and four and a half watches. At dawn, the night in the west is divided into three periods, each consisting of ten *muhūrtas*.

Because it is difficult to understand, we shall follow the fivefold division of the day to make it easier for those who seek to know. These are: the time when the sun rises; the time for the morning meal; the time of the forenoon; the time when midday is about to arrive; the time of exact midday; the time when midday has passed; the time of the afternoon shadow; the time of the late afternoon; the time after the late afternoon; and the time of evening twilight. If a bhikṣuṇī, throughout this day and night, does not inspect the monastic bedding and furniture at each respective interval, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) if the items are not damaged;
if they are damaged, she incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).
15. The Training Rule on Not Putting Away Grass Mattings. The fifteenth training rule concerning not putting away grass mattings. The setting is the same as before.
There were two bhikṣus who, for the purpose of paying homage to the Buddha, were traveling toward Śrāvastī; when evening fell on the road, they entered a monastery to stay the night.
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw from afar, they assigned rooms and bedding to the elder, while giving the younger one only a room without bedding.

These two bhikṣus were by nature diligent and energetic; they sought out dry grass to spread as a thick and warm mat, and having done so, they departed at dawn. Subsequently, a swarm of ants took refuge in this grass mat and burrowed through, ruining the dwelling.
The Buddha, wishing to inspect the bedding of the Saṃgha and to establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), saw the grass strewn about as described in detail above.
After rebuking them, he said: "I now establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited thus:

'If a bhikṣuṇī, within a monastery cell, spreads grass or leaves herself or instructs another to spread them, and upon departing does not remove them herself nor instruct another to remove them, and if there is no other bhikṣuṇī to whom she has entrusted them, it is a pāyattika.'"

After the Blessed One had thus established the training rule for the bhikṣus, there were many bhikṣus traveling through the countryside who were invited by a certain householder to stay. He provided them with a great quantity of dry grass piled up to their knees; when dawn broke, they departed without informing him.
When the elder saw this mockery, the Buddha said:
"One should inform the owner and it must be discarded.
If one acts contrary to this, one incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
Furthermore, there were many bhikṣus traveling through the countryside; as described at length previously, they stayed overnight in a certain monastery and wished to discard their grass mats.
The host replied, "I sought this grass from afar for the sake of guests; it is truly difficult to obtain, so you should not discard it lightly."
The visiting bhikṣus replied, "You are ignorant;
having committed offenses yourselves, do you wish to cause us to commit offenses as well?
Having rebuked them thus, they took the grass and cast it outside.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"This should not be discarded. If there is a bhikṣu who has been entrusted with the task, you may discard it only after he has been sent to do so.
Should you act otherwise, you will incur an offense of transgression against the Dharma."
The former was an original enactment; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated thus:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, within a monastery dwelling, should herself spread or cause another to spread grass or leaves."

If one departs without lifting up [the bedding] oneself or instructing another to lift it, and if there is a bhikṣuṇī present who has not been informed, except for other extenuating circumstances, it is a pāyattika offense.
“Nun” refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
“Monastery” refers to the dwelling place of the Tathāgata’s disciples, wherein it is suitable for performing the four modes of deportment: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
"Reclining materials" refers to grass and leaves.
The rest is as explained above.
The characteristics of the offense herein are also the same as previously stated.
If one spreads grass on a hard surface made of brick, or upon sand and stones where there are no insects or ants, there is no offense even if one does not inspect it frequently. 16.
The Training Rule on Forcefully Annoying or Offending Others. The sixteenth training rule concerning forcefully annoying or offending others; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
Then the Venerable Udāyin went to where those many young bhikṣus were and exhorted them, saying:
"Come, let us travel together through the human world."

The full account continues until the young bhikṣus all went out to lie down in the open air; during that single night, they endured the sufferings of cold and other hardships, as detailed in the Bhikṣu-vinaya.
After the Buddha had rebuked her, he established a training rule for the two assemblies, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that other bhikṣuṇīs are already residing in a monastery, should later arrive there and intentionally cause them distress or annoyance by sitting or lying down upon their bedding with the thought:
'If they experience discomfort, they will surely avoid me and leave.'"
"A *pāyattika*.
"Nun" refers to a nun within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as above.
"Knows" means to have understood the matter.
"A bhikṣuṇī who previously resided in this place" refers to one who had already stayed there as a lodging.
"One who arrives later" refers to someone who forcibly occupies the space by lying down or sitting.
"One who dislikes suffering" means one who is distressed and finds it unpleasant.
"He shall avoid me of his own accord" means that he does so for this specific reason and not for any other matter.
The meaning of *pāyattika* is as explained above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī clearly understands the matter as previously described, up to the point of [the man] saying, "Go away from me," she incurs a pāyattika offense.

17. The Training Rule on Sitting or Lying Down with the Body Unrestrained on a Bed with Detachable Legs. The seventeenth training rule concerning sitting or lying down with the body unrestrained on a bed with detachable legs; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
Then the Venerable Upānanda went to where those many young bhikṣus were and exhorted them, saying:
"Come with me to travel through the human realm; we shall surely defeat the doctrines of other schools and attain renown for ourselves."

"If you wish to engage in recitation, chanting, or meditative reflection, as well as for whatever necessities may arise regarding food, clothing, or medical care, I shall ensure that none of these are lacking.
Although the young men heard this exhortation, they all knew that Upānanda was of a wicked nature and unfit to live with; consequently, not a single person consented to go together with him.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who lived on alms; hearing that [the Buddha] was seeking companions, he said to Upānanda, "I shall travel through the human realm together with the Venerable One."
A fellow traveler informed the one seeking alms, saying:
"This Upānanda is a man of evil conduct; if you follow him now, you will surely encounter distress and provocation."
He then replied to his fellow practitioners of the holy life:
"I have completed ten years since full ordination; I do not rely upon others for dependence, nor do I go to them to request instruction in the teachings. What, then, could they possibly do for me?"
The acquaintance replied, "Do not speak such words;
you shall know for yourself later. Disregarding this advice, he went along with him.

The full account continues as described in the Bhikṣu-vinaya, up until the point where Upānanda lay upon an upper platform and, knowing the bed had removable legs, sat down carelessly, causing the leg to slip out and strike another’s head, and so forth.
For this reason, the Blessed One rebuked them in various ways and established a training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, in a dwelling place belonging to the Saṃgha, knowing that it is an upper story or a loft, should sit or lie down with her body fully extended upon a bed with removable legs or other seating furniture, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
“Knows” means either she acts herself at some time or is instructed by another.
“Multi-storied dwelling” refers to a multi-leveled building that is dilapidated and decayed.

Regarding "beds with detachable legs on a shelf": this refers to beds whose legs are not connected to the upper cover. In the Western Regions (India), the legs of a bed are fixed at the four corners, and the cover above is joined to those legs; it is because of this difference that [such beds] are excluded, as are other types of seats.
"Releasing the body while sitting or lying down" means to stretch the body out excessively while either sitting or lying down, thereby causing one's feet to protrude and injure others.
The term *pāyattika* (波逸底迦) is explained in detail as above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is a bed with detachable legs in a monastic dwelling, sits or lies down upon it with her body fully extended in order to annoy others, she incurs a *pārājika* offense in every case.
If it is a wooden shelf, or a brick floor, or if the feet are supported by a board, or if it is placed face up—in all these cases, there is no offense.
18. The Training Rule on Using Water with Living Beings. The eighteenth training rule concerning the use of water containing living beings was established at Kauśāmbī.

At that time, the Venerable Channa used water containing living beings to sprinkle upon grass, soil, cow dung, and other such things. Those who possessed few desires collectively felt revulsion and contempt, saying:
"How can he use water with living beings to sprinkle upon grass and the like, doing it himself or commanding others to do so, showing no regard for the lives of sentient beings?"
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
On account of this, the Buddha questioned her regarding the facts and rebuked her. He then established a training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains living beings, herself sprinkles it upon grass or soil, or mixes it with cow dung, or instructs another to do so, it is a pāyattika."
The remainder is as stated above.

Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī perceives water containing insects as such, whether she uses it herself or instructs another to use it, she incurs a pāyattika; the same applies if she is in doubt.
If one perceives water that is free of insects as containing insects, one incurs an *āpatti* of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); the same applies if one is in doubt.
The Nineteenth Rule of Training on the Exceeding of Limits in Constructing Large Monasteries. The setting and circumstances are the same as before. As the Blessed One has said:
"Those who cultivate merit shall always experience peace and happiness in both this life and future lives."
"Those without merit constantly encounter suffering and affliction.
At that time, the bhikṣus instructed the brahmins and householders to establish dwellings for the sake of the Saṃgha.

At that time, the six bhikṣus spoke of various faults, observing that the entrance to this monastery was poorly arranged. As explained at length in the Bhikṣu-vinaya, up until the World-Honored One’s reprimand, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī constructs a large dwelling, she must install a crossbar at the side of the door-post, as well as windows and drainage channels.'"
"If, when building a wall, it is made of wet mud, it should be two or three layers high, level with the place where the horizontal bolts are inserted.
If it exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The remaining meaning is as above.
"Great" refers to two kinds:
first, greatness of the object given; second, greatness of physical dimension.
This refers to greatness of physical dimension.
Regarding the "dwelling place," it refers to a location where one may perform the four modes of conduct: walking, standing, sitting, and reclining.
Regarding the "builder," whether acting for oneself or employing others, one should install horizontal bolts, windows, and drainage outlets at the sides of the doorposts.

If the wall being constructed consists of wet clay, starting from the initial preparation of the ground and the laying of the foundation, one should apply two or three layers of the supporting framework and the trench.
If this limit is exceeded, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The explanation of the meaning is as above.
In this case, the characteristics of the offense are identical in detail to those for the fully ordained monks (bhikṣu).
The twentieth training rule concerning eating after one night has passed (*ekarātra-vipravāsa-bhakta*). The setting was in Śrāvastī.
The World-Honored One manifested great supernormal powers, whereby the non-Buddhists were utterly defeated and all fled in dispersion to dwell in the borderlands.
At that time, an elder constructed a dwelling place for the non-Buddhists, where a false teacher of the non-Buddhists resided together with sixty followers.
Later, a friend of the householder arrived at the householder’s residence from Śrāvastī and said to him:
"Do you currently have any superior field of merit here whom you may honor?"
The elder then led him to the place where the heretics were.
His acquaintance informed him, saying, "These are people of inverted views; they are not true fields of merit.

He then spoke to the elder at length regarding the noble and exalted virtues of the bhikṣus, continuing until he informed the six groups that they had all arrived. Consequently, the elder’s mind was stripped of pure faith, and he further beat the non-Buddhists and drove them away.
The bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha.
On account of this incident, the Buddha rebuked them in various ways and established a training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, at the dwelling place of non-Buddhists..."
"One may stay for one night and take one meal;
if one exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the time had come to subdue that householder, instructed the Venerable Śāriputra to preach the Dharma to him. Having heard the Dharma, he attained the vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana*). Furthermore, he preached the Dharma to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, and they all realized the Truths.
When the time had passed and she did not eat, wind-disorders arose and she fell ill; [the full account] is explained at length. The Buddha said:
"The former was the initial prohibition, and this is the subsequent allowance. It should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stays at the dwelling place of non-Buddhists for one night and takes one meal, except in the case of illness.'"
"If one exceeds [this limit], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Nun" refers to a nun within this Dharma.
"The dwelling place of non-Buddhists" means those who do not practice the holy life together.
"One night and one meal" means receiving food and lodging from that assembly while observing the limits of time and occasion.
"Except for the cause of illness" means on account of the matter of preaching the Dharma or being ill.
Regarding the *pāyattika* (offense entailing expiation), it is explained in detail as stated above.
What are the characteristics of the offense and its specific instances?
If a bhikṣuṇī has already accepted a single meal at a separate residence and stays there for an additional night, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) offense.
If one eats [the food], one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one stays overnight here and receives food elsewhere, there is an *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing) at the time of staying, but no offense at the time of eating.
If one stays overnight elsewhere and eats here, there is no fault at the time of staying, but one incurs a *pāyattika* offense at the time of eating.
If one stays in another place and eats in another, there is no offense if one comes here only temporarily.

If this dwelling is a communal property for many people, or if the host requests that one stay, or if this residence was built by a relative, there is no offense even if one eats beyond the permitted time.
The third summary verse says:
Encouraging [others] to eat their fill and eating separately from the community; eating at improper times, touching food with unwashed hands, and not receiving [food);
[seeing] insects, non-Buddhists, and observing one's own attire.
21. The Training Rule on Receiving Food in Excess of Three Alms Bowls. The twenty-first training rule concerning receiving food in excess of three alms bowls was established in Śrāvastī.
Since the Blessed One had realized unsurpassed wisdom and enlightenment, his fame had spread everywhere.
At that time, there was a great merchant leader from the north who arrived at the outskirts of this city and halted there.

When the group of six monks heard of this, they went together to his location and preached the Dharma for him. He then invited them to take a meal; once they had accepted the food, they continued to look upon one another and preach the Dharma for him.
The merchant leader earnestly invited him to accept food, but he replied once more,
"I have no need for food," and manifested a sign to request clothing.
The merchant abandoned him and departed, following behind and reciting this verse:
"One should not travel on the perilous roads of the borderlands; even if one must go, do not stay there.
Not only is that place unfit for travel, but one should not form friendships with those people."
The inhabitants of the mountainous wilderness may find it pleasing at first sight, like gold freshly polished on stone;
yet those dwelling in the central lands are not thus, remaining as immovable as mountain peaks from beginning to end.
When the merchants heard these words, they replied to the noble ones,
"For what reason do you harbor resentment and subject us to such mockery?
The group of six replied:
“O virtuous ones! You have briefly expressed your sentiments toward me, causing me to neglect my wholesome practices.
Having repeatedly preached the Dharma for them and manifested various signs, he eventually obtained the robes.
The merchants, bowing and nodding in agreement, gave him everything they had; their provisions for the journey were completely exhausted, and they subsequently encountered bandits and were plundered.
When the other merchants heard these words, they all joined in censuring and disparaging him.
This is the origin of the rule; the precept had not yet been established.
The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was an elder in this city who married a wife, but she died shortly thereafter. This continued until he had married a wife for the seventh time, and all of them passed away.

At that time, everyone called her "the wife who causes obstacles," and when others wished to marry wives, no one would give them to her. Eventually, she even managed to find a girl who was blind in her right eye.
A friend of hers spoke this verse:
"If a person sleeps with their head pointing west while using *pārasī* wood to clean their teeth; [she will become a wife who causes obstacles]."
A woman with a squinting right eye was taken as his wife; these are all signs of ill fortune.
When two evils meet, there will surely be harm, like a blade and a stone cast together.
Both husband and wife are people who cause injury; had he married her, he would certainly have met with death.
At that time, although her friend heard these words, he paid them no heed and continued to press for the marriage without ceasing.

The parents of the one-eyed girl prepared food and drink, intending to marry off their daughter; however, when the group of twelve arrived for the meal, they consumed everything and failed to complete the wedding ceremony, leading the laypeople to voice their derision and resentment.
The detailed exposition continues until the Blessed One rebuked them and established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a number of bhikṣuṇīs go to the home of a layperson, and there a faithful brahmin or householder earnestly invites them to accept cakes, parched grain, and boiled rice..."
A bhikṣuṇī who requires [food] should accept two or three bowls.
If she accepts more than that, it is a pāyattika offense.
Once she has received it and returned to her dwelling place, if there are other bhikṣuṇīs, they should share the food together; this is the proper time.
“Nuns” refers to the group of twelve or other nuns; when there are more than two, it is termed “a multitude.
“Lay families” refers to the households of white-robed laypeople, Brahmins, and so forth.
"Going there" means arriving at their location.
"Pure faith" means believing in the Triple Gem with a profound heart of devotion and respect.
"Sincere diligence" means the mind reaching its ultimate limit.
"To request" means to speak words of direct entreaty.
"Barley flour and cakes" refers to the food to be given as an offering.
"To desire" means to have a mind of affection and delight.
Regarding "two or three bowls," there are three kinds of bowls:
namely, superior, middling, and inferior.
The superior bowl is one that can receive two *śrona* measures of rice from the kingdom of Magadha.
The "medium" [portion] refers to accepting one and a half *śronas* of cooked rice;
the "small" [portion] refers to accepting one *śrona* of cooked rice.
The phrase "two or three bowls" indicates the limit.
"Returning to one's dwelling place" means arriving at the monastery.
"If there are bhikṣuṇīs with whom one should share the food" means distributing it together with those who practice the same holy life.
Regarding the offense of *pāyattika* for receiving more than the permitted amount, the details are the same as previously stated.
In this context, the characteristics of the offense are as follows: when receiving with two large bowls, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing);
if one then swallows or consumes it, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture).
22. The Training Rule on Sufficient Food (Paryāpta-bhakta-śikṣāpada). The twenty-second training rule on sufficient food. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"When I eat in a single sitting, I always obtain few desires, remain free from illness, have light and agile movements, possess robust physical strength, and dwell in peace and happiness."
As the Buddha had taught that there are such benefits to eating in a single sitting, all the bhikṣus then ate in a single sitting.

However, during the meal, if they saw their two teachers or other senior elders, they would immediately leave their seats; thinking it was because they had already finished eating, they did not dare eat more. Because they ate so little, their complexions became sallow and their bodies grew emaciated.
The Blessed One, having seen this and knowing it, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"I eat in a single sitting and thereby attain a state of dwelling in comfort; I instruct the bhikṣus likewise to eat in a single sitting so that they may attain a state of dwelling in comfort."
"For what reason are the bhikṣus so pale in complexion and emaciated in body?

Ānanda replied, "At that time, the bhikṣus were eating in a single sitting as instructed by the Buddha. While they were in the midst of eating, they saw two teachers and various elders arrive, and they immediately rose from their seats."
"Once he had left his seat, thinking it was sufficient food, he did not dare eat more. Because he ate so little, his complexion became sallow and his body grew emaciated.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"When a bhikṣu eats, he may eat as much as he desires until he is full."
"Once you have finished eating, you must not rise again.

Following the Buddha’s instruction that they must not rise, the bhikṣus considered themselves to have had enough as soon as they received any amount of soup, vegetables, or cooked beans; having risen, they did not dare to eat further. Due to these circumstances, their bodies all became emaciated and weak.
Having seen this, the Blessed One asked Ānanda:
"I have instructed the bhikṣus that whenever they wish to eat, from the time the salt has been served until they are no longer hungry, they may eat as much as they please to their satisfaction."
"If one has finished eating, one should not rise again.
For what reason are the bodies of the bhikṣus so emaciated and unable to be nourished?
Then Ānanda reported the preceding circumstances in detail to the World-Honored One, and the Buddha, on account of these circumstances, said to Ānanda:
“There are five kinds of *khādanīya* food, which means that which is chewed and bitten; if one eats these, it does not constitute having finished a meal (*pūrvabhakta*).
What are the five? Namely: first, roots; second, stalks; third, leaves; fourth, flowers; and fifth, fruits.”
Eating at these five times does not constitute having finished one's meal (*paryāpta-bhojana*).
If a bhikṣu has first eaten the five kinds of chewed foods (*khādya*), he may later eat the five kinds of masticated foods (*bhojya*).
However, if he has first eaten the five kinds of masticated foods, he should not further eat the five kinds of chewed foods.
"If one eats further, one incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.

As the Blessed One had taught that five kinds of chewed food do not constitute "sufficient food" while five kinds of masticated food do constitute "sufficient food," at that time, the bhikṣus, having received food and eaten only a small amount, would stop as soon as they had a reason to rise, thinking they had already reached sufficiency and daring not to eat more; consequently, their bodies all became emaciated.
The World-Honored One, having seen this and knowing it already, intentionally asked Ānanda:
"I have taught that five kinds of chewed food do not constitute a full meal, whereas five kinds of masticated food do constitute a full meal; in both cases, one should eat until satisfied."
"For what reason, Bhikṣus, are your bodies so emaciated?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha:

"As the Buddha has taught, if five kinds of food are chewed they do not constitute 'having had enough,' whereas five kinds of food that are swallowed do constitute 'having had enough. At present, when the Bhikṣus receive food, they eat only a small amount; as soon as they have finished with some business, they consider themselves to have had enough and dare not eat more. Due to these causes and conditions, their bodies have become thin and wasted."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“There are five conditions by which one’s meal is considered complete, and another five conditions by which it is not.
What are the five conditions by which a meal is considered complete?”
1. Knowing this is food; 2. knowing there is a person who bestows the food; 3. knowing that one has received it and is eating; 4. knowing what constitutes the prohibition of food;
5. knowing the relinquishing of the formal posture.
How does one know the food?
It means knowing these five types of food: that which is chewed and that which is eaten.
How does one know the person who gives the food?
This refers to knowing whether [the recipient] is a woman, a man, or a *paṇḍaka*, and so forth.
How does one know that food has been received before eating?
It means that two types of the five kinds of food have been received from another before being eaten.
How is it known that food is refused?
It means refusing two sets of five kinds of food.
How is it known that one abandons formal deportment?
That is to say, one leaves this seat and rises;
possessing these five conditions is called "having finished eating" (*paryāpta-bhojana*).
What are the five types that do not constitute having finished eating?

That is to say: knowing it is not food; knowing there is no one to give it; knowing one has received it but has not yet eaten it; knowing that eating is not prohibited; and knowing one has not yet left one's seat—these are called the five kinds of "insufficient for eating."
Furthermore, there are five kinds of "sufficient food" (*paryāpta-bhakta*).

What are the five? First, pure food; second, food slightly mixed with impure elements; third, food not touched by what is unwholesome; fourth, food slightly mixed with what is unwholesome; fifth, having left one's original seat—these are called the five kinds of sufficient food.
Furthermore, there are five cases that do not constitute having finished eating. What are these five? First, impure food;

second, food mixed with much that is impure; third, food touched by what is unwholesome; fourth, food mixed with much that is touched by what is unwholesome; and fifth, when one has not yet left one’s original seat.
These are called the five kinds that do not constitute having finished eating.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of having finished eating. What are the five?
This refers to when one sees someone distributing food;
the bhikṣu replies,
"I do not need it."
Some said: "Go. Others said: [Go. Or they said: [Go.]
"Stop," or "I have had enough."
Or one might say, "I have finished.
These five are all expressions of definitive refusal and lack of further need; when such words are spoken, it is termed "having had enough to eat" (*paryāpta-bhakta*).
Furthermore, there are five kinds of improper food. What are the five?
They are as follows: when one sees a person distributing food, a bhikṣu says:
"I do not yet need it," he said; or he said,
"Go for now."
Some said, "Let it rest for now. Others said:
"Wait for the meal," or "Wait until it is finished."
"These five [statements] are all incomplete and not definitive; when such words are spoken, it is not called 'having finished eating'.

As the Blessed One has said, a bhikṣu should not, after having eaten his fill, receive more food. At that time, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs, regardless of whether they were full or not, continued to eat further.
The bhikṣuṇīs of few desires, hearing this, felt revulsion and shame, and spoke thus:
"How can one contravene the Buddha's instructions?
They informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

For this reason, the Buddha, as before, assembled the bhikṣuṇīs, questioned them regarding the facts, and rebuked them; he then spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her meal, eats again, it is a pāyattika."

After the Blessed One had thus established the training rule, there was a time when a householder invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to his home for a meal. Many bhikṣuṇīs were afflicted by the suffering of illness; their attendants also went to that meal, and having eaten themselves, they returned carrying food for the sick.

At that time, the sick were unable to finish their meals, and the attendants, having already eaten their fill, did not dare to eat more. Furthermore, as there were no śrāmaṇeras or lay attendants (karmadāna) available to hand out food, they simply cast the leftovers aside. Consequently, crows and birds vied with one another to come and devour them, resulting in a great clamor.
The Buddha said,
"I permit you to perform the *śeṣa-bhakta-vidhi* (the ritual for leftover food) and eat as you wish.
Following the Buddha's words, they were permitted to perform the *śeṣa-bhakta-vidhi*.
Not knowing how to proceed, they informed the Buddha of the circumstances. The Buddha said:

"If there is a bhikṣuṇī who has already finished her meal, and a donor further offers her five kinds of solid foods and five kinds of soft foods that are delicious, and she desires to eat them, that bhikṣuṇī should wash her hands clean, receive the food, and go before a bhikṣuṇī who is currently eating and has not yet left her seat, standing before her and speaking as follows:"
"Venerable one, please take note!
I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], having already finished eating my fill, have further received this *khādanīya* (solid food) and *bhojanīya* (soft food), and I desire to eat more."
"Venerable One!
Please perform the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food) for me.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī should immediately perform the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* for her; having eaten two or three mouthfuls, she should say:
"You may go; this is your own property, so eat as you please.
Then, having performed the ritual, that bhikṣuṇī took it to one side and ate her fill at her leisure.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having already finished her meal, desires to eat more and eats without performing the *kṛtāvaśeṣa* (remaining-food) ritual, she incurs an offense of transgressing the Dharma.
There are five causes and conditions by which the *kṛtāvaśeṣa* ritual is not validly performed.
What are the five? They are: staying outside the boundary;

being at a distance or in a screened place; being behind [the monk]; being at his side; or when the person addressed has left their original seat. In these cases, the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa-vidhi* (the ritual for consuming leftovers) is not accomplished.
There are five causes and conditions for performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of making food "leftover"). What are these five? They are:

being within the same boundary (*sīmā*); being in a nearby place free of obstructions; not being behind [the person]; not being at their side; and the person facing one must also not have left their seat.
This constitutes the formal procedure for making food "leftover" (kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣa).
Furthermore, there are five conditions under which the formal procedure for making food leftover is not accomplished. What are these five?

That is to say: if one is outside the boundary, or in a distant or obstructed place, or if the food is not contained in a vessel, or if it is not held in the hands, or if the person being addressed has already left their seat—these do not constitute the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa-vidhi* (the ritual for consuming leftover food).
There are five causes and conditions by which the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the formal act of declaring food as "leftover") is accomplished;

these should be understood as the reverse of the aforementioned [five]. If one person has performed the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* and many bhikṣuṇīs subsequently arrive to eat together with him, none of them commit an offense; do not harbor any doubt regarding this.
The Blessed One, praising the observance of the precepts, addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"The former was the initial formulation; this is the subsequent allowance. It should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her meal, eats again without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual of leftover food), it is a *pāyattika* offense.'"
“Nuns” refers to the group of twelve; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
“Having finished eating” means that after having eaten until full, one has left one’s original seat.
“Not performing the *kṛtapiṇḍa* (remaining-food) rite” means not taking two or five portions of food and performing the formal ritual before another person.
"Further eating" refers to swallowing.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī perceives that she has had enough to eat or has doubts about it, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If she perceives that she has not had enough to eat or has doubts about it, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"If one has not eaten enough but perceives that one has not eaten enough, or if one has eaten enough but perceives that one has not eaten enough, there is no offense.
At that time, Upāli addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What kind of gruel is called 'sufficient food'?
The Buddha told Upāli:

"If the gruel is freshly cooked such that a spoon set upright does not fall over, or if the marks drawn with a finger or similar object do not disappear, eating this gruel is called 'sufficient food'."
“Venerable Sir!
What kind of flour-based food (saktu) is considered ‘enough food’?
The Buddha said:

"If, when first mixing with water and stirring, the spoon stands upright without falling over, or if the traces left by the five fingers do not disappear, eating this gruel at such a time is called 'sufficient food' (paryāpta-bhakta)."
Furthermore, Upāli!
Any thin gruel or thin flour paste is not considered sufficient food.
The Twenty-third Training Rule on Encouraging Another to Eat Until Satiated. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, a laywoman went to the place of a bhikṣuṇī and said:
"Noble Lady,
I wish to go forth."
The nun took this girl to her preceptor and granted her the going forth.
She then said to her disciple,
"You must instruct her."
At that time, an elder invited the Buddha and the Sangha to his house for a meal. After they had eaten as much as they desired, he obtained some leftover food and took it toward the edge of a pond.
There, the teacher asked the elder, "Do you wish to have some?"
He replied,
"I wish to obtain it.
The Master said:
"Are you straining water,
or are you performing the ritual for leftover food?
The senior disciple replied:
"I shall perform the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite; you, Master, may take water.
He then entered the water and performed the *kṛtapiṇḍa* rite for his own portion, but not for the Master's portion.
After the teacher had taken water, he immediately took some food.
Once the teacher had finished eating, the elder addressed him, saying:
"Teacher, you have now committed an offense; you should repent according to the Dharma."
The teacher said,
"I do not see any offense.
He replied:
"I did not perform the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* ritual.
The teacher said, "I am truly without fault; according to this principle, you must be at fault."
She immediately reported this matter to the bhikṣuṇīs; the bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.

On account of these circumstances, as previously, the Buddha assembled the Saṅgha, questioned her regarding the facts, and after reprimanding her extensively, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
“If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī has finished eating and has not performed the *kṛta-śeṣa* (remaining-food) rite, encourages her to eat more, saying:”
"Venerable one!
You should eat this food.
If, by such means, one intends to cause another to commit an offense and thereby produce distress, it is a *pāyattika*.
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“Knows” means either knowing by herself or being informed by another.
“Having finished eating” means having already eaten one’s fill.
"Without performing the *kṛtapiṇḍapāta* (the ritual for leftover food)" means not taking food from another person in their presence.
"To urge" means to send [someone] to eat more.
With this cause and condition, one intends to cause another to commit an offense; the definition of the offense and its detailed explanation are both as before.

Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī knows that another has finished eating and has not performed the *kṛta-śeṣa* rite, yet she encourages them to eat these various kinds of chewable or edible foods, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
