The Twenty-fourth Śikṣāpada: On Eating in a Group Apart from the Community. The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, within that boundary, Devadatta ate separately from the community with five hundred bhikṣus.
The bhikṣus of few desires were filled with resentment and shame, and they reported these matters in detail to the World-Honored One.
The Blessed One assembled the community of both monks and nuns, questioned them regarding the facts, and having rebuked them, declared:
"I now establish this training rule for the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; it shall be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī eats separately from the community, it is a pāyattika.'"
After the Blessed One had thus established the training rule, there were at that time bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs afflicted by the suffering of illness. The Buddha said:
"Except in the case of being ill."
Some were traveling on a journey, while others were engaged in manual labor; they all abstained from food. The Buddha said:
"Except for those traveling on a journey and those working.
Some were traveling by boat; the Buddha said: [“Except for those traveling by boat.”]
“Except when traveling by boat,” and so on, up to “except during a great almsgiving assembly.

At that time, King Bimbisāra had not yet attained the vision of the Truths (dṛṣṭi-prāpti); he had offered the Bamboo Grove Monastery to the naked ascetics (nirgrantha), but once he had attained the vision of the Truths, he subsequently abandoned the heterodox practitioners and offered it to the Buddha and the Saṅgha for their use.

At that time, King Bimbisāra’s maternal uncle had gone forth among the non-Buddhist ascetics; having conceived a heart of faith and reverence, he invited [the Buddha] to receive offerings and even addressed the Buddha, who said:
"Except when a śramaṇa is receiving a meal."
At that time, the Blessed One, having praised those with few desires and those who revere the precepts, taught the Dharma and addressed the bhikṣus:
"The former was the original prohibition; this is a subsequent allowance. I now establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī eats separately from the community, except at the appropriate times, it is a pāyattika.'"
The exceptions are:
when one is ill, when working, when traveling on a road, when traveling by boat, during a great communal meal, or during a śramaṇa’s almsgiving assembly; these are the appropriate times.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Eating in a separate group" means eating individually.
"Except at other times" means excluding those specific occasions.
Regarding "when one is ill": it refers to being unable to sit comfortably during a single mealtime.

Regarding "when one is working": it refers to either at a *stūpa*, or in communal affairs, down to sweeping a patch of ground as large as a mat, or occasionally smearing and cleaning a place as large as where a cow lies down.
Regarding the time spent traveling on foot: it refers to traveling half a *yojana* to and fro, or traveling one full *yojana*.
Regarding the time spent traveling by boat: it refers to riding in another's boat for half a *yojana* or one full *yojana*.
"Great assembly" refers to the gathering of many people.

"Śramaṇa" refers to those outside the Buddha-dharma, namely the various classes of non-Buddhist practitioners, who are also called śramaṇas because they exhaust their bodies in the pursuit of the Way.
This is a concession; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the transgression and its specific details?
If a bhikṣuṇī, within a boundary, perceives it as being within the same boundary—or entertains doubt—and then partakes of a separate meal for a group, she incurs a pāyattika.
If one is outside the boundary but perceives it as being inside, or is in doubt about it, one incurs an *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one is outside the boundary and perceives it as being outside, or is inside the boundary but perceives it as being outside, there is no offense.
Generally speaking, there are two kinds of residences:
first, the primary residence; second, the external residence.
When a bhikṣuṇī is eating at her primary residence, she should ask whether the bhikṣuṇīs from the external residence have come to eat with her.
If one eats without having asked, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
When bhikṣuṇīs outside the monastery are eating, one should ask the bhikṣuṇīs residing there whether they will come to eat together.
If one eats together with four people without having asked for permission, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If three people eat and one does not eat, or if three are fully ordained (*upasampanna*) and one is not fully ordained, there is no offense in all such cases.
If one sends food to them—even as much as a single spoonful of salt or a handful of grass leaves—to be eaten by that community, there is no offense.
Or, at times, a donor may say:
"I shall give food to everyone who enters."
At times, a donor may construct a separate room and offer it as a gift, saying,
"I shall provide food for all who reside within my room.
This, too, is without fault.
25. The Training Rule on Eating at Improper Times. The twenty-fifth training rule concerning eating at improper times.

The setting is the same as before. At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana ordained seventeen followers. During the morning mealtime, they donned their robes, took up their alms bowls, and entered the city to beg for food. They were reviled and scolded by Brahmins, elders, and others; unable to obtain any alms, they returned with empty bowls and consequently fasted.
In the presence of the multitude, he rubbed his own belly and spoke this verse:
“The Buddha has spoken the most wondrous words, Which pervade the realms of humans and devas;
‘Hunger is the ultimate of sufferings’— This statement is indeed the most wondrous.”
...until seventeen members of the community went to a certain householder’s residence and ate their fill at an improper time.
The World-Honored One, having rebuked them in various ways, addressed them, saying:
"I shall now establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī should eat at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.
The remaining meaning is as above.
Regarding "at an improper time," there are two limits:
1. After midday has passed; 2. before the appearance of the morning light. The offense is established as previously stated.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the transgression?
If one eats at an improper time while perceiving it as such, or when in doubt, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one eats at a proper time while perceiving it as improper, or when in doubt, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one perceives a proper time as proper, or an improper time as improper, there is no offense.
**The Training Rule on Eating Food Touched Previously (Śikṣāpada 26)** The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣu Kara had this constant custom: whenever he went for alms in a village or town, he would carry both his bowl and his bowl-bag. If he obtained moist rice, he would receive it in his bowl; if he obtained dry rice, he would place it in the bag. All the moist rice he received was eaten on the same day, while the dry rice he would dry in the sun and store in a basin.
If they encountered wind, cold, or rainy weather, they would immediately soak their food in warm water and eat it.

Once they had eaten their fill, they would then experience the subtle bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), liberation (*vimokṣa*), sameness of mind (*samādhi*), and attainment (*samāpatti*). Thereupon, the Blessed One rebuked them in various ways and declared:
"I shall now establish a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) for my disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:"
“If a bhikṣuṇī should eat food that has been previously touched, it is a pāyattika.
The remaining meaning is as above.
Regarding “food that has been previously touched,” there are two kinds of touching: [the touching by hand and the touching by mouth].
1. Receiving food before midday that has been touched after midday; 2. Receiving food after midday that has been touched after the watch of the night.
If a bhikṣuṇī knows that this is food already touched, yet swallows it again without performing the proper ritual procedure, the offense is established as previously described.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and its specific details?
If a bhikṣuṇī eats food that has been previously touched, while perceiving it as such or having doubt regarding it, she commits a pāyattika offense.
If one has not touched [the object] but forms the perception that one has touched it, or if there is doubt, one incurs an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
If one has not touched it and does not perceive that one has touched it, or if one touches it but perceives that one has not touched it, there is no offense.

If one uses a bowl that has been previously touched and has not been properly cleansed—whether it be a small bowl, a spoon, a bronze cup, or a salt container—to eat from, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense in all such cases.

If one touches a bowl-bag, a wiping cloth, a mendicant’s staff, a door-key, or a lock, and having thus touched or grasped such objects, fails to wash the hands and then grasps other food or drink, even down to fruit, at the time of swallowing it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in every case.
If a bhikṣuṇī wishes to drink water but has not thoroughly cleansed her mouth, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense at the moment of swallowing.
If she rinses and cleanses with soap-nuts (*kaṣāya*), earth, or other such pure substances, there is no offense.
27. The Training Rule on Not Accepting Food. The twenty-seventh training rule concerning not accepting food. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣu Mahākāla always used the śmaśāna (cremation ground) as his alms-bowl—meaning he considered it a place for discarding corpses; the old translation "Śītavana" is erroneous. He made use of the clothing, food, and bedding found at the śmaśāna.
What is meant by "using a skull-bowl"?
If someone has died, one takes a clay bowl or a sacrificial vessel to serve as a bowl.
What is meant by "the clothing of the dead"?
They take the clothing offered to the corpse, wash, dye, and sew it to make their own garments.
What is the food of the dead?
It is the five morsels of food that these kinsmen offer as a sacrifice to the deceased spirit, which they take and consume for sustenance.
What is the bedding?
This Mahākāla always sleeps in a place where corpses are kept;
this is called the bedding of the Śmaśānapātra for food and clothing.
When many people were dying, Mahākāla’s body became robust and stout, and he no longer went frequently into the city to beg for food.
When no one was dying, his body became emaciated, and he went frequently into the city, wandering from door to door to beg for food.
At that time, the gatekeeper of the city thought to himself:
"Does Mahākāla eat the flesh of the dead?
Then, a certain Brahmin in the city passed away and was carried to the charnel ground, where his wife and daughter stood weeping at one side.
At that time, Mahākāla was watching over the burning corpse.
When the girl saw him, she said to her mother,
"This holy man is like a blind crow, staying here guarding the corpse."
At that time, someone who had heard this came to inform the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.

The Buddha said, "That brahmin woman has brought harm upon herself. My śrāvaka disciples possess virtues as lofty as Mount Sumeru, yet she addressed them with coarse and evil words, mutually disparaging and reviling them. Due to this evil karma, she shall remain a blind crow for five hundred lifetimes."

At that time, people from near and far all heard what the World-Honored One had prophesied; as it was explained at length, they even said, "Do not let the jackal devour our sacrificial offerings," and they immediately hurried away to drive off that jackal and take back the sacrificial food.
The people replied,
"Whatever it is you eat, the sound of 'you are eating people' will resound throughout the city.
Having said this, they departed together.
He addressed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"It is because my śrāvaka disciples do not accept food that this fault has arisen."
"Therefore, I now command my disciples to receive and take appropriate food so that others may witness and know it.
Following the Buddha's instruction, they received and took the food before eating.
Not knowing how [the aggregates] constitute feeling, the Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of feeling: [feeling born of contact with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body]."

1. Receiving with the body and receiving with the body; 2. Receiving with the body and receiving with an object; 3. Receiving with an object and receiving with the body; 4. Receiving with an object and receiving with an object; 5. Receiving by placing on the ground.
There are five ways in which the formal acceptance of food is not accomplished.

What are these five? They are: being outside the boundary; being at a distance or in a screened place; being at the side; being behind [the donor]; or joining one’s palms [at the wrong time]. These are called the five ways in which the acceptance of food is not accomplished.
The full account continues until it says that he obtained the fruit but did not accept it.
The Buddha said, "You should accept it and you should perform the ritual of purification (pariśuddhi). He did not know how to perform the purification.
The Buddha said:
"There are five kinds of purification.
What are the five?
These are: purification by fire, purification by knife, purification by nails, purification by withering, and purification by pecking by birds.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of preparation for purity:
purification by uprooting, purification by hand-breaking, purification by cutting off, purification by splitting, and purification by making seedless.
"As the Buddha has taught, one should accept and eat what is offered," yet the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs ate whatever they took for themselves, regardless of whether it had been formally accepted.
The bhikṣuṇīs of few desires, seeing this, felt revulsion and shame; they reported the matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.

On account of this matter, the Buddha assembled the bhikṣuṇīs as before and, having questioned them regarding the facts, rebuked them. He spoke at length, up until the point where he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, without having received food, places it in her mouth and swallows it, it is a pāyattika."
After the Blessed One had thus established the training rule, there was a bhikṣuṇī who, having received neither water nor tooth-sticks from anyone, entered a village to seek them. The Buddha said:
"Except for water and tooth-sticks."

Furthermore, there were those traveling through the countryside who, upon encountering a perilous road where no one offered them food, were given fruit by monkeys, bears, and brown bears. The nuns refused to accept it and returned; eventually, they reported this to the Buddha. The Buddha said:
"If sentient beings know whether food has been offered or not yet offered, all may accept it; do not harbor doubts."
The former was an original enactment; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated thus:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, without having received food, places it in her mouth and swallows it—except for water and tooth-sticks—this is a pāyattika."
"Ni" refers to those within this Dharma.
"Not having received" means not having obtained it from another.
"Eating" refers to the two sets of five [precepts] and so forth.
"Eating and swallowing" refers to the act of ingesting.
"Excepting water and tooth-sticks" means that, with the exception of these items, all other things must be formally accepted.
If one receives fresh, moist branches, they should be purified by fire before being accepted; the offense for violating this rule is the same as previously stated.

Regarding the characteristics of offenses herein: if one perceives food as not having been formally received (*apratigrāhita*) when it has not been so received, or harbors doubt regarding this, there are two grave offenses and two light offenses; for the latter two cases, there is no offense, as explained in detail above.

28. The Training Rule on Drinking Water Containing Insects. The twenty-eighth training rule concerning drinking water containing insects was established while the Buddha was staying at the Ghoṣitārāma in Kauśāmbī.
At that time, the bhikṣu Chanda used water containing insects.
At that time, the bhikṣus saw this and said to him,
"For what reason do you intentionally use water containing living beings?
He replied:
"Who delivered these insects within this water to me?
Why do they not go to other jars, basins, rivers, streams, ponds, or the waters of the four great oceans?
They are born and die of their own accord; what fault is there of mine?"
Having heard these words, they were all filled with resentment and shame, and reported the matter to the Buddha.

On account of this, the Buddha assembled the disciples of both divisions and, after questioning them to ascertain the facts, rebuked them. He spoke at length, up to the point where he established the training rule, saying:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that water contains living organisms, should use it, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
“Knows” means either she knows it herself or has been informed by another.
Regarding “water with insects,” there are two kinds of insects: [the *udakajantu* and the *pāṇaka*].
First, one sees it immediately upon looking; second, one sees it only after straining with a filter.
"Water" refers to all types of water.
There are two ways of using water:
First, internal enjoyment; second, external enjoyment.
What is internal enjoyment?
It refers to all that is enjoyed by the internal body.
"External" refers to all things for use outside the body:
washing robes and alms bowls, laundering or dyeing robes, sprinkling the ground, or smearing it with cow dung, and so forth.
*Pāyattika*: the explanation of the term is as above.

Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī uses water containing living beings while perceiving it as having living beings, or while harboring doubt about it, she incurs a *pāyattika*.

If there are no insects in the water, yet one perceives them as being present or suspects their presence, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing); in the other two cases, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī knowingly consumes roasted flour, honey, molasses, oil, vinegar, water-gruel, fermented milk, curd, cakes, fruit, or similar items that contain insects, she incurs a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) in all such instances.
29. The Training Rule on Giving Food to Naked Ascetics, Male and Female. This twenty-ninth training rule was established with its origin in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were several merchants within this city who came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and sat to one side.
Then the World-Honored One preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the merchants, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening them before remaining silent.
Having heard the Dharma, they were filled with deep joy in their hearts; they paid homage to the Buddha and departed.
He then went to where Ānanda was, prostrated, and sat down. The Venerable One expounded the essential points of the Dharma for him, until [the youth] addressed him, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
To which human region does the Blessed One intend to travel on his journey?"
Ānanda said: "Virtuous ones, you may go yourselves to question the World-Honored One.
They replied:
“The World-Honored One, our Great Teacher, possesses such majestic and solemn authority; how would we dare to venture to question him?
Ānanda said, “Judging by his physical demeanor, it appears that the World-Honored One will soon be heading toward Śrāvastī.”
When the summer retreat had concluded, the World-Honored One set out on the road with his great assembly.
At that time, there were naked ascetics among the traveling merchants who also accompanied him; being unable to obtain food, they manifested signs of hunger.

The bhikṣuṇīs had leftover food in their bowls, which they each took and gave away; they filled their vessels with cakes, fruits, and other such items. A detailed account follows until, on the road, they encountered a naked ascetic who asked them, "Noble ones, who has provided you with provisions for the journey?"
He replied,
“The shaven-headed daughters of the Śākyas.
When the naked ascetics heard these words, they were filled with indignation and spoke this verse to the non-Buddhists:
"Why does your body not sink into the earth?
Why does your tongue not split into a hundred pieces?
Why did the various deities, upon seeing this matter, not strike your body with a thunderbolt?"
The jackal constantly eats the leavings of the lion, yet it always harbors thoughts of harming him;
though the assembly of the Ten-Powered Sage sustains you with food, you now revile me and remain ignorant of my kindness.
He has certainly realized all-knowledge; his mind is impartial toward friend and foe alike.
Even you, O outsiders—despicable people—still rely upon him and receive his aid and sustenance.
If a person does not recognize kindness and righteousness, know that such a type is worse than a dog;
a dog understands how to repay the kindness shown by humans, while you are like a venomous snake, constantly spitting out poison.
This was the origin of the event, at which time the precept had not yet been established.
At that time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the human realm and arrived at Śrāvastī.
There, five hundred people from the village invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha; as extensively described, they heard the Dharma and realized the Truths.
At that time, there were two naked ascetics (nirgrantha), one old and one young, who came to beg for food.
Ānanda did not carefully examine the cakes to see if they were stuck together; he gave one to the old woman and two to the young woman.
The elder said, "The prince-bhikṣu gave me one cake, yet you received two; I know for certain that he has conceived a fond affection for you, so you should adorn yourself."
The youth said, "Do not speak such words.
This prince has now abandoned the imperial palace and its inner chambers to leave the home life and grow weary of worldly俗事; he has cast off the dust of toil like one discards snot or spittle."
At that time, the bhikṣus reported the matter to the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for my disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, with her own hands, gives food to a naked ascetic or to other male or female ascetics, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
“With her own hand,” etc., means giving food with the hand.
The meaning of “eating” is the same as previously explained.

"Those without clothing" refers to the naked ascetics and other various classes of non-Buddhists; for [giving to] them, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. The remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī gives food with her own hand, she incurs a downfall offense (*pāyattika*) in all such cases.
If it is a relative or a sick person, there is no offense in giving;
or if one wishes to eliminate that person's wrong views by means of food, there is likewise no offense in giving.
30. The Training Rule on Viewing Armies. The thirtieth training rule concerning viewing armies. The occasion was at Śrāvastī.
At that time, King Prasenajit ordered a great general to lead his troops in a military expedition.
At that time, when the six bhikṣus heard that the troops were about to depart, they said to one another,
"We should go and watch," and they went to the place on the road.
Seeing the elephant army approaching, he asked,
"Where are you going?
They replied:
“Venerable One!
There is currently a border region that has not submitted; the King has commanded us to go and wage war against it.
The group of six replied:

"Judging by your current circumstances, it appears you will depart without returning. You should first return for a brief time to bid farewell to your kinsmen; only after performing mutual sacrifices with *arkasvatī* water may you join the army."
The full account continues until the Blessed One questioned her about the facts, rebuked her, and addressed the bhikṣus:
"I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions;
it should be recited as follows: 'If a bhikṣuṇī goes to view an army in formation, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to one who belongs among those who follow this Dharma.
“To array the army” means to prepare for battle by donning armor and accoutrements, and arranging the military formation.
There is one type of army that consists solely of elephants.
There are two types of armies, namely those that additionally include cavalry.
There are three types of armies, namely those that additionally include chariots.
There are four types of armies, namely those that additionally include infantry.
"To go and view" means to head toward that place.
The offense is established as described above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī views an army in full array, she incurs a pāyattika.

If a bhikṣuṇī, while on her almsround, sees an army approaching; or if the monastery is near a main road and an army enters it; or if the bhikṣuṇī is summoned by a king; or if she is invited by a queen, a crown prince, a minister, or other persons—should she see an army in these circumstances, there is no offense in any case.
When seeing an army, one should not speak of its strengths or weaknesses.
Furthermore, there is no offense if one sees [an army] when any one of the eight difficult circumstances has arisen.
The fourth summary verse says:
Concealing an offense, visiting a layperson's home, lighting a fire, giving consent (*chanda*), and stating that the giving of consent is not an obstructing factor. 31.
The Training Rule on Staying Two Nights or More among an Army. The setting for the thirty-first training rule is the same as before.
At that time, King Prasenajit personally led his army to the frontier city; having arrived there and laid siege, the city had not yet surrendered. A minister said to the king:
"The householder Anāthapiṇḍada possesses great power of merit; if he were to come, they might perhaps surrender."
When the imperial decree arrived, summoning them, although they were in the midst of the army, they thought only of the noble Saṃgha.

King Prasenajit then sent a letter to the community of monks; having heard it, the group of six monks went to the king’s military camp. Upon seeing an elephant, they seized its trunk and threw it to the ground; seeing the cavalry approaching, they seized their tails and cast them aside;
seeing the chariot troops approaching, they said: "This is a broken cart."
He immediately seized the axle and pulled it to the side of the road.
Seeing the infantry approaching, he regarded them as mere straw figures; he then gripped one by the neck and threw him outside the army.
When those four soldiers saw themselves thus humiliated, they were utterly helpless.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, for this reason, assembled the community of bhikṣus; the dialogue was as before, and he declared:
“Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the two communities, which should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī has a legitimate reason to go among the military forces, she may remain for no more than two nights.’”
"If she stays overnight, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Nun" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
"Having a reason" means being summoned by anyone from the king down to the common people.
"Within an army" refers to when the military forces are about to engage in battle.
The four types of troops are as previously described.
"Staying for two nights" means one should remain there for two nights; beyond this, it is not permitted. If one stays longer than that, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if one stays within an army for more than two nights, one incurs a *pāyattika* (falling) offense.
However, if the king or others invite one to stay overnight, or if there are the eight kinds of calamities, staying overnight is not an offense.

32. The Training Rule on Disturbing Military Troops. The third-twelfth training rule concerning disturbing military troops. The setting is the same as before; the remainder is as explained above, up until [the incident where they] went together to observe the troops to see whether they were brave or cowardly, and having previously hidden and waited in ambush, they terrified the army and caused mutual disturbance. The full account continues until the World-Honored One’s reproach, after which he gathered the assembly as before and addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
“I now establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī stays overnight in an army for two nights and observes the troops preparing for battle, or sees the vanguard flags and watches the arrayed or scattered soldiers, it is a pāyattika.’”
“Nun” refers to one who belongs to this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
There are four kinds of banners:
first, the lion banner; second, the great bull banner; third, the whale banner; and fourth, the garuḍa banner.
There are four kinds of troops:
namely, elephants, cavalry, chariots, and infantry.
There are four kinds of battle arrays:
First, the spear-point formation; second, the chariot-pole formation; third, the half-moon formation; fourth, the garuḍa-wing formation.
If one observes such military arrays, one incurs an offense of downfall.

Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if one stays within an army for two nights, if one observes the four divisions of troops who have not yet donned armor or taken up weapons, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing);
if one observes those who are fully equipped, it is a *pāyattika* (offense of expiation).
If the king or others invite one to remain and dwell, or if there are the eight difficult circumstances (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), seeing [the offense] does not constitute a transgression. 33.
The Training Rule on Striking a Bhikṣuṇī. The third training rule on striking a bhikṣuṇī; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana ordained seventeen groups of people as renunciants. When he was traveling through the human world on his own, he told them:
"When I am not present, you should dwell in reliance upon the virtuous Sangha."
He then relied upon Udāyin, who replied:
"Come here and perform such-and-such tasks?
They replied: [as instructed].
"I cannot carry out any of these instructions.
Then Udāyin seized one person, whereupon seventeen people cried out loudly; [the account continues] at length until the Blessed One rebuked him:
"How can a bhikṣu, with a mind of anger, strike another bhikṣu?"
Having assembled the community of bhikṣus, he addressed them, saying:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for my disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger and displeasure, strikes another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
“Angry” means when the mind is entangled in resentment and gives rise to indignation and vexation.
“Striking” means to strike or beat.
"An ordained nun (bhikṣuṇī)" refers to one who has received full ordination within this Dharma; the explanation of the offense is as above.
Regarding the characteristics of the transgression herein: it may be committed by means of one's own body parts, or by means of external objects, or by both combined.
Regarding the internal [parts]: if one strikes with a single finger, one incurs one *pāyattika* offense;
if with two fingers, two; and so on, up to five fingers, one incurs five *pāyattika* offenses.
Whether using the fist, the elbow, the head, the shoulder, the hip, the knee, or even the toes of the foot, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in each case.

Regarding "external objects": if one strikes or hurls another from a distance using a fine blade of grass, an arrow shaft, or other implements—even as small as a jujube pit or a handful of mustard seeds—whenever any of these makes contact, one incurs a *pārājika* offense; this is what is meant by "external objects."

Regarding "both": if one strikes another person with a hand-held weapon such as a blade or staff, or with various other types of objects such as grass, stalks, or tree leaves, a *pāyattika* offense is incurred for whatever part is struck; this is called "both."
If one strikes another person in order to cause them fear, or for the sake of accomplishing a mantra or incantation, there is no offense in any of these cases.
34. The Training Rule on Gesturing Toward a Bhikṣuṇī. The setting for this thirty-fourth training rule is the same as before; the rest is as explained above.
At that time, Udāyin became enraged and, lashing out with his hand toward one person, all seventeen of them fell down at once and wailed loudly.
The bhikṣus felt contempt for this and reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha then rebuked her and, eventually, addressed her, saying:
"Observing ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:

"We have not died here to be reborn elsewhere; rather, it is through the power of the accomplishment of this extraordinary Great Being that our bodies and minds are freed from suffering and have attained happiness."

Once faith has arisen, they are able to extinguish all the sufferings of the hells and receive superior and wondrous bodies within the realms of humans and devas; they constantly serve as vessels for the Dharma and are able to perceive the principles of the Truths.

Those who ascended went upward as far as the Heaven of the Four Great Kings, the Heaven of the Thirty-three, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin Heaven, and even up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.
Wherever he went, light issued forth from him, proclaiming the dharmas of suffering, emptiness, impermanence, and non-self, and further reciting these two gāthās:
"You should seek renunciation And diligently practice the Buddha's teaching;
Subdue the army of birth and death, As an elephant destroys a thatched hut."
"In this Dharma and Vinaya, by always practicing heedfulness,
one can exhaust the ocean of afflictions and reach the ultimate end of suffering.
Then that radiance, having illuminated the trichiliocosm, returned to the presence of the Buddha.

if he speaks of matters concerning the hells, the light enters through the soles of his feet.

If he was to speak of the affairs of a Cakravartin King of Power, the light would enter through the palm of his left hand;

Then the Venerable Ānanda, with palms joined in reverence, addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Did you see the two youths who led me?

Upon hearing these words, all the merchants thought to themselves:

The World-Honored One, on this account, again comforted him so that he might be freed from sorrow and fear.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"It was not only today that I startled the traveling merchants; in ages past, I have likewise caused others to be terrified and flee in all four directions, and I have comforted them to free them from their distress."
Listen, all of you!
In a past age, by the side of a certain body of water, there was a grove of *piṇḍa* fruits. Within this grove lived six rabbits who dwelt together as close friends, relying upon one another.

At that time, the fruit of a *bimbi* tree ripened and fell into the water, making a sound. Hearing the sound of the falling fruit, six rabbits—small in body and timid in spirit—were seized with great terror and fled in all four directions.
At that time, there was a jackal who saw him running away and asked him the reason for his flight.
The hare said, "I heard an extraordinary sound within the water; could it not be a fierce beast about to come and harm me?"
"Because of this matter, we have fled.

Not far from there, in the midst of the mountain valleys, lived a fierce lion king. At that time,

They all recounted the matter.
Siṃha replied,
"In what place did you make that evil sound?"
The beasts replied, "We do not know either.
[The man said,] "If you are not certain, do not run away for now; I shall investigate for myself."
He then questioned him in succession, and the hare replied, "This terrifying sound was personally witnessed by me; it is not something heard by hearsay.
[The king said,] "Let us go together to the place where the sound originated."
At that time, all the beasts gathered together and paused for a moment; then, hearing again the sound of fruit falling into the water, they said, "This is merely the sound of fruit falling;

"O bhikṣus, do not harbor other thoughts. He who was the lion in the past was none other than myself.

"...up to the occasion of illness.

"If a bhikṣuṇī, not being ill, for her own sake, should kindle a fire herself or instruct another to kindle one, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who is a member of this Dharma; the remaining meanings are as stated above.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī plays with the tip of a flame or fashions the shape of the sun or moon discs, she incurs a *pārājika* offense in all such cases.

If one extinguishes the fire, one also incurs an offense of falling.

"I am extinguishing the fire."

If one grasps the tip of a flame and moves it forward, or pulls back the tip of a flame, or turns over burning coals, or turns over fire such as that from chaff or husks—whatever action one performs, such as preparing food, boiling water, lighting a lamp, or burning incense—at the moment of contact, it constitutes a *duṣkṛta* offense.
If one discards hair, body hair, nails, saliva, or similar substances into fire, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).

"We ought to perform the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against him.

39. The Training Rule on Staying Overnight for More Than Two Nights in the Same Room with One Who Has Not Yet Received Full Ordination. The third and final training rule: "The training rule on staying overnight for more than two nights in the same room with one who has not yet received full ordination. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by a great assembly as he preached the Dharma; his words were exquisite and beautiful, causing the multitude to delight in hearing them, such that the listeners forgot their fatigue as bees savor honey.
At that time, there was a poor laborer who, having heard the Buddha’s Dharma, spoke these words:
"The appearance of the World-Honored One is solely for the sake of the wealthy; had the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preached the Dharma at night, I would have been able to hear it."
The Buddha said, “One should recite the sūtras at night, or preach the Dharma for others; one should light lamps and candles so that it is not dark.

At that time, there was an elder bhikṣu who slept without mindfulness and consequently uttered delirious speech regarding unwholesome matters. When the laypeople heard this, they became critical and disparaging, and no longer listened to the Dharma.
They reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Because of sharing a room for lodging and lighting lamps and candles with those who have not yet received full ordination, such faults arise;
therefore, I now forbid bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs from sharing a room for lodging or lighting lamps and candles with persons who have not received full ordination."
This was the origin of the event, at which time the precepts had not yet been established.
At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra had two śrāmaṇeras:
one was Cunda and the other was Rāhula.
When they were about to enter the summer retreat, the great assembly gathered and divided the dwellings among themselves.
These two novices did not receive a share, and their hearts were filled with distress. Eventually, Cunda asked Rāhula, "For what reason do you remain so sorrowful?"
He replied, “Virtuous one, you possess merit and great majestic power; you can transform a grass hut that is fit for lodging, but as I lack such power, what can I do?”
Cunda said, "It is not possible to see the Buddha at an improper time for the purpose of inquiry.
However, there is a pure donor who has smeared a latrine with exquisite fragrant clay; you may stay there to pass this single night."
He then entered the latrine and lay down for a while.
That very night, a heavy rain fell from the heavens.
Not far from there, a large venomous snake was dwelling within a hole in the ground.
When the hole was filled with water, the snake emerged and went straight to the latrine.
The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, possessing a mind free from forgetfulness, thought to himself:
"If that venomous snake were to bite Rāhula, he would surely die and exist only in name."
Furthermore, those of the Śākya clan, relying on their own high status and becoming arrogant, gave rise to disbelief and spoke thus:
"If Rāhula had not gone forth into homelessness, he would have succeeded to the position of a Wheel-Turning King."
"Now that he has gone forth as a renunciant, he is without support or protection; lying upon a latrine, he was bitten by a snake and died an unjust and painful death.

Having thought this, the Buddha extended his right hand like the trunk of an elephant king, lifted the body, and placed it upon his own bed. That night, the Buddha remained walking and sitting until daybreak.
There was another bhikṣu who went to where the Blessed One was, wishing to pay his respects.
It was the Blessed One’s constant practice that, when he intended to establish a training rule for the śrāvakas, he would not allow anyone who had not yet arrived to depart until they had assembled.
When the novice Rāhula awoke, he realized it was the Buddha’s bed; he immediately sprang up in alarm and stood there trembling with fear.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"For all novices and novice nuns, there is neither father nor mother; you who practice the holy life together are their only companions, mutually caring for one another. If they are not protected by you, who else would feel concern for them?"
"Therefore, I now permit the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs to stay overnight for up to two nights with those who have not yet received full ordination without committing an offense.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus stayed for more than two nights; when the bhikṣus of few desires heard these words, they felt contempt and disparagement, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu fail to uphold the Buddha's teachings?"
They reported the matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and, having rebuked them, declared:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī again sleeps in the same room as a person who has not yet received full ordination for more than two nights, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who is a member of this community.
There are two types of those who are fully ordained (*upasampanna*):
namely, bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs; others are not fully ordained, such as śrāmaṇerīs and so forth.
There are four kinds of dwellings:
1. Fully covered and fully enclosed, such as various houses and multi-storied pavilions, which are completely covered on top and have all four walls shut off.
2. Fully covered and mostly enclosed, where few windows or doors are installed among the four walls.

Third, the "mostly covered and fully enclosed" [dwelling] refers to a four-sided house; walls are erected on the four sides with pillars standing in the center, and the four eaves either recede inward or are level-headed.
4. "Much covered and much obstructed" refers to a dwelling with three sides, meaning that one side is missing from what would otherwise be a four-sided dwelling.
If it is half-obstructed and half-covered, or if it is mostly obstructed and less covered, or if it consists of such things as a mere eaves-edge, in all these cases there is no offense.
If one stays overnight with someone who is ill, there is no offense even if it exceeds two nights.
40. The Training Rule on Not Abandoning Wrong Views Despite Being Admonished. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣu Animitta gave rise to a pernicious view and spoke these words:
"Regarding what the Buddha has said—that 'dharmas which constitute obstacles should not be practiced'—I know that when these dharmas are practiced, they do not constitute obstacles."
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"The community should carry out a formal admonition against him.
Should there be other monks or nuns of a similar kind, they should be dealt with in this same manner."
He went to where he was and said to him:
"Do not speak such words as:
'Regarding the dharmas that the Buddha has declared should not be practiced because they are obstacles, I know that when these dharmas are practiced, they are not obstacles.'"
"Do not misrepresent the Blessed One!
It is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.

The Blessed One does not say that obstructive factors are not obstructive; rather, through various skillful means, he has declared that if one practices those factors which are obstructive, they will certainly constitute an obstruction."
"You should now abandon such an evil view.
Thus should one offer admonition.
Having received these instructions, he departed; however, that person persisted in his attachment and would not relinquish it.
The Buddha said:

"You should admonish him through a formal motion followed by three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman), following the same procedure as in the Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya, up to the performance of the act of suspension (pratisaṃharaṇīya-karman).
If he then remains obstinate and refuses to relinquish his position, you must report the circumstances to the Buddha."
The Buddha assembled the community and, after reproaching them in various ways, addressed them, saying:
"Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions.
It should be recited as follows: 'If a bhikṣuṇī should speak thus:"
"If I understand the Dharma taught by the Buddha, that 'desire is an obstacle,' it is not an obstacle when one practices it.
The bhikṣuṇīs should say to that bhikṣuṇī:
"Do not speak such words."
"I understand what the Buddha has said: 'Sensual desires are obstacles'—yet when one practices them, they are not obstacles.
Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak thus; rather, the Blessed One has declared, by means of countless methods, that all sensual desires are obstacles.
You should abandon such an evil view.
When the bhikṣuṇīs have admonished her in this manner, it is well if she relinquishes [the matter].
If she does not relinquish it, they should admonish her correctly up to two or three times;
they should instruct her correctly so that she relinquishes this matter.
"If he renounces it, it is well;
if he does not renounce it, it is a *pāyattika*.
The remaining meaning is as above.
"One who speaks these words" refers to one who explains the matter.
"I know the Dharma taught by the Buddha" refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Dharma" refers to that which was spoken by the Buddha or spoken by a Śrāvaka.
This statement clarifies the meaning.

"Obstructive dharmas" refers to the four *pārājika* offenses, the various *saṃghāvaśeṣa* (formal meetings) rules, the thirty-three *niḥsargika-pāyattika* (forfeiture and confession) rules, the one hundred and eighty *pāyattika* (confession) rules, and so forth, up to the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*).
"Not being an obstacle during the time of practice" means that it cannot obstruct the noble fruits of a śramaṇa.
"Slander" refers to uttering unreasonable speech.
"Unwholesome" means that it brings about an unpleasant ripening of karma.
When the bhikṣuṇīs see this speech, they should perform a formal admonition (pratyekapratideśanā).
If she does not relinquish it, they should perform a formal ritual admonition (karmavācanā-pratideśanā), continuing until the conclusion of the procedure, as explained in detail previously.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if one speaks such words as,
"I know what the Buddha has taught," it is well if they relinquish [the position] when admonished;
If one does not relinquish [the position], one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

During the formal act of admonition (*kamma*), if one does not relinquish it during the motion (*ñatti*) or the first and second proclamations (*kammavācā*), one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense in each case;
however, when the third proclamation is completed, one incurs a *pācittiya* offense.
If it is not a legal matter and so forth, there is no offense.
The fifth summary verse says:
"Dwelling together with one of evil views; a novice with dyed robes."
Seizing [a monk’s] bowl, washing [a monk], animals, causing distress, pointing at water, and staying overnight together.
41. The Training Rule Concerning One Who Has Been Suspected and Set Aside (Pratiniḥsargika-pācattika-dharma 41). The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, having received the formal ritual (karmavācanā), the bhikṣu Animitta sat with his cheek propped upon his palm, dwelling in sorrow.
When the group of six saw him, they asked:
"For what reason do you dwell in sorrow?"
He replied, "The Black-bowl monks have performed the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against me; they treat me as an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*) and will no longer have any dealings with me."
The group of six replied:

"Even if one were to perform the ritual of suspension (*pratikṣepa-karman*) against cities, villages, and all sentient beings within the three realms, would that mean these cities and so forth do not exist?"
"Do not be distressed.
Thereupon, they conversed together, partook of food and clothing, and lay down in the same room.
At that time, those of few desires felt mutual disdain and contempt, and reported the matter to the Buddha. [The account continues] at length until the Buddha said:
“Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:

‘If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a person who speaks in such a manner has not yet acted in accordance with the Dharma and has not abandoned their evil view, should engage in conversation with them, dwell together with them, share resources with them, or sleep in the same room with them, it is a pāyattika.’”
The remaining meanings are as above.
"One who has not yet performed the conforming dharma" refers to one who has not yet performed the conforming rite of confession (*pratideśanā*).

"Not abandoning wrong views and engaging in conversation with them," etc., means performing acts such as providing instruction or serving as a formal refuge (*niśraya*), sharing a room among the four types of dwellings until dawn; the matter of the offense and its classification are all as described above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that such a person has not yet performed the act of compliance, yet engages in conversation, stays overnight with them, or performs similar acts, she incurs an offense of downfall (pāyattika).
If one nurses a person who is ill, there is no offense;
or if one causes a co-resident to abandon wrong views, this also constitutes no offense. 42.

The Training Rule on Accepting a Novice Girl Who Does Not Abandon Wrong Views. The forty-second training rule concerning the acceptance of a novice girl who does not abandon wrong views. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the group of six monks had two novices:
one named Śaṇḍa and the other named Phalgu.

There was once a bhikṣu who went for alms and lived together with these two, engaging in playful conversation and frivolous behavior with them. Later, he felt remorse and reproached himself; rousing a mind of heroic vigor, he severed all afflictions and realized arhatship. Having attained great supernormal powers, he traveled through the air to the place where the two novices were, and related everything in detail, up until his attainment of the fruits of supernatural power.
Upon hearing this, the śrāmaṇera thought to himself:
"In the past, he committed such and such unrighteous acts together with us.
How is it that he has now obtained a superior fruit?"
"For this reason, I understand that what the Buddha has taught—that 'indulging in various sensual desires is an obstacle'—is not actually an obstacle.
He reported this matter to the Buddha, who said:
"What these two śrāmaṇeras have said is unreasonable; you should admonish them separately to bring them to understanding."
If there are others of this kind, they should also be admonished in this way:
"You, [Name], do not speak such words as:
'I know that which the Buddha has taught as being an obstacle—namely, sensual desire—is not actually an obstacle.'"
"Do not speak such words to slander the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to slander the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not say such a thing; rather, the Buddha has taught through various skillful means that the pursuit of sensual desires is an obstructive dharma."
"You two must now abandon this evil view.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, they went to them and delivered the message; however, at that time, the two novices stubbornly clung to their position and would not relinquish it.
They reported this matter to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"A *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal motion followed by three proclamations) should be performed," as explained in detail above. "That bhikṣuṇī should also act in this manner:"
“‘Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
These śrāmaṇerikās, so-and-so by name, have themselves given rise to such evil views and spoken thus:
“I know that which the Buddha has taught as being an obstacle—namely, sensual desire—is not actually an obstacle.”’”
When the bhikṣuṇīs were giving her a formal admonition, she still stubbornly clung to her evil view and refused to relinquish it, saying:
"This alone is the truth; all else is false."
"If the Saṃgha deems it timely and grants its permission, the Saṃgha should authorize that it now performs the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* for him to instruct him in this matter.
Having spoken at length up to the formal motion (*jñapti*), he announces:
"The Saṃgha has finished performing the formal motion for you; you should now abandon your evil view."
"If he relinquishes it, that is well;
if he does not relinquish it, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) shall follow.
Thus, at the conclusion of the first proclamation, he is questioned as before; at the conclusion of the second and third proclamations, he is likewise questioned as before.
Having carried out the instruction, they reported to the Buddha that she still stubbornly clung to her evil views and would not relinquish them.
The Buddha said,
"You should perform the formal act of suspension for not relinquishing evil views (*adhyāśaya-aviniścaya-pratikṣepa-karman*) against that śrāmaṇerī."
It should be performed in this manner:
ring the *ghanṭā* to assemble the community, and one *bhikṣuṇī* shall perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable *bhikṣuṇī* Saṃgha, listen!..."

That certain śrāmaṇerī [Name], having conceived an evil view as described in detail above, when the Saṃgha performed the formal admonition and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* to instruct her, stubbornly clung to it and refused to relinquish it, saying:
"This matter is true; all else is false."

"If the Saṃgha deems the time appropriate and grants its consent, may the Saṃgha permit that the Saṃgha now perform the formal act of *pravāsanīya-karman* (banishment) against him for not relinquishing his evil view.
When this is concluded, one should tell them:
"From this day forward, you must no longer say:..."
"One should not say, 'The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my great teacher.
Furthermore, one should not follow behind a bhikṣuṇī along the same path, nor should one share a room with her for two nights, as other śrāmaṇerīs do with mahābhikṣuṇīs."
"You do not possess such qualities now; you foolish person, depart at once!
Thus it was announced.
[The procedure] is the same as previously described for the formal inquiry.
If she does not relinquish it, the formal ritual (karmavācanā) should next be performed according to the procedure for the motion (jñapti).
Once one round has been completed, a bhikṣuṇī must again be sent to inform her:
"The community has already performed the first formal ritual for you; you should relinquish this evil view."
The full exposition is as above, continuing until the conclusion of the third *karmavācanā*, with the concluding formula applied accordingly.
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, they performed the *pravāsanīya-karman* (act of banishment) for him, yet he did not relinquish his evil views.
The bhikṣu Upānanda provided for him, made offerings to him, conversed with him, and shared a bed with him.
The bhikṣus reported this matter to the Buddha,
and the Buddha questioned him regarding the facts and rebuked him, saying:
“Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī, seeing a śrāmaṇerī making such a statement as:
“I know that which the Buddha has taught as being an obstacle—namely, sensual desire—is not an obstacle when one practices it,” [that bhikṣuṇī shall be dealt with according to the rule].’”
The bhikṣuṇīs should say to that śrāmaṇerī:
"Do not speak such words as:
'I understand what the Buddha has taught—that those things which are obstructive dharmas are not obstructions when one practices them.'"
"Do not misrepresent the Blessed One; it is unwholesome to misrepresent the Blessed One.
The Blessed One does not speak thus; rather, the Blessed One has declared in countless ways that all sensual phenomena are obstacles."
"You should abandon such an evil view.
When the bhikṣuṇīs speak thus to that śrāmaṇerī, it is well if she abandons this matter;
if she does not abandon it, they should instruct her correctly and admonish her correctly up to two or three times to make her abandon this matter.
If she relinquishes it, that is well;
if she does not relinquish it, the bhikṣuṇīs should say to that śrāmaṇerī:
"From this day forward, you must not say: [the rest of the quote follows]."
"The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is my great teacher.
If there are elders or fellow practitioners of the holy life, she should not follow after them; however, as other śrāmaṇerikās may do, she may stay overnight with a bhikṣuṇī for two nights.
"You do not possess such qualities now; you foolish woman, depart quickly!
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that this śrāmaṇerī has been expelled, nevertheless accepts her, benefits her, or shares a room with her for the night, it is a pāyattika.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Buddha" refers to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
"Speaker" (śāstṛ) carries the meaning of one who guides and instructs.
The Dharma refers to what is spoken by the Buddha or what is spoken by the śrāvakas.
"Sensual desires are obstacles" means they refer to the five sensual desires.
"Practicing them" means performing those actions.
"Not being an obstacle" means that it cannot obstruct the noble fruits of a śramaṇa.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
"Speaking to that śrāmaṇerī and others" refers to recounting her evil views and administering both individual admonition and formal communal admonition.
If he does not relinquish [the offense], a formal act of banishment (*pravāsanīya-karman*) should be performed, and he should be addressed as follows:
"From this day forward, you shall explain the matter at length; it is improper for us to travel or stay together with you."
"You are a foolish person; you should depart at once.
"Knows" means either knowing it oneself or hearing it from another.
"Accepts" means providing him with formal reliance (*niśraya*).
"Benefiting" means providing food and clothing.
"Staying in the same room" means sharing a bed within any of the four types of rooms; the offense incurred is the same as previously described.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense here: if one knows she is a *śrāmaṇerī* who has been expelled, yet still stays in the same room with her, it is a *pāyattika*.
If they are kinsmen, or if they are currently ill, or if one temporarily accepts them for the purpose of causing them to abandon wrong views, there is no offense in any of these cases. 43.
The Training Rule on Wearing Dye-dyed Robes. The forty-third training rule concerning the wearing of dye-dyed robes was established with its causal setting in Rājagṛha.
At that time, there were two dragon kings in this city:
the first was named Kṛtī and the second was named Balākā.
King Bimbisāra then constructed two divine shrines for them in a grove by a spring outside the city.
Twice each year, on the days of the festivals, all the people from the six great cities would gather like clouds.
Once, on such a festival day, musicians from the south arrived at the royal city and said among themselves:
"If we recount the extraordinary deeds of the Great Man, we can cause the hearts of the multitude to be filled with joy and affection, thereby obtaining much wealth."
He went to where the group of six monks was, prostrated at their feet, and said:
"Noble ones, please explain for me the sublime conduct that the Buddha practiced when he was formerly a bodhisattva."
The group of six asked,
"For what purpose do you ask this?
The musicians replied:
"I wish to set it to music and compose it into songs.
He replied, "Fool!"
"You must take these supreme matters of my Buddha-dharma and set them to song.
You may depart at once; there is no need for further discussion.
She then went to the bhikṣuṇī Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra and related everything in detail, from her birth until her attainment of enlightenment.
Upon hearing this, the musicians all took it up in song; they gathered many people to perform various musical entertainments, and those of respectful faith were struck with wonder, all exclaiming:
"How marvelous!"
"The musician is skilled at singing.
He bestowed upon him gifts of money and valuables beyond the measure of ordinary men.
Furthermore, he reflected again:
"One must ultimately lead those who lack faith [to the truth].
He then assumed the appearance, movements, and conduct of the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*).
When those who lacked faith saw him, they all laughed loudly and squandered much of their precious wealth.
When the six groups of monks heard this, they went to the two shrines, dressed themselves in lay clothing, and all performed as dancers and musicians.
The great assembly rushed there like clouds, abandoning their own performance venues, and thus the monks obtained many articles of clothing.
A young musician looked down on him with disdain, saying:
"How can a bhikṣu wear the white robes of a layperson?
[The Buddha] spoke at length until the World-Honored One rebuked him, saying:
"Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for my disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī obtains a new robe, she must apply one of three types of dyed, discolored stains:
either blue, mud-colored, or madder-red.'"
"If one uses [a garment] without applying the three kinds of discoloration, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Nun" refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
Regarding "new garments," there are two kinds of new: [the new by nature and the new by acquisition].
First, it refers to an item that is a new garment; second, it refers to one newly obtained from another.
Here, "new" means a new garment.
There are ten types of garments, as fully explained above.
"Blue" refers to blue color;
"clay" refers to red stone;
"red" refers to the red bark of trees.
"Staining with a discolored hue" means to alter its original color.
If one uses it without having altered the color, the offense is the same as before.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if one obtains a robe and does not stain it with any one of the three prescribed colors, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
44. The Training Rule on Taking Valuables. The forty-fourth training rule concerning taking valuables. The setting is the same as before.

At the first part of the day, Upānanda took up his robes and bowl and entered the city to beg for food. On the way, he saw several young boys who had set aside various ornaments and were playing together.
Seeing it, Upānanda thought it was the property of a yakṣa and took possession of it.
Then the boys each vied with one another to pull at his hands and feet, scattering dust and dirt over him; this is related in detail until the World-Honored One rebuked him and said:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī should herself take hold of, or cause another to take hold of, a jewel or anything resembling a jewel, it is a pāyattika.
At that time, the Blessed One traveled from Vaiśālī to Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jetavana Grove.
At that time, Viśākhā Mṛgāramātṛ, hearing that the Buddha had arrived and wishing to pay him homage, adorned her entire body with various necklaces and ornaments.

However, as she was by nature modest and felt a sense of shame upon about to see the Buddha, she subsequently removed her ornaments and entrusted them to her attendants; she then prostrated before the Buddha, listened to the Dharma, and departed from her seat.
At that time, the attendant placed the necklace beneath the flowering tree and forgot to return home.
When Ānanda saw this, he thought to himself:
"The rule established by the World-Honored One shall now be relaxed on account of this."
He immediately took it and went himself to inform the Buddha. The Buddha said, "Excellent!
Although I had not yet granted permission, you already knew the proper time."
The Buddha spoke at length, and so on until the World-Honored One, for these reasons, assembled the community and praised the observance of the precepts, declaring:
"The former was the initial enactment; this is the subsequent allowance."
It should be stated thus:

"If a bhikṣuṇī herself takes hold of, or causes another to take hold of, precious objects or things belonging to precious objects, except when inside a monastery or in the house of a layperson, it is a pāyattika."
If, within a monastery or in the house of a layperson, one sees treasure or what resembles treasure, one should form this thought before taking it:
"If anyone claims it as their own, I shall give it to them."
"This is the proper time" refers to one who is among those who practice this Dharma.
"Jewels" refers to the seven precious gems.
Regarding "precious objects," this refers to various types of weaponry such as bows and swords, as well as musical instruments such as drums and flutes.
Whether one takes them up oneself, causes another to do so, or incurs the offense through other means, the details are as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, while in a monastery or a layperson’s house, sees jewels or other valuables, she is permitted to think:
"I shall take them up; if their owner comes, I will return them to him."

Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if one grasps a precious object with one's own hand or causes another to grasp it after it has already been polished or treated, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling);
if it has not yet been polished or treated, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing).
Even to grasp an imitation lapis lazuli incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*duṣkṛta*).
If one grasps ornaments for adorning the body, such as necklaces, one incurs an offense of falling (*pāyantika*).
Even to grasp a garland made by knotting barley stalks incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If one takes up various musical instruments such as the lute (*vīṇā*) that possess strings and frets, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if they lack strings, it is a *dukkaṭa*.
This applies even down to a single-stringed lute made of bamboo; to hold such an instrument also constitutes a *dukkaṭa*.
If conch shells are fit to be blown, holding them constitutes a *pāyattika* offense; if they are not fit to be blown, it is an *dukkaṭa*.
The same applies to various drums and musical instruments.
If a statue contains relics, holding it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.

If one carries [the relics] without the thought that they are the Teacher's remains, it is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). However, if one carries them while perceiving them as the Great Teacher himself, there is no offense.
The Forty-fifth Training Rule: Bathing at Improper Times. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there were three hot springs by this city:
first, one where the king himself bathed; second, one for the women of the royal palace; and third, one for various other people.
The bhikṣus also bathed at the place where the king washed, and the bhikṣuṇīs also bathed at the place where the palace women bathed.
At that time, when the group of six monks and the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs went to bathe, they thought to themselves, "Let us test the depth of the King's faith.

Intending to cause him annoyance, they lingered for a long time and did not emerge promptly. Consequently, the King sent someone to fetch water elsewhere to bathe, rather than entering the hot spring.
Having finished bathing, he went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, listened to the sublime Dharma, and took his leave of the Buddha to depart.
At that time, Ānanda reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"Because the bhikṣus bathed, this fault arose; one should not bathe."
Because his body was unwashed, it was covered in much grime and oiliness. While he was on his almsround, a lay traveler saw him and asked, "Do you consider this grime and oiliness to be pure?
The Buddha said:
"One should bathe once every half-month.
Because they did not wash frequently during the heat, the same situation arose as before, and the Buddha said:
"One should wash during the hot season."
There was a bhikṣu who was ill; a physician told him to wash, but he replied, "The World-Honored One does not permit it.
The Buddha said:
"One should wash when ill.
Or, while performing communal work or at a stūpa, if one's body was soiled and impure that others saw it and felt disdain, the Buddha said:
"One should wash while working."
While traveling on the road, he became utterly exhausted from coming and going and lay down to rest. When the people saw this, they were astonished.
The Buddha said, "When traveling on the road, one should wash."
...until, when he was blown by the wind, his body became covered with much dust. The Buddha said:
"When there is wind, one should wash.
Again, when he was touched by rain, and again when his body was soiled by mud during wind and rain, he reported these matters to the Buddha as before. The Buddha said:
“If it rains, or if it is raining and windy, one may wash as one pleases.

At that time, the Blessed One praised the observance of the precepts, and so forth, until he said: “Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited thus:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī should bathe more than once every half-month, she commits an offense.’”
Therefore, for one who bathes in contravention [of the rule], it is a *pāyattika* offense, except during the remaining times.

The remaining times are: the time of heat, the time of illness, the time of work, the time of travel, the time of wind, the time of rain, and the time of both wind and rain; these are the [permitted] times.
“Nun” refers to one who belongs to this Dharma.
“Should bathe once every half-month” means that bathing is permitted once every fifteen days.
“Therefore, to contravene it” means to act in violation of the instruction.
Regarding "except at other times": if it is at another time, there is no offense.

"Time" refers to when one month and a half remain of spring—meaning when one month and a half remains, one should enter the rains retreat from the first day of the fourth month until the middle of the fifth month—as well as the first month of summer—meaning the first month of the rainy season from the sixteenth day of the fifth month until the middle of the sixth month. These two and a half months are called the period of extreme heat.
"Being ill" refers to one who has a disease such that frequent bathing does not bring about comfort.
"Engaged in work" refers to performing tasks for the Triple Gem, ranging from sweeping an area as large as a mat, to occasionally smearing [the ground] like a cow's resting place.
"Time of walking" refers to walking one *yojana*, or returning from half a *yojana*.
"Time of wind" refers to even until the wind blows so that the corner of one's robe moves.
"During rain" refers to even two or three drops falling upon one's body.
"During wind and rain" means that both are present.
"This is the proper time" refers to following the permission to hear the Dharma.
The offense is established as previously described.

Regarding the characteristics of the transgression herein: whenever it is the permitted time for bathing, a bhikṣuṇī must always maintain the vow through mental reflection and verbal expression, saying:
"During such-and-such a period, I shall bathe."
If one does not maintain the vow, and washes the body with water, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) is incurred if the water has not reached the navel;
if the water reaches the navel, an offense of falling (pācittiya) is incurred.
If there is a necessary reason to cross water that reaches above the navel, there is no offense.
46. The Training Rule on Killing Animals (Tiryagyoni-vadha-śikṣāpada), the forty-sixth. The occasion for this rule occurred in Śrāvastī.
At that time, Udāyin, while on his alms round, went to an archery hall and took up arrows to shoot at crows, until the laypeople began to criticize and disparage him.
The World-Honored One rebuked him and said:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī again intentionally takes the life of a sentient being belonging to the animal realm, it is a pāyattika.
The remaining meaning is as above.
"Intentionally" clarifies that it was not an error.
"Animals" refers to birds or other species of fowl and beasts.
"Taking life" means severing their life-faculty; the explanation of the offense is the same as before.
Regarding the characteristics of an offense herein, "taking the life of a sentient being" refers to employing the three types of means—
internal, external, and both— to initiate the application of effort that severs their life-faculty.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to kill, harms an animal even with a single finger, and it dies as a result, she incurs a pāyattika;
or if it does not die at that time but dies later as a result of this, she also incurs a pāyattika offense;
if it does not die later, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
This is explained in detail as in the previous training rule regarding the taking of human life.
47. The Training Rule on Annoying a Bhikṣuṇī: The forty-seventh training rule concerning annoying a bhikṣuṇī has the same setting as the preceding one.
At that time, the group of seventeen approached the group of six and said to them,
"Do such a thing.
They replied:
"I cannot do it. Thus, he was dismissed and not permitted to dwell with them.
At that time, the group of seventeen followed him to another location to engage in recitation. Nanda went to Upānanda’s place and said:
"These young masters do not accept my words.
He replied, "You should cause each of them to feel distress and regret so that they abandon their studies; you must act in this manner."
He spoke at length regarding the causes of the provocation, causing [the offender] to feel remorse.
He reported the matter to the Buddha, who spoke at length until he questioned [the offender] about the facts and reprimanded him, saying:
"I shall consider ten benefits and establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of malice, intentionally causes another bhikṣuṇī distress, even for a brief moment,
and acts with this as her motive, it is a pāyattika."
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
Therefore, "to cause distress" means to cause the mind to give rise to remorse through bad conduct.
"To be unhappy for even a short time" means that one's state of being is not at peace for even a brief moment.
Regarding "taking this as the condition," it refers to no other circumstance.
The offense is established as described above.
In this context, the characteristics of the offense are as follows: first, one asks about a specific matter; second, one asks about that which accords with the Vinaya teachings.
What is the inquiry regarding its particulars?
If a bhikṣuṇī, with a mind intent on causing disturbance, approaches another bhikṣuṇī and speaks thus:
"Venerable one!..."
"Do you remember such-and-such a king and such-and-such a householder?
He replied, "That was long ago; I do not remember them."
He replied: "Venerable one!
That which you do not recall over such a long period is precisely that you received full ordination before your age had reached twenty; it may be received once again."
One incurs an offense of falling (pāyattika).
If one asks in this manner:
"Do you remember such-and-such a time, a solar eclipse, a lunar eclipse, a year of famine, or a year of plenty?"...
The detailed explanation is as above.
What is meant by "inquiring in accordance with the Vinaya teachings"?
For example, if one acts with a mind of malice, one asks:
"In what place did you previously receive full ordination?
He replied, "In such-and-such a place."
He replied:

"In that place there was no great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) nor was a formal boundary field (*sīmā-bandha*) established; since the great assembly did not gather, it constitutes a separate residence, and thus the full ordination (*upasampadā*) was not properly received.
You should receive it again."
He asked again,
"Who are your ācārya and upādhyāya?
He replied:
"He was our second teacher.
