He replied, "That man violated the precepts and was unfit to be a teacher; therefore, you cannot be said to have properly received full ordination."
He asked again,
"Did you go to such-and-such a place?
He replied:
"Go! If you go to that place, they will all be foolish people who have broken their precepts, or base and evil types who are not virtuous companions.
You, too, must certainly have broken your precepts."
When one utters such words as these to disturb another, whether that person is actually disturbed or not, if they merely hear and understand them, one incurs a downfall offense.
He asked again:
"Venerable one!
Will you take the robes of the two teachers?"
He replied, "I took it. He was told:
"If you take it, because you have a thieving mind, you commit a defeat (pārājika) offense.
He asked: "Venerable sir!"
“Have you ever spoken of the impermanence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the selflessness of all dharmas (*dharma-nairātmya*), and the tranquility of nirvāṇa?
He replied, “I have spoken of them.”
He replied:
"If you speak of such superhuman states (uttara-manuṣya-dharma), you commit a pārājika offense.
If there is a bhikṣuṇī who asks other bhikṣuṇīs such a question:
"Venerable one!
Do you remember such-and-such a king and such-and-such a householder?
He replied:
"I do not recall," he replied, saying,
"Venerable sir!"
"Even though you do not recall it because it was a long time ago, he has indeed completed twenty years and has properly received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
Furthermore, one should understand as above regarding solar and lunar eclipses, and the abundance or scarcity of harvests throughout the years; this is called "inquiring about specific matters."
For example, if a bhikṣuṇī goes to another bhikṣuṇī and asks:
"Venerable one,
in what place did you previously receive full ordination?"
He replied, “In such-and-such a place.
The other said:
"I know that at such-and-such a place there was previously a great boundary and an established site for ordination; you may now properly receive full ordination.
Thus he asks the two masters about the location to which they are directed.
Question: "Is it permissible to take the teacher's robe? Answer:
"In all these cases, there is no fault."
He asked again:
“Venerable sir!
Do you say that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, and so on, up to: that nirvāṇa is peace?”
He replied, "I said it. The other responded:
"Did you not claim for yourself that you had attained this state of a superior person? He replied, "No."
"If it is thus, there is no fault in speaking; this is called a question that accords with the Vinaya teachings.
The forty-eighth rule concerning striking or tickling others with a finger. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who tickled another with his fingers, causing the other’s death.
The World-Honored One rebuked him and, for the sake of the disciples of both divisions, established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again tickles another with her fingers, it is a pāyattika."
The remaining meanings are as above.
"Striking with a finger" refers to a physical action (*kāyakarman*).
The determination of the offense is as above.
Regarding the characteristics of offenses herein: if one uses a single finger, one incurs one *pāyattika* offense; likewise, up to five fingers result in five offenses.
However, if one points with the tips of the fingers to indicate the location of a mole or the site of a wound, there is no offense in any of these cases.
49. The Training Rule on Playing in Water. The setting for this forty-ninth training rule is the same as before.
At that time, among the group of seventeen monks, there was a senior bhikṣu named Upāli. Having severed all afflictions and realized the fruit of arhatship, he thought to himself:
"I shall first examine those who dwell with me in the practice of purity; within this assembly, who possesses roots of goodness?"
"Who lacks roots of goodness?
Having observed that there were indeed such people, he considered to whom they belonged;
knowing they belonged to him, he employed skillful means to guide them as companions, and together they went to the Ajiravatī River to filter water for filling the jars.
Having observed the water, they applied their minds with right mindfulness for the purpose of bathing; once the bathing was finished, they stood to one side.

At that time, the sixteen men also all bathed; having entered the river, they floated and submerged, went to the opposite bank or returned to this bank, moved with the waves or went against the current, played the water-drum, struck the water-frog, made water-ropes, or made water-mortars—performing various such musical entertainments, their bodies and hands agitated as they laughed and played together.
At that time, King Śreṇika, from atop his high tower, saw their performance from afar and said to Queen Vaidehī:
"Observe for a moment those who are the field of merit you hold in such high regard."
The lady said to him:
"Great King!
These youths possess full and vigorous countenances; that you do not marvel at their ability to practice the holy life (brahmacarya) is truly extraordinary."
"Although the King is advanced in years, he has not yet attained tranquility; why then should his sporting in the water be censured?
At that time, Upāli, having perceived the King's thoughts, addressed the people, saying:
"Each of you should adjust your robes, take up water-jars together, and return to our residence."
Then Upāli, by means of his supernormal powers, ascended into the air together with his fellow practitioners of the holy life and flew past above the king’s palace.
At that time, Queen Vaidehī looked down at their shadows and gazed up in wonder at this marvel, and she said to the king:
"Your Majesty, behold these most excellent fields of merit as they soar through the sky."
The King said,
"My lady! How could there be anyone who has realized arhatship playing in the water?"
The lady replied:
"This is indeed what Your Majesty has heard and known; however, there are matters you have not yet heard and do not know.
The king said:
"What do you mean?

The lady replied, "The mind is like a flash of lightning, changing in an instant; yet with firm concentration as steadfast as a diamond, one shatters the delusions of ignorance in a single kṣaṇa. Your Majesty should not find this strange."
Having heard these words, the king remained silent and gave no reply.
Then Queen Śrīmālā sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One would take me into his compassionate mindfulness."
At that time, the World-Honored One, having understood this, assembled the community and questioned them regarding the facts.
Having rebuked them, he declared: "Observing ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions.
It should be recited as follows: 'If a bhikṣuṇī again engages in playing in water, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding "playing in water," all details are as stated above; in each case, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

As for the characteristics of the transgression herein: if one enters the water with the intention of playing in it, from the moment of entry until before one has submerged, it constitutes an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one's body is submerged, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Even making a sound by snapping one's fingers constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one plays with water contained in a jar or vessel, that too is a *pāyattika* offense.
If one makes a clinking sound while stirring soup or broth in a bowl, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
There is no offense if one does so with the intention of cooling it.
The fiftieth training rule: On sleeping in the same room as a man. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, Āniruddha, having severed all fetters and delusions and realized arhatship, took up his robes and bowl and traveled through the human world until he arrived at a certain village.
In this village lived an elder who had two sons and one daughter; when the daughter reached maturity, her conduct was neither chaste nor disciplined.
Because those two brothers were competing with others, someone told them:
"Your sister, though not yet married, has been having illicit relations with an outsider.
Having heard this, they questioned their sister about its truth or falsehood, and she immediately replied:
"I am truly pure and restrained; it is only the people of the world who speak falsely of me.
Later, she became pregnant, and her brothers asked, "You claim to be pure and restrained; from where did you obtain this?"
The sister said,
"A shaven-headed man once forced himself upon me, and because of that, I became pregnant.
Subsequently, she gave birth to a son.
At that time, people called her "The Mother of the Bald.
When the Venerable Āniruddha arrived at this village, as the sun was about to set, he sought a place to stay for the night.
Then the young boys replied,
"Venerable One!
That house of the bald woman over there will surely allow you to stay the night."
Following his words, they stayed the night there.
The bald woman’s mother then allowed them to dwell together, but she conceived improper thoughts and, during the night, sought to embrace him.

At that time, the Venerable One, perceiving her evil intent, rose into the air by means of his supernormal powers. When the woman saw this, she was filled with wonder and sought his mercy, offering her apologies; [the text continues] at length until it says that, having witnessed this transgression, the Venerable One thereafter no longer stayed overnight in the houses of the laity.
She reported the matter to the Buddha. On this occasion, the Buddha, as before, assembled the community and praised the observance of the precepts, then declared:
"Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī again sleeps in the same room as a man, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Together" means including the other party.
"A man" refers to either an adult male or a boy, meaning one who is capable of engaging in sexual intercourse.
Regarding "staying overnight in the same room," there are four types of rooms as mentioned above.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.

As for the characteristics of the transgression herein: if one stays overnight with a man, and one's body is on the upper floor while the man is on the lower floor, one should pull up the ladder so he cannot ascend, or secure the door with a bolt and lock, or dispatch someone to keep watch.
If it were otherwise, until the appearance of the dawn light, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
if the dawn light has passed, one incurs a *pāyattika* (offense of falling).

If a bhikṣuṇī is on the lower floor while a man is on the middle floor, or if a bhikṣuṇī is on the middle floor while a man is on the upper floor, or if the situation is reversed—these cases are explained in detail as before.
Alternatively, if a bhikṣuṇī is in the room and a man is under the eaves, all matters are as previously stated, with the single exception of the ladder.
If a man is inside the room and a bhikṣuṇī is under the eaves, one should fasten the door from the outside; the rest is as previously explained.

If she is under a porch, with the bhikṣuṇī inside the door and a man outside the door, she should secure a bolt from within; conversely, if the situation is reversed, she should fasten it from without. All other matters are as previously stated.
Even if they share the same room, there is no offense if there is a wife present to guard her.
The sixth summary verse says:
"Fear, concealment, anger, the two paths, digging the earth, and the four-month invitation."
Refusing instruction and eavesdropping on words, she silently rose from her seat. 51.
The Training Rule for Frightening a Bhikṣuṇī. The fifth and final training rule concerning frightening a bhikṣuṇī; the setting of the缘 (nidāna) is the same as before.

At that time, the group of seventeen monks was diligently engaged in recitation. When the group of six monks learned of this, they turned their woolen blankets inside out during the first watch of the night and made terrifying sounds.
The group of seventeen monks were each greatly alarmed. [The full account] is related at length until the World-Honored One rebuked them and said:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be stated as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, whether by herself or by instructing another, causes fear in another bhikṣuṇī—even if done in jest—this is a pāyattika."
The remaining meaning is as explained above.
"Another bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who is a member of this Dharma.
Regarding the characteristics of an offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to terrify another, assumes various frightening forms, namely those of diverse kinds; [this constitutes an offense].
If one burns a tree stump or creates various images of spirits and ghosts, saying, "Come and eat you!
Cut off your life-root!
then regardless of whether that bhikṣuṇī is frightened or not, this bhikṣuṇī incurs a pāyattika offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī, with the intent to terrify another, produces various kinds of fearsome sounds—namely, the sounds of lions, tigers, leopards, and various ghosts and spirits—and says, "Come and eat you!
[she commits an offense.]
The rest is the same as before.
If one produces various fearsome odors—
namely, the odors of feces and urine, or the odors of spirits and ghosts;
Or they may act with the intent to terrify others, creating unpleasant tactile sensations— such as coarse and stiff mats or the malevolent touch of various spirits and ghosts— saying,
"Come and harm you!"
The rest is the same as before.
Or they may manifest various lovely forms—namely, the likenesses of kings, ministers, elders, householders, devas, and so forth—and say:
"This one has come to harm you."
Whether that bhikṣuṇī is frightened or not, she incurs an offense of wrongdoing (duṣkṛta).
If she produces pleasant sounds— such as those of the lute, the sheng, the flute, or the voices of devas and nāgas— and says,
"These various sounds are coming to harm you," [she incurs an offense].
If they produce pleasant odors—namely, the fragrances of sandalwood, aloeswood, camphor, saffron, celestial incense, dragon incense, and so forth, or even foul odors—they will come to harm you.
If one encounters pleasant tactile sensations—namely, the exquisite touches of fine silks, delicate cotton, and the like, as well as the touches of devas, nāgas, and so forth—one should say:
"These various tactile sensations are coming to harm you."
Whether that bhikṣuṇī feels fear or not, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.

However, if she intends to cause the other person to develop a sense of revulsion and, for that purpose, speaks of the various sufferings and pleasures found in the realms of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas to induce a feeling of dread, there is no offense in any of these cases.

52. The Training Rule on Concealing the Robes and Alms Bowls of Other Bhikṣuṇīs, etc. The training rule on concealing the robes and alms bowls of other bhikṣuṇīs, etc., is the fifty-second. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, a householder invited the Buddha and the Sangha to his residence for a meal. The group of six and the group of seventeen followed behind at a leisurely pace until they reached a pond.
The group of six then said to the group of seventeen, "There is no need to hurry away;
let us enter the pond together and bathe slowly."
Having entered the pool, he said to the group of seventeen:
"Dive in together with you; who shall be the last to surface?

When the group of seventeen were last, the group of six emerged quickly, took their clothes, and hid them beneath a thicket of grass. [The full account] continues until the World-Honored One rebuked them, saying:
“Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:
‘If a bhikṣuṇī herself hides the robes, bowl, or other requisites of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, or causes another to hide them, it is a pāyattika.’”

Furthermore, after the Blessed One had established this training rule, there was a bhikṣu who entrusted his robe to another bhikṣu; that bhikṣu, however, hid only his own robe and did not hide the other's.
At that time, some bandits arrived and stole the robes of others; because of this, the bhikṣu who had been entrusted with them was deprived of his belongings. The Buddha said:
"Except in cases of such circumstantial necessity, there is no offense for one who stores [the items]."
The former was an original enactment; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated thus:

"If a bhikṣuṇī herself hides the robes, bowl, or other requisites of a bhikṣu, a bhikṣuṇī, a śikṣamāṇā, a śrāmaṇera, or a śrāmaṇerī, or causes another to hide them, except for other extenuating circumstances, it is a pāyattika."
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
The five groups of practitioners, beginning with the bhikṣus, are all persons within this Dharma.
There are seven kinds of robes, three types of waist-bands, and other miscellaneous items, all of which are as described above.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī herself hides the robes, bowl, or other requisites of another bhikṣuṇī, or instructs another person to hide them, she incurs a pāyattika offense in all such cases.
"Except for other circumstances" means that there is no offense in cases such as the eight difficult conditions (aṣṭāvakṣaṇa).
The fifty-third training rule concerning the accusation of a pure bhikṣuṇī with a saṃghāvaśeṣa offense. The setting was in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the Venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain, walking to and fro along the edge of the Śilāpuñja Pond.
Then, the Bhikṣuṇī Utpalā saw the Venerable One approaching from afar and paid him her respects.

Not long after that bhikṣuṇī had shaved her hair, as she was bowing her head in prostration and about to rise, she rose with the head-dress of Śrīgupta’s outer robe upon her head, which even reached the ground.
When the two bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they returned to their residence and said to the other bhikṣus:
"Venerable friends!
In whom do you wish for us to place our faith and confidence?"
"I myself saw the venerable Sthavira Śrīgupta touching the body of the bhikṣuṇī Utpalā.
He related the matter in detail until the Buddha ordered him to be interrogated, whereupon he replied:
"It was because I harbored a heart of malice, resentment, and anger that I spoke thus."
The Blessed One rebuked her and said:
"Perceiving ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī is pure and without offense, should defame her with a groundless *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, it is a *pāyattika*.'"
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Malicious" refers to harboring resentment and anger.
"A pure bhikṣuṇī" refers to one who is a member of this Dharma community.
"Without basis" means lacking the three bases:
matters seen, heard, or suspected.
The remainder is as explained above.

Regarding the characteristics of an offense herein: it refers to slandering a person known to be pure with groundless charges. There are ten matters that constitute an offense and five matters that do not constitute an offense; these matters are as explained above.
54. The Training Rule on Traveling with a Man on the Same Road. The fifth and final training rule on traveling with a man on the same road. The setting is the same as before.

At that time, there was a weaver in this city who was by nature coarse and difficult to live with. He treated his wife with such hardship that she never found any pleasure. Once, seeing a bhikṣu heading for Śrāvastī, he immediately accompanied him and traveled along with him on the road.
At that time, the weaver followed his tracks and pursued him in haste, seeing a bhikṣu traveling along the road with his wife.

Seeing them from afar, the weaver waited until they reached a village, where he called upon his acquaintances to beat the bhikṣu together; they nearly brought him to the point of death. [The full account] is related at length, until the World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts and declared:
"I shall establish a training rule for my disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī should travel along the same path with a man, without another woman present, even for the distance of a single village, it is a pāyattika."
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"A man" refers to one who is capable of engaging in sexual intercourse.
"There is no other woman" means that there are only two persons present.
"Road" refers to a remote and distant path.
Regarding the characteristics of the offense herein: if one accompanies a man along such a remote and distant path, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If there is one *krośa* between villages, and this continues up to seven, if [the distance] is not yet complete, one incurs an *duṣkṛta*; if it is complete, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If, at that place, another person sends a man to act as a guide, or if a man comes to provide directions because he is lost on the road, in all these cases there is no offense.
The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School, Scroll Fifteen.
The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Scroll Sixteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.
The Fifty-fifth Training Rule: On Traveling with Robbers. The fifty-fifth training rule on traveling with robbers; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

There was a bhikṣu who had completed his summer retreat in Rājagṛha. At that time, there was a merchant intending to travel toward Śrāvastī; this merchant was a smuggler, but the bhikṣu did not know it and accompanied him.
Traveling by a path frequented by thieves, they were subsequently apprehended and bound together and brought before him. [The account] is related in detail until the Blessed One said:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions; it should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī travels along the same road with a caravan of thieves, even for the distance of a single village, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meaning is as explained above.
"To associate with thieves" refers to those who destroy villages or steal customs duties.
"Traveling together on the same path" means traveling as companions through remote areas; if they do so for even the distance of one village, it constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
If one takes a thief as a protector or guide, there is no offense in traveling together with them.
Or, if one has lost one's way and the other comes to provide directions, there is likewise no offense even if they travel along the same path.
56. The Training Rule on Degrading Cultivated Ground. The fifth and sixth training rules concerning degrading cultivated ground share the same setting as before.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus dug the earth with their own hands or instructed others to do so. Lay travelers saw this and mocked them, until [the matter] was reported to the Buddha.
The Buddha assembled the bhikṣus and, through various skillful means, praised the observance of the precepts, fewness of desires, and contentment, while censuring excessive desire. He declared:
"Having considered ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī digs the earth with her own hands, or instructs another to dig it, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meanings are as explained above; the distinction between self and others is as before.
As for "ground," there are two types:
namely, ground that has been tilled and ground that has not been tilled.
What is "cultivated ground"?

It refers to ground that is naturally cultivated, or ground that has been excavated and has undergone heavy rains from the heavens during the three months [of the rainy season]; this is called cultivated ground.
If there have been no rains, it is only after six months have passed that it is designated as cultivated.
The explanation of the offense is as above.
Regarding the characteristics of the transgression herein, what are its specific details?
If a bhikṣuṇī digs into or damages cultivated earth, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If it is not native soil, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one lifts the surface of the ground, or if it is connected to the nature of the earth, it is an offense of expiation (pāyattika);
if it is not connected, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If a bhikṣuṇī drives in a wooden peg, it is a pāyattika;
if she pulls one out, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī draws lines on the ground without cause, she incurs a duṣkṛta offense.
If one merely counts them lightly, there is no offense.
If cow dung adheres to the ground and one disturbs it, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing);
if one merely takes up the cow dung, there is no offense.
If a riverbank collapses and damages cultivated ground, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it cracks and then collapses, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a nun stirs up the mud in a river or pond, she incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she lifts up a jar that is situated in the mud, she incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
If one drives a stake into a wall, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one lifts up cow dung attached to a wall, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one pushes against a wall that is connected to dampness, one incurs a *pāyattika*.
If there are cracks or fissures, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one paints on a wall, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing;
however, if one forms the mental perception of it being a numerical record, there is no offense.
If one damages or disturbs green plants growing on a wall, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If one digs into a stony ground where stone predominates and earth is scarce, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if earth predominates and stone is scarce, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If it consists entirely of stone, there is no offense.
If one digs into sandy ground where the sand is scarce and the soil is abundant, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if the sand is abundant, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
If it consists solely of sand, there is no offense.

If a bhikṣuṇī engaged in construction wishes to establish the foundation and, having obtained an auspicious constellation and a favorable moment, finds no *kappiyakāraka* (pure person) available, she may herself drive a stake into the ground to mark the boundary to a depth of four finger-widths; in this case, there is no offense.

57. The Training Rule on Soliciting Food for More Than Four Months. This fifty-seventh training rule concerning soliciting food for more than four months was established with the city of Kapilavastu as its setting.
At that time, the Śākya Mahānāma invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha to provide them with food and drink for three months, along with all necessary requisites, ensuring that nothing was lacking.

At that time, for three months, the group of six monks constantly consumed fine food in accordance with the physician’s instructions. When the three months had concluded, they still demanded choice delicacies from the kitchen staff. Mahānāman criticized and disapproved of this, noting that after having already accepted an invitation, they were improperly and insistently demanding more. He reported the matter to the Buddha, who said:
"Do not again persistently beg from donors, causing them to give rise to resentment and distress."
Having related the previous circumstances at length and having issued various reprimands, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī has been invited for four months, she may accept it when the time is right.'"
"If one receives more than this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
After this rule had been established, King Śreṇika Bimbisāra invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha for three months of offerings.
At that time, there was a donor who invited a bhikṣu again.
The Buddha said, "I now grant permission accordingly; if it is a separate invitation, one may accept it without offense.
Furthermore, there were guests who arrived and, not having been invited by the king, went out to beg for food, whereupon the king saw them.
He asked, "I have invited the community of monks; for what reason do you beg for alms?
He replied:
“I do not accept your invitation.
The king said,
“I now invite you once more for a meal.”
The Buddha said,
"If you invite me again, I shall accept.
When the king had invited him with such earnest and repeated entreaty, the Buddha finished his meal and went forth to beg for alms.
The King invited him again as before, and the Buddha said, "If he invites you constantly, you should also accept.
The World-Honored One praised the observance of precepts and few desires, and rebuked excessive desire, addressing the bhikṣus:
"Previously this was established as a new rule, and now it is further permitted; it should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī receives an invitation for four months, she may accept it when necessary.'"
If one accepts more than that, except at other times, it is a *pāyattika*.
"Other times" refers to a special invitation, a repeated invitation, a persistent invitation, or a regular invitation; these are the [permitted] times.
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Four months" refers to a period limited to four months.
"Requests acceptance" means to request permission for that matter.
"If it exceeds [the limit]," it means requesting beyond the established time frame.
"Except for other times" refers to the time of a special invitation, which is distinct from others.
"Repeated invitation" means inviting again and again.
"Entreated with earnestness" means to entreat again with renewed earnestness and the full exertion of one's heart.
"Constantly entreated" means to invite for a long duration.
"This is the proper time" refers to the time as it is permitted.
The explanation of the offense is as above.
Regarding the characteristics of the transgression herein, what are the specific circumstances?

If a nun is invited by another to eat coarse food, yet requests something fine and delicious, there is an *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) at the time of requesting; upon eating it, she incurs a *pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation).
If another person gives one fine food, yet one asks for coarse food, there is an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) at the time of asking, but no offense at the time of eating.
Likewise, if one is given milk and so forth, yet asks for curd and so forth, there is an *dukkaṭa* at the time of asking, but a *pāyattika* (offense involving forfeiture) at the time of eating.
If the patient has committed no offense,
and while she is begging for alms from house to house, the host sees her and comes out with food, the nun who feels desire should say to him:
"There is no need for further rice."
If he should reply with a counter-question: "Noble one,
what else do you require?"
The phrase "thus" constitutes a formal request; if one seeks out what is required according to necessity, there is no offense. 58.

The Training Rule on Prohibiting the Transmission of Teaching (Śikṣamāṇā-śikṣā-pratisedha-śikṣāpada). The fifty-eighth training rule concerning the prohibition of transmitting teachings was established in Rājagṛha.

It is the natural law of the World-Honored One that when a training rule (śikṣāpada) common to both divisions is being established, the Saṃghas of both divisions must assemble together; yet, although this training rule is shared by both divisions, the community of nuns did not assemble.
The Buddha addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
"You should say to Cūḍapanthaka:
'You must take these rules of training and go before the community of bhikṣuṇīs to proclaim them.'"
Having received the Buddha’s instruction, he went to the nunnery intending to proclaim the Buddha’s teaching.
On the way, he encountered the group of six monks and asked:
“What training rule is this?”
He then explained it for her:
"If a bhikṣuṇī has an invitation for four months, she should accept it when the need arises.
If she accepts it beyond that period, except during other [permitted] times, it is a pāyattika; this is what constitutes 'other times.'"
Having finished speaking thus, the group of six replied:
"You are foolish, lacking clarity, and incompetent; how could we possibly use your words?"
"If I were to see another who is well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, I would follow their words and undertake the training rules.
Having spoken thus in derision, she departed.
She then went to the place of the group of twelve nuns, and they likewise spoke improper words.

The rest of the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, having heard this, rejoiced and received it with devotion, practicing accordingly. This was explained in detail, until the World-Honored One questioned them regarding the facts, rebuked them, and declared:
"I perceive ten benefits in establishing this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī hears other bhikṣuṇīs speaking in such a manner:'"
"Venerable one!
You should train yourself in this precept.
He then says these words:
"I truly cannot accept and practice the training rules according to what you—who are foolish, lacking clarity, and unskilled in understanding—have said.
If I see others who are well-versed in the Tripiṭaka, I shall accept and practice them according to their words."
To say this constitutes a *pāyattika*.
If that bhikṣuṇī truly wishes to seek understanding, she should inquire about the Tripiṭaka; this is the proper time.
The remaining meaning is as explained above.
“Venerable one!
You should now train in such precepts” refers to the precepts that have been transmitted.
“I cannot employ your foolishness,” and so forth, means that thinking what should not be thought, speaking what should not be spoken, and doing what should not be done is called “foolishness.”
If one does not uphold the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras, it is called "delusion.
If one does not understand their meaning within the Tripiṭaka, it is called "lack of clarity.
If one is not skilled in making definitive determinations regarding the Tripiṭaka, it is called "lack of proficiency in understanding."
The remaining text is easy to understand; even the explanation of the offenses is as stated above.
What are the characteristics of the offense in this context?
If a bhikṣuṇī says to another bhikṣuṇī:
"You should practice and train in such precepts. He then replied,
"I cannot follow your words."
If one speaks of each of the four matters, such as being "foolish" and so forth, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense for every instance.
However, if the person before one is actually foolish and so forth, there is no offense in speaking of it.
59. The Training Rule on Listening in Silence to Quarrels. This fifth and ninth training rule concerning listening in silence to quarrels was occasioned in Śrāvastī.
At that time, among the group of seventeen monks, some members of the group of six had passed away, and Udāyin came to reside with the great assembly.

At that time, the group of seventeen remembered their previous mistreatment and deliberated together in the dining hall, intending to perform a *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (a formal act of censure) against Upānanda. He went to the window and listened by pressing his ear to it; he then entered the hall and subjected them to severe reproach.
Thus, whenever these seventeen groups were engaged in discussion in various places, they would all go there to eavesdrop and incite discord.
[The text] explains at length until the Blessed One rebuked them and declared:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be spoken thus:"

“If, moreover, a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that other bhikṣuṇīs have begun to deliberate on a matter, remain there seeking faults, causing turmoil, and engaging in contention, should go there in silence to listen to what they say with the thought:
‘Having listened, I shall cause them to fall into strife.’”
"If one acts on this basis, it is a *pāyattika*.
The remaining meaning is as above.
Regarding the phrase "a matter of deliberation," it refers to beginning a deliberation upon first seeing an unpleasant thing.
"Seeking faults" means searching for transgressions and shortcomings, and speaking of them to one another.
"Causing agitation" means failing to maintain forbearance in one's heart and bringing the matter to light.
"Contentious rivalry" means entering the gateway of strife through these disputes, forming factions for oneself, and mutually inciting one another.
To "dwell in contention while listening in silence" means to eavesdrop on their words and follow along with what they say.
To "cause strife and confusion" means to desire that disputes remain unresolved and do not cease.
The explanation of the offense is as above.

Regarding the characteristics of the violation herein: if a bhikṣuṇī is on an upper story engaged in discussion and another bhikṣuṇī ascends the story, she should tread upon the steps making a sound, or cough, or snap her fingers.
If one ascends the pavilion without performing such actions, merely hearing the words without understanding their meaning constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta);
if one understands the meaning of the words, one incurs an offense of falling (pāyattika).
The detailed explanation is as previously stated, up to the offenses of light and heavy gravity regarding gate-houses; these should be understood according to the specific circumstances.
Whether at a place for walking meditation or in a quiet grove, one should likewise recognize them by analogy with these matters.

If they deliberate together while traveling along a road, it should be understood that all rules of conduct for when a bhikṣuṇī arrives later are to be applied according to the regulations for ascending a multi-storied building; if she fails to do so, the gravity of the offense shall be as described above.
If there has been no prior enmity or grievance, and one happens to hear of it, or having heard it, desires to employ skillful means to cause the dispute to be extinguished, there is no offense.
The Sixtieth Rule: The Training Precept on Departing in Silence Without Having Granted Consent. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, Udāyin severed all fetters and delusions, as described in detail above.
Eventually, the group of seventeen monks consulted together; having assembled the community of bhikṣus, they went before the Elder and made this announcement:
"We now have something to interrogate him about... [and so on] ...until we wish to perform the *jñapti-karman* of suspension against Upānanda."
Having heard this, Nanda became terrified; he rose from his seat in silence and departed. [The full account] continues until the Blessed One rebuked him, saying:
"Considering ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal discussion according to the Dharma, should rise from her seat and depart in silence, it is a pāyattika.'"

After this rule had been established, the bhikṣuṇīs remained for long periods within the assembly, causing the attendants who cared for the sick and those who managed communal affairs to neglect their duties.
On account of this circumstance, the Buddha further permitted:
"If there is a valid reason, one should entrust [the bowl] and depart.
The World-Honored One praised the observance of the precepts, and so forth, as explained at length.
"The former was an original enactment; this is a subsequent allowance. It should be stated thus:

'If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal deliberation on a matter according to the Dharma, should rise from her seat and depart in silence without having entrusted another bhikṣuṇī [with her affairs], except for other extenuating circumstances, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"The assembly" refers to the disciples of the Buddha.

"Discourse in accordance with the Dharma" refers to formal procedures consisting of a single motion (*jñapti*), a motion followed by one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*), or a motion followed by three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"To depart from one's seat in silence" means to go beyond the limits of propriety.
"Without having made an announcement" refers to a nun who departs without informing those present.
The explanation of the offense is the same as before.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?

If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the Saṃgha is engaged in a formal discussion and deliberation on a matter in accordance with the Dharma, should rise from her seat and depart in silence without having informed another bhikṣuṇī, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing) for every step taken until she reaches a place where her voice can still be heard.
When one abandons this place, one incurs a root offense.
The seventh summary verse says:
Disrespect toward food and drink, entering a village and going to another house.
The ear-pieces for the head-covering, the bed-legs, and the cotton bedding. 61.
The Training Rule on Lack of Reverence. The sixthty-first training rule concerning lack of reverence was established with its causal context in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there were two bhikṣus who knew that the bhikṣus had gathered in the dining hall intending to settle a dispute; one followed the community's command, while the other disobeyed the instruction and did not go to the assembly.
She reported this matter to the Buddha. On account of this, the Buddha rebuked her as before and established a training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī is disrespectful, it is a pāyattika."
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding "lack of respect," there are two types:
first, the assembly; second, an individual. When one shows disrespect toward either of these two, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
Regarding this, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that the great assembly has gathered to deliberate on a matter, is summoned to attend the assembly but fails to come, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense.

If one calls for someone to stay and they do not stay, or sends them away and they do not go; if one sends for bedding and they refuse to take it, yet when not sent for it they forcibly take it; and if they act similarly regarding being sent to their quarters or other matters—in all such cases of defying the community's instructions, one incurs an offense of downfall (pāyattika).

If a bhikṣuṇī sees her two teachers—the preceptor (upādhyāya) and the instructor (ācārya)—and they speak thus: "Come here," yet she does not come, or otherwise acts in opposition to the instructions of these individuals regarding matters such as entering a room, in each case she incurs an offense of wrong-doing (duṣkṛta).
If one makes a formal announcement based on the correct reasoning, it is not a lack of respect; in such cases, there is no offense.
62. The Training Rule on Drinking Alcohol (Śikṣāpada on Drinking Alcohol), the sixty-second. The setting was in Śrāvastī.

There was an elder named Pūra who was immensely wealthy with abundant riches and ample food and clothing. Not long after he had married his wife, a daughter was born to them; she was of such upright countenance that all people loved and delighted in her.
When she reached adulthood, she was married to the son of the householder Anāthapiṇḍada as his wife, and later gave birth to a son.
Seeing him, her father rejoiced and exclaimed: "Welcome!"
"Welcome!
At that time, his kinsmen gave him a name accordingly, calling him Svāgata.
Due to the power of this child’s meager merit, all of the family's property gradually vanished, and both his parents passed away.
When the multitude of people saw him in such a state, they called him "Evil-Coming" (Acala). He became a companion to beggars, seeking his livelihood by begging.

[The account continues] at length until, through the cultivation of the meditation on the blue object (*nīlavarṇa-bhāvanā*), the mental image appeared before him. The World-Honored One further expounded for him the essentials of the Dharma, instructing, benefiting, and gladdening him; he then realized the vision of the Truths (*satyadarśana*). Having left the household life and renounced worldly affairs, he practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*), exerting great vigor and maintaining a firm mind. During the first and last watches of the night, he contemplated without weariness, severing the fetters and delusions to realize the fruit of Arhatship. He then spoke this verse:
"In the past, in the presence of various Buddhas, I merely maintained a body of clay or iron;
now, having heard the World-Honored One’s teaching, it has been transformed into a body of pure gold.
Within the cycle of birth and death, I shall no longer undergo further existence."
Upholding the untainted Dharma, one peacefully proceeds to the city of Nirvana.
If a person desires precious jewels, rebirth in heaven, or liberation, they should draw near to virtuous friends;
then all that is wished for will be fulfilled according to their intent.
At that time, those who lacked faith and respect gave rise to disparaging remarks:
"The śramaṇa Gautama ordains even the poor,
the lowly, and the foolish as renunciants, making them his servants!"
The World-Honored One, wishing to manifest the virtue of "Welcome" (svāgata), caused the poisonous dragon to be subdued, until the dragon accepted the Three Refuges along with the Five Precepts.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Among my disciples, the śrāvakas, he who has subdued the poisonous dragon is foremost in being 'Welcome'."
At that time, the people of the remote and nearby regions of Mount Samala, including brahmins and others, saw that the venomous dragon had been subdued and that the multitude was free from harm.

Then, a certain brahmin invited Svāgata and, with the utmost sincerity, provided him with excellent food and drink until he was fully satiated. Desiring to ensure that the food would be quickly digested, he placed a small amount of *gaja-mada* (elephant-liquor) into the drinking water.
Svāgata did not realize this; having drunk the gruel, he fell intoxicated upon the ground.

Since the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, possess mindfulness that is never lost at any time, they immediately manifested a grass hut at the place where Svāgata lay, covering his body so that no one could see him.

Then the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "You should observe what Svāgata has done: he subdued the poisonous dragon Āmrapālī on Mount Gaṅgāvarana; how could he now possibly tame a mere small crab?"
"O bhikṣus! For those who drink alcohol, there are such great failings as these.
He then took the hand of King Puṇyaviśeṣasaṃpanna, which was adorned with the marks of the thousand-spoked wheel and webbed fingers, and stroked the crown of Svāgata’s head, saying:
"Welcome! Why do you not observe yourself and realize that you have fallen into such distress?
At that time, Svāgata regained a small measure of clarity and followed behind the Buddha to the Jetavana Grove.
After the Buddha had washed his feet, he sat upon his usual seat and addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
"You should observe that those who drink alcohol possess such faults as these."
Having praised the observance of the precepts, he spoke at length until: "I, considering ten benefits, have established this training rule for the disciples of both divisions;
it should be recited as follows: 'If a bhikṣuṇī drinks any kind of intoxicating liquor, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meanings are as explained above.

Regarding "various liquors," this refers to rice-based fermented liquors, or those made by blending roots, stalks, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits; when these various liquors are consumed, they cause a person to become dazed and intoxicated.
"Drinking" refers to swallowing.
The explanation of the offense is as before.
In this context, what are the characteristics of the transgression and its specific instances?
If a nun drinks any kind of liquor that can cause intoxication, it is a *pāyattika*;
if she drinks that which does not intoxicate, she incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.
If a nun sees such liquors possessing the color, smell, and taste of alcohol, and they are capable of causing intoxication, it is a *pāyattika*.
If one does not become intoxicated, one incurs three *duṣkṛta* offenses.
When a *bhikṣuṇī* drinks various liquors that possess the color, smell, and power of intoxication of liquor, if it is capable of causing intoxication, it is a *pāyattika*;
if it is not capable of causing intoxication, she incurs two *duṣkṛta* offenses.

If a bhikṣuṇī drinks various types of liquor, even if it has only the color of liquor, if it is capable of causing intoxication, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense; if it is not capable of causing intoxication, she incurs one *dukkaṭa*.
If she eats wine dregs and becomes intoxicated, she incurs a *pāyattika*; if she does not become intoxicated, she incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
If a bhikṣuṇī consumes any roots, stalks, leaves, flowers, or fruits that can cause intoxication, she incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs:

"If you take me as your teacher, you must not drink any kind of liquor yourselves, nor give it to others; you must not even place a drop of liquor on the tip of a blade of grass and put it in your mouth. If you intentionally violate this, you shall incur a *vinayātikrama* (transgression of the discipline)."
If a bhikṣuṇī drinks vinegar that has the color of wine, there is no offense in drinking it.
If she drinks well-boiled wine, this likewise constitutes no offense.
"If it is a physician who causes one to swallow wine or applies it to the body, there is no offense.

63. The Training Rule on Entering a Village at an Improper Time Without Informing a Bhikṣuṇī. The sixth-third training rule: "Entering a village at an improper time without informing a bhikṣuṇī. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there was a brahmin from another region who came to this city to marry a wife and live together; before long, he gave birth to a daughter.
As she gradually grew up, she went with other young girls to the Jeta Grove and arrived before the gate of the monastery.
At that time, seeing the woman’s beautiful countenance and graceful form, Udāyin gave rise to a lustful mind; he immediately touched her body and kissed her mouth.
Then the young girl desired to engage in unrighteous conduct, but Udāyin would not consent to it.
The girl, harboring resentment and anger, proceeded to tear at her own body with her fingernails;
having returned home, she said to her father, "Udāyin has violated me."
The father immediately informed five hundred brahmins, who, harboring mutual anger and resentment, gathered in one place, intending to beat Udāyin.
At that time, the five hundred men went to his location and all together pulled and dragged him; yet they were unable to move him even so much as the breadth of a footstep.
The World-Honored One, having known this, thought to himself:
"This is the final instruction for Udāyin.

The Buddha diminished his strength so that he was rendered incapable of resistance; seeing his weakness, the brahmins beat him severely together until he was nearly dead, and dragged him to the king's gate.

At that time, while the king was sleeping during the day atop a high tower, the Buddha used his supernormal powers to startle him awake; he then preached extensively, until finally Queen Śrīmālā urged him to repent and reform.

Upon hearing this, he reproached himself and gave rise to a mind of heroic vigor; before long, all his delusions were severed and he realized the fruit of Arhatship. He extensively delivered sentient beings, and the World-Honored One declared him to be the foremost among those who teach and transform others.
Later, because he entered another's house at night, he was killed unjustly and cast away in a heap of refuse.
At that time, when the World-Honored One had arrived at his dwelling, he addressed the bhikṣus:
"This was due to traveling at an improper time, which brought about this great calamity."
The full explanation continues until: “Having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions;
it should be recited as follows: ‘If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village at an improper time, it is a pāyattika.’”
Once this rule had been established, the bhikṣuṇīs who were tending to the sick were unable to enter the village at improper times, and consequently failed to provide care;
those managing monastic affairs likewise neglected their duties.
She reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"If there is a bhikṣuṇī present, she should entrust you with her care before you go.
You should tell her: [as follows]."
"Venerable sir, please take note!
Due to the occasion of visiting a sick person, or for the sake of communal affairs, I must enter the village at an improper time.
I inform you, venerable sir, of this."
He replied, "Aupagika.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu who had previously deposited his robes and bowl inside a layperson's house; when the house suddenly caught fire at an improper time, he immediately went to retrieve them.
While on the way, he remembered that he had not been instructed, so he immediately turned back; his robes and bowl were completely consumed by fire. The Buddha said:
"This is excepted due to special circumstances.
What was previously established as a prohibition is now further permitted according to the situation. It should be stated thus:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters a village at an improper time without having informed another bhikṣuṇī, except when there is a valid reason, it is a pāyattika."
The remaining meanings are as stated above.
Regarding "the improper time," there are two limits:
namely, from after midday until the appearance of the dawn light has not yet occurred.
The meaning of "village" (*grāma*) is as explained above.
"Entering" means arriving at the village gate.
"Other bhikṣuṇīs" refers to those who are already present in that place, yet [the visitor] does not inform them.
Regarding the "exceptional circumstances": this refers to situations involving difficulties; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
What are the characteristics of the offense in this context?
If a bhikṣuṇī, during a non-time, perceives it as a non-time or has doubt about it, she incurs the root offense.
If, at that time, one perceives it as a non-proper time or has doubt regarding it, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* offense.
In the other two cases, there is no offense.
There are other past causal circumstances, which are the same as those explained for the bhikṣus.
64. The Training Rule Concerning Invitations Before and After a Meal. The training rule concerning invitations before and after a meal is the sixty-fourth. The setting is the same as before.
At that time, there was a householder in this city who was very wealthy, possessed of much property, and lived in abundance.
At that time, Udāyin happened to arrive at her house while begging for alms and preached the essentials of the Dharma to her:
"One who gives food obtains five merits, namely: long life, beauty, strength, happiness, and eloquence."
Having heard this, the householder took food and offered it as a gift; with a heart of profound joy, he prostrated at his feet, took refuge in the Triple Gem, and received the five precepts.
Later, on another day, when Udāyin came to the householder’s home again, the householder said to him:
"I have invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to take a meal at my residence; you may come early."
He then went to the house of the elder early in the morning and informed him, saying:
"I have some business and shall visit another household for a short while; if I have not returned, you need not serve the meal."
The Buddha led the great assembly to the house of the elder. At that time, the bhikṣus said to the elder, "You should announce the *pravāraṇā*.
The elder replied:
“Noble One! I have prepared these seats and mats for the great assembly.
The Buddha said:
"This concludes the proclamation of the *pravāraṇā*; you should now take your seats.

At that time, Udāyin arrived just as the meal was about to be served. Some of the bhikṣus ate a little, while others did not eat at all. After the Buddha had recited the verses on giving for the elder, he rose from his seat and departed.

Upānanda remained right there and did not go to the monastery. At that time, it was the fifteenth day, the day for the *poṣadha* ceremony of the Saṃgha; he did not come to the assembly, nor was there anyone to carry his proxy-vote (*chanda*). The assembly sat for a long time, which obstructed and neglected the Dharma-affairs. They searched for him but could not find him, causing the assembly to become weary. [The Buddha] spoke at length, even unto: "I, considering ten benefits, shall establish a training rule (*śikṣāpada*) for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having accepted an invitation to a meal at a layperson's house, should go to another house before or after the meal, it is a *pāyattika*.'"

After this rule had been established, there were those who attended to the sick and those who managed monastic affairs who encountered the same fault as before. When the Buddha heard of this, he said:
"The former was the initial prohibition; now I grant a further exception. It should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, having accepted an invitation to a meal, goes to another house before or after the meal without informing [her host], except for a specific reason, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Invited to a meal" means being summoned by another.
"Before the meal" refers to the period before noon; if, while traveling, one passes through two households, one incurs an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
"Having finished eating" refers to the time after midday; if one goes out and passes by more than three houses, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
"Without having made an announcement" means not informing another person; one should announce to the donor, saying:
"I am going to such-and-such a place."
Or if one instructs a bhikṣuṇī, saying,
"Go to such-and-such a place," the offense is established as described above.

Regarding the characteristics of an offense herein: if one has accepted an invitation to a layperson's home, and before the meal goes past two other households, or after the meal goes past three other households, without having made a formal announcement, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
If one does not invite [a nun] by making this particular bhikṣuṇī the primary figure, there is no offense. 65.
The Training Rule on Entering a Royal Palace. The sixth and fifteenth training rule concerning entering a royal palace; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, Udāyin, being unaware of the situation, heard the sound of the bells and clappers of the troops at night; he immediately woke up in alarm and thought to himself:
"Is it not the case that the King’s forces have some business and are departing elsewhere?"
Thinking it was already dawn when it was not yet so, he took up his robes and bowl and entered the royal palace.
Upon hearing this, Queen Śrīmālā went out to welcome him and respectfully received his teachings; she repeated this over and over again even before the break of day.
The palace attendants criticized him, saying:

"Although the King respects and has faith in him, his affection for him is unswerving; yet this bhikṣu, failing to recognize the proper timing, arrived in the middle of the night. Before the King had even put away his treasures and various precious objects, he arrived abruptly at the palace gate."
The Buddha spoke at length on this occasion, addressing the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs:

"There are ten kinds of faults in entering the royal palace. The full details are as set forth in the Mahābhikṣu-vinaya. Furthermore, having considered ten benefits, I establish this training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī enters the threshold of the palace gate before the dawn has appeared and while the Kṣatriya consecrated king has not yet put away his treasures or precious objects, it is a pāyattika."
After this rule had been established, on another occasion, the King invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
The World-Honored One did not go himself, but sent Śāriputra to travel together with the assembly.
Having arrived at the royal gate, he did not dare to enter abruptly; the king ordered him to proceed.
Śāriputra thought to himself:
"The World-Honored One has established a precept forbidding one from entering the palace gates abruptly."
"Now that I have received Your Majesty’s command, I cannot again refuse to comply.
For this reason, the Buddha may perhaps grant permission.
Having said this, he entered the palace.
They returned to the place where the Buddha was and recounted the aforementioned matters.
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"Excellent!"
I have not yet granted you permission; you should know that the time has come.
You must understand that what was previously established as a primary prohibition is now further relaxed by this supplementary allowance. For the sake of my disciples, it should be said thus:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, before the appearance of the dawn light and while the consecrated Kṣatriya king has not yet hidden his treasures or precious objects, should enter past the threshold of the palace gate, except for other extenuating circumstances, it is a pāyattika offense."
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Before the appearance of the dawn" means that the sky has not yet brightened; there are three types of such appearances.
The king, the jewels, and so forth are all as described elsewhere.
Regarding the threshold of a palace gate, there are three distinctions:
namely, the city gate, the royal gate, and the palace gate.
"To cross over" means to lift one's foot and step beyond it.
"Except for other circumstances" means except when one has attained superior dharmas, such as Śāriputra and others.
The explanation of the offense is as above.

Regarding the characteristics of the violation herein: if a nun, while unaware or suspecting that she is unaware [of the time], passes through the city gate, she incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing) offense.
If one has the perception or doubt that it is not yet dawn, one incurs an *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
The same applies to the royal gate.
If one passes through the palace gate with the perception or doubt [that it is not yet dawn], one incurs the primary offense (*pārājika*).
The next two cases constitute offenses of wrong-doing;
the final two phrases involve no offense.
Furthermore, there is no offense if one is summoned by the queen, the crown prince, or a high minister.
66. The Training Rule on Pretending Not to Know. The sixth and final training rule on pretending not to know. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
The Buddha said:
"Every half-month, the Prātimokṣa precepts should be recited."
They spoke accordingly as instructed.
When the group of six monks heard the precepts, they said:
"Only now do we know that this rule is recited within the Sūtra of the Precepts."
The bhikṣus asked,
"Venerable sirs, have you not heard what has been happening lately?
They replied:
“Is it permissible for us to do nothing but listen to this and have no other matters?
Thus the Blessed One rebuked them and established a training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
“If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Prātimokṣa Sūtra is being recited every half-month, should speak thus:”
"Venerable one!
It is only now that I have learned that this rule is taught in the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
If the bhikṣuṇīs know that this bhikṣuṇī has performed the poṣadha ceremony with them two or three times, let alone more than that, they should say to her:
"Venerable one!
You cannot escape this offense by claiming ignorance; you must confess and repent for the transgression you have committed according to the Dharma.
Thus should he be exhorted.
"Venerable one!

This Dharma is rare and difficult to encounter. When you were reciting the precepts, you listened to the teaching without respect, without mental stability, without earnestness, without focused attention, without single-mindedness, without lending an ear, and without applying mindfulness."
...is a *pāyattika*. The remaining meaning is as explained above.

"When reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra" refers to reciting the essential rules in their proper sequence, from the eight *pārājikas* down to the seven methods for settling disputes (*saptādhikaraṇa-śamathāḥ*).

Regarding the phrase "I have only now come to know," it means that although the group of six monks had repeatedly listened to the precepts together with other bhikṣus, they intentionally said, "I do not know," intending to cause others to feel distress and regret, thereby creating a disturbance among the assembly.
Regarding the phrase "the bhikṣus should exhort them," this clarifies that there is a deficiency when one fails to show respect and so forth.

As for the characteristics of an offense herein: if a bhikṣuṇī sees [a bhikṣu] reciting the eight *pārājika* rules, and continues in this manner up to the twenty-one *saṃghāvaśeṣa* rules and the seven methods for settling disputes (*adhikaraṇa-śamatha*), and speaks in such a manner, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense for each instance she speaks.
If one truly does not understand [the offense] and is like a foolish person, there is no offense in speaking the truth.
67. The Training Rule on Making Needle Cases. The setting for this sixty-seventh training rule is the same as before.

There was an artisan named Dharma who was skilled in working with ivory and bone. Previously, he had conceived a sense of reverence and faith toward the non-Buddhist teachings; however, having come to the monastery to listen to the essential points of the Dharma, he abandoned those false doctrines and took up affinity with the True Vehicle.
He thought to himself: "Since my family is poor, it is difficult for me to cultivate meritorious deeds. I ought to exert myself and employ my own labor to benefit others."
He said to the bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs:
"I am skilled in working with ivory and bone; if you require needle cases, I shall gladly fashion them for you."
At that time, the artisan fell into such poverty that his clothes could not cover his body and his food did not suffice for his mouth.
Seeing him, the non-Buddhists asked, "In former times your household was prosperous; now, because you have followed the tonsure, you have fallen into destitution."
"Judging by this, who is the superior friend?
Having explained this at length, the Blessed One rebuked him and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be spoken thus:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī should make a needle case from bone, ivory, or horn, it shall be broken; this is a pāyattika.
The remaining meaning is as above.
Their bones, teeth, and horns may be understood according to the facts.
There are two kinds of needle cases:
first, a case (tong), and second, a tube (guan).
If one uses bone, ivory, or horn to make them, both types are prohibited.
Whether for oneself or for others, one should not make them under any circumstances.
If they have already been made, they must be smashed to pieces, and the offense must be confessed and expiated.
The person being addressed should be asked:
"Have you broken your needle case?
If one does not ask this, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

If one regrets [the action] only after having asked, the nun should use a bamboo tube or a piece of felt and the like to hold the needle; she may check it from time to time to ensure no grime forms. In these cases, there is no offense.
68. The Training Rule on Making Oversized Beds. The sixth and eighty-eighth training rule concerning making oversize beds. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu traveling through the human world who arrived at the Jeta Grove when evening fell and the gates were closed.
He sat down beneath the porch of the gatehouse, washed his feet on a low-legged stool, withdrew his body into meditative concentration, and entered *samādhi*.

A snake, fond of coolness, was staying before the bed; seeing the bhikṣu with his head hanging down, it bit him on the forehead, whereupon he passed away and was reborn in the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
The full account was related to the Buddha, who said:
"One should not lie down to sleep on a small, low bed, nor should one wash one's feet at the foot of the bed. Whoever violates this incurs an offense of transgression against the Dharma."

When the group of six monks heard this prohibition, they subsequently made high beds with legs seven cubits long, which they ascended and descended by means of ladders; worldly travelers criticized and disparaged them.
The World-Honored One rebuked them and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be spoken thus:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a bed or a stool, the legs should be no higher than eight finger-breadths of the Buddha's measure.
If she makes them exceeding that height, they must be cut down; it is a pāyattika."
After this rule had been established, at that time Udāyin was tall and large in stature; when sitting on that bed, his chin rested against his knees. The Buddha said:
"This is further permitted as an exception, except for the entry into the wooden frame; if it exceeds [the limit], it should be cut off, and it is a *pāyattika* offense."
The remaining meaning is as explained above.
Regarding the making of large or small beds, this refers to making them oneself or having others do so.

As for the requirement that these large beds and small seats be eight finger-breadths high according to the Buddha’s measure: "the Buddha" refers to the Great Teacher; these eight finger-breadths are equal in length to one cubit (*hasta*) of a person of medium height.
"Except for the entry into the mortise of the bed-legs": this refers to the portion of the bed-leg that enters the mortise; this is not counted as part of the measurement.
If it exceeds [the prescribed length], meaning if the measurement is exceeded, it should be cut off.
An offense involving downfall (pāyattika) should be confessed.
Regarding the characteristics of this transgression: whether it was made for the sake of the Saṃgha or for oneself, if it exceeds the measure of eight finger-breadths, it should be cut off.
The confession of that offense shall be explained.
When confessing the offense, one should be asked:
"Have you cut off the legs of the bed?"
If one does not ask [for permission], one incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense; this offense should not be confessed.
If one makes [the bed] according to the prescribed measure, there is no offense.
The sixty-ninth training rule concerning the use of cotton from grasses or trees to stuff a bed. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, Upānanda received a large bed and lay down upon it after stuffing it with cotton wool as a mattress.

When an elder came who was entitled to a bedding place, Upānanda removed the stuffed mattress and spread out the loose cotton wool for him to rest upon; consequently, both his body and his robes were entirely white.
Having reported this matter to the Buddha, the Buddha said:
"Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī should store cotton or similar materials upon a monastic bed or seat, she must remove them; [otherwise, it is] a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
Regarding "storing materials," there are five types:
first, *śamālī*; second, reed mats; third, *aṅka*; fourth, *tūla* (cotton or reed fibers); and fifth, wool.
If a bhikṣuṇī stores these five kinds of items herself or instructs others to store them, she incurs a pāyattika offense.
Regarding the offenses herein: if a bhikṣuṇī, whether for the sake of the Saṃgha or for herself, scatters materials such as cotton down upon a bed or seat, she incurs a pāyattika offense.
The stuffing should be removed, and the offense should be confessed; the rest is the same as before. 70.

The Training Rule on Making a *niṣīdana* (Sitting Mat) of Excessive Size. The seventy-first training rule on making a *niṣīdana* of excessive size. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
As the Blessed One said:
“If one uses bedding or other articles belonging to the Saṃgha, or even personal items, one should use a *pratyaṃśuka* (undergarment) as a substitute.

Not knowing its proper measure, they made it too large; when it was small, they would discard it, or find it too long or short. [The Buddha] spoke at length until the Blessed One established this training rule for the disciples of both divisions, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a niṣīdana, she should make it according to the proper measure.
Herein, the measure is: two spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and one and a half spans in width."
"If one exceeds this measure, it is a *pāyattika* offense.

After this rule had been established, the nun Khujjuttarā was tall in stature; whenever she went to sleep, she would use various tree leaves as a mattress beneath her feet to protect her bedding. Thereupon the Buddha said:
"I grant you further permission for this: increase the length by one additional span (*hasta*)."
"If one makes it exceeding [the prescribed measure], it should be cut down;
this is a *pāyattika* offense.
The remaining meaning is as above. "Naiṣadana" refers to a sitting mat.
Whether one acts for oneself or causes another to act, the offense is incurred in all cases equally.
Regarding the measurement, it may be understood from the text.
One *hasta* of the Buddha is equivalent to three *hastas* of an ordinary person; thus, the total length is nine *hastas*, which amounts to four and a half *cubits*.
"A width of one and a half handspans" refers to four handspans plus six finger-widths for a person of medium stature.
If one constructs it exceeding this measurement, the excess material must be cut away and the offense must be confessed; all other questions and answers are as explained above.
The eighth summary verse says:
Covering sores, the Buddha’s robe measurements, garlic, shaving, washing hands, and slapping;
cooking for oneself, sprinkling water, raw grass, and discarding [waste] outside the wall.
71. The Training Rule on Making a Scarf for Covering Sores. The seventh training rule concerning the making of a scarf for covering sores. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
As the Blessed One has said:
"One shall make a scarf for covering sores."
The bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs did not know how they should proceed;
the measurements were sometimes too large and sometimes too small.
Thereupon, the Blessed One established this rule of training, which should be recited as follows:
Furthermore, if a bhikṣuṇī makes a wound-covering robe, it must be made according to the proper measurements.
The measurement therein is four spans of the Buddha’s hand in length and two spans in width.
"If one makes it exceeding [the prescribed measure], it should be cut down; this constitutes a *pāyattika* offense.
The remaining meaning is as explained above.
"A wound-covering cloth" refers to a cloth for covering sores or scabs on the body.
That Buddha’s span of the hand and its variations, as well as the explanation of the offenses and so forth, are as extensively described above.
72. The Training Rule on Making Robes the Size of the Buddha’s Robe. The setting for this seventy-second rule is the same as before.
At that time, Upānanda made a robe equal in size to the Buddha’s; he wore it with only one side draped over his body, while the rest was gathered upon his shoulder.
On account of this incident, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Observing ten benefits, I shall establish a training rule for the disciples of both divisions. It should be stated as follows:”
"If a bhikṣuṇī should make a robe equal in measure to the Buddha’s robe, or exceeding it, it is a pāyattika.
Herein, the measure of the Buddha’s robe is ten spans of the Buddha’s hands in length and six spans in width; this is the measure of the Buddha’s robe."
The remaining meanings are as explained above.
"Buddha-cīvara" refers to the robe of the Great Teacher.
Its length is ten *hasta* of the Buddha, which corresponds to thirty *hasta* of an ordinary person, or fifteen *cubit* (*aratni*).
Regarding the sixth point concerning the width: it should be eighteen handspans, which is nine cubits, or even more than this; in all such cases, one commits a *pāyattika* offense.
The details regarding the width are as explained above.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, Fascicle Sixteen.
The Vinaya of the Bhikṣuṇīs of the Mūlasarvāstivāda School,
Volume Seventeen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Command.
73. The Training Rule on Eating Garlic. The training rule on eating garlic, the seventy-third: The Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was an elder whose livelihood was the cultivation of garlic; in his garden, many excellent vegetables grew.
At that time, there was a famine in the world and it was difficult to obtain alms through begging. Whenever the householder saw the bhikṣuṇīs returning with empty bowls after their rounds for food,
he said to them,
"Noble ladies!..."
"In my garden, I have planted many garlic plants, but other vegetables have grown as well; you may take them as you please.
The bhikṣuṇīs went to that garden frequently and took much of the fine vegetables.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulmavilāsinī also went there to take vegetables and took some garlic as well. When the other bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they said to her:
“Venerable one, are you taking garlic?
The nun replied, “The vegetable is the garlic; the garlic is the vegetable.”
