Upon seeing this, the householder was filled with indignation; he beat her severely, seized the vegetables and garlic, and drove her out of the garden, reviling her in various ways:
"How can a bhikṣuṇī eat garlic?"
The nuns reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha. On account of this, the Buddha assembled the community of bhikṣuṇīs.

The Buddha, who is the knower and the seer, asks what he knows and does not ask what he does not know; he asks at the proper time and does not ask at an improper time; he asks when there is benefit and does not ask when there is no benefit. To breach the embankment of concealment and to eliminate doubt, he questioned the nun Tullānandā:
"Is it true that you committed such an unseemly act and ate garlic?"
He replied, "It is indeed so,
Venerable Sir!"
The World-Honored One then rebuked her in various ways:
"This is not the dharma of a śramaṇī, nor is it the dharma of pure conduct, nor is it a matter of dignified decorum.
He then addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
“Having considered ten benefits—as explained at length elsewhere—I establish this training rule for my disciples, the bhikṣuṇīs, within the Vinaya;
it should be recited as follows: ‘If a bhikṣuṇī should eat garlic, it is a pāyattika.’”
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
“Eating garlic” means swallowing it as food.

*Pāyattika* (offense requiring expiation) carries the meaning of being scorched and boiled and falling away; that is to say, one who commits this offense falls into the evil realms of hell, the animal kingdom, or the realm of hungry ghosts, where they undergo the suffering of being scorched and boiled.
Furthermore, if one commits this offense and does not earnestly confess and eliminate it, it will obstruct all wholesome dharmas; for these reasons, it is called a *pāyattika*.
In this regard, what are the characteristics of the offense and how does it occur?
If a bhikṣuṇī eats garlic, she incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
“I only wish that the Venerable One would explain the past causes and conditions for how the nun Tullānandā, out of greed, was beaten by another and driven out of the park.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“It was not only in the present that the nun Tullānandā encountered such misfortune due to her greed; in the past as well, she met with calamity and suffering that led her to the brink of death.”
"Listen attentively! I shall explain it for you.

Long ago, there was a thief who bored a hole through a wall and entered a royal palace. He stole much gold, silver, and various exquisite treasures, wrapped them up, and carried them out. However, he had forgotten a ladle by the side of the hole; when he returned to retrieve it, he was captured by the guards. He was brought before the king, who ordered the judicial officer to cut off his hands and feet."
At that time, a deva spoke a verse, saying:
"One should not harbor excessive greed; Greed is a sinful and evil matter.
If one indulges in excessive greed, Whatever one has acquired will all be lost."
"Just as he who sought the lost ladle subsequently encountered manifold sufferings and hardships.
"Bhikṣus, what do you think?
Who else could the thief of that time have been?"
The nun Tullā is she.
Because of her greedy mind, she obtained suffering without profit; now it is the same for her once again.
Furthermore, monks, because this nun harbored greed, she frequently encountered misfortune and suffered the loss of what she had acquired.
Listen attentively!
I shall now speak further.

In the distant past, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a goldsmith who, not long after marrying a wife, gave birth to a daughter whose appearance was upright and whose complexion was so transcendent that she was exceedingly lovely.
When the girl had grown up, her father passed away, and she was reborn in the realm of geese as a goose king.
The girl endured extreme poverty and great hardship; the father, now the goose king, recalled his previous life and pondered how he might provide for the girl's sustenance.
Seeing that he was impoverished and suffering various afflictions, he flew to a treasure island out of love for his wife; at dawn, he took a precious jewel in his beak and placed it beneath her door.
The woman gathered the precious jewels and hid them away securely.
In this manner, the king of geese delivered them every morning, yet the woman continued to store them away without ever spending any.
Thus, the woman came to possess many precious jewels, and she thought to herself:
"Who gave me these jewels? he thought.
Thereupon, during the final watch of the night, he waited by the side gate. He then saw the goose arrive and had this thought:
"The body of this goose is entirely a treasury of jewels; it comes to the gate every time and discards one before departing. By what means might I capture it and take all the precious jewels?"
In order to capture the goose, he secretly set a net; when the Goose King saw the net, he thought to himself:
"This wicked creature, ungrateful for my kindness, wishes to harm me."
He then immediately flew away and did not return again.
A deity spoke this verse:
"One should not harbor excessive greed; greed is a sinful and evil matter."
"If one becomes excessively greedy, whatever one acquires will be lost;
now that you have seized the goose, the precious jewel has been severed.
"What do you think, monks?"
Was that woman of former times anyone else?
She was none other than the bhikṣuṇī Tullānanda.
Because of her greedy mind, she lost all her precious possessions; now, because of her greedy mind, she has been beaten by another, driven out of the garden, and her hopes have been severed.
For this reason, bhikṣuṇīs should not be excessively greedy. 74.
The Training Rule on Shaving the Hair of the Private Parts. The setting for the seventy-fourth training rule on shaving the hair of the private parts is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā shaved the hair from under her arms in a public place.
When the other nuns saw it, they asked, "Who shaved the hair from under their arms and discarded it here?"
The nun Thullanandā replied, "It was I.
The nuns asked again:
"For what reason?
He replied, "The hair in my armpits was troubling me; therefore, I shaved it off."
The nuns said,
"Venerable sister!
Is this a pure matter?"
She replied,
"Whether it be clean or unclean, I have already finished shaving it.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the nun Cūḍāpanthaka:
"Did you truly shave the hair from your armpits?
She replied:
"It is truly so, Venerable Sir!

Having rebuked her in various ways, the Blessed One spoke at length, up to: "For the sake of my disciples, the bhikṣuṇīs, I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada) in the Vinaya; it should be spoken thus:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, shaves the hair of the private parts, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover," refers to the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"Secret parts" refers to those that are not exposed.
"Shaving the hair" means removing the hair; the offense of falling (pācittiya) is as previously described.
Furthermore, what are the characteristics of the transgression and its specific details?
If any bhikṣuṇīs shave the hair of the private parts, they all incur a pāyattika offense.
The seventy-fifth training rule: On the matter of washing not exceeding the prescribed measure. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā’s lustful mind was intensely inflamed; while washing herself, she immediately inserted her finger into her birth canal, imagining it to be for the sake of pleasure.
While doing so, she subsequently developed an ulcerous swelling and suffered great pain and distress.
She said to her disciples, "You should seek other fragrant substances, such as sandalwood or grass incense, for I have an ailment."
The disciples asked,
"Venerable One!
What ailment do you have now?"
She then recounted the matter in full, and the nuns said, "Noble lady!
Is it proper to perform such an act? Should it not accord with the pure Dharma?"
She replied,
"I have already finished what is pure and what is impure.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her:
"All these faults arise from washing; therefore, one should not allow a bhikṣuṇī to wash.

After the World-Honored One had established this rule, at another time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūrṇa-nandā was preaching the Dharma to the wife of a householder. Her body emitted a foul odor that others could not endure, so they asked her:
"From where does this odor come?
He then asked the nun:
"Is it possible that the World-Honored One has prohibited nuns from washing so that they retain such foul odors?"
The nun said, "It is so.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"For this reason, I now further establish a training rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī, when performing cleansing, shall do so [only] up to the length of two finger-joints.'"
If one exceeds this, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Nun" refers to the nun Khemā, or any other nun.
"It should be limited to two finger-joints" means that it must not exceed that measure.
If it exceeds two finger-joints, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense in all cases.
The remainder is as previously explained. 76.
The Training Rule on Striking the Private Parts with the Hand. The training rule on striking the private parts with the hand, the seventy-sixth: the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the nun Thullanandā’s lustful mind was intensely inflamed; she struck her private parts with her hand, and while doing so, a swelling and ulcer formed, causing her great suffering. The questions and answers were the same as before.
...up to:
"Noble One, what ailment do you have now?
He then explained the matter in detail.
The nuns asked,
"Is it proper to perform such an act in accordance with the pure Dharma?
They replied:
"I have already completed the purification and the non-purification.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, as described in detail above, up until: "I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī again slaps her private parts with her hand, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to the nun Tullā or any other nun.
The meaning of "private parts" is as explained above.
Regarding "striking," it refers to striking with the hand; the offense of downfall (*pāyattika*) is as previously stated.
If a nun strikes her private parts with her hand, she incurs an offense of downfall in all such cases.
77. The Training Rule on Cooking Raw Food with One’s Own Hands. The setting for this seventy-seventh training rule is the same as before.
At that time, there was a man who was fond of gardens and groves;
he instructed his cook, saying, "I wish to go out for an excursion; come early in the morning and prepare food and drink."

He then provided the payment for the provisions and sent those who prepare the food; they all came to his residence, and he instructed them that everything must be fully prepared. Having given these orders, he departed for the Fragrant Garden (*Gandhavana*).
At that time, the family members prepared what was required and waited for the cooks, but as the time passed and they did not see them arrive, they remained there in anxiety.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulmavilāsinī entered his house while going for alms and said:
"O noble sir! May you be free from illness."
"You may give me some food.
His wife replied,
"Noble One!"
"I am now filled with sorrow; how can I provide food?
The nun said, "O virtuous one!"
"What is the matter that you worry about?
She then explained it in detail, and the nun said,
"Sister!..."
"Do you know only how to handle needles and thread,
and nothing else? He replied,
"Noble one, do you know how to prepare food?"
The nun said,
"What craft is there that I do not understand?
The woman replied:
"Noble one! If that is so, out of compassion, please grant me the means to prepare food and drink.
The nun said:
"If I prepare food, shall I give it to you? He replied, "I will."
"And what about the one who guards the room?
He replied, "I shall give it to him as well."
The nun asked,
"What kind of food shall we prepare?
He replied:
"She should prepare various kinds of ghee-based fruit platters and assorted cakes.
Whatever was required, the nun prepared it all for them.
Once the preparations were complete, she took the food and returned to the monastery.
When the food-preparer arrived later, the family members informed him, saying,
"The meal has already been carefully cooked by the Therī Tittiriyā.
Upon hearing this, the food-preparer spoke various words of derision and uttered harsh speech:
“How is it that a female ascetic of the Śākya clan deprives others of their livelihood, being neither a true female ascetic nor one of pure conduct?
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, as explained in detail above, up until: "I shall establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī herself cooks raw food with her own hands, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to the nun Thullanandā or any other nun.
“Raw food” means cooking it with one’s own hands until it is cooked.
The offense of downfall (pācittiya) is as previously described.

There is no offense if it is for the sake of the bhikṣu-saṃgha or other fellow practitioners of the holy life; if one wishes to cook food in a private room where no outsiders can see, there is no offense.
78. The Training Rule on Sprinkling Water Upon Others. The setting for this seventy-eighth training rule is the same as before.
At that time, there was an elder who, despite having been married for a long time, had no children.
Having lost all his kinsmen and exhausted his wealth, impoverished, solitary, and aged, with no one to whom he could appeal, he rested his cheek upon his hand and thought to himself:
"I am now advanced in years; what use have I for wealth?"
"You should go forth into the homeless life and aspire for the supreme state.
He said to his wife,
"O virtuous lady!"
"I wish to leave the household life; what will you do?
His wife replied, "I too shall leave the household life."
He then took his wife to the place of Mahāprajāpatī and said to her:
"Noble Lady! This is my wife;
she wishes to seek ordination, and thus has come to consult you."
Then Mahāprajāpatī ordained her as a nun.
Her husband also went to a teacher to seek ordination, and he thought to himself:
“I previously made an agreement with her that we would inquire after one another from time to time; I should go and see her now.”
Having formed this thought, he went at once to the place where the bhikṣuṇī was. Seeing him from afar, the bhikṣuṇī came out to meet him herself and prepared a seat for him.
The bhikṣu sat down, and the bhikṣuṇī stood to one side and preached the sublime Dharma to him. Having heard it, he wished to depart.
Women by nature tend to accumulate possessions; whatever they have acquired, they store away in their rooms.
The nun then said, "Please stay a short while and accept a small meal from me."
As she served various foods and drinks to the bhikṣu, she stood before him fanning him with a cool breeze and holding a water flask; the bhikṣu then smiled.
The nun immediately asked, "What did you see that made you smile?"
The bhikṣu replied, “She served me while she was a householder, and now she does so again; it is for this reason that I smile.
The bhikṣuṇī then became indignant and said in retort:
"I shall serve as a field of merit and provide for you with a devout heart, yet you instead laugh at me.
He then scooped up water in his cupped hands and sprinkled it over the bhikṣu, and further struck him with the water jar.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, as extensively described above, up until: "The training rule should be formulated and spoken thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī sprinkles water upon those who are superior [in rank], it is a pāyattika.'"
Regarding the term "senior assembly," it refers to those who have gone forth first and thus occupy the superior position.
"Sprinkling with water" means taking water and sprinkling it upon the body.
The offense of falling [into a transgression] is the same as previously stated.
If one sees [a person] fainting and sprinkles [water on them], there is no offense. 79.

The Training Rule on Voiding Excrement or Urine upon Living Grass. The seventh and ninety-first training rule concerning voiding excrement or urine upon living grass. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

In front of the nunnery, there was a patch of grassy ground where various brahmins and young sons of householders would come to engage in improper conversation and mutual mockery, creating a great clamor that disturbed and vexed the nuns.
When Tullānandā saw this, she gave purgatives to all her disciples and caught the impurities in a large vessel.
Seeing that it was filled to the brim, she immediately went before the monastery and scattered it upon the wild grass.
Those brahmin sons of elders all came as before and, together with him, played and rolled about on the ground, saying to one another:
"There is a most foul odor; there is much impurity here."
"Who has done this? Why has he not been destroyed!
Seeing them from afar, Tulludhananda laughed loudly; the people asked: [Why do you laugh?]
"Noble One, why do you laugh?
Is it because this green grass has been defiled?
He replied:
"Who else but me? You wicked people deserve to be dealt with exactly as you are.

When those men heard this, they were all displeased; each returned to his own home and related the matter in detail to their parents, kinsmen, brothers, and sisters, and all of them mocked and censured him.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them as extensively as described above, up until: "I shall establish a training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī voids excrement or urine, or spits or sneezes upon living grass, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhananda or any other nun.
“Upon living grass” means upon green, living ground.
“Defecating or urinating” refers to various impurities.
The offense of downfall is the same as before.
There is no offense except in the case of a cause related to illness. 80.
The Training Rule on Discarding Impurities Outside a Wall. The setting for this eighty-first training rule is the same as before.

At that time, the Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, whether for the sake of managing communal affairs, providing instruction, or teaching recitation, remained awake through much of the night; consequently, her food and drink were not digested, she suffered from abdominal distress, and she discarded all her impurities outside the wall.
King Prasenajit had a minister named Śrī who had ridden the king’s elephant without permission. Enraged, the king drove him out;
as he walked near the monastery wall, the refuse discarded by the nun Thullanandā fell upon the minister’s head, defiling him.
When the bhikṣuṇīs learned of this matter, they deliberated among themselves, saying:
"This great minister now possesses immense power; we shall surely meet with calamity and misfortune."
Filled with resentment and shame, the minister went to the river to bathe.
At that time, the minister Mṛgāra, for the sake of his auspiciousness, addressed the King, saying:
"That minister is loyal and diligent, having rendered great service to the state; I only pray that Your Majesty will forgive him for the transgression of riding the elephant."
The king approved of his proposal and dispatched an envoy to pursue him.
The envoy went and announced:
"The Great King remembers you and has sent me to summon you back."
The minister, anxious and fearful as to the king’s unpredictable intentions, immediately put on wet clothes and hurried to the king’s presence.
Upon seeing him, the king was pleased and restored him to his official rank, returning the White Lotus Elephant for him to ride.
Śrīpramoda further thought to himself:
"From where have I regained this official honor?
It is because I abandoned impurities that had defiled my body through that holy life (brahmacarya) that I have obtained this karmic fruit."
Having departed from the royal palace and gone to the nuns' residence, she said to the nuns:
"Venerable ladies!
Which nun today cast this impurity upon my head?"
When the nun Tullānandā saw him questioning her, she was greatly alarmed and terrified; she closed the door and spoke from behind the crack of the panel:
"There was an old nun who did not know good from bad and did not realize she was throwing this; it has soiled you, O Noble One, but please do not be angry."
The minister said, "I truly have no ill will toward him; I came to inquire because I wished to offer him clothing. It is because of this stain that I have received such high office and honor."
Upon hearing these words, the nun stepped out through the door and, beating her breast with her hand, replied:
"It was my own coarse mind that committed this transgression.
Seeing the nun depart, the minister took off his robes and offered them to her himself.
The minister again smiled and spoke these words:
"It is by the power of the Noble One’s impurity that I attained this exalted position and received the king’s favor.
Later, on another occasion, the nun Tārā engaged in a quarrel with a group of nuns and reviled them, saying:
"I now observe you and find you not even equal to my excrement.
The nun informed the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, and after explaining at length, he established the rule of training, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, without careful inspection, should discard impure matter outside a wall, it is a pāyattika.
"If a bhikṣuṇī" refers to the Bhikṣuṇī Toulani, or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"To discard outside" means to discard it beyond the wall.
"Not observing" means not looking closely.
"Impure" refers to human excrement, which is impure.
The offense of downfall is as previously described.
If one wraps the object in cloth and discards it outside, there is no offense.
The ninth summary verse says:
There are five kinds of being alone; there are four ways by way of whispering.
If one harbors a mind of malice, pushing against the chest, none of these are permissible.

81. The Training Rule on Standing in a Secluded Place Alone with a Man. The eighth training rule concerning standing in a secluded place alone with a man. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā was standing alone with a man in a secluded place.
When the brahmins, householders, and the general public witnessed this, they became suspicious and discussed it among themselves, saying:
"This is not the conduct of one who has left the home life in tranquility; she stands alone with a man in a secluded place."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them as extensively described above, up until: "I shall establish a training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī stands alone with a man in a secluded place, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to the nun Thullanandā or any other nun.
“Alone with a man” means with a layman or a male householder.
“Standing in a concealed place” refers to five kinds of concealments: [the five types of physical screens].
First, fences; second, walls;
third, curtains.
Fourth, deep forests;
fifth, dark places.
"Standing" refers to remaining standing; [if one acts] up to this point, one incurs an offense of downfall.

82. The Training Rule on Standing Alone with a Bhikṣu in a Secluded Place. The eighth-twelfth training rule concerning standing alone with a bhikṣu in a secluded place; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Guptā was standing in a secluded place with Udāyin.
When the brahmin householders and other men saw this, they felt revulsion and discussed it among themselves, saying:
"This nun is not one who has left the home life in tranquility; she is standing in a secluded place with a bhikṣu, and they must surely be making an appointment."
Those who lacked faith engaged in various forms of derision and slander.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them at length, as described above, up until: "I shall establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī should again stand in a secluded place alone with a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to the bhikṣuṇī Guptā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"Monk" refers to the monk Udāyin.
"Standing in a secluded place" refers to the five types of seclusion as explained above.
Even down to merely standing [in such a place], one incurs an offense of downfall (pārājika).

83. The Training Rule on Standing Alone with a Man in an Exposed Place. The eighth and third training rule concerning standing alone with a man in an exposed place; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā was standing alone with a man in an open space.
When the brahmins, householders, and others saw this, they were filled with disdain and said to one another in discussion:
"This nun is not one who has left the home life in tranquility; she has gone so far as to meet with a man alone in an open space."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them as extensively described above, until the Blessed One established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands alone with a man in an open place, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, regarding 'a bhikṣuṇī,' this refers to the nun Tāpanā or any other nun.
Regarding 'alone with a man,' this refers to a layman."
"Standing in an open place" means standing in an exposed area where there are no obstructions.
Even if one merely stands [with a bhikṣu], one incurs an offense of transgression.
The Eighty-fourth Training Rule: Standing Alone with a Bhikṣu in an Open Place. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gopā was standing alone with the bhikṣu Udāyin in an open space.
When the brahmin householders saw them, they discussed the matter as before, even going so far as to arrange a meeting between them.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them at length as described above, until the World-Honored One established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī stands in an open place together with a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Guptā or any other nun.
“Bhikṣu” refers to Udāyin or any other bhikṣu.
“Standing in an exposed place” has the same meaning as explained above; in all such cases, one incurs a *pārājika* offense.
There is no offense if the bhikṣu has a companion or if the bhikṣuṇī has an attendant. 85.
The Training Rule on Staying Alone in a Single Room. The eighth and final training rule on staying alone in a single room; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

When the bhikṣuṇī Maṇicūḍanandā, wearing exquisite robes and moving with dignified and composed deportment, was walking for alms, a man selling incense saw her appearance and conduct; his mind became filled with lustful attachment, and with a blazing desire, he felt no shame as he stepped forward slowly and spoke in a low voice:
"Noble Lady!..."
"You may engage in private sexual pleasure with me.
The nun said, "I am one who has left the household life; how could I engage in such base matters with you?"
His resentment flared up again, and he said:
"You worthless man! Why did your father not kill you?
Now you utter such coarse words in my presence."
"Why do you not play and frolic together with elephants, tigers, lions, venomous snakes,
and other such malevolent creatures? The man replied, "Noble One!"
"What is so strange?
All men speak in this way.
The nun thought to herself:
"This is no virtuous person who has already vexed me; I shall vex him in turn.
Let us make an appointment. Having formed this thought, he said:
"O noble sir!"
"My room is located at such-and-such a place; you should know the time for yourself and come there to play together.
When evening had fallen, all the bhikṣuṇīs paid homage to the caitya, and at that moment, the man entered the room.
The nun was chanting together with others; as the night grew late, she entered her room and sat upon her bed, whereupon the man came and took her hand.
The nun then cried out in a loud voice,
"A thief has entered my room!
The man, in a state of panic, quickly fled from the room and spoke these words:
"This nun is a habitual liar; having made an appointment with me, she has come here and cried out that there is a thief.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her as extensively described above, up until the World-Honored One established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī stays alone in a single room, it is a pāyattika."
"If again a bhikṣuṇī" refers to the bhikṣuṇī Gulmavati Nandā, or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"Dwelling alone in a single room" means staying overnight without a second bhikṣuṇī; the offense incurred is the same as before.
Even down to one who has stayed overnight, all incur an offense of downfall (*pāyattika*).
There is no offense if the second companion nun dies, or is expelled, or renounces the path on her own accord.
86. The Training Rule on Whispering with a Man. The eighth and sixty-sixth training rule concerning whispering with a man. The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulmavilāsinī entered the city of Śrāvastī during the morning meal; while maintaining proper deportment as she went for alms, she whispered with various laypeople.
When the brahmins, householders, and those who were faithless and disrespectful saw this, they became indignant and deliberated among themselves, saying:

"Look at this bhikṣuṇī; she is not one who has left the home life in tranquility. Having abandoned her own wholesome qualities, she converses in whispers with these men; she must surely be making an appointment."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them as extensively described above, until the World-Honored One established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī whispers in the ear with a man, it is a pāyattika."
"If again a bhikṣuṇī" refers to the nun Tullā or any other nun.

"Whispering in the ear with a man" means whispering in the ear with a male person and mutually engaging in such communication; even down to merely speaking [in this manner], all incur a *pārājika* offense.

87. The Training Rule on Receiving Whispered Words from a Man. The eighth and final training rule concerning receiving whispered words from a man. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the nun Thullanandā entered the city to beg for alms with the same dignified demeanor as previously described, yet she received whispered words from a man. When those who lacked faith and respect saw this, they reviled her, as described at length above, even to the point of making appointments with others.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them as extensively described above, until the World-Honored One established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again receives whispered words from a man, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to the nun Thullanandā or any other nun.
“Receiving whispered words from a man” means to take a man’s speech into one’s ear; the offense of downfall is the same as before.
In all such cases, the recipient incurs an offense of transgression. 88.
The Training Rule on Whispering with a Bhikṣu. The eighth and eighty-eighth training rule concerning whispering with a bhikṣu; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Guptā, like the nun Tārā, was begging for alms within the city when she began whispering with a bhikṣu.
Those who lacked faith saw this and reviled her, saying:
"Look at this nun; she is not one who has left the household life in tranquility, but is instead making a secret appointment for illicit affairs."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them as extensively described above, until the Blessed One established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī whispers in the ear of a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to the nun Guptā or any other nun.
“Whispering with a bhikṣu” has the same meaning as explained above; in all such cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The eighty-ninth training rule concerning receiving whispers from a bhikṣu. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Gopā went on her alms round as before and accepted whispered instructions from a bhikṣu.
Those who lacked faith, having seen this, criticized and disparaged her. [The full account] is related at length until the establishment of the training rule, which should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī accepts whispered instructions from a bhikṣu, it is a pāyattika offense."
“Nun” refers to Guptā or any other nun.
“Receiving whispered instructions from a bhikṣu” has the same meaning as explained above; in all such cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The Ninetieth Rule: Beating One’s Chest. The setting for this rule is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs quarreled with one another, speaking of each other's faults; filled with resentment, they beat their breasts and cried out in pain.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, out of anger, beats her own breast so as to produce physical pain, it is a pāyattika."
"Furthermore, 'a bhikṣuṇī' refers to a nun within this Dharma.
'Because of anger, she strikes her own breast' means that upon hearing something contrary to her wishes, she cannot tolerate it and strikes her breast with her hand, causing extreme pain."
As before, up to: those who perform these acts all incur a *pāyattika* offense.
The tenth summary verse says:
"Oaths, not examining the matter, sitting on a bed, and using resin."
In the four types of lay households, one should not lie down together with someone who has not been attended to during their illness.
91. The Training Rule on Oaths. The ninety-first training rule on oaths; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs would all go to the homes of householders and brahmins—whether for the purpose of begging for alms, inquiring after the sick, or preaching the Dharma—and upon arriving at their houses, the laypeople would see them coming and offer respectful salutations, saying with devout reverence:

"It is most difficult to encounter the Noble Ones. We are fortunate to have the merit to see you coming and going within our homes; we pray that out of compassion you will come here often so that we may behold you."
At that time, when these nuns saw others praising them and addressing them as "Noble Lady," each harbored conceit and became greatly arrogant.
The lay travelers spoke again, saying:
"We fear that once the Noble Ladies have departed they will not return; if they must come, let them do so under a solemn oath."
The bhikṣuṇīs said, "If she goes and does not return,
our cultivation of the pure precepts will be without fruit or benefit.
Having thus made a solemn oath regarding their own holy life (*brahmacarya*), the assembly collectively censured them with disdain.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī makes a vow or an oath by means of her own holy life (brahmacarya), it is a pāyattika."
The nuns and so forth are as described above.
"By one's own holy life" means not practicing the acts of censure.
Regarding "oaths," this refers to uttering words of cursation oneself; the meaning is as explained above, and in all such cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The offense regarding skillful means is as usual. 92.

The Training Rule on Not Interrogating Others Without Observation. The ninety-second training rule on not interrogating others without observation; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
The bhikṣuṇīs lived in harmony, and the faithful householders and brahmins all showed them reverence and respect, providing offerings of robes, food, bedding, and the cost of medicine, saying:
"Noble ladies!..."
"Accept this payment for medicine; if you have any illness, use it as you wish to provide for your own body.
When the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs saw this occurrence, they felt jealousy and thought to themselves:
"For what reason do we not receive the respect, offerings, clothing, food, bedding, and payments for medicine from laypeople to provide for our meals?"
Having had this thought, they consulted with one another, saying:
"Let us devise a plan so that the elder brahmin will develop even greater pure faith toward us, and will honor, revere, and respectfully offer gifts to us."
Having deliberated thus, they took what was not seen, heard, or suspected to be seen, heard, or suspected, and interrogated the bhikṣuṇīs:
"Such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī has this fault; such-and-such a bhikṣuṇī has committed such an offense; she is not permitted to remain in the assembly during the time of the Poṣadha and the Pravāraṇā."
He interrogated the bhikṣuṇī with groundless charges and remained in a state of reproach.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her regarding the reproach and, after explaining it at length, established the training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, interrogates another without having properly examined the matter, it is a pāyattika.
The term "bhikṣuṇī" and so forth are as explained previously.
"Without properly examining" means not having scrutinized [the facts].

Regarding "interrogating others": this refers to forcefully interrogating and reproaching another with groundless matters. The meaning is as explained above; in all such cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense. 93.

The Training Rule on Sitting or Lying Down Without Examining the Bed or Seat. The ninety-third training rule concerning sitting or lying down without examining the bed or seat. The setting and circumstances are the same as before. At that time, after the bhikṣuṇīs had completed their summer retreat, the Buddha permitted them:
"Once the bhikṣuṇīs have finished their retreat, they may travel through the human world."
Traveling by stages, he arrived at a village.
As evening was approaching, he requested a place to stay from an elder.
The elder replied:
"The noble ones may reside within the reception hall.

Having received this permission, they did not check whether anyone had already arrived at the location; being exhausted from the journey and suffering from the heat and exhaustion, they were unable to remain inside and went outside to sleep.

During that night, wind and rain suddenly arose and the four quarters became dark; everyone was struck with great terror and entered the inner hall, where they could not see one another. A layperson who had previously been staying in the hall also rose, and he took hold of the bhikṣuṇī’s hand.
The nun cried out in fear, "Who is this reckless person seizing my hand?
King Prasenajit honors the nuns as he does his own queens; how could he tolerate a fool acting with such force?"
They even went so far as to report this to the authorities, who investigated the matter and cut off that man's hand.
Once the bhikṣuṇīs had arrived in Śrāvastī, they reported these circumstances to the nuns.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, speaking at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī sits or lies down in a secluded, dark place without first inspecting the seat, it is a pāyattika."
The nuns and so forth are as previously described.
"In a secluded place" means where there is a covering or obstruction.
"Without observing" means without careful examination.
"Regarding sitting or lying down": this refers to spending the night; the remaining meanings are as explained above, and in all such cases, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense.
The ninety-fourth training rule: Regarding the use of tree resin to make a male organ. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika went to the house of a householder while on her almsround and said to his wife,
"May you be free from illness and long-lived.
Knowing that her husband was not at home, she asked:
“O virtuous lady!
Since her husband is no longer here, how will she survive?
The woman felt ashamed and remained silent, offering no reply; the nun then lowered her head and departed, going to the royal palace where she told Queen Śrīmālā: [text continues]
"May you be free from illness and long-lived.
Having thus offered mutual greetings, he spoke privately to the consort, saying:
"The King has gone on a distant journey; how do you find comfort?"
The consort said:
“Noble One! Since you have already left the household life, why discuss worldly matters?”
The nun said, "Noble and powerful as you are, and being young with no consort, it is truly difficult for you to pass the days; I am deeply concerned.
The consort said:
"Noble Lady!
If the King is not present, I shall take tree resin and have that skilled craftsman fashion a phallus for me to satisfy my desires.
Upon hearing these words, she went to the wife of the craftsman and said:
"Please make for me a life-member [vagina] out of resin, similar to the one you made for Lady Śrīmālā.
The artisan’s wife replied,
"Noble One!..."
"What use does one who has left the household life have for such things?
The nun replied,
"I have something that I require."
The wife said, "If that is so, I shall have it made.
She then informed her husband that he should have a life-prosthesis made. The husband said:
"Is it that I am insufficient that you seek this further?
His wife said, "I have an acquaintance who has come to rely on me; it is not for my own need."
The carpenter gave it to his wife, and she in turn handed it over to the nun.

At that time, after Tullānandā had finished her meal, she entered her inner chamber; she then took a tree resin dildo, fastened it to her heel, inserted it into herself, and experienced sensual pleasure, falling asleep as a result.

At that time, a fire suddenly broke out within the nunnery, and a great clamor arose. The nuns were startled awake and, forgetting to remove their birth-giving organs (*janapada*), emerged from their rooms.
When the crowd saw them, they broke into loud derision. Then some children saw them and cried out:
"O Noble Ones!"
"What is that on your foot?
Upon hearing these words, the nun felt extreme shame.
She informed the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī fashions a male organ out of tree resin, it is a pāyattika."
The case for a *bhikṣuṇī* is the same as before.

Regarding "making a phallus out of resin," this refers to using various tree resins or even other materials to fashion the shape of a male organ; the remaining meaning is as explained above. If one uses it, one incurs a *pāyattika* offense;
if one makes it but does not use it, one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.
Regarding all the offenses involving skillful means therein, they should be understood according to the specific circumstances.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!..."
"I only pray that you will explain why this Tullā-nī caused the assembly to laugh.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This Tullā-nī has not only caused the great assembly to laugh at this time; it was likewise so in the past."
Listen attentively!
I shall now speak for you.

In the distant past, there was a brahmin in a certain village who, shortly after marrying, fathered a son endowed with eighteen kinds of evil physical characteristics. When the boy had grown up, he traveled to other regions to study and seek mastery of the arts.
In a certain village there was a great brāhmaṇa who was exceptionally proficient in the four Vedas.
His wife gave birth to a daughter, and the father thought to himself:
"If there is a brāhmaṇa who is well-versed in the treatises of the four Vedas, I shall give this daughter to him as a wife."

That brahmin youth gradually traveled until he arrived at this village, where he went to the great brahmin to study the four Vedas until he was thoroughly proficient in them. The brahmin thought to himself:
"I previously made a vow that if a son of pure conduct masters the four treatises, I shall give my daughter to him as a wife."
"Now this youth is of pure conduct and lineage, and moreover is versed in the four Vedas;
he is a suitable husband for her.
They were then married. After some time had passed, the Brahmin again thought to himself:
"Since this son-in-law of mine is ugly in appearance, many people would mock him if he were at home.
Furthermore, seeing that her daughter had behaved with a lack of chastity and propriety, she said to the son-in-law:
"You may now take your wife back to your own residence."
He then thought to himself:
"My wife’s nature and conduct are not chaste or pure; she constantly engages in jesting and laughter with others even in my presence. Now I should take her back to her parents' home."
Having had this thought, he immediately said to his wife:
"O fair-faced one!
You should prepare yourself; tomorrow morning we shall go together to visit the fragrant garden."
The wife said, "So be it.
When morning dawned the next day, he ordered his wife to mount a donkey so they might return to their own home; the wife then said:
"Where are you now taking me?
her husband replied,
"I am now taking you to my parents' home."
The wife then thought to herself:
"Calamity has come upon me; while I am here in a state of autonomy where I can act as I please, I may now engage with another man according to my own will."
If you now take me to that house, I will be guarded by my parents and various kinsmen; how then could I wander about at will?
She then struggled with her husband, wailing and weeping bitterly:
"I will never go!
Her husband became greatly enraged and bound her crosswise with a rope; he made her lie face up on a donkey and drove it forward.

Driven by lustful desire, the husband committed an act contrary to the Dharma; in order to wash himself clean, he took a jar and poured water over himself. As the water flowed out, it made a sound, which the donkey heard and fled in alarm. The husband pursued it but could not catch it; the donkey entered the village where everyone saw it together and was filled with shame. "Why is this so? he asked.
The husband then gave a full account of the matter; upon hearing the sound of the water in the jar, the donkey suddenly bolted in terror.
Those who heard this burst into laughter and spoke this verse:
“When the water from a jar was poured out with a sound, the donkey heard it and fled in terror;
because of this meager merit, this woman is so hideous she makes people laugh.”
“O bhikṣus, do not harbor any other thoughts. Was the wife of that ugly brahmin in the past someone else?
She was none other than the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇadattā here now.”
"O Bhikṣus! In the past, the nun Tullā also caused a great deal of clamor and laughter among the multitude.
Listen further!"
I shall now speak again.
Long ago, in a certain village, there was a brahmin who had recently married; later, at another time, he wished to travel elsewhere.
His wife, who had previously been unchaste and lacking in propriety, heard that her husband intended to leave and told outsiders:
"My husband wishes to travel to another village; you may come and stay the night with him."
That man followed her words and arrived at their home that night. The husband returned and called to his wife to open the door, asking, "Who is there?
Recognizing their husband's voice, both were struck with terror; they then placed the outsider inside a cow-dung basket before finally opening the door for him.
Now, after he had entered the house, his wife brought water to wash his feet for him.

Suddenly, the house caught fire; the husband hurriedly moved his wealth and goods out, but the wife said to her husband, "All these excellent treasures are inside this granary; you ought to bring them out first."
He then attempted to carry it away together with the cart, but the grain basket shattered violently. The man outside fled, striking his head against a pillar; wounded and bleeding, he departed.
At that time, a crowd of people spoke this verse:
"This woman previously committed an illicit act;
having placed a person inside a grain basket, she was carried out by fire, where her head was shattered and known by all."
“Monks, what do you think?
Was the Brahmin’s wife of that time someone else?
She was none other than the bhikṣuṇī Pūrṇa-nanda.”

95. The Training Rule on Not Entrusting One’s Bedding and Seating When Preaching the Dharma in the Homes of Laypeople. The ninety-fifth training rule concerning not entrusting one’s bedding and seating when preaching the Dharma in the homes of laypeople; the setting of the缘 (nidāna) is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā frequently went to the homes of householders and brahmins to preach the Dharma for them.
When a householder’s wife saw the nun arrive, her reverence increased all the more; she prepared an exquisite seat, and the nun then expounded for her the profound meanings within the sūtras.
While listening to the Dharma, his mind was preoccupied with household affairs and he grew impatient that the time was too long, thinking to himself:
"I have secular duties; I cannot remain here for much longer."
She then rose and departed.
After the nun had finished reciting the sūtra, she did not see the listener; she left her seat in silence and went away, whereupon a thief later came and stole the sitting mat.
When the woman saw the nun, she asked her for the seat-cloth, to which the nun replied,
"At that time, as we did not meet, I left the seat and returned. The nun informed the bhikṣu,
and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while preaching the Dharma in the home of a layperson, departs without entrusting the master of the house to take care of the bedding and seats, it is a pāyattika."
The nuns and so forth are as described above.
"One who expounds the Dharma" refers to one who explains the meaning of the sūtras.
"Requisites for bedding" refers to items spread out for sitting and lying down.
"Leaving without having informed [the owner]" means not notifying the owner.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth is as extensively described previously. 96.
The Training Rule on Sitting Down Without Permission. The ninety-sixth training rule concerning sitting down without permission; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā was wandering for alms.

There was a brahmin who delighted in the dharma of purity; as the nun entered his house for alms, she found within his reception hall a pure bed and seat covered with a white woolen cloth (*śveta-karpāsa*).
There was another woman who held a fly-whisk to brush away flies so as not to cause any damage or defilement.
The woman asked the nun,
"Noble Lady!..."
"What brings you here?
The nun replied, "I have come for alms; you may bring them."
The woman said,
"Noble one! If I take food, I fear the flies will defile your seat."
The nun said, "I removed the flies so that there would be no filth.
The woman then entered her house; the nun’s feet were impure, and she sat upon the bed, leaving bloodstains upon it.
A brahmin saw him and asked, "Venerable one!
Your feet are covered in dust; why do you sit upon this clean bed without washing them?"
The nun said,
"Since you have already taken a seat, why should I, a practitioner of the holy life (*brahmacārinī*), not be allowed one?
She then rose from her seat.
At that time, a brahmin saw the seat stained with blood and criticized her in various ways, saying,
"I observe that this nun has no sense of shame or modesty.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while in the home of a layperson, sits down abruptly upon a bed or seat without the host's permission, it is a pāyattika."
The nuns and so forth are as described above.
If it is a bed or seat in the home of a layperson, one should not sit upon it without first being permitted by the other.
Regarding the explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth, it is explained in detail as previously stated.
97. The Training Rule on Staying Overnight Without Asking the Host. The setting for this ninety-seventh rule is the same as before.
At that time, several bhikṣuṇīs were traveling through the countryside and arrived at a village seeking a place to stay overnight.
While the weaver was away, his wife took liberties with him, sleeping in the same room as a nun.
When the weaver returned at night and lay down with his wife with the intent to engage in unrighteous conduct, he grasped her by the hand, whereupon she let out a cry.
Upon hearing this, the nun smiled. Her husband asked his wife, "Who was that who smiled?
She replied:
"This is one who has gone forth.
Thereupon, the husband became enraged and drove the nun out.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī stays overnight in the house of a layperson without having asked the host's permission, it is a pāyattika."
The term "nuns" and so forth is as explained above.
"Without asking the owner" means not consulting or requesting permission from the master of the house.
"Staying overnight" means lying down or sitting within that place.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is set forth in detail as previously described.
Regarding those who are exempt from the offense: this excludes women who, being without a husband, act as the mistress of their own household.

98. The Training Rule on Knowing that a Bhikṣuṇī Was Already Present in a Layperson’s House and Then Causing Her to Leave. The ninety-eighth rule; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣuṇīs were traveling through the countryside and arrived at a village seeking a place to stay; consequently, an elder granted them permission to remain there.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā followed after them, also seeking lodging.
The villagers said to her, "There are other nuns staying at that house; Noble Lady, you should also go there to seek lodging."
The nun then went forward and informed the other nuns, saying:
"May I be permitted to stay the night?
The nuns replied:
"This place is narrow and cannot accommodate you," said the nun Thullanandā. She replied,
"It will suffice as it is."
When the nuns heard this, they knelt down to make way for her.
Then the nun Pātayantī pushed and shoved the resident nuns with her hands and feet, whereupon the nuns said to her,
"Venerable One!..."
"Why do you press me so?
He replied,
"If you cannot remain here, then go wherever you please."
The nuns deliberated, saying, "This nun Tullā is robust and possesses great strength; if she continues to oppress us, our lives will be in peril.
Thereupon, the nuns rose up and departed all at once.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another bhikṣuṇī is already present in the home of a layperson, subsequently causes her to leave, it is a pāyattika."
The term "nuns" and so forth is as explained above.
"Those who were previously in the house of a layperson" refers to those who arrived first at a secular home.
"Causing them to leave" means that those who arrive later cause the former occupants to depart.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed before. 99.
The training rule regarding failing to attend to a sick disciple. The ninety-ninth training rule concerning failing to attend to a sick disciple. The setting for the occasion is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā was ill, and her personal disciples as well as those she relied upon attended to her.
Once her illness had been cured, at a later time, the disciples suffered from having no one to care for them; filth lay scattered about, and they did not clear it away.
The bhikṣuṇīs asked one another,
"Who is the sick one?
They replied:
"She is a disciple of the nun Thullanandā.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her; the full account is as previously detailed, up to: "He shall establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, seeing that her own disciple or her resident disciple is ill, does not attend to them, it is a pāyattika."
The nuns and so forth are as described above.
A "close disciple" refers to one who has been granted full ordination (*upasampadā*).
An "attendant disciple" refers to one who dwells in dependence [upon her].
"Sick" refers to the disharmony of the four great elements.
"Not attending to them" means failing to provide care and nourishment with a compassionate heart.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense, it is described in detail as previously stated.
100. The Training Rule on Two Nuns Lying on the Same Bed. The training rule on two nuns lying on the same bed, number one hundred. The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the two bhikṣuṇīs, Pāpā and Uttara, lay together on one bed, like a man and a woman engaging in amorous play.
Later, one nun became pregnant; when the months were complete, she gave birth to a mass of flesh from which no sense organs, hands, or feet had yet emerged.
Upon hearing this, the other nuns expelled her from the monastery.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"She need not be expelled for now; you should examine her thoroughly."
"Place this mass of flesh in the sun; if it dissolves, then there is no pregnancy, but if it does not perish, there will truly be a fetus.
Following the Buddha's instruction, the nun placed it in the sun, and it was completely digested.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after a detailed exposition, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī lies down on the same bed with another bhikṣuṇī, it is a pāyattika."

Thus, after the Blessed One had established this training rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, there were many bhikṣuṇīs who, traveling at twilight, sought lodging for the night from a certain householder; the householder consented and gave them a large bed.
A certain nun lived alone, and another nun requested her room.
The householder replied, "My household is large and there is no extra space; since the Venerable One’s quarters are cramped, why do you not share a bed?"
The nun said,
"The World-Honored One does not permit nuns to sleep on the same bed.
Because of this matter, the nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"If one obtains a large bed that is difficult to lift or move, a bhikṣuṇī may stay in the same place; she should sleep with a cloth partition between them, maintaining mindfulness, and must not touch one another. If small beds are used with a partition installed, it is likewise permissible to sleep together."
The eleventh summary verse says:
Two rainy-season retreats, two fears, the temple, not having reached the required age,
keeping a retinue, two types of married women, and the Sangha not granting the unlimited [permission].
101. The Training Rule on Wandering Before the *Varṣā* is Over. The training rule on wandering before the *varṣā* is over, number one hundred and one. The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Gulmavilāsinī was observing the summer retreat in Śrāvastī; before the *pravāraṇā* ceremony had even taken place, she traveled through the countryside.
Various non-Buddhists, brahmins, elders, and householders all criticized and disparaged her, saying:
"Now we see that this nun does not delight in the life of renunciation; at this time, when insects cover the ground everywhere, she wanders through the villages, causing endless destruction."
Even small birds like these remain hidden in their nests during the summer rains;
yet this śramaṇī lacks compassion and harms sentient beings—whom else would one have the heart to respect, honor, and provide for?
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, while the summer retreat has not yet concluded its *pravāraṇā*, travels through the countryside, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
The term "nuns" and so forth is as explained above.
"Summer retreat" refers to the three-month retreats at the beginning and end of the summer.
"Not having performed the *pravāraṇā*" means not having carried out the ritual of invitation and confession.
A human wanderer is one who travels according to the dictates of the mind.
The explanation of the characteristics of offenses is as extensively detailed before.
Regarding those who are exempt from offense: if any one of the eight difficulties occurs, there is no offense in wandering.
102. The Training Rule on Not Traveling After the Completion of the Rain Retreat. The setting for this one hundred and second rule is the same as before.
At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs had finished the summer retreat and wished to travel among the people, they said to the bhikṣuṇī Gulatrandā:
"You may travel among the people."
The nun Thullanandā said,
"Why should I now wander among the people?
The nuns said:
“The Buddha has ordered you to leave; for what reason do you disobey?
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, speaking at length until he established the training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the summer retreat, does not depart from her former location to travel among the people, it is a pāyattika.
The term "bhikṣuṇī" and so forth are as explained above.
"Completion of the summer retreat" means the conclusion of the *varṣā*.
"Not departing from one's former location" means not wandering among the people.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth, they are explained in detail as previously stated.
103. The Training Rule on Traveling While Aware of Danger. This is the one hundred and third training rule. It was set in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having become a great enemy of Vaiśālī, intended to launch a military expedition against it; he beat the drums and issued a proclamation to the people, saying:
"Whoever goes from within my territory to Vaiśālī shall have their head cut off."
He ordered that all major thoroughfares be guarded so that those caught could be dealt with according to the law.
At that time, a large number of bhikṣuṇīs were traveling from Rājagṛha toward Vaiśālī when they encountered bandits on the road; they were all terrified and cried out in a loud voice.
The guards, hearing the sound, arrived immediately; seeing the king’s army, the thieves scattered and fled in all directions.
They asked the nuns, "O Noble Ones, have you not heard the king’s command that anyone going toward Vaiśālī shall have their head cut off?"
"Furthermore, we have stationed guards within our territory; if I am not present, could it be that the Noble One is captured by bandits?
The nun informed the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is a place within a kingdom where there is fear of bandits, should travel there, it is a pāyattika."
The term "nun" and so forth are as explained above.
"Knowing there is a place of fear from bandits within the kingdom" refers to a situation where two kingdoms are at enmity.
"Wandering" means traveling to another country.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed before. 104.

The training rule concerning traveling when aware of the presence of tigers, wolves, or lions. Regarding the training rule on traveling when aware of the presence of tigers, wolves, or lions, the fourteenth case has the same setting as before.

There were groups of bhikṣuṇīs traveling along remote paths who frequently encountered the perils of tigers, wolves, and lions; lay travelers criticized and disparaged them. [The Buddha] gave a detailed discourse, up to the point of establishing this training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that there is danger from tigers, wolves, or lions at a certain place, should travel there, it is a pāyattika."
The term "nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*) and so forth are as explained above.
"Knowing that it exists" means knowing that tigers or wolves are present.
The remaining meanings may be understood accordingly.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is also as stated above. 105.
The Training Rule on Going to a Shrine for Debate. This one hundred and fifth training rule concerning going to a shrine for debate was established while [the Buddha] was staying in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā was traveling among the temples of the gods and the dwellings of the non-Buddhists, engaging them in debate.
As evening drew near, she arrived at the nunnery and said to her disciples:
"I am now exhausted and my limbs ache all over; relieve my fatigue by massaging and rubbing my hands and feet."
The disciples asked,
"Venerable One, why are you so exhausted?"
He replied,
"I went to the celestial shrines and the dwellings of the various non-Buddhist practitioners to debate with them.
He was asked again:
“Noble One! Is it appropriate to go to the temples of the gods or to the dwellings of the non-Buddhists?
He replied:
"I have already gone back and forth regarding whether it is appropriate or not.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and reproached her, and after speaking at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again engages in debate within a temple of the gods, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" and so forth are as explained above.
"Within a temple of the gods" refers to a dwelling place of celestial deities or non-Buddhist practitioners.
Regarding "engaging in debate," this refers to putting forward difficult questions.
The explanations concerning the characteristics of the offense and so forth are all as stated above.
106. The Precept on Granting Ordination and Full Acceptance to One Not Yet of Age. The sixteenth case: The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there were bhikṣus who, being less than ten years of age, granted others the going-forth and the full ordination; the bhikṣuṇīs did likewise.
At that time, the disciples of the twelve bhikṣuṇīs were extremely numerous; they went to the dwelling place of the six bhikṣus, and the six bhikṣus said to them:
"Your followers have gathered in great numbers around you."
The nuns said:
"Just as the Noble Ones and others grant others the going forth and the full ordination, we do likewise.
They asked:
"Are you no different from us? He replied,
"I am not different."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, being less than twelve years [of standing], grants another person the going-forth and the full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
The nuns and so forth are as described above.
"Causing another to go forth" refers to receiving the training rules of a śrāmaṇerī.
"Receiving full ordination" refers to the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations).
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is set forth in detail as previously described.
107. The Training Rule on Taking Disciples Arbitrarily. The setting of this one hundred seventh rule is the same as before.
At that time, the Blessed One ordained that bhikṣuṇīs who had completed twelve years of seniority were permitted to grant others the going-forth and the full ordination.
However, if a bhikṣuṇī, though having completed twelve years of seniority, was foolish, lacked clarity, and was incompetent, yet still granted others the going-forth and the full ordination.

If one is not self-disciplined yet wishes to discipline others; if one is not personally tranquil yet wishes to bring tranquility to others; if one has not yet crossed over [to liberation] oneself yet wishes to ferry others across; or if one cannot save oneself yet wishes to save others—none of these things are possible.
At that time, those nuns, lacking any actual virtue or capability, arbitrarily ordained disciples.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"If a bhikṣuṇī has the strength and capability to instruct a disciple, she should request it from the Saṃgha; in this manner, the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for authorizing her to maintain a following should be granted. The entire Saṃgha must assemble, numbering at least twelve, or even more."
Having paid homage in due order, that nun joined her palms before the senior nun, squatted down, and spoke these words:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!

I, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], having completed twelve years of residence in the rains retreat and being capable of instructing disciples, now request from the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha the formal act (*karmavācanā*) for maintaining a following.
May the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣuṇī [Name], the formal act for maintaining a following.
Thus he spoke three times.
Then, one bhikṣuṇī performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī [Name], having completed twelve years since her full ordination, wishes to maintain female disciples.
This [Name] now requests from the bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha the formal authorization to maintain female disciples.

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permit that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grant [this] to [Name], who has completed twelve years of seniority, the rule of maintaining a female disciple.
"I declare it thus.
Next, perform the *karmavācanā*:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!

This bhikṣuṇī [Name], having completed twelve years since her full ordination, wishes to maintain female disciples; she now requests from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs the formal authorization to maintain female disciples.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grants [the name] so-and-so the full twelve-year period for maintaining a disciple according to the Dharma.
If the venerable ones consent to granting so-and-so the full twelve-year period for maintaining a disciple according to the Dharma, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.

"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already completed the formal procedure for [the nun] so-and-so to have a full twelve years of seniority and to take on a female disciple. The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold this."
Thus, the Blessed One granted permission for a bhikṣuṇī who has the capacity to instruct a disciple to request from the Saṃgha the formal authorization to maintain a following.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇā, not yet having received from the Saṃgha the authorization to maintain a following, arbitrarily allowed others to go forth and receive full ordination.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after a detailed exposition, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha has not yet granted her the authorization to take on disciples, should nevertheless take on a disciple, it is a pāyattika."
The term "nun" and so forth are as explained above.
"The Saṃgha has not yet granted the authorization to keep followers" means that the community has not yet given its permission.
"To keep a disciple without authorization" means to grant another person the going-forth (pravrajyā) or to confer full ordination (upasampadā).
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed before. 108.

The training rule concerning the ordination of a woman previously married who is less than twelve years of age. The one hundred and eighth training rule concerning the ordination of a woman previously married who is less than twelve years of age. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, when the foolish and wicked Ajātaśatru slaughtered the Śākya clan, many Śākya women, finding themselves without any support, were permitted to go forth. They grieved for their kinsmen, remembering them with sorrowful weeping; later, having realized the Dharma, their anxieties gradually vanished as they sought to receive full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*).
The bhikṣuṇīs said,
"You must wait until you have reached twenty years of age before receiving full ordination.
They replied:
“Noble lady!
To wait for twenty full years is an exceedingly long time.
The nuns said:
"If one has reached twenty years of age, one is then able to serve an upādhyāya and an ācārya.
The nuns said, "If we were at home, we could still manage our husbands' business affairs; how then could we not now serve our preceptors and instructors?"
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a woman who has previously been married is twelve or eighteen years of age, she should be granted the two years of the *śikṣamāṇā* training before being ordained into full *upasampadā*."
It should be granted in this manner: when the Saṃgha has assembled in its entirety, have that person perform prostrations in due order and speak these words before the Elder:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!"
I, [name], now for the sake of this matter, take Venerable [name] as my preceptor.

I now request from the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha the six rules and the six secondary rules to become a *śikṣamāṇā*. May the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha grant me, [name], the six rules, the six secondary rules, and the training rules of a *śikṣamāṇā*, with [name] as my preceptor.
"May those who are capable of compassion please show us mercy.
Thus it is said three times.
Next, one bhikṣuṇī performs the formal motion (jñapti-karman):
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!

This śrāmaṇerikā [Name], who has reached the age of eighteen, with [Name] as her upādhyāyā, now requests from the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha to train in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas for a period of two years."

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their consent, let the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permit that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grant [the status of] Śrāmaṇerī to [Name], who is eighteen years of age, so that she may train in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas for two years, with [Name] acting as her Upādhyāyī.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!

This female śrāmaṇerī, so-and-so, who has reached the age of eighteen, with so-and-so as her upādhyāyī, now requests from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs for a period of two years to train in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas, with so-and-so as her upādhyāyī.

The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grants [the status of] śrāmaṇerī to [Name], who is eighteen years of age, to train in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas for two years, with [Name] acting as her upādhyāyī.

Venerable sirs, if you approve that the śrāmaṇerī [Name], who has reached eighteen years of age, be granted the training in the six rules and the six secondary rules for two years, with [Name] acting as her upādhyāyī, remain silent;
if you do not approve, speak.

"The community of bhikṣuṇīs has already granted [the status of] śrāmaṇerī to the maiden so-and-so, who is eighteen years of age, for the training in the six dharmas and six secondary dharmas over a period of two years, with so-and-so acting as her upādhyāyī."
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its permission; by reason of their silence, I now hold it to be so.
Next, one should say:
"Listen, [Name]!
From this day forward, you should train in six rules:

first, you must not travel alone on a road; second, you must not cross a river alone; third, you must not touch the body of a man; fourth, you must not sleep in the same room as a male; fifth, you must not act as a matchmaker for marriages; sixth, you must not conceal a grave offense committed by a bhikṣuṇī.
The summary verse says:
One should not travel on a road alone; one should not cross a river alone;
one should not intentionally touch a man; one should not sleep with a man.
Do not act as a matchmaker for marriages; do not conceal the grave offenses of a bhikṣuṇī.
Furthermore, say:
"Listen, you, [Name]!
