From this day forward, you should train in the six secondary rules (*anuvartana-dharma*):

first, one must not handle gold or silver that belongs to oneself; second, one must not shave the hair of the private parts; third, one must not dig into the earth; fourth, one must not intentionally cut living plants or trees; fifth, one must not eat food that has not been formally received.
"Sixth, one must not eat food that has been handled by another.
A summary verse says:
"Not grasping gold and the like; not removing hair from the private parts;"
One shall not dig the earth, nor damage living plants and trees;
one shall not eat food that has not been formally received, nor food that has already been touched.

Thus the World-Honored One ordained that a woman who has previously been married must undergo training for two full years in the six rules and the six secondary rules; only after having correctly completed this training in the rules may she receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
At that time, the nun Thullanandā ordained a girl who was less than twelve years old and conferred full ordination upon her.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman who has previously been married is less than twelve years of age, grants her the going forth, it is a pāyattika."
The term "nuns" and so forth is as explained above.
"A woman who has previously married" refers to one who has already been wedded to another family.
"Not yet full [of years]" refers to one whose age is not yet twelve.
Regarding "granting [ordination] to one who has gone forth," the meaning is as explained above.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is detailed as previously stated. 109.

The training rule concerning not granting the *śikṣamāṇā* dharma and full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*) to one who has reached twelve years of age. The setting and circumstances are the same as before. The hundred and ninth [training rule]: not granting the *śikṣamāṇā* dharma and full ordination to one who has reached twelve years of age. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā, knowing that a woman who had previously been married and was twelve years of age could receive the going forth, thought to herself:
"The World-Honored One has permitted her to receive full ordination."
If one confers full ordination (*upasampadā*) without first granting the rules of training for novices (*śikṣamāṇā-dharma*),
the nun informs the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus inform the Buddha.
The Buddha questions her and rebukes her, and after explaining the matter at length, he establishes the rule of training (*śikṣāpada*), which should be stated as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman who has previously been married is twelve years of age, should confer full ordination upon her without first granting her the *śikṣamāṇā* training, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
The nuns and so forth are as described above.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is set forth in detail as previously stated.
110. The Training Rule on Unauthorized Retention of Many Disciples. The setting of this one hundred and tenth rule is the same as before.

At that time, the nun Thullanandā gave the going forth and the full ordination to others without limit, yet she did not assign them names such as Buddhaguptā, Dharmaguptā, or Saṃghaguptā; she merely engaged them in work, calling out to them:
"Hey! [Name]!"
"Disciples! Hearing this, they did not know whom he was calling;
some even called out in reply:
"Ho! Śrāmaṇerikā! Ho!"
"O student of the True Dharma! Ho!
Young man!"
As for the phrase "one year," it refers to calling out [the age] as "one year," and so on, up to "ten years."
When they were called in this manner, none of them knew who the teacher was calling;
one nun said to them,
"Noble ladies!..."
"Since you have already conferred full ordination upon her, why not assign her a name? For what reason do you cause such a commotion?
Tullā said, "I have many people; how am I to give them all names?"
The nun said, "Noble one!
How could it be appropriate to maintain an unlimited number of followers as a 'pure' dharma?"
She replied,
"I have already finished what was pure and what was impure.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not maintain a following without limit.

However, if a bhikṣuṇī wishes to maintain an unlimited following, that bhikṣuṇī must request from the Saṃgha the procedure for maintaining an unlimited following; only after obtaining it from the Saṃgha may she maintain a following."
If they are capable of doing so, the Saṃgha of nuns should assemble, with a minimum of twelve or more members.
That nun, having paid her respects in order, should join her palms before the senior nun, squat down, and speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha of nuns, please listen!"

I, [Name], have reached the age of twelve and am capable of maintaining a community of disciples; I pray that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha will grant me, [Name], the rule of maintaining an unlimited number of disciples, out of compassion for me.
Thus it was said three times.
Then, one bhikṣuṇī performed the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*):
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, wishes to maintain an unlimited number of disciples.
This so-and-so now requests from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs the formal procedure for maintaining an unlimited number of disciples.

If it is the proper time for the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha and they grant their consent, may the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha permit that the Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grant [the nun] so-and-so the rule of maintaining an unlimited number of disciples.
The motion is thus made.
Next, the *karmavācanā* is performed:
"Venerable Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣuṇī, so-and-so, wishes to maintain an unlimited number of female disciples.
This so-and-so now requests from the saṃgha of bhikṣuṇīs the formal authorization to maintain an unlimited number of female disciples.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha now grants such-and-such a person the rule of maintaining an unlimited number of disciples.
If the venerable ones consent to granting such-and-such a person the rule of maintaining an unlimited number of disciples, let them remain silent; if they do not consent, let them speak.
"The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has already completed the procedure for [the nun] so-and-so to maintain unlimited disciples.
The Bhikṣuṇī Saṃgha has granted its consent, as indicated by their silence; thus do I now uphold this."

"Thus, the Blessed One has permitted bhikṣuṇīs to request from the Saṃgha the method for maintaining an unlimited number of followers; however, until the Saṃgha grants permission, one may not maintain an unlimited number of followers."
At that time, the nun Thullanandā, although the Saṃgha had not yet granted her permission to maintain an unlimited number of followers, kept them under her care on her own authority.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, explaining at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, when the Saṃgha has not yet granted her the permission to maintain an unlimited number of followers, should nevertheless maintain many, it is a pāyattika."
The term "nun" and so forth are as explained above.
"Sangha" refers to the disciples of the Tathāgata.
"Not yet granted" means not yet having received the authorization of the community.
"Without limit" means according to one's own discretion as to how many.
"To keep a multitude of followers recklessly" means to keep more followers than the prescribed limit.
"Dharma" refers to the formal procedure of *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is set forth in detail as previously described.
The twelfth summary verse says:
"Ordaining a pregnant woman, failing to provide instruction, not protecting her, and not following her."
The two young girls, the wicked person, And the many anxieties—the twelve dharmas.
111. The Training Rule Concerning a Pregnant Woman. The setting for this training rule, number one hundred and eleven, is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā gave ordination to a pregnant woman, who subsequently gave birth to a girl.
When a brahmin householder saw this, he criticized and disparaged her, saying:
"The daughters of the Śākya śramaṇas are truly not pure; within a single monastery, there are two kinds of practices."
"This refers to worldly dharmas and the dharmas of pure conduct.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established the precept, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again ordains a pregnant woman, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūranā-Dhanandā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"One who is pregnant" refers to one who is carrying a fetus.
"A woman" refers to a female.
"One who has gone forth" refers to one who has been granted the precepts for a śrāmaṇerī.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed above. 112.
The Training Rule on Not Providing Instruction. The training rule on not providing instruction, number one hundred and twelve: the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, when people came to her, the nun Pūraṇa-Dhananda would ordain them and grant them full admission (upasampadā) without discriminating between their families; she neither instructed nor guided them. Consequently, they wore their robes improperly, with the upper and lower garments not aligned or adjusted correctly, and lacking knowledge of the proper rules, they departed immediately wherever they pleased.
When the bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they criticized her and asked,
"Whose disciple is she?
She replied:
"This is an *utpala* nun.
The nuns then said, "Noble Lady!"
"Why do you not instruct them so that they may come to know the Dharma?
He replied, "I now have many disciples; how could I possibly teach them all?"
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains another person and grants them full admission (upasampadā), yet does not instruct them in the precepts, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūranā Nandā or any other nun.
“To grant another the going forth” means to cause another to receive the training rules (*śikṣamāṇā*) of a female novice (*śrāmaṇerī*).
“To receive full ordination” (*upasampadā*) refers to the formal procedure of the motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
"Failure to instruct" means failure to admonish.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth is as extensively described previously.
113. The Training Rule on Failure to Protect: The setting for this one hundred and thirteenth rule is the same as before.

At that time, whenever women came to the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā, she would ordain them and grant them full admission (upasampadā), yet she did not take charge of or protect them; they departed as they pleased. Some remained waiting at the gate, some stayed in the corridors, some went up to the upper stories, and some peered out from the windows, continuing in this manner day and night.
The other nuns saw this and mocked her, asking,
"Whose disciple are you?
She replied:
"It is the nun Thullanandā. The nuns said,
"Why does the Noble One not accept and protect her disciples?"
He replied, "My disciples are so numerous; how could I possibly take them all under my care?
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again grants another person the going forth and the full ordination, yet does not provide for their care and protection, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
Regarding “going forth,” etc., the meaning is as explained above.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is also the same as before in detail.

114. The Training Rule on Not Carrying [an Object] with One. The one hundred and fourteenth training rule concerning not carrying [an object] with one. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā ordained a woman who had a husband. After she had been ordained, she said to the nun Thullanandā:
“Noble Lady!...”
"If my master learns that I have left home to come here, he will surely create obstacles for me; I pray that the Noble One will take me to another region.
Toulanī said, "Why must you go elsewhere now?"
"Leaving home and departing from the secular world is itself another direction.
Later, at another time, when her husband came and saw her, he had her remove her dharma robes and put on secular clothing, and then took her back to his house.
Some bhikṣuṇīs entered her house while on their almsround; seeing them, she paid them homage, whereupon the bhikṣuṇīs asked:
"For what reason have you now returned to the life of a laywoman?"
"If I were to increase my virtuous qualities within every thought-moment of the Buddha-dharma, I would now be burdened by worldly entanglements and further ensnared.
The woman replied, "I am not my own mistress;
I belong to another. At that time, I repeatedly petitioned the Venerable Tullā-nī, requesting that she take me elsewhere so that I would not encounter obstacles."
"Because we were not protected, we have now come to this state.
The nuns went to the monastery and said to the nun Khuddakā (Tulā):
"O Noble One!"
"Why do you not take her away to another region, thereby causing her to return to lay life and creating an obstacle to her renunciation?
Tālapuṇyā replied, "I have no other business;
must I take every single person who renounces the world to another region?"
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī ordains another and does not take her with her when she departs, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
“Gives another person the going-forth” has the same meaning as explained above.
“Does not take [the person] along with her” means that due to difficult circumstances, she does not take [the person] to another region.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed above. 115.

The training rule concerning the full ordination of a girl who is less than twenty years of age. The one hundred fifteenth training rule concerning the full ordination of a girl who is less than twenty years of age. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā ordained a girl of eighteen years of age; she granted her two years of training in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas, yet she conferred full ordination upon her before she had reached twenty years of age.
The bhikṣuṇīs said:
“As the Blessed One has taught:

‘A girl of eighteen years should be granted two years of training in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas; only when she has reached twenty years of age shall she receive full ordination (upasampadā).’”
"How does the Venerable One know that she has not yet reached the required age and yet confers full ordination?
Can this be considered pure?
He replied:
"I have already conferred full ordination upon her, both pure and impure.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after a detailed exposition, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a girl is less than twenty years of age, confers full ordination upon her, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"A maiden" refers to one who has not yet married into a husband's household.
"Less than twenty years of age" refers to one who receives full ordination (*upasampadā*) at nineteen; the remaining meanings are as explained above.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is, in detail, the same as before. 116.

The Training Rule on Granting Full Ordination Without Imparting the Six Rules of Training. Regarding the training rule on granting full ordination without imparting the six rules of training, number 116: the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā gave the going-forth to a girl who was twenty years of age, and she thought to herself:
"If one were eighteen years old, they may receive the six rules and the six secondary rules;
since she is now twenty years of age, why is it necessary to grant her two more years of the *śikṣamāṇā* training?"
She then received full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her; after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a girl has reached twenty years of age, should confer full ordination upon her without having first had her train for two years in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to the nun Dhanika, or perhaps another nun; the remaining meanings are as stated above.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense, the details are identical to those previously mentioned.

117. The Training Rule on Ordaining Women of Evil Character. The training rule on ordaining women of evil character, number one hundred and seventeen. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Dhanika was begging for alms in the city of Śrāvastī when she saw a woman who was by nature prone to anger, fierce and coarse, and fond of quarreling. She was engaged in a dispute with another woman; her hair stood on end as she let out a cry like a jackal, and upon hearing the sound, other people immediately fell to the ground.
Upon seeing this, the nun Thullanandā thought to herself:
"If I can lead him forth as a renunciant, he will surely provide me with the strength to assist me in our conflict.
She then employed skillful means to ordain him.
Later, at another time, the nun Thullanandā had a minor dispute with another nun, while a newly ordained nun stood watching in silence.
Thullanandā said to her, "You cannot survive on your own;
I ordained you, so why do you stand here in silence now, not coming to my aid?"
The nun said: "Noble one!
I do not know the background of this matter; how can I assist you?"
The nun Thullanandā said,
"If I compete with the nun Mahāprajāpatī, you may insult me by calling me 'the one who shaves her head in secret'."
Regarding the nun Utpalavarṇā, one should rebuke her by saying, "She prostituted herself for sustenance in the six great cities";
regarding the nun Dharmadinnā, "It was because of her that [the rule] for receiving full ordination was established";
and regarding the nun Gaṅgāpālī, "She was forced by others to eat the flesh of her own son"—one should assist in the reproach with these words.
When the nuns of ill character heard that the nun Thullanandā had quarreled with others and was inciting other nuns to engage in mutual strife and contention, many nuns said:
"Who ordained such a person of ill character who delights in quarreling, allowing her to go forth?"
In response, he said:
"Except for the nun Thullanandā, who else would ordain her?
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman of bad character is fond of quarreling, should grant her ordination and confer full admission (upasampadā), it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or any other nun.
“A woman of evil character” refers to one who is fond of quarreling.
“One who has gone forth” refers to one who has received the status of a śrāmaṇerī as well as the other precepts.
The meaning of "receiving full ordination" (*upasampadā*) is as explained above.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth is also the same as before. 118.

The Training Rule on Ordaining Women with Excessive Grief. The training rule on ordaining women with excessive grief, number one hundred and eighteen; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the nun Thullanandā ordained a woman who had no relatives and was burdened with grief; she constantly dwelt upon thoughts of her kin, weeping and shedding tears throughout both the first and last watches of the night.

Many bhikṣuṇīs were frequently startled awake; hearing that sound of weeping, their minds became distracted and they could no longer maintain mindfulness, which acted as a thorn to those in meditative concentration.
Many nuns admonished her:
"Do not weep and lament; this is not the dharma of those who have left the household life."
The nun did not accept this, replying:

"You do not understand the suffering of others; with father deceased, mother dead, brothers, sisters, husband, and sons all having abandoned me, my heart is pierced with pain—how could I not be grieved?"
The bhikṣuṇīs asked one another,
"Who ordained such a woman, so full of grief and distress?
A nun replied:
“This is the nun Tūlā who has ordained her.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman is subject to much sorrow and distress, ordains her as a renunciant, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūraṇa-Dhananda or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"One who has much grief and affliction" means one who constantly harbors sorrow.
"One who has gone forth [into homelessness]" has the same meaning as explained above.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth is also extensive, as before.
119. The Training Rule on Granting Full Ordination (*upasampadā*) to One Who Has Not Yet Completed the Training Period. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

The nun Tullānandā ordained another woman as a renunciant; although she had not yet completed two years of training in the six rules and the six secondary rules, she conferred upon her the full ordination (upasampadā).
He then addressed him, saying:
"Venerable One!
I am still in the process of training and have not yet attained mastery."
The nun Thullanandā said, "Simply receive full ordination;
the training for female novices will be fulfilled of its own accord.
She then immediately conferred full ordination upon her.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after explaining the matter at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman has not yet completed two years of training in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas, confers full ordination upon her, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or any other nun.
“Less than two years” means that she has not yet completed the training in the six rules and the six secondary rules.
“To grant full ordination” refers to the formal procedure consisting of one motion and three proclamations (jñapti-caturtha-karman).
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is set forth in detail as previously stated.

120. The training rule concerning not conferring full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon one who has completed the period of training (*śikṣamāṇā*): The setting for this one hundred twentieth rule is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā ordained another woman as a renunciant and provided her with two years of training in the six rules and the six secondary rules.
When the period was complete, she said:
"Noble Lady!..."
"You may receive the full ordination from me.
She then replied to that nun:
"You should study further until you have mastered it thoroughly; then you shall receive the full ordination."
That nun remained silent.
Later, at another time, many bhikṣuṇīs said to her:
"Since you have already completed your training in the Dharma, why do you not receive full ordination?"
He replied,
"I have already consulted the Venerable Tullānanda.
He said:"
"You should study further until you have mastered it; then you shall receive full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the precept (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a woman has completed two years of training in the six dharmas and the six secondary dharmas, does not confer full ordination upon her, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūrṇaśailā Nandā or any other nun.
“Knowing that a woman has been a student for two years” means that although her training in the Dharma is complete, she does not grant her full ordination (upasampadā).
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively set forth previously.
The thirteenth summary verse says:
"Giving me robes before they have been released; collecting [robes] and receiving them annually."
Desiring to be without monks for half a month, [one should not] perform the *pravāraṇā* at the end of the rainy season retreat.
121. The training rule regarding ordaining a person without the husband’s permission. The one hundred and twenty-first [rule]: The causal narrative was set in Śrāvastī.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā, while entering another household for alms within the city, saw a woman who had been beaten by her husband and was confined inside a room.
When he was about to go outside, Toraṇanda said to him:
"O worthy one!
May you be free from illness."
"You may give me some food.
The woman replied,
"Noble one!"
"I am now distressed with grief; there is no way for me to eat.
He asked, "What is your grief?"
She then related the matter in full, and the nun said,
"If that is so, why do you not go forth?
She replied:
"This is what I desire.
Tullanandā then took her away and ordained her as a nun.
Later, when the husband came looking for his wife and could not find her, the family members informed him:
"He has gone forth into homelessness.
He asked again,
"Who ordained him?"
He replied, "The nun Tullānandā. [The other asked,] "If she were to leave,
who would know how to manage the household affairs?"
Later, at another time, as that nun was going out for alms, he saw her and asked:
"Noble Lady! Since you have become a renunciant for the sake of my wife, who will look after the household affairs?"
Filled with resentment and anger, he wrung the nun’s neck with his garment and dragged her along, saying:
“Since you have gone forth as a renunciant from my wife, come now and perform domestic labor for me!”
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after explaining the matter at length, he established this training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that another woman’s husband has not yet released her, ordains her into the homeless life, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
“Knowing another woman” means knowing her to be the wife or concubine of another.
“The husband has not released her” means that the husband has not given his permission.
"Going forth" refers to such acts as shaving the hair and so forth;
the rest is as explained previously.
122. The Training Rule on Soliciting Robes. The one hundred and twenty-second training rule concerning soliciting robes has the same setting as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā had a female trainee (śikṣamāṇā) who, after completing two years of training, went to Tullānandā’s quarters and said:
"Venerable One!
I have completed my training; I pray that you will grant me full ordination."
The nun Thullanandā said,
"If you give me a robe, only then may I grant it to you.
She replied:
"I have obtained so little due to my lack of merit; where can I find a robe?
The nuns asked her, "For what reason did you not receive full ordination?"
He replied:
"I have already requested the Venerable Upananda to grant me full ordination.
He said:"
"If you give me a robe, only then will I confer full ordination.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If, moreover, a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a certain woman desires to receive full ordination, should say to her:
'Give me your robe and I shall grant you full ordination.'"
"Whoever [says this], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Nun" refers to Pūrṇa-nandā or any other nun.
"One who desires to receive full ordination" means one who seeks to advance in the training rules (*śikṣāpada*).
"Those who give me robes" refers to any one of the seven types of robes as requested.
"When conferring full ordination" refers to performing the formal ritual of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* after the robes have been obtained.
The remainder is as explained previously. 123.

The Training Rule on Causing Another Woman to Take Charge of Household Affairs. The Training Rule on Causing Another Woman to Take Charge of Household Affairs, Number One Hundred and Twenty-Three. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Śrī-gautamī was wandering through this city for alms and arrived in due course at the house of a great householder.

The householder had passed away and his wife was now the mistress of the household; though she was immensely wealthy with abundant riches and many servants, slaves, and attendants, she lived there filled with grief.
Seeing Śrī Gautamī, she neither extended respectful greetings nor offered her food.
The nun said:
"Sister!..."
"For what reason is your distress so great?
The woman replied,
"Noble one!"
"My husband has died and my kinsmen have all perished; I do not know what I should do now.

The poisonous arrows of affliction have pierced my inner heart, and I am constantly filled with grief and distress. Although I possess wealth, servants, and property, since my husband has turned his back on me and my kin have departed, of what use are these things?"
The nun said,
"If that is so, why do you not go forth?
The woman replied:
“Noble One!
Please grant me the going forth.
The nun said:
"If one can withdraw from household affairs and cast off the worldly nets, then even the path of renunciation will not be difficult.

She then took all her storehouses and assets and offered them as gifts to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the poor, the orphaned, and the widowed. Having relinquished everything, she went to the nunnery and approached the nun Śrī-gautamī, requesting ordination.
The nun said, "I cannot ordain you now; you should go to another nun.
The woman thought to herself:
“Having exhausted my family’s wealth, I have come seeking to leave the household life.
Since she was not granted permission, she remained there in distress.
At that time, many nuns saw her and asked:
“O virtuous one! What is the cause of your sorrow?
He then answered her in detail.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them; having explained the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī says to a laywoman:"
"You should manage your household affairs; I shall allow you to go forth into homelessness.
If, after these instructions have been carried out, he does not ordain him as a renunciant, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Ni" refers to Śrī-Gautamī or other nuns.
"Informing a laywoman" means causing a housewife to take charge of her household affairs.
"When I shall grant you the going forth" means to promise to ordain her.
"Having completed it according to the instructions" means that the woman acted in accordance with the nun's words.
"Not ordained" means that she was not granted the going forth later on.
The explanation of the characteristics is as before.
124. The training rule regarding granting ordination and full admission (*upasampadā*) every year. The setting for this one hundred twenty-fourth rule is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā would, throughout the year, ordain others and grant them full admission (upasampadā) without bestowing upon them names.
Whenever there was business to attend to, she would simply call out:
"Hey! [Name]!"
Śrāmaṇerikā! Ho! Śikṣamāṇā!
"Ho! Young man! he said.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they said to the Therī:
"Noble Lady, why do you ordain others every year?"
She replied to the nuns, saying,
"I have allowed my enemy, whose neck was bound [with shackles], to go forth as a renunciant.
A nun asked her:
"Who is my enemy? He replied,
"You yourself are my great enemy, for you have shown me such intolerance."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, during the course of a year, grants another person the going forth or the full ordination, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
“During each year” means that throughout every year she grants others the going forth and the full ordination.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and other matters are as previously stated.
*Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*, Fascicle Eighteen. *Mūlasarvāstivāda-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya*.
Fascicle Nineteen.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree. Precept 125:
The Training Rule on Giving Consent after Spending the Night. The setting for this precept is the same as before.
At that time, there was an urgent matter for the Saṃgha, and the entire assembly of bhikṣuṇīs gathered together. They addressed the bhikṣuṇī Pūrṇā, saying:
"Noble Lady!..."
"When the assembly of nuns has gathered, you may go to join them.
The nun Thullanandā replied, "I have already given my consent according to the Dharma; let whatever needs to be done be performed accordingly."
On the following day, when the community of nuns was required to assemble, the nun Khuddakā did not go among them to perform her duties.
The nuns said:
"Noble lady!..."
"You should grant your consent.
The nun Thullanandā said,
"I have already granted my consent according to the Dharma yesterday."
The nun asked,
"Can it be accomplished by giving the *chanda* after the night has passed?
He replied:
“Is it possible that desire could become rotten and fail to be accomplished?
The nun informed the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha. The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, explaining at length until he said:
“If a bhikṣuṇī should convey her consent (*chanda*) after having spent the night [without the presence of the recipient], it is a *pāyattika* offense.”
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
“Having spent the night” means having passed the night.
“To give one’s consent” (yad-ṛcchā) means to express one’s intention.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and other matters are as stated previously.
126. The Training Rule on Requesting Instruction. The training rule on requesting instruction, number one hundred and twenty-six, has the same setting as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā, traveling through the countryside with a large retinue of nuns, arrived at a certain village.
There being a dwelling place there, she sought lodging; she then remembered that today was the fifteenth day, on which the *poṣadha* (confession and purification) ceremony ought to be performed.
The other nuns said to her,
"Noble lady! Come,
let us go together to the monastery to seek someone to give us instruction."
The nun Thullanandā said, "I am well-versed in the Tripiṭaka;

how could I not know this? Why should I seek another to act as my instructor? Whether a matter should be done or should not be done, I understand it all clearly; there is no need to trouble yourself by going to request [instruction]!"
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after a detailed discourse, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not seek instruction every half-month, she commits an offense."
"If one does not seek [to have it removed], it is a *pāyattika* offense.
"Nun" refers to Pūranāndā or any other nun.
"Every half-month" means on the fifteenth day of both the dark and light fortnights of each month.
"One who should seek instruction" refers to one who ought to seek a person from whom to receive instruction.
"If one does not seek it" means that one does not go to request it.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth is as extensively detailed before.

127. The Training Rule on Performing the Poṣadha in a Place Where No Bhikṣus Are Present. The one hundred twenty-seventh training rule on performing the poṣadha in a place where no bhikṣus are present; the setting and circumstances are as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā, traveling through the countryside with a large retinue of nuns, arrived at a certain village where there was a nunnery situated outside the settlement.
It happened to be the fifteenth day, the day for the Poṣadha ceremony; the other nuns said to Thullanandā, "Noble Lady!..."
As the Blessed One has said:
"A bhikṣuṇī should not perform the poṣadha where no bhikṣus are present.
You may come with me to the temple of the great saṃgha.
The nun Thullanandā said, "I am well-versed in the Tripiṭaka;
how could I not know the rules for the Poṣadha ceremony?
Why trouble yourself to go there again just to ask about it?"
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and reprimanded them, and after explaining the matter at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī performs the *poṣadha* ceremony in a place where no bhikṣus are present, it is a *pāyattika* offense."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
“A place where there are no bhikṣus” means a place where the great saṃgha of monks is absent.
“Performing the poṣadha” means reciting the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed before. 128.

The Training Rule on Observing the Rainy Season Retreat (*Varṣā*) Where No Bhikṣus Are Present. The one hundred twenty-eighth training rule on observing the rainy season retreat where no bhikṣus are present; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā was traveling with her companions when they arrived at a village.

There was a householder there who was very wealthy and possessed great riches; he provided for the community of nuns by constructing a dwelling place for them. Upon seeing the nuns, he approached and paid his respects, saying:
"Noble ladies!"
"You may stay here and observe the rains retreat.
Having heard this, the people wished to stay there, but a nun reported,
"Noble ones!..."
As the Blessed One has said:
"The bhikṣuṇīs should not observe the rainy-season retreat (varṣā) in a place where no bhikṣus are present.
We should go together to a place near the great community of monks (bhikṣusaṃgha).
The nun Thullanandā said, "I am well-versed in the Tripitaka;
how could I not know the rules for the rainy season retreat?
Why trouble myself to go again to the place of the bhikṣus?"
The nuns accepted these instructions.
When the rainy season retreat had concluded, the nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should observe the rainy-season retreat in a place where no bhikṣus are present, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūranā-Śailā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"A place where there are no bhikṣus" has the same meaning as explained above.
"One who observes the rains retreat" refers to the three-month summer *varṣā* retreat.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth, it is detailed as previously stated.

129. The Training Rule Regarding Not Performing the *Pravāraṇā* Ceremony Before the Two Assemblies on Three Matters. This is the one hundred and twenty-ninth training rule. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs had completed their summer retreat, they wished to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony on the fifteenth day.
Another bhikṣuṇī said to Pūrṇa-nandā:
"Noble Lady!..."
"You may come and go within the monastery to perform the *svairī-karman* (the rite of communal consent).
He replied, "Let us simply do it here; why trouble ourselves with going?"
The nun said,
"As the World-Honored One has taught:
'A bhikṣuṇī should perform the invitation ceremony (*pravāraṇā*) before the two assemblies by declaring three matters— namely, what has been seen, heard, or suspected.'"
The nun Khuddakā said, "I am well-versed in the Tripitaka and skilled in debate;
how could I not know how to perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony? Why would I go among the two assemblies [of monks and nuns] for that purpose?"
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
“If a bhikṣuṇī, having completed the rainy season retreat, does not perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony before both assemblies by means of the three matters, it is a *pāyattika* offense.”
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or any other nun.
“The rains retreat is concluded” means that the three-month *varṣā* has ended.

“Not before the two assemblies” means not within the assembly of monks and nuns performing the *pravāraṇā* (invitation for criticism) regarding the three matters—what was seen, heard, or suspected—as previously explained.
130. The Training Rule on Rebuking the Assembly. The setting for this one hundred and thirtieth training rule is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā spoke various words to rebuke the assembly of nuns, engaging in improper livelihoods and mutually inducing them [to do so], saying to the other nuns:
"You are foolish and lack skill; you do not know what should be given or what should be done."
"You are unskilled in various affairs.
The nuns admonished her, saying,
"Venerable One!..."
"How could it be appropriate to speak such words of reproach?
The Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā replied,
"Whether it is appropriate or not, I have already finished speaking."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and reprimanded them at length.
... [He continued] until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, reviles the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Sthūlanandā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"Rebuking the assembly" refers to rebuking the *saṃgha*.
The remaining explanations are as previously stated.
The fourteenth summary verse says:
The five kinds of stinginess in reviling the assembly; the rules regarding praising householders and temple food;
eating again after having been provided for; and washing the lower robe while having another wash clothes.
131. The Training Rule on Reviling the Assembly. The setting for the one hundred and thirty-first training rule on reviling the assembly is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā, harboring malice, reviled the assembly, saying:

"Because you were unable to sustain yourselves, you sought to have your hair shaved; you are a destitute and evil lineage who has gone forth into homelessness. You have no share in the Noble Dharma; with a mind intent on thievery, you delude others. You are truly not pure, but are violators of the precepts."
The other nuns said to her,
"Noble lady! Why do you harbor such anger and speak these vulgar words?"
The nun Thullanandā said:
"I was born into the Śākya clan, a lineage of noble and high standing; it is according to the Dharma that I should be reviled.
Do you not know what clan I belong to?"
She merely heard the insults and endured them in silence.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, reviles the Saṃgha, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Sthūlanandā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
Regarding "reviling the assembly," it refers to uttering malicious words.
The explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth is, in detail, the same as before.
132. The training rule on giving rise to a jealous mind upon seeing another praised; the setting for this one hundred and thirty-second training rule is the same as before.

At that time, the brahmins, householders, and lay devotees praised the Bhikṣuṇīs Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, Utpalavarṇā, Dharmadinnā, and Gaṅgāpālā, extolling their virtuous conduct as being like Mount Sumeru.
Upon seeing this, the nun Thullanandā immediately spoke with derision and jealousy.
The other nuns replied,
"Venerable One, why do you utter such slander?"
The nun Thullanandā said:

"I am one who has gone forth from the Śākya clan; I am well-versed in the Tripiṭaka as a great Dharma teacher, and in all debates and dialogues I am unimpeded. It is right that you praise my virtues, yet instead you praise others."
The nuns said: "Venerable One!
Why is it necessary to praise your virtues?"
She replied,
"Those who speak falsely without basis invite great calamity upon themselves.
The nuns said:
"Why are you stingy, envious, and unable to endure the prosperity of others?
The nun reported this to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, and after a detailed exposition, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, upon seeing another being praised, gives rise to a mind of stinginess or envy, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūranānandā or any other nun.
Regarding "giving rise to a mind of stinginess and envy by praising others," this refers to being stingy regarding the ethical virtue and qualities of others.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth is as extensively detailed previously.

133. The Training Rule on Stinginess Regarding Households (Gṛhamaṭsuṣṭhu-śikṣāpada). The one hundred and thirty-third training rule on stinginess regarding households; the setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs, while going on their alms-round, entered the home of a wealthy person of faith, who offered them pure and exquisite food and drink.
Having received the food, they quickly returned to their own monastery.
The nun Thullanandā saw them and asked,
"From whose family did you obtain this exquisite food?
The bhikṣuṇīs explained in detail where they had obtained it.
The nun Thullanandā reviled, disparaged, and rebuked them, saying:
"One should go to such-and-such a family; one should not go to such-and-such a house;
one should not enter such-and-such a residence. The nuns said:
"Noble one! Why are you so stingy with these many households?
He replied:
"What is the fault?
I am the preceptor of this gate; do not cause him fatigue, lest he lose his respectful faith.
The nun reported this to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī is stingy regarding households, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
“Miserly toward households” means being stingy regarding others’ houses.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is detailed as previously stated.
134. The Training Rule on Stinginess Regarding Monasteries. The setting for the one hundred thirty-fourth training rule on stinginess regarding monasteries is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā constructed a nunnery; a nun was residing on an upper story, and when she walked upon it, there was a great noise.
Upon hearing this, the nun Thullanandā became angry and resentful, saying:
"Where could there be such a worthless person, walking like a female elephant and making noise with her footsteps?
It is because she has received no instruction."
The nuns said: "Noble One!
For what reason do you speak such harsh words out of stinginess regarding the monastery?"
He replied, "What fault is there in my anger?
Since I built this monastery, my hands and feet have cracked and my body is exhausted; it is because of these various hardships that I am stingy."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after explaining at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī is stingy regarding the monastery, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or any other nun.
“Miserly regarding the monastery” means being miserly toward the dwelling places of monks and nuns.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed before.

135. The Training Rule on Stinginess Regarding Gains and Food. The training rule on stinginess regarding gains and food, number one hundred and thirty-five. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs put on their robes and took up their alms bowls at the time of the morning meal, went for alms in succession, and returned to the monastery after they had finished begging.
At that time, because the nun Pātayantī was greedy for much food, she was unable to sleep during the first or last watch of the night, and only lay down after a long time.
Every time the nuns returned to the monastery after begging for alms at sunrise, the nun Khujjuttarā saw them and thought to herself:
"These nuns have gone out begging very early; there is nothing I can say to them now. I should employ a skillful means to go begging first so that they arrive later."
While giving them instruction, he said:

"Because you steal the food and drink of others, you cannot sleep through the long night; you think only of food and drink and do not contemplate the meaning of the Dharma. You do not serve your preceptors, nor do you revere the Buddha, nor do you smear the altar ground, nor do you praise or recite the scriptures."
"I only know how to rise early, take up my alms-bowl, and go on alms-round; what kind of ritual procedure is this?
Having heard this, the nun replied, "Noble one!"
"What you have said is most excellent.
[The nun] did not dare to beg for alms prematurely.
Then, on another day when the sky had just turned light, the nun Khuddā put on her robes, took up her bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

At that time, there was a brahmin who, having selected an auspicious day, intended to travel to another region. Just as he was departing the city, he encountered the gatekeeper; their mutual encounter gave rise to feelings of resentment, and the brahmin was immediately seized and severely beaten by him.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī is stingy regarding gains, food, or drink, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhanandā or any other nun.
“One who is stingy regarding gains and food” means one who begrudges the gifts offered by others.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed before.
At that time, all the bhikṣus were filled with doubt and requested the World-Honored One, saying:
"Venerable Sir!
Observe how the bhikṣuṇī Tullānandā, out of stinginess regarding the food and drink offered by others and due to her own greedy mind, was severely beaten by a brāhmaṇa."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only in this present life that this nun was beaten by others due to her greedy mind; it was also the same in the past."
Listen attentively!
In the distant past, there was a large green pigeon who saw a cart of black sesame seeds overturned at the head of a road; other green pigeons then came wishing to eat them.
The great myna bird said:
"Do not gather this black sesame by the side of the road.
As evening approaches, there will surely be carriages, horses with saddles, and elephants passing by here; they will trample you to death."
The other birds replied,
"As you have said, sir," and they all flew away in different directions.
Having instructed him thus, he went there at night himself to eat the sesame seeds.
At that moment, a cart passed by; because he was so intent on eating, he failed to exercise caution and was run over and killed by the vehicle.
At that time, a celestial being spoke in verse:
“Lacking wisdom and understanding yourself, You stubbornly attempted to instruct others;
Because of your greed for eating sesame at night, You have encountered this suffering of the chariot wheel.”
"O bhikṣus! For this reason, whatever you say, you should act accordingly; you should train yourselves thus. 136.
The Training Rule on Stinginess with the Dharma (Dharmamātsarya-śikṣāpada). The setting for this one hundred and thirty-sixth rule is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇīs requested the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇa, saying:
"Noble Lady! You should instruct us in recitation and other such matters."

Having heard this, when the time came for instruction, he had all the bhikṣuṇīs perform various tasks: some he sent to warm their backs by roasting near a fire, some he sent to hand him eye-salve tubes, some he ordered to sweep the rooms, some to fetch water, and others to spread out bedding or dry clothes in the sun; in this manner, he assigned them all sorts of chores.
The nuns thought:
"Now this noble lady is stingy with the Dharma toward us;
she does not provide instruction, but merely makes us perform menial tasks."
"We should ask him together.
They then asked immediately:
"Why did you not instruct us?"
The nun Thullanandā said:
"Do you think the Dharma is easy to obtain?
For many years I endured various hardships and labored day and night to serve my enlightened teacher; only after such a long time did I finally succeed in obtaining it."
Yet she did not provide instruction at all.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, then addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
"One who is stingy with the Dharma shall incur five kinds of faults:

first, being born blind; second, lacking wisdom; third, being far removed from the Buddha-dharma; fourth, having enemies within one's own home; and fifth, failing to enter the ranks of the noble ones."
Upon the dissolution of the body at the end of life, she will fall into hell; [this is] explained in detail up until the establishment of the training rule, which should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī is stingy with the Dharma, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dhananda or any other nun.
“One who is stingy with the Dharma” means one who does not reveal or instruct.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively described above.
137. The Training Rule on Eating Again After Having Finished a Meal. The setting for this training rule is the same as before.

At that time, the nun Khujjuttarā took her alms-bowl in the early morning and entered the city to beg for food. Having obtained food, she placed it in her dwelling and ate at her leisure; she then immediately went for a walking meditation (*caṅkrama*). When the walking meditation was finished, she returned to eat again, and when the food in her bowl was exhausted, she threw herself down and lay there.
The nuns said, "Venerable One!
Do you walk after finishing your meal, eat again after walking, and then lie down once you are full?"
Having heard this, Tullānandā reviled and rebuked the other nuns with harsh words.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, and after a detailed exposition, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, having finished her meal, eats again, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūlananda or any other nun.
"Having finished eating, to eat again" means to eat once more after having already eaten one's fill.
The explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth is as extensively detailed before.
138. The Training Rule on Caring for Another’s Child (Śaikṣa 138). The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
The nun Thullanandā entered another’s house while begging for alms and saw that the woman there had given birth not long before.
Thullanandā said to her:
“Noble lady!”
"I pray that you may be free from illness; please grant me some food.
The woman replied, "Noble One!"
"The child cries much; what do you intend to do?
The nun said, "Since you know how to give birth to a child, why do you not know the methods of raising one?"
The woman said, "Noble one!
Do you perhaps know a method for ceasing this weeping?"
The nun said,
"If I understand even the supreme Dharma that exists in the world, how could I not be knowledgeable about raising a child?
If you intend to teach and raise him, will you provide me with food?"
She replied,
“I will give it.
The nun said:
"Will you also give food to the nun who attends upon me? She replied, "I will."
"Is food also given to the person who guards the room?
He replied, "It is also given."

The nun then took the child and sat him upon her lap; she anointed his body with warm oil, rubbed it with flour, and washed him clean with warm water. She laid him down securely under a coverlet, and the child fell asleep.
Whatever the woman had promised, she gave it all to the nun.
Later, on another occasion, the nun Mahāprajāpatī also entered this house while going for alms.
The householder’s wife said:
“Noble one!
Is it possible to bring peace and security to this child?
The nun replied:
"This is not the conduct of one who has gone forth; have you ever seen a person who has gone forth engage in such an undertaking?
The woman replied, "Noble One!"
“The nun Thullanandā previously committed such an act against me.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her at length, and so forth, until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī again provides sustenance for another's child, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūrṇa-nandā or any other bhikṣuṇī.
"Providing for another's child" means attending to the wife or children of another.
The explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth is as extensively detailed previously. 139.

The Training Rule on Not Keeping a Washcloth (*Na-cīvara-dhāraṇa-śikṣāpada*). The thirteenth-nineth training rule concerning not keeping a washcloth. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, there were many bhikṣuṇīs bathing in the Ajiravatī River together with several laywomen. Pointing at one another with their fingers, they gazed upon the bhikṣuṇīs' breasts, waists, bellies, calves, and so forth, praising and commenting on these features according to their observations.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her about the facts and rebuked her; having explained the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not keep a bathing skirt, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“Not keeping a bathing skirt” means not having a skirt for bathing.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth, it is explained in detail as previously stated.

140. The Training Rule on Having a Washerwoman Wash Clothes. The training rule on having a washerwoman wash clothes is the one hundred and fortieth. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, twelve bhikṣuṇīs dreamed of sexual intercourse with men; as a result, they discharged impurities that stained their robes, and they had a washerman wash them.
The man then washed the bhikṣuṇīs’ saffron-colored robes together with the white robes of laypeople, whereby they became soiled and ruined.
The owner of the garment came and asked,
"Who ruined my garment?
The washerman replied:
"I washed my nun's robe in the same place [as the lay robes], and because of this, it has been ruined by dye.
The householders criticized and disparaged them, saying, "Look at these renunciants; they are not tranquil."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them regarding the facts and rebuked them, and after explaining at length, he established this training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī causes a washerman to wash her clothes, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“To have a washerwoman wash clothes” means to have another person wash any one of the seven types of robes.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth is as extensively detailed before.
The fifteenth summary verse says:
The upper robe and the saṃghāṭī; Two types of sick robes and begging for them;
Not sharing when departing, and not dividing [the robes]; Quarreling, not entrusting, and learning incantations.
141. The Training Rule on Exchanging Clothes with Senior Members of the Community. The setting for this rule is the same as before.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī named Kālī who had a son named Vatsa, whom she also ordained;
she further had four daughters, whom she likewise ordained.
The one named Kālī had made a new saṃghāṭī and, having put it on, went to her mother’s place.

When her younger sister saw that her brother’s robe was so bright, fresh, and radiant, a feeling of affection arose within her. She asked her brother for the robe, but when he would not give it to her, she immediately began to weep.
The mother said to her son,
"Why do you not give him the garment and cause me distress?
The son, reflecting that he must not disobey his mother’s sincere instruction, immediately gave the garment to his younger sister to wear.
The younger sister nun in the monastery said, "Sister, you are wearing your own great robe; please give this robe to me.
Since she refused to give it, the younger sister immediately began to weep bitterly.
The mother then said, "You may give it; do not cause me distress.
Not disobeying her mother's instruction, he immediately gave her the garment.
The bhikṣuṇīs asked,
"Where did you obtain these exquisite, fine, and pure garments of the Śuddhāvāsa devas, all of which you wear with such attachment?
She replied:
"I wish my elder brother were free from illness and at peace; as for these robes, who would even mention them?
The nun informed the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her regarding the truth or falsehood of taking the robes from her elder brother, and she replied:
"It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked her in various ways, and after speaking at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī exchanges robes with those of higher standing, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“Superior assembly” refers to those who are above oneself.
“Exchanging robes” refers to bartering.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is set forth in detail as previously described. 142.
The Training Rule on Unlawfully Giving Robes to Laypeople: The four hundred and twelfth training rule concerning unlawfully giving robes to laypeople; the occasion for this occurred in Rājagṛha.
At that time, the musician asked the nun Tullā for a robe, and she gave him one.
Having obtained it, he immediately put on the robe as a śrāmaṇera and mocked the group of six bhikṣus.
When the group of six monks discovered that the bhikṣuṇī had given the clothes to the musician, they each harbored resentment, saying:
"It was only this nun who mocked and ridiculed us; it was not that musician."
Then, on one occasion, she encountered the nun Thullanandā in a secluded place and was beaten by her severely; her body became swollen all over, and she lay bedridden.
The other nuns asked her, "Noble lady!..."
"What is the trouble? He replied,
"I was beaten by the group of six."
"He is my elder brother; if he does not instruct me, who else should hold me accountable?
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should again arbitrarily give the saṃghāṭī robe of a śramaṇa to a layperson, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Tullanandā.
"The dharma-robes of a śramaṇa" refers to the dharma-robes of monks and nuns.
"Giving them to laypeople" means bestowing them upon white-clad persons so that they may wear and use them.
Regarding the explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth, it is explained in detail as previously stated.

143. The Training Rule on Not Keeping a Sickness Garment (Glānapraticchādana-cīvara). The four hundred and forty-third training rule concerning not keeping a sickness garment was established with its causal origin in Śrāvastī.

At that time, while the bhikṣuṇīs were going on their alms-round, the blood from their menstrual flow stained their undergarments. When brahmins and householders saw this, they all spoke in derision and reproach.
The bhikṣuṇīs reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:

"As long as afflictions have not been eliminated, one follows the flow of karma; women all discharge impurities every month. Therefore, the bhikṣuṇīs should keep 'sickness-clothes' (glānapraticchādana-vastra)."
Thus the Blessed One prescribed that one should keep a sick-cloth.
Tullanandā did not keep it in accordance with the instruction.
A nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her about the facts and rebuked her, explaining at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not keep a sick-cloth, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
“Not keeping a sick-cloth” refers to an undergarment.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense, it is described in detail as previously stated.
144. The Training Rule on the Private Use of the Community’s Sick-Clothing. The setting for this rule is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā said to Lady Śrīmālā, "The World-Honored One has prescribed that nuns must keep a robe for illness, yet I do not see one now.
The lady took a robe and offered it to Thullanandā and the assembly; however, they all took it for their own private use.
Furthermore, a great number of bhikṣuṇīs went to the lady’s quarters and said,
“We pray that you will grant us robes for the sick.
The lady replied:
"I have already given everything in total.
He asked, "To whom did you give it?"
She replied,
"It was Tullānandā.
The nuns asked her for it, but she would not give it to them.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them regarding the facts and rebuked them; he spoke at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī takes clothing intended for the sick from the community and uses it for her own private purposes, it is a pāyattika."
"Ni" refers to Pūranāndā or any other nun.
"Robes for the sick belonging to the Great Assembly" refers to those bestowed upon the Saṃgha by others.
"To take for private use" means to divert them into one's own possession; the rest is as previously explained.

145. The Training Rule on Begging for *Kathina* Cloth from the Poor. The four hundred and forty-fifth training rule concerning begging for *kathina* cloth from the poor; the setting of the occasion is the same as before.

At that time, there was a lay devotee who had been wealthy in the past but was now poor with meager resources; nevertheless, whenever the bhikṣuṇīs were spreading the kaṭhina robe, he would regularly provide offerings.
Later, when the time for the distribution of robes arrived within that year, the nun went to the householder’s place and said,
“You may offer a robe of solid material.
The householder replied:
"I see that I have nothing at present, but if I should have anything in the future, I shall certainly offer it as a gift.
The nun said, "The *kaṭhina* robe season has now arrived; it cannot be delayed. You may simply offer it to the field of the Sangha immediately, and you shall repay the debt later."
The householder replied,
"So be it," and immediately entered into an agreement to borrow money from another.
Later, when the time limit had expired, the creditor dragged him along. Others asked,
"Why are you being dragged?"
He replied, "I thought you were offering me a robe.
The other then answered:
“If one gives rise to pure faith toward a female disciple of the Śākya ascetic, such suffering and hardship will be encountered.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her about the facts, rebuked her, and gave a detailed discourse up to the point where he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a person is poor, should beg from them for kaṭhina cloth, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun within this Dharma.
"Knowing this person to be poor" means that they currently possess no goods, yet one begs from them for *kaṭhina* cloth.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense and so forth is detailed at length as in other [sections]. 146.
The Training Rule on Not Sharing the Cloth (The Fourteenth-Sixth Training Rule on Not Sharing the Cloth). The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, a great number of bhikṣuṇīs gathered together;
as the Blessed One had said, "When the bhikṣuṇīs have completed their rains retreat, they should travel through the countryside.
They then set out on their journey, but encountered bandits along the way.
They returned to the nunnery and informed the bhikṣuṇīs, who in turn reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I now authorize that bhikṣuṇīs who have encountered bandits shall be given their share of the kaṭhina robe."
Upon hearing this, all the bhikṣuṇīs gathered together and called out to the bhikṣuṇī Pūraṇa-Dhanadā, saying:
"Noble Lady, please come;
let us go together to distribute the kaṭhina robe."
She was unwilling to come.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her regarding the facts, rebuked her extensively, and so forth, until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī does not participate in the distribution of the kaṭhina robe, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Pūrṇaśailā (Tulanandā) or any other nun.
"Regarding 'not participating in the distribution of the *kaṭhina* robe': this means not assembling together with them.
The explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth is as extensively described previously. 147.
The Training Rule on Not Sharing the Distribution of Robes (Caturdaśottaraśatamaṃ Śikṣāpadaṃ na-saha-vibhajana-vastu). The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, when the bhikṣuṇīs were taking out the kaṭhina robe and wished to share it collectively, Pūrṇa (Tulānanda) refused to come and share it.
The other nuns grew weary from being summoned back and forth repeatedly, and the nun in charge of the robe became distressed in her heart.
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her about the facts, rebuked her, and gave a detailed discourse, concluding with: "I shall establish this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
'If a bhikṣuṇī does not share clothing with others, it is a pāyattika.'"
"Ni" refers to Pūraṇa-Dharmadinnā or any other nun.
"Not sharing the distribution of robes with others" means not joining together with them to create an obstacle to the distribution.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively described above.
There is no offense if it was not one's intention to take a share of the robe.
**The 148th Training Rule: On Not Exhorting Those Fighting to Cease.** The setting and circumstances are the same as before.

When a dispute arose among the bhikṣuṇīs, they split into two factions and ceased practicing wholesome qualities; they all went to the nun Dhanika to express their respective intentions to one another.
Because Dhanika possessed great influence, she did not cause them to cease their quarrel, nor did she ultimately exhort them to do so, until the conflict persisted.
Thullanandā said,
"As I observe this now, have you subdued me?
The nun reported this to the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her about the facts and rebuked her, speaking at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing she has the power to do so, sees other bhikṣuṇīs fighting and does not exhort them to cease, it is a pāyattika."
“Nuns” refers to Pūrṇāśā Nandā and others.
“Knowing oneself to have the power” means having the capacity to subdue them.
“Seeing other nuns fighting and not exhorting them to cease” means seeing nuns forming factions and fighting one another, yet failing to use skillful speech to exhort them to stop.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively detailed before. 149.

The training rule on abandoning one’s residence without having made an announcement. The four hundred and forty-ninth training rule on abandoning one’s residence without having made an announcement. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā abandoned her former residence without making a formal entrustment of her quarters and traveled through the countryside with a group of nuns.
After she had departed, a fire broke out and the monastery buildings were burned down; all her robes, bowls, and requisites were completely consumed by the flames.
Later, when the nun returned to the monastery and saw that it had been burned by fire, the other nuns said to her,
"Venerable One!
Why did you not entrust the place to us before you left?"
"The property belonging to the Saṃgha has been consumed by fire.
The Bhikṣuṇī Thullanandā said, "It would rather have been burned by fire; I will not give my own property for you to use."
The bhikṣuṇīs informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned them about the facts and rebuked them, and after speaking at length, he established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī abandons her residence without having entrusted it to another, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūranā-Nandā and others.
“Abandoning the dwelling place” means leaving the monastery quarters where the nun resides.
“Without having made an announcement” means not informing other people when departing, as explained previously.
150. The Training Rule on Receiving Spells from Laypeople. The one hundred and fiftieth training rule concerning receiving spells from laypeople. The setting is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā learned a spell from a layman who understood incantations. The spell said:
“Hiri hiri pū pha (pronounced with a *hu* sound) svāhā.”
Having received it once, she received it again. The nuns said to her, "Noble Lady!

We have heard that you are a person of great intelligence and wide learning, possessing vast knowledge and a powerful memory, and that you can recite the Tripiṭaka. For what reason do you repeatedly ask this person to grant you such a minor spell?"
The nun Thullanandā said, "It is not that I do not remember;
it is that I love this man and wish to speak with him.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned her about the facts and rebuked her, speaking at length until he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī learns the art of incantations from a layperson, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Pūranā-Nandā and others.
“To receive instruction in the art of spells from a layperson” means to seek and receive the transmission of spells from a householder.
Regarding the explanation of the nature of the offense, it is explained in detail as previously stated.
The sixteenth summary verse says:
Teaching spells, selling roasted flour, managing affairs for others, and having a nun do so;
spinning thread, weaving, and walking with a parasol; sandals, sores, and ordaining a courtesan.
151. The Training Rule on Teaching Laypeople the Art of Incantations. The setting for this rule is the same as before.
At that time, a layperson came to the nun Tullānandā and requested instruction in the art of incantations.
The nun granted it to him, and the incantation was: “Hiri hiri, svāhā.”
Having heard this, the layperson accepted it immediately; the nun then bestowed it upon him once more.
He then replied, "Noble Lady!"
"I have already received it; there is no need for you to bestow it again.
Although the nun heard this, she continued to bestow it without ceasing. The layperson became enraged and replied, "I have no need for incantations!"
At that time, another nun asked,
"Noble Lady! For what reason do you repeatedly bestow this mantra-method upon others?"
He replied, "I love this person; it is because I wish to converse with him that I grant these frequent instructions.
The nun informed the bhikṣu, and the bhikṣu informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Cūḍapanthaka:
"Is it true that you have repeatedly bestowed the Dharma upon others in this manner?
He replied:
"It is indeed so.
This is explained at length, up until: "The training rule (śikṣāpada) is hereby established and should be recited as follows:
