'If a bhikṣuṇī teaches the methods of incantation to a layperson, it is a pāyattika.'"
“Nun” refers to Sthūlanandā and others.
“Teaching a layperson the methods of incantation” means bestowing spells upon another.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively described before.

152. The Training Rule on Selling Flour-Based Foods; The Training Rule on Selling Parched Grain-Based Foods. The one hundred and fifty-second [rule]. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā, while wandering for alms, saw a person buying parched grain (*saktu*) intending to eat it.
Tullānandā said to him, "Follow me; I will give you excellent parched grain."
He immediately sold it to him.
That man then cried out in a loud voice amidst the great assembly:
"There is fine flour for sale inside the nunnery!"
Having heard this, other people came to the monastery seeking to buy parched grain flour (saktu). They then saw the Venerable Mahāprajāpatī and asked her,
"Noble Lady, do you have any parched grain flour for sale?"
The nun said,
"Where have you ever seen a nun selling parched grain?
The man replied:
“Venerable One!
Do you not know for yourself that Thullanandā has sold flour?
All the people in the city are fully aware that the nun has flour for sale.”
The Great Leader Bhikṣuṇī said,
"A bhikṣuṇī has now arrived at this place where flour is being sold.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha questioned and rebuked her, and after explaining the matter at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī sells parched grain, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Sthūlanandā and others.
“Selling food” is as commonly understood, or it may refer to bartering by taking gold, silver, coins, and so forth.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense, it is explained in detail as before.
153. The Training Rule on Engaging in Domestic Affairs. The setting for this one hundred and fifty-third rule is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā went to another's house while begging for alms and said to the wife there:
"May you be free from illness; please give me some food."
The woman replied, "I am currently unacquainted with the domestic affairs of a lay household; I do not know what ought to be done.
The nun said:
"Sister! Do you know only how to sew with needle and thread, and not know how to perform other tasks for managing household affairs?
The woman replied:
"Noble one! Are you perhaps skilled in managing household affairs?
The nun replied:
"What business does my household have that I should not know?
The woman said, "If that is so,
I wish for you to assist me."
The nun said, "I will do work for you; can you provide me with food?
She replied:
He replied, "I can. He further asked,
"Can you also provide for my attendants and the keepers of the quarters?"
He replied, "I shall also give it.

He then set aside his robes and bowl, drew water to examine for insects, swept everywhere, and washed all the earthenware vessels; he also prepared food, drinks, soups, stews, and pickled vegetables, completing everything.
She then washed her hands and feet, burned incense to make offerings to the household deities and spirits, and distributed sacrificial food before returning to the monastery with the remainder.
Later, on another occasion, the nun Mahāprajāpatī also entered this house while begging for alms. Upon seeing her, the elder’s wife said:
"Noble Lady!"
"Help me manage the household affairs.
Mahāprajāpatī said,
"Where have you ever seen a nun managing the household affairs for a layperson?"
The woman said,
"The noble Tullānanda once managed my household in such a manner that no one else could equal her.
Mahāprajāpatī said:
"How could a nun go so far as to manage affairs for another?
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha then questioned Pūrṇaśailā (Tulandanda):
“Is it true that you are actually managing household affairs for other laypeople in this way?
She replied,
“It is indeed so.”
The Blessed One rebuked her and, after speaking at length, established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī manages the domestic affairs of a layperson's household, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Tullanandā and others.
“Managing the household affairs of laypeople” means performing worldly tasks for those who live as householders.
Regarding the explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth, it is explained in detail as previously stated.
154. The Training Rule on Moving Seats and Beds. The setting for this training rule, the one hundred and fifty-fourth, is the same as before.

At that time, the nun Tullānandā was instructing the nuns; she would have those who came to receive the Dharma move their seats and beds outside the room, and then move them again to place them outside the door, or have them placed under the veranda, or on the upper gallery.
All the bhikṣuṇīs were weary, exhausted, and distressed, and they collectively expressed their resentment, saying:
"Night and day we have moved our beds and seats, yet we have received no instruction."
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Pūraṇa-Dhanadā:
"Is it true that you caused those nuns to move their beds and seats?"
He replied, "It is truly so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him, and after speaking at length, up to: "I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada), which should be recited as follows:"
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, causes other bhikṣuṇīs to move their seats or couches to the point of exhaustion, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Tullānandā and others.
Regarding "causing the moving of a seat or bed": this refers to dispatching a nun to lift and carry [the furniture] so as to cause her exhaustion.
The explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth is as extensively detailed before.
The 155th Rule: The Training Precept on Spinning Thread with One's Own Hands. The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the nun Tullānandā was spinning thread with her own hands and selling it to a weaver.
When another weaver saw this, he asked,
"Where did you obtain such fine thread?"
He replied,
"I purchased it from a female ascetic.
Later, when the weaver saw the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, he asked her:
“Noble one! Do you have any spun thread?
I wish to purchase it.”
The nun said,
"Where have you seen a nun selling spun thread?
And yet, you ask me about it now."
She replied, "O śramaṇī, everyone knows that Toraṇadā constantly spins and sells [yarn]; have you not heard?
Mahāprajāpatī thought to herself:
"We have now arrived at such a place.
On this account, the nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha then questioned Pūrṇa-nandā:
"Is it true that you yourself spun this thread with your own hands and sold it to a weaver?
He replied, "It is indeed so."
The Blessed One rebuked her and, after speaking at length, established this training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī should twist thread with her own hands, it is a pāyattika."
“Nun” refers to Tullānandā and others.
“Twisting thread with one’s own hands” means twisting the seven kinds of thread.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense, it is explained in detail as previously stated.
There is no offense if one uses it for oneself and twists it in a secluded place. 156.
The Training Rule on Weaving and Netting. The setting for this fifteenth-sixth training rule is the same as before.
The nun Tūlanandā wove a web with her own hands and was criticized by the laity; the precept was established as before: "It should be stated thus:
'If a bhikṣuṇī weaves a web herself, it is a pāyattika.'"
The remaining meaning is the same as before. The 157th training rule on walking while carrying a parasol: the setting and circumstances are the same as before.

At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Muktakaśikhā-Nanda was walking for alms while holding a parasol. When some Brahmins and householders who lacked faith and respect saw her, they reviled and disparaged her, saying:
"Though this bald śramaṇī has shaved her head and left the home life, she is still entangled and tormented by desire."
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Zhujì Nántuó:
"Is it true that you carry this parasol while begging for alms?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him, and after speaking at length, up to the point where he established the training rule, it should be stated as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī walks while carrying a parasol, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to such individuals as Śikhinanda and others.
"Walks while carrying a parasol" means to carry one of two kinds of parasols: [the royal parasol or the common parasol].
The first is a parasol made of bamboo, grass, or leaves;
the second is a parasol made of silk or fine cloth.
Regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the offense, it is set forth in detail as previously described.
158. The Training Rule on Wearing Colorful Shoes. The setting for this training rule, the one hundred and fifty-eighth, is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Māluṅkyāputra (Zhūjì Nántuó) was walking for alms while wearing colorful shoes. When brahmins and householders saw her, they spoke with derision:
“Although these shaven-headed śramaṇī women have had their hair cut, they do not possess pure conduct; they are entangled by desire.”
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Juḥi Nanda:
"Is it true that you go on almsround wearing shoes dyed with colors such as these?"
He replied, “It is truly so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him and, after speaking at length, established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī wears dyed shoes or sandals, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to [those such as] Cūḍapanthaka’s mother, Nanda, and others.
"Regarding those who wear dyed footwear": this refers to wearing and walking about in footwear that is variegated with various embroidered patterns.
The explanation of the nature of the offense and so forth is as extensively detailed previously.
There is no offense if one wears [the garment] within one's own room.
The 159th Training Rule concerning having a wound and causing it to be repeatedly untied and tied. The setting for this rule is the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Maṇicūḍanandā developed a sore on her right upper arm. She sent a messenger to summon a physician to prepare a healing ointment for the flesh.
The physician then applied a lump of it to the sore and bound it with a piece of old cloth.
Not long after it had been tied, the nun said, "It is too tight;
untie it for a moment and make it loose.
When the physician untied it, she spoke again:
"Too loose.
Thus he caused the other to untie and tie it again and again.
The physician became enraged and said:
"Noble one!
Whether the wound heals or not is none of my business," he said, and departed.
The nuns asked, "Venerable one!
For what purpose do you cause others to be repeatedly released and repeatedly bound?"
She replied,
"Out of affection for this person, I wished to speak with him, and so I had him untied.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Nanda Maṇicūḍa:
"Is it true that you have caused others to repeatedly loosen and repeatedly tie his wound?
He replied:
"It is indeed so.
The Blessed One rebuked her and, having spoken at length, even up to the point of establishing the training rule, declared:
"If a bhikṣuṇī has a sore on her arm and causes another person to repeatedly loosen and repeatedly tie it, it is a pāyattika offense."
“Nuns” refers to Śuklā-Śikhandinī Nandā and others.
“Having sores on the arms” means having rashes, scabs, and the like.
“Causing another to repeatedly untie and tie them” means causing them to be untied and tied again and again.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offense is as extensively described above.
Regarding "no offense": if one ties [the hair] tightly or loosely according to reality, and unties it so that it is no longer tied, there is no offense.
160. The Training Rule on Ordaining Prostitutes. The sixteenth training rule, concerning the ordination of prostitutes, has the same setting as before.
The nun Tullānandā ordained a courtesan and went on alms-round with her.
When men who were addicted to sensual pleasures saw them, they reviled and disparaged them, saying:
"This woman previously engaged constantly in unrighteous conduct with laymen; now she has gathered together with one who has gone forth."
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Pūrṇa-dharmadinnā:
"Is it true that you have thus ordained a courtesan as a nun and gone forth together with her to beg for alms?"
He replied, “It is truly so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him and, after speaking at length, established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:
"If a bhikṣuṇī, moreover, ordains a courtesan, it is a pāyattika.
"Bhikṣuṇī" refers to Tullānandā and others.
"Courtesan" refers to a woman who was previously unchaste.
"One who has gone forth" refers to one who has received the training rules (*śikṣāpada*) of a *śrāmaṇera*.
The explanation of the characteristics of the offenses and so forth is as extensively set forth previously.
The seventeenth summary verse (*uddāna*) says:
A nun is not permitted to rub her body; there are five distinctions regarding persons; [regarding] perfumes and sesame-water;
and one must always ask before using worldly ornaments. 161.

The training rule concerning having a bhikṣuṇī rub one’s body. The six hundred and first training rule concerning having a bhikṣuṇī rub one’s body. The setting for the origin of this rule is the same as before.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā had other nuns rub her body, and when they touched her, she gave rise to a sense of pleasure.
The nuns informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha asked Cūḍapanthaka:

The summary verse says:
Milk, curd, and fresh butter; Ripe butter, oil, sugar, and honey;
Fish, meat, and dried meat; Obtained from families of those who have received the precepts.
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, twelve bhikṣuṇīs, though not ill, went out to beg for food for their own bodies and requested milk from others, drinking it as they pleased.
The various non-Buddhists, along with the laypeople, brahmins, and others who did not have faith or respect, collectively mocked them, saying:

"These bhikṣuṇīs do not practice pure conduct; they merely nourish their own bodies by begging for milk from others and drinking it themselves. Who would not desire such refined and delicious flavors?"
When the nuns heard these criticisms from the lay travelers, those nuns of few desires reported the matter in detail to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked the nuns:
"Is it true that you, while not actually ill, begged for milk from others for your own sake and then drank it at will in the homes of laypeople?"
He replied, “It is indeed so.
The World-Honored One rebuked him, and after speaking at length, he established the training rule, which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, being not ill, for her own sake goes to the home of a layperson to beg for milk, or causes another to beg it for her to drink, that bhikṣuṇī must return to the residence outside the village, go to where the other bhikṣuṇīs are, and address each of them individually, saying:
'Venerable ladies!'"
"I have committed an offense that requires confession; this was not what I should have done, and I now confess it before you.
This is called the "Dharma of Confession.
Thus, after the Blessed One had established the training rule for the bhikṣuṇīs, at a later time, there was a sick bhikṣuṇī, and another bhikṣuṇī went to inquire after her illness.
“Noble one! Has your illness been relieved?
The sick nun replied:
"I previously used milk as my food and drink, and my illness was thereby cured.
Now that the World-Honored One has prohibited nuns from begging for it, how can my illness be healed?
She reported this matter to the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus reported it to the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"I now permit nuns who are ill to beg for milk and drink it as they wish; what was previously prohibited is now again granted.
As explained extensively above, this is called the 'Teaching by Confrontation' (pratideśanīya), except in cases of illness."
“Nun” refers to a nun within this Dharma.
“Not being ill and going to the house of a layperson to beg for milk” means that, being free from physical illness, she requests milk from another.
"If she causes another to beg for food and eat it" means she causes another person to beg.
"That bhikṣuṇī" refers to a nun who has committed this training rule.
"She should return to the residence outside the village" means she should go to the place where the other nuns are.
"To address each individually" means to speak of the confession separately.
"Venerable sir, I have committed an offense that requires individual confession" means to state the characteristics of the transgression committed.
"This was not what should have been done" means that it was contrary to the Dharma.
"Confessing face-to-face" (*pratideśanā*) means to disclose it oneself without concealment; this is called "confessing face-to-face.
"The rule" (*dharma*) refers to pointing out the specific matter.
"Except during times of illness" means when one is suffering from disease.
If those who are healthy beg for food, all incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*); this is called the "Exposition of the Dharma.
If one who is ill begs and one who is healthy eats, the beggar incurs an offense of wrong-doing, while the eater commits no offense.
If one requests on behalf of a healthy person but eats while ill, the requester incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa), while the eater commits no offense.
If one requests on behalf of a sick person but eats while healthy, the requester commits no offense, but the eater should confess the transgression.
There is no offense for begging on behalf of a sick person, nor for a sick person eating [the food].
If a bhikṣuṇī begs for milk and then further solicits curd, the one who begs incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing); the one who eats it should confess the transgression.

If a nun obtains curd and further requests fresh butter from the same person, the one who asks incurs an *duṣkṛta* offense, and the one who eats it must confess the transgression by reciting the appropriate formula.
If a nun obtains fresh butter and further requests clarified butter from the same person, the offense incurred is the same as before.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having received matured butter (*ghṛta*), further begs for oil, it is as explained above.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having received oil, further begs for granulated sugar (*guḍa*), the offense is the same as before.
If a bhikṣuṇī, having received sugar, further demands honey or meat, she incurs an offense as before.
Having obtained honeyed meat, he further begged for fish; this was also as described above.
Having obtained fish, he further begged for meat; this was likewise as above.
Having obtained meat, he begged for dried jerky; this was also as above.
Having obtained dried meat, if one begs for various refined foods, it is as explained above.
Having obtained refined foods, if one further begs for coarse foods, in all such cases there is an *duṣkṛta* (offense of wrong-doing).

There is no offense for one who acts on behalf of the community, or one who is insane, mentally deranged, or afflicted by intense pain. This is the first method of confession through face-to-face declaration (*pratideśanīya*).

In this way, it should be understood that curd, fresh butter, clarified butter, oil, sugar, honey, fish, meat, and dried meat—these ten pairs of teachings on the dharma—constitute offenses for the beggar, as explained in detail above.
The setting was the city of Vaiśālī.

In this city there was a householder named Siṃha who had realized the principles of the Truths (satyadarśana). He conceived deep and correct faith in the Buddha and the community of Śrāvakas, and offered all his wealth and possessions as offerings to the Triple Gem. By making such gifts, his household wealth was completely exhausted and his assets were entirely depleted.

At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana, while traveling through the human realm, arrived at Vaiśālī. When Siṃha heard that the two honored ones had arrived, he went quickly to invite them, requesting that they partake of a meal the following day.
The worldly travelers criticized and disparaged him, saying:
"The Elder Siṃha’s clothing does not cover his body and his food does not suffice for his mouth; all of this is due to his making offerings."
Having heard this, the bhikṣus informed the Buddha. The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!
You may perform the *karmavācanā* for the Lion family; others of a similar kind should be treated in the same way."
As is customary, having assembled the community, one bhikṣu should perform the formal motion (*jñapti-karman*) as follows:
"Venerable Ni-saṃgha, listen!

This householder Siṃha possesses profound faith and a pure, virtuous intention; he bestows whatever he has upon the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha without ever a thought of stinginess, and likewise provides for all who seek it. Consequently, his provisions of food and clothing have been entirely exhausted."

If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to listen, may the Saṃgha grant its permission; the Saṃgha shall now perform the *śikṣādattaka-karman* (the formal act of declaring one a "learner") for the householder Siṃha.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
The formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) should be performed according to the preceding announcement (*jñapti*).

If a bhikṣuṇī knows that the Saṃgha has performed the *śaikṣakula-karman* (the ritual for a family under training), she must not go there to receive food, drink, bedding, or seats, nor should she preach the Dharma; whoever violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense.

Furthermore, because the group of twelve nuns went to this household to eat without having first received an invitation, they reported the circumstances to the Buddha. The Buddha questioned them and rebuked them, establishing this training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:

"If a bhikṣuṇī, knowing that a family is a 'householder's family' (*śaikṣa-kula*) for whom the Saṃgha has performed the formal act of the 'householder's family' (*śaikṣa-karmavācanā*), should go to that house and, without having first received an invitation, accept food with her own hands and eat it."
This bhikṣuṇī should return to her residence outside the village, go to where the bhikṣuṇīs are, and address each of them individually, saying:
"Venerable ladies!
I have committed a transgression that requires confession; it was improper for me to do so, and I now confess and repent before you."
"This is called the 'teaching in response' (prātimokṣa).
All the bhikṣuṇīs neither went there nor accepted [the food] for them. The Buddha said:

'One should accept it for them so that they may eat while seated on a bed or chair; if there are leftover vegetables or leaves, these may also be accepted for them; and small boys and girls should be given portions of the remaining food.'"

The people of Vaiśālī all heard that because Siṃha had provided offerings, he had now encountered poverty and hardship; yet, by personally engaging in farming, he had gathered grain so that his granaries were overflowing.
At that time, Siṃha went to the place where the World-Honored One was and said:
"Venerable Sir!

Previously, I possessed goods which I had entirely exhausted for making offerings to the fields of merit—the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha. Now, however, my household has harvested a great abundance of grain."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One, out of compassion for me, will revoke the 'householder's prohibition' and permit the monks and nuns to accept my offerings.
The Buddha said,
"The bhikṣus should revoke the householder's prohibition for the general."
It should be granted in this manner:
When the Saṃgha has assembled, have Siṃha pay homage in due order; then, crouching before the Elder and joining his palms, he should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, please listen!"

My teacher Siṃha previously conceived deep faith toward the Triple Gem; with a pure and virtuous intention, he always delighted in giving, and it was through his giving to the Triple Gem that he fell into poverty.

"Because the Saṃgha, out of compassion for me, performed a formal act (*karmavācanā*) to ensure that the noble assembly would not enter my home, my wealth and provisions have now returned to abundance.
However, my preceptor Siṃha first obtained the communal rules; I now beg the great assembly to revoke this formal act."
"I only pray that you will explain the *karmavācanā* for me out of compassion!
Thus he said three times.
Having made this formal announcement (*jñapti*), he prostrated to the assembly and departed.
At that time, the great assembly should appoint one person to perform a *jñapti-dvitīya-karman* (a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) to lift the restriction.
Once the lifting has been performed, the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs may, as before, go back and forth and accept offerings; none of them will be guilty of an offense.
"Furthermore, 'a bhikṣuṇī' refers to a nun within this Dharma; the rest is as explained above.
'A learner' (śaikṣā) refers to one who has faith in the Three Jewels and has realized the vision of the Truths."
"Family" refers to the four castes.
"Nun" refers to a disciple of the Buddha.

Regarding the *karmavācanā*, it refers to the formal procedure consisting of one motion and one proclamation (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*). If one goes to such a family to receive food without having previously accepted an invitation, one incurs an offense.
Regarding the offense herein: when one receives and consumes two sets of five foods at such a place, the offense incurred is the same as before, and the confession is as described above.
If one attains the method of liberation, there is no offense in eating at all.
Furthermore, regarding those who do not commit an offense, it is as explained in detail previously. "Venerable sirs!
I have now recited the eleven *pāṭidesanīya* dharmas."
Now I ask the venerable ones:
"Are you pure in this matter?
Thus he asks three times: "Venerable ones!"
"In this matter, we are pure; because we remain silent, I now hold it to be so.
The Fourth Section is concluded. The Fifth Section: The Rules of Training for the Assembly. "Venerable sirs! [Listen well...]"
"These rules of training (śaikṣa-dharma) are recited every half-month within the Prātimokṣa Sūtra.
A summary verse says:
"Food, clothing, and physical decorum; Proper conduct when visiting the homes of the laity."
Protecting the bowl, except for those who are ill; [avoiding] spitting or expectorating on trees taller than a person.

At that time, the World-Honored One established numerous rules of training (*śikṣāpada*) for the bhikṣus concerning all protocols, such as wearing robes and eating food; all bhikṣuṇīs must likewise train according to them.
At that time, although the bhikṣuṇīs had heard the instruction, they were unable to follow it according to the Dharma and wore their robes too high.
When faithful brahmins and others saw that they were not properly adjusted, they began to mock them, saying:
"These bhikṣuṇīs do not wear their robes properly; they are just like shameless people."
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard this, they informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
“One should train oneself not to wear the robes too high.”
He then put on his robe too low, and the laity again criticized and disparaged him. The Buddha said:
"One should not wear the robe too low like a newly married woman; this is how one should train."
At times they let the front [of the robe] hang down long like an elephant’s trunk; at other times they made fine pleats at the waist like *tāla* leaves.
The laypeople criticized and disparaged them, so the Buddha said:
"One should not do so."
At times, they would gather one corner of the robe and tuck it behind their waist like the head of a snake;
the Buddha said, "One should not do so.
At other times, they would grasp the upper corner and roll it around their waist like a ball of beans; the Buddha said:
"One should not wear one's robes in this manner; you should train yourself accordingly.
The setting and circumstances are the same as before.
At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Pūrṇaśailā wore her robes so as to expose her abdomen, appearing just like a courtesan.
When the other bhikṣuṇīs saw this, they spoke with derision, saying:
"Noble lady!
You should wear your robes in such a way that it constitutes a pure practice."
The nun Thullanandā said,
"I have seen women within the palace dressing in such a manner.
The nun informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Bhikṣuṇīs should not wear their robes so as to expose their bellies; you should train yourselves accordingly.
At that time, some bhikṣuṇīs entered the homes of laypeople with upraised gazes or loud voices, causing the laity to criticize and resent them. The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself not to look up haughtily when entering the house of a layperson.
One should train oneself to wear the five robes in a neat and orderly manner.
The setting for this account is the same as before.

At that time, twelve bhikṣuṇīs were begging for alms at the houses of brahmins and householders. They looked about in all four directions without decorum; their senses were restless and they did not watch where they were going. Upon entering the houses of others, they saw handsome men, and their lustful desires became so intense that impurity flowed out. Whether they had obtained food or not, they quickly departed from outside.
When the laypeople saw this, they criticized and disparaged her, saying:
"This shaven-headed female ascetic is not truly pure in conduct, yet she falsely claims to be pure.
The bhikṣuṇī informed the bhikṣus, and the bhikṣus informed the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If a bhikṣuṇī’s menstrual period is approaching, she should not go to the homes of others; this is how she should train.

At that time, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs entered the homes of laypeople with their heads covered, with one shoulder of their robes bared, with both shoulders bared, with their hands on their hips, or with their hands clasped over their shoulders—behaving like those who are shameless or like newlywed brides.
When the bhikṣuṇīs heard and saw this, they felt revulsion and asked,
"Venerable ladies, is it appropriate to act in such a manner?"
He replied, "All men and women who indulge in sensual beauty act in this way; however, we did not know that we were being asked to learn it.
He reported this to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should train oneself: not to enter the homes of laypeople with one's head covered, nor with one shoulder bared, nor with both shoulders bared, nor with hands on the hips, nor by slapping the shoulders."

At that time, the twelve bhikṣuṇīs walked on their haunches, walked on their toes, walked by leaping, walked on the balls of their feet, and walked with their bodies hunched; this led to public censure and reproach, to which they replied as before.
The Buddha said:

"One should train oneself thus: one must not enter the house of a layperson while squatting, nor while pointing with the toes, nor while hopping, nor while walking on the heels, nor while arching the body."
At that time, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs entered the houses of laypeople swaying their bodies, dangling their arms, shaking their heads, jostling their shoulders, and holding hands.
When people saw this, they mocked them, as described previously.
The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself not to sway the body, not to swing the arms, not to shake the head, not to jostle shoulders, and not to join hands when entering the house of a layperson."
At that time, Upānanda, having dressed and taken his bowl at the hour of the morning meal, entered the city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
There was a brahmin who by nature delighted in purity; he had a bed and seat in his house, and Upānanda entered and sat upon it.
The brahmins saw this and spoke with derision.
The Buddha said, "When in the house of a layperson, one should not sit unless invited to do so; this is how you should train.

At that time, the Venerable Udāyin was invited by a brahmin of pure faith to take a seat. Without careful observation, he sat down abruptly, and there being a small child on the bed, he pressed it to death.
The Buddha said:
"When in the house of a layperson, one should not sit down without careful observation; this is how you should train.
At that time, the World-Honored One, together with the assembly of śrāvakas, accepted the offerings in the palace of King Śuddhodana.
At that time, the Venerable Udāyin failed to restrain his body properly, causing Lady Gopī to find his conduct improper and strange.

Later, on another occasion, he went alone into the palace; the lady had him sit on a dilapidated chair, and as he sat down with full force, the chair broke and he fell to the ground, leading to public ridicule and disgrace. The Buddha spoke at length until he said:
"Noble sister, when sitting in a layperson's home, you should not sit down with full force; you must observe carefully. This is how you should train."

Some sat with their feet crossed in lay houses, some sat with their inner and outer ankles overlapping, some drew up their feet too tightly, some stretched them out too far, and some sat with their bodies exposed; the laypeople criticized and disparaged this. The Buddha said:
"This should not be done; a training rule must be established."

In the house of a layperson, one should train oneself not to cross the legs, not to place the inner ankles together, not to place the outer ankles together, not to draw the feet up too tightly, not to extend the feet too far, and not to expose the body.
At that time, there was a donor who invited the Buddha and the community of monks and nuns to his residence for a meal.
One of those distributing the food was not attentive and carelessly cast a mouthful of delicious rice into the bowls.
The bhikṣuṇīs did not treat their alms bowls with respect or care, and consequently many were damaged or broken. The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself to receive food with respect.
At that time, the group of twelve bhikṣuṇīs entered the house of the householder Bodhi to beg for food.
When a householder gave food, he filled the bowl with rice and further offered soup and condiments; the bowl then overflowed, spilling onto the ground and causing public reproach.
The matter was reported to the Buddha, who established this training rule (*śikṣāpada*), which should be recited as follows:

"One must not receive rice until the bowl is full and then add soup and vegetables so that the food overflows; one should leave a space around the rim of the bowl equal to the width of a finger, and receive food with due care. This is how one should train."
Some would extend their bowls in advance before the food had even arrived, appearing like beggars exhibiting gluttonous behavior; consequently, they incurred reproach and shame. The Buddha said:
"I shall establish a training rule (śikṣāpada). It should be stated thus:
'One should train oneself not to extend the bowl in advance when the distribution of food has not yet arrived.'"
"One should train oneself not to leave the alms bowl unsteady upon the food.
Furthermore, when eating, one should not manifest signs of arrogance, such as those of small children or courtesans.
The Buddha said:
"One should not eat with such arrogance; one should eat with reverence, and you should train yourselves accordingly.
Furthermore, when eating, [the mouth] may be too small, or the food entering the mouth may be too large, like that of a poor beggar.
The Buddha said, "It should not be done thus. One should train oneself to eat with food balls that are neither too small nor too large, but rounded and well-formed.
At that time, there was a donor who invited the Buddha and the Sangha to his home for a meal.
At that time, the bhikṣu Upānanda was sitting next to an elderly bhikṣu (mahallaka).
The elderly bhikṣu opened his mouth wide and looked upward; thereupon, Upānanda took a clod of earth and hurled it from a distance into his mouth, saying, "Eat this for now."
The Buddha said:
"One should not keep one's mouth wide open in anticipation; if food has not yet arrived, one should not wait with the mouth agape. You should train yourselves thus.
At that time, the twelve bhikṣuṇīs of the group spoke while their mouths were full of food, which caused the laypeople to criticize and disparage them.
The Buddha said:
"It should not be so. One should train oneself not to speak with food in the mouth."

Or again, having gone to the house of a donor and seeing that the soup and vegetables were meager, fearing they would not be sufficient, he first requested some soup and covered it with rice, hoping to receive more.
The laypeople criticized and complained about this.
The Buddha said:
"You should not act in this way. You must train yourselves thus: one must not cover the soup or vegetables with rice, nor cover the rice with soup or vegetables in the hope of obtaining more."
At that time, a donor invited the bhikṣus for a meal.
The food was excessively sweet, so the group of twelve immediately made a clicking sound with their tongues and said to one another,
"This food is extremely sour, or perhaps even over-sour."
The group of twelve immediately made smacking sounds to one another, saying that the food was very sweet.
On another occasion, when a donor invited the two assemblies of monks to a meal, the food was excessively hot; the group of twelve then blew on it and said to one another, "The food is very cold."
They would eat only after scolding it for being hot. Or,
when their food was too cold, the group of twelve would immediately blow upon it, telling one another,
"This food is very hot."
He blew upon his food before eating.
All such instances were inverted explanations of the facts that distressed the donors. The Buddha said: "This should not be done.
A training rule (śikṣāpada) shall be established: [One should not blow upon food]."
"One should train oneself not to eat by flicking the tongue, not to eat making smacking sounds, not to eat blowing air upon the food, and not to eat puffing air upon the food. On one occasion,
when the group of six was receiving an invitation for a meal, they used their hands to scatter and disperse the rice as they ate, like chickens or birds, or they said, "This food is bad."

They reviled one another, or else stuffed their cheeks with food and ate it bit by bit; or else, while eating, they bit off half a morsel and left the other half behind; or else they stuck out their tongues to lick their lips and mouths.
The Buddha said:
"You should establish this training rule:
one should train oneself not to scatter food with the hand, not to disparage food, not to stuff the cheeks with food, not to bite off half a morsel, and not to lick the tongue while eating."

At that time, there was a naked ascetic lay follower (*upāsaka*) who, having recently conceived faith and taken refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, invited the Buddha to his home for a meal. He served various foods and drinks, as well as balls of parched grain, thin cakes, and radishes.
At that time, the group of six intended to mock the donor; they fashioned a stūpa out of balls of parched grain, placed a radish on top, and covered it with a thin pancake.
They then said to one another, "This is the stūpa of Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, the naked ascetic from among the evil destinies."
As they gradually began to pull it up, the radish overturned;
they then cried out to one another, "This was a stūpa erected by a naked ascetic, and now it has collapsed!"
When the donor saw this, his mind of reverence subsided.
The Buddha said:
"A training rule should be established: one should train oneself not to eat in the shape of a stūpa."

On certain occasions, when the group of six monks accepted invitations to eat, if there were delicious leftovers remaining on their hands, they would lick them repeatedly with their tongues; they did the same with their alms bowls.
Alternatively, they would shake their hands or shake their bowls, splashing water from the bowls onto others and soiling their robes, because they felt envy toward the fine garments of those others.
The Buddha said:
"All such things as these should not be done; you should train yourselves accordingly.
At that time, there was a donor who provided a meal for the community of monks and addressed them, saying:
"Noble one!
There is plenty of fine food; do not accept so much parched grain.

The group of six did not believe him and accepted a great deal of the parched grain. Later, seeing the fine food, they wished to discard the parched grain, while a mahallaka bhikṣu sitting nearby looked around at them.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus took balls of parched grain and placed them inside their bowls until they were overflowing, leaving no room to receive any more.
The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself to always watch one's bowl while eating."

At that time, there was a bhikṣu whose alms bowl was full during the mealtime; the group of six observed him from the side and together gave rise to contempt, saying, "This mahallaka can eat his fill."
The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself to observe the food in the bowl of one's neighbor with a mind free from contempt.
At that time, the group of six bhikṣus held a pure water flask with unclean hands, causing flies to swarm around it and inviting public reproach.
The Buddha said:
"One should train oneself not to grasp a pure water vessel with soiled hands.

At that time, a bhikṣuṇī was at Mount Jiangzhu, eating on the high terrace of the householder Bodhi; she discarded the water used for washing her bowl onto the fine ground, which caused the donor to feel resentment.
The Buddha said:
"A training rule should be established: when in the house of a layperson, one must not discard the water used for rinsing the alms bowl unless one has asked the host; this is how you should train.
The occasion for this occurred in Śrāvastī.
At that time, there was a Brahmin boy who fell ill. A lay follower (*upāsaka*), who was a close friend of his, came to him and said:
"If your child is ill, you should go to the monastery and beg for water from the bowls of the bhikṣus; have him wash and bathe with it, and he will surely recover."
Then the brahmin went to seek water and saw Upānanda begging for bowl-water from him.
Upānanda then placed the remnants of his flour cakes into the water in the bowl and handed it to him.
Seeing the turbid water, he conceived a feeling of loathing and spoke these words:
"My son would rather die; who could possibly bathe him with such vile and foul things?"
He reported the matter to the Buddha, and the Buddha said:

"One should not give such defiled water as an offering to others. However, if someone comes to beg for bowl-water, one should wash the bowl thoroughly, place pure water within it, and recite the essential verses from the sūtras—the *ārya-gāthās*—three times over it. When bestowed upon that person, whether they wash with it or drink it, it can eliminate ten thousand ailments."
Regarding the *ariṣagāthā*: these are verses spoken by the Buddha that have been extracted from the Noble Teachings (*ārya-śāsana*).
When recited, they possess great power; any other instances where one is instructed to recite verses elsewhere are all of this same category.

For instance, when bathing or drinking water at rivers, ponds, or wells; when resting briefly under a tree to seek coolness before departing; when staying in a guesthouse; when entering a shrine hall, treading upon a maṇḍala, or stepping on the shadow of a Buddhist stūpa; when one’s own shadow obscures the venerable countenance of the Buddha; when the great assembly disperses; when entering a city or village; when performing prostrations before the sacred image at dawn or dusk; when finishing one's daily meal; or when sweeping and cleaning a stūpa or temple—regarding all such matters, their specific requirements are indeed manifold; in every case, one must recite a gāthā and perform the practice to obtain merit.
If one deliberately violates [the precepts] out of arrogance, one incurs the offense of *dukkaṭa*.

However, because this practice was not previously observed among the monastic community of Dongchuan, the following statement was added to indicate that the existence of the sacred teaching is known through its presence in the *gāthās*, as it is said in the verse:
"The pleasures of the five worldly desires, Or even the pleasures of the various devas;..."
Compared to the bliss of the exhaustion of craving, it does not equal even one-thousandth part.
From accumulation arises suffering; from suffering, accumulation arises again.
Through the Noble Eightfold Path, one transcends them and reaches the wondrous state of Nirvana.
Whoever practices giving will surely obtain its benefit;
if one gives for the sake of happiness, they will surely attain peace and joy in the future.
The Buddha said:
"One must not place leftover food into the water within the bowl; this is how you should train.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who placed his bowl on the ground without a protective base beneath it. This led to public reproach and caused the bowl to deteriorate quickly.
The Buddha said:
"A training rule should be established: one must not place a bowl on the ground without a mat; this is how you should train.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who stood while washing her bowl; she lost her grip, and it fell to the ground, breaking it.
The Buddha said:
"One must not wash the bowl while standing; this is how you should train.
At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who placed her bowl on a precarious cliff edge. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one should train oneself not to place the bowl on a dangerous riverbank.
Because the river current was swift, he scooped water against the flow with his bowl and consequently broke it. The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one must train oneself not to scoop water against the current."
The group of twelve nuns sat while the others stood, yet they preached the Dharma to them.
At that time, Brahmins and lay devotees who had faith in the Triple Gem criticized and rebuked them.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one should train oneself thus: 'When others are seated and I am standing, I shall not preach the Dharma to them.
At that time, there was a sick person who was unable to stand for long while listening to the Dharma. The Buddha said:"

"If a sick person sits or lies upon high or low ground, on a path or a non-path, or in a carriage; or if they wear boots, cover their head, wear flowered crowns or necklaces of pearls, carry a parasol, sword, or staff, or don armor and the like."
If it concerns one who is ill, there is no offense in speaking [of the precepts] regardless of which posture they are in.
It is not permissible for one who is not ill.
To establish the training rule (śikṣāpada), it should be stated as follows:
One should train oneself thus: "When another is seated and I am standing, I must not preach the Dharma to them, except in cases of illness.
One should train oneself thus: "When another is lying down and I am seated, I must not preach the Dharma to them, except in cases of illness."
"One should train oneself: when another person is on a high seat and one is on a low seat, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness.
One should train oneself: when another person is walking in front and one is walking behind, one must not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness."
"One should train oneself: 'If another person is on the path and I am off the path, I shall not preach the Dharma to them, except in the case of illness. One should train oneself:

'I shall not preach the Dharma to one who has covered their head, nor to one who has tucked up one side of their robe, nor to one who has tucked up both sides of their robe, nor to one with hands on hips, nor to one with hands on shoulders, except in the case of illness.'"
"One should train oneself: except in cases of illness, one shall not preach the Dharma to those riding elephants, nor to those riding horses, nor to those in palanquins, nor to those in carriages."
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to those wearing wooden clogs, boots, shoes, or sandals.
One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to those wearing hats, crowns, or topknots, or those with their heads wrapped or adorned with flowers.'"
"One should train oneself: 'Except in the case of illness, I shall not preach the Dharma to one who is wearing a sunshade.
The setting was the city of Kapilavastu.
At that time, Pūtanā stood while defecating or urinating; when the laypeople saw this, they all spoke in derision and reproach.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one should train oneself not to stand while defecating or urinating, except when ill.
At that time, the nun Thullanandā took her own used clothes and had a washerman wash them.
He refused to wash it and, giving rise to a mind of anger, intentionally discharged impurity into the water where she was washing clothes.
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one must not defecate, urinate, spit, or expectorate in water, except in cases of illness; this is how you should train."
The setting was in Śrāvastī.
At that time, a donor invited the Saṃgha for a meal. A temple attendant, finding the delay strange and fearing that the time for the meal would pass, climbed a tall tree to watch for their return.
At that time, some lay travelers saw this and mocked him, saying:
"A śramaṇa son of the Śākyas climbing a tall tree—how is he any different from a worldly person?
The Buddha said:
"One should not do so; one must not climb a tree higher than a person's height.

At that time, there was a bhikṣuṇī who, fearing she might tangle her dyeing cord, did not dare to climb a tree. Furthermore, when the danger of tigers and wolves approached, she still did not dare to climb, and as a result, she was harmed. The Buddha said:
"One must not climb a tree higher than a person's height, except in the event of an emergency; this is how you should train."
7. The Seven Methods for Settling Disputes A summary verse concerning the seven methods for settling disputes states:
Face-to-face settlement, recollection, The sane mind, and the confession of an offense, The majority decision, and the self-accusation, And the covering over with grass—these settle all disputes.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣuṇīs:
“There are seven methods for the settlement of disputes that you should practice and study.
‘One should grant the *vinaya* of presence; one must grant the *vinaya* of presence.’”
Where the *smṛtivinaya* (settlement by recollection) should be granted, the *smṛtivinaya* shall be granted.
Where the *amūḍhavinaya* (settlement for one no longer insane) should be granted, the *amūḍhavinaya* shall be granted.
Where the Vinaya for seeking the nature of the offense should be granted, the Vinaya for seeking the nature of the offense shall be granted.
Where the Vinaya of the majority opinion should be granted, the Vinaya of the majority opinion shall be granted.
One who should be granted the *pātimokkha* by confession should be granted the *pātimokkha* by confession;
one who should be granted the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) should be granted the *tṛṇaprastāraka*.
"If a dispute arises, you should use these seven methods to follow the Great Teacher’s instruction and extinguish it in accordance with the Dharma and the Vinaya:
'Patience is the highest among ascetic practices; it leads to the state of Nirvana.
One who causes distress to others while claiming to have left the household life is not called a bhikṣuṇī.'"
This is the *Prātimokṣa Sūtra* as spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Awakened One, Vipaśyin:
“As one with clear vision avoids dangerous paths, And is able to reach a place of safety;
So the wise person, within the realm of birth, Is able to remain far removed from all evils.”
This is the Sūtra of the Precepts as spoken by the Tathāgata Śikhin, the Samyaksaṃbuddha:
"Do not revile, nor do harm; Guard the Sūtra of the Precepts well.
Know moderation in food and drink; Use humble bedding and seats."
"Exert yourself in the cultivation of higher concentration; this is the teaching of all Buddhas.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata Viśvabhū, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
"Just as a bee gathers from a flower, Without harming its color or fragrance,
But taking only its nectar to depart— So should a nun enter a village.
This is the precept scripture spoken by the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha Krakucchanda.
"Do not oppose others; do not look at what they have done or left undone.
But observe your own conduct alone—whether it be right or wrong.
This is the *Dhammapada* (Sūtra of the Precepts) spoken by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kanakamuni.
"Do not be attached to the concentrated mind; diligently cultivate the state of tranquility.
One who is capable of saving others has no sorrow, and shall always ensure that mindfulness is not lost.

Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhū, Krakucchanda,

The seven Buddhas were all heroic and fierce, Able to rescue and protect the world.

All Buddhas and their disciples Together revere and honor the precepts.
